en: The *Cakrasaṃvara Tantra*, Chapter One: The Procedure for Entering the Maṇḍala.
Om! Homage to the glorious Cakrasaṃvara!
Now, therefore, I shall explain the secret in brief, and not in detail:
the union with Śrī Heruka, which accomplishes all desires and goals. (1)
A Commentary on the Śrī Cakrasaṃvara. Homage to the illustrious Cakrasaṃvara!
O Hara, destroyer of passion, do not plunge me into the ocean of attachment; O Hari, do not consort with the serpent of hatred.
"Do not remain in the net of delusion, O Brahmā; O enemy of Bala [Indra], do not conceal the fire of envy!
Delight in Mind-Only, which is devoid of self and cause, where vows have vanished.
May Heruka, whose glorious body possesses four faces, protect the world by thus instructing them.
For those yogis who possess faith and reasoning, afflictions such as leprosy and other physical and mental diseases come to an end through this treatise.
Who is capable of measuring the jewels of excellence contained within this treatise?
Who is able to perform the calculation of the drops of water in the ocean?
Like the temple of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), this abode of meaning is inaccessible to mere words;
it is as if this system were uttered from the mind by the Wielder of the Thunderbolt (Vajrapāṇi).
The burden of his purpose was entrusted by my teachers to me, though I am of dull intellect,
just as a treasure might be found even within a heap of ashes.
If it were not stolen by lack of vigilance— as if by a thief who has forgotten his weapon— I shall now explain it by dividing it.
The meaning of the words is indeed difficult to grasp for one whose intellect is firmly set on annihilation;
without instruction, the study of the Tantra is like [trying to contain] fire in a jar.

For nowhere is activity observed to occur without seeing a purpose. And thus: "Of every scripture or indeed of any action whatsoever, as long as the purpose has not been stated, so long is it not accepted through reasoning."

For even one of dull intellect does not engage in a means without perceiving a purpose, according to the saying: "Even a fool does not set his mind to action without aiming at an effect. Therefore, for those engaging in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara*, the commentators must state that [purpose] as a prerequisite for engagement. And so it has been said:

"The purpose, the summarized meaning, the meaning of the words along with their connections, the objection, and the rebuttal—these must be stated by those who explain the meaning of the sūtras" (*Nāmasaṃgīti* 1.12–13).

And that is well-explained by first providing the discussion on the naming and so forth; furthermore, this was stated by the Blessed One himself through such phrases as "atha ata" (now, therefore). Therefore, we shall here first explain the words in pairs, and we will relate that. As for the summary meaning (*piṇḍārtha*), it should be expanded upon through reflection based precisely on the stated proof beginning with "from the position, in the sūtra," and the explanation of the meanings of the words and so forth follows the order of the commentary. The teacher is the Great Vajradhara, appearing in the form of the future Caturmukha and others.

And he himself is directly established in the state of emanation (*nirmāṇa*). This *tantra*, existing as something to be taught since beginningless time, sometimes remains hidden due to the lack of merit of sentient beings, and sometimes it manifests through merit. Furthermore, this conduct of the Tathāgatas—consisting of the taught, the teacher, and so forth—is like an illusion and is inconceivable. Moreover, the Blessed Lady Vajravārāhī is the requester, and Vajrapāṇi is the compiler, because the latter has been entrusted with the teaching in a general sense.

Alternatively, it is established that the Tantra—which expresses the entirety of its meaning through the teachings on the partial and the whole of the bodies of Caturmukha and others—is taught by the Sugatas, but not created by them, such as [the categories of] cause and effect, pleasure and pain, passion and hatred, and virtuous and non-virtuous deeds. And it is said here:
"The well-spoken words of ten million Buddhas and of ten million Heroes. Elsewhere:
That which was spoken by the Buddhas of the past, which those of the future will speak,
and which the perfectly awakened ones of the present speak again and again.
"That which is fully proclaimed in this *Māyājāla-mahātantra*" (*Nāmasaṃgīti* 1.12–13).

Here, "speaking" (*bhāṣaṇa*) refers specifically to teaching. Thus, the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-tantra* descends [into the world] being taught for an unlimited period of time, both in its meaning and in its textual form, through the cognition of identical words and so forth. Desiring to teach it in this manner, the Blessed One said: "Now, therefore," and so on.

The Blessed One, having extracted this from the Root Tantra consisting of one hundred thousand [verses] for the sake of those devoted to the Śrī Cakrasaṃvara, teaches it because they have a preference for brevity; this is the response of the Blessed One, requested by Vajravārāhī, beginning with the words "Now, therefore" (*atha-ataḥ*). The word *atha* (now) signifies immediate succession. The word *ataḥ* (therefore) is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*) used with the elision of a suffix ending in *-lyap*. The connection is as follows: immediately after the teaching of the Root Tantra, taking the Root Tantra itself as the source, I shall speak the secret.

For it is possible to translate the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-tantra* from that [original] into another language, since its meaning is fully contained within this very [work]; the difference lies merely in the condensation of the text. Alternatively, it should be construed as: "Because I have been requested by Vajravārāhī, for that reason I shall speak the secret. This refers specifically to the request, based on the statement in the tantra, "Listen to what has been declared," for the teaching of the Dharma by one who has not been requested is not conducive to spiritual welfare, as such a teaching of the Dharma might lead to pride and the possibility of disrespect.

If it is asked what the rule regarding the goddess who requests [the teaching] is, it is heard from the lineage of gurus that in the Root Tantra she alone is the requester; therefore, it is understood that she alone is so here as well. Some maintain that the Blessed One is the requester and the Blessed Lady is the teacher; for the intention of the Tathāgatas is indeed inconceivable.

Regarding the term *rahasya* (secret): time, place, and intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) are not within the sphere of all people. "Time" refers to the past and so forth; that specific time is expressed by the word *tu* and so on. "Place" refers to a location, which is expressed by terms such as *rahasya*. "Intrinsic nature" is one's own form, characterized by the meditation on Śrī Heruka, the site, the observance of commitments (*samaya*), the request for instruction, worship, and so forth. Alternatively, Mahāvajradhara is denoted by the word *rahaḥ*, because his intrinsic nature is inaccessible to all ordinary people. Therefore, since he is beyond the comprehension of common folk, there is "solitude" (*vijanatva*).

In that regard, "the secret" (*rahasya*) refers to whatever is to be spoken therein: the meditation on Śrī Heruka accompanied by twenty-four heroes (*vīra*) and thirty-seven heroines (*vīriṇī*), as well as the places of practice, the rules of conduct (*samayācāra*), and so forth; for this very reason, this alone is the subject matter (*abhidheya*). And this indeed is the essential body of the meaning of the *Śrī Cakrasaṃvara*.

"I shall speak"—that is, I shall embody the expression. To embody the expression is precisely to illuminate the expressed; for this very reason, there exists between the expression and the expressed a relationship characterized as that of the signifier and the signified. Herein, the purpose of the expression is the non-erroneous presentation of the expressed; the purpose of the expressed is the direct realization of that very [expression] once it has been fully understood; and the purpose of that [realization] is the accomplishment of the welfare of the world through teaching and other such means.

That which has been directly realized in solitude can be communicated to another; or else, the relationship is characterized by the means (*upāya*) and the goal (*upeya*). Here, the "means" refers to the previously mentioned mandala-circle and so forth. And that [means] is favorable because the objects of enjoyment are practiced according to one's inclination. The "goal" is non-abiding nirvana (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*). Thus it has been said:
"The teaching that expresses the human goal possesses a means consistent with the relationship."
"Speech is authorized for examination; therefore, anything else is unauthorized.

If it is argued that "I have stated that very thing [in brief] because a request was made for a concise meaning in order to dispel doubts regarding Vajravārāhī," he says: "In summary" (*samāsāt*). "Summary" (*samāsa*) is a collection of all things in the sense of brevity. To the question, "In what way? Is it by way of meaning or by way of the text? he replies: "But not at length" (*na tu vistarāt*). The word "not" (*na*) is used for emphasis, and not in the sense of excluding either the meaning or the collection. Thus, a summary has been made of the words for the purpose of removing uncertainty regarding the meaning, but not of the meaning itself.

The intention is that only the equality of the text is desired, not the equality of the meaning. How is this known? He says: "Because of the elaboration. Elaboration has been accepted here; if the meaning were condensed here, then the intended meaning would not be established. One's own system (*svasamatantra*) would not be drawn forth. The *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-tantra* is the mantra for those devoted to it, being condensed from its own system in terms of the text. For the teaching of the Teacher proceeds according to the liberation from objects.
Thus, for those to be trained by passion and so forth, there is indeed the teaching of passion and so forth. And so he said:
"Just as those burned by fire are purified again by fire,
so too those burned by the fire of passion are purified by the fire of passion.
There is no other evil in the three realms equal to dispassion.
Therefore, you should never cultivate a state of detachment.

Explaining the aforementioned meaning through the term *rahasya* (secret) with some further detail, he says: "Śrī," and so forth. Conventionally, the application of arms, faces, and so on is *saṃyoga* (union); here the suffix *-ghañ* is used in the sense of an action (*karman*). The syllable *Śrī* denotes the locus of non-duality; the syllable *He* denotes the emptiness of causes and so forth; the syllable *Ru* denotes the absence of aspiration (*apraṇidhāna*); and the syllable *Ka* means "not situated anywhere. Thus, it is established as *Śrīheruka*. As it has been said: "The syllable *Śrī* is non-dual gnosis; *He* is the emptiness of causes and so forth;
the syllable *Ru* is that from which mental proliferation (*vyūha*) has departed; and *Ka* means not situated anywhere."
Furthermore: the syllable ŚRĪ is non-dual gnosis; the syllable HEKĀRA is devoid of cause;
the syllable RUKĀRA is free from form; and the syllable KAKĀRA is beyond the instruments of action.
It is called *rūpa* because it is transformed (*rūpyate*). The instruments are the sense faculties and so forth. Alternatively:

"He who has conquered the enemies that are the Māras with his fangs, filling the quarters of space [with their sound], and who is free from the net of conceptual construction—he is celebrated as Heruka."

Thus is Heruka. Śrī is Vajravārāhī; Heruka joined with her is Śrīheruka. This is a compound in which the middle term is elided (*madhyamapadalopī samāsa*), as in the case of the mantra that removes fever, called "the fever-mantra" (*jvaramantra*). Indeed, the relationship of qualifier and qualified arises from the intention to express the qualified through their very conjunction. He is both Śrīheruka and the conjunction; thus he is so designated. Śrīheruka is one part of the referent of the word "secret" (*rahasya*); the connection is made with the preceding verb "I shall speak" (*vakṣye*).

Having pointed out Śrī Heruka as one who has accomplished his own welfare (*svārthasaṃpanna*), the author speaks—beginning with "all," etc.—to further qualify him by way of his accomplishment of the welfare of others (*parārthasaṃpad*). The desires (*kāma*) of all beings—whether enemies, friends, or neutrals, or even gods, asuras, and so forth—are their inclinations; that is to say, their wishes. Their "object" (*artha*) is the sphere of those [desires]. And that consists of the attainment of non-existent happiness, the non-separation from what is not yet attained, and the non-occurrence of what is undesirable. He is the "accomplisher" (*sādhaka*) of that, meaning its direct realizer. (1)
Even higher than the highest is the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*, which abides eternally within the self of all, in the supreme and most delightful secret. (2)

He asks whether this means of accomplishment (*sādhaka*) is uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) or common (*sādhāraṇa*), and says: "Superior even to the superior," and so forth. For the excellence of the engagement is what causes one to proceed. If it were not excellent, those who are devoted to it would not engage, even though they are being taught about something excellent. Nor would they have the notion of excellence regarding it. However, because those who are devoted to it are taught that it is indeed excellent, they do proceed. This is the very nature of things (*dharmatā*) that it is described as uncommon.

For there are indeed other deities who are superior [to others], and the meaning is that this deity Śrī Heruka is superior even to them. Alternatively, by the statement "the Blessed One is superior to the Śrāvakas and others due to his possession of the accumulations of extraordinary merit and gnosis," the perfection of the means for achieving one's own welfare is demonstrated.

To the question, "Why is there a successive progression? he says: "Ḍākinī," and so forth. She is called a *ḍākinī* because her nature (*śīla*) is to take possession of non-referential gnosis (*nirālambana-jñāna*). Through etymological derivation, the letter *ka* results in the form *ḍākinī*. Since the verbal root *ḍai*, meaning "to move through the air," is employed here, those who possess the means for similarity with birds—which move through the sky (*vihāyasaḥ*)—are themselves called "those of the sky" (*vihāyasaḥ*). And here, they traverse the path that is without support by means of their wings; likewise, yogins directly realize non-referential gnosis through skillful means.

Their knowledge is "in the sky" (*vaihāyasa*); therein lies movement and abiding. Here, the root *gam* has the sense of "abiding," and that is rest. Having directly realized non-reliant knowledge, there is the cessation of wandering elsewhere.

At that time, because there is no other [existence], that gnosis (*jñāna*) has the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*). *Ḍākinī* is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and *jāla* is skillful means (*upāya*). For by a net, the capture of fish and so forth is accomplished; likewise, by skillful means, the fish of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth are restrained and rendered powerless. Because it conceals (*saṃ-vṛṇoti*) bliss (*sukha*) from those things to be avoided that stand outside, it is called *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*. Since the verbal root *saṃskṛ* denotes bliss, *saṃ* is bliss, according to the traditional teaching: "Bliss is designated as *sam*."

This worldly word *śam* is exclusively palatal (*tālavya*). Alternatively, it is called *dhātu* because it holds (*dadhāti*) within itself the manifestation (*nirmāṇa*) of the *ḍākinīs*, such as Lāmā and others. By means of this perfection of the means for the fulfillment of the welfare of others, there is an explanatory commentary on the term *pada* everywhere.

In this context, "junction" (*sandhi*) refers to the underlying intention; "objection" (*codya*) refers to the turning away from hearing, reflection, and so forth, as well as a question posed by way of an opposing view. The "response" (*parihāra*) is the refutation of that objection. This should be inferred for oneself within the context of what has been said and what is yet to be said. To the question, "Where situated shall I speak all of this?", he says: "The secret" (*rahasya*), and so forth. By the word "secret" (*rahaḥ*), there are the thirty-seven yoginīs—both with heroes (*savīrā*) and without heroes (*nirvīrā*)—who preside over the five wheels and are designated as Knowledge (*jñāna*), Mind (*citta*), Speech (*vāk*), Body (*kāya*), and the Cremation Ground (*śmaśāna*).

In this context, *rahasi* means "secret" (*rahasyam*), meaning that which is suitable for the abiding of the *yoginīs*. And that is the *kūṭāgāra*. To the question "What by this? he says: "Supreme" (*parama*). "Supreme" refers to *nirvāṇa*. It is "supreme" because it measures (*māti*) [all things] as an effect in some way or other. Alternatively, "others" (*pare*) are enemies; these are the afflictions (*kleśas*). Therefore, it is "supreme" (*paramam*) because by it others are measured, fully measured, and rendered light.

That by which one delights is "delightful" (*ramya*); it is so called because it appears like an illusion (*māyā*). Since it is but a single part [of the whole], even though it is delightful, there is no bliss in every respect even when it is directly perceived; thus he says, "in its entirety" (*sarvātmani*). That whose self (*ātman*) is present in all things—whether stable or moving—is the "Sattva-self" (*sattvātman*), which is the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*). Abiding therein, one ceases from going elsewhere, because there is no other place to go apart from that. "Always" (*sada*) means throughout the duration of saṃsāra. || 2 ||
The being consisting of all ḍākinīs is Vajrasattva, the supreme bliss;
for he is the self-arisen Blessed One, the Hero, the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*. (3)

*Sthitiḥ* means abiding. He says that even when [the practice] is accomplished, there is no other state of accomplishment—this is expressed by the passage beginning with *sarvaḍākinī*. All *ḍākinīs*, such as Ḍākinī, Lāmā, and so forth, are its constituent parts, because they have the nature of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) regarding the body and so on. Its greatness consists in having them as its constituents. Alternatively, according to the principle that "a speaker who speaks with witnesses attains authority," he describes the assembly by the passage beginning with *sarvaḍākinī*.

He states that there is no greatness in being a teacher because of acting for the sake of others—namely, "Sattva. He is called *sattva* because he is engaged in accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings (*sattva*). Nevertheless, one whose purpose is not certain does not possess that [greatness]; thus he says "Vajrasattva. The sense is that his intention (*āśaya*) is indivisible and his resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) is indivisible. Since even an indivisible resolute conviction is not sufficient on its own, he says "Supreme" (*parama*). He delights in the welfare of others (*para-artha*), hence he is "supreme" (*parama*). This is an adverbial modifier; the meaning is: "Vajrasattva in such a way as to be supreme."

"Even conceptualization regarding the ultimate reality is not sufficient for the establishment of the object," he says with the word *sukham*. *Su* means "well," and *kham* means "empty," because it is devoid of both attachment to the ultimate and the non-ultimate. This too is an adverbial modifier. The connection is: "I, being endowed with the [proper] place and so forth, shall speak the union of Śrī Heruka. Anticipating the objection, "If the union of Śrī Heruka has not been directly realized by you, how will you speak of it? he says *asau* and so forth.

The word *hi* is used for emphasis; this very Śrī Heruka-saṃyoga is indeed that. "I myself, by my own self, shall speak of the Śrī Heruka-saṃyoga"—the meaning is that it is through the instruction of that very form which has been directly realized. And since that is so, he says "[I am] Bhūḥ" to show that you are not the locus of qualities. To the question, "How could I be such a one who is the ground (*bhū*) of the Buddha-qualities, such as the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses? he says "Bhagavān. [He is so called because he possesses] complete sovereignty, beauty, fame, and splendor.

"Furthermore, the traditional teaching is that *bhaga* consists of knowledge (*jñāna*), effort (*prayatna*), and the six [perfections]. Because he possesses these *bhagas*, he is the Blessed One (*bhagavān*). To the question "From what does his state of being the Blessed One arise?", he says: "The Hero (*vīra*). He is a hero because he causes the destruction of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Thus it has been said: "He is the Blessed One because he shatters the four Māras, beginning with the afflictions. This refers to the shattering of the Māras of the afflictions, the aggregates (*skandha*), death, and the son of a god (*devaputra*). Furthermore: "He states that *bhaga* is 'shattering' (*bhañjana*) because of the shattering of the Māra of the afflictions and so forth. To the question "Why is there specifically a shattering of the afflictions?", he says: "The *Ḍākinī*," and so forth.

*Ḍākinī* is wisdom (*prajñā*), which consists both of the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) and the nature of suchness (*tathatā*). *Jāla* refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*). Therefore, the restraint (*saṃvara*) or protection of the mind by means of the *ḍākinī* acting as the instrument is the *ḍākinījālasaṃvara*. He speaks of the *ḍākinījālasaṃvara* as it truly is: "the Hero" (*vīra*). The meaning is that he will explain the union with Śrī Heruka. Accordingly, it is said: "The afflictions are to be overcome by wisdom; therefore, wisdom is called the Blessed One (*bhagā*)."

And from these [senses] comes the conquest of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the protection of the mind; for even though "net" (*jāla*) signifies delusion (*moha*), all afflictions are included therein. This is because the root of the afflictions is the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*). Thus it has been said:
"The birth of all classes of faults arises from the view of a real body (*satkāyadarśana*).
That [view] is ignorance (*avidyā*); from that comes attachment (*sneha*); and from that, the occurrence of faults and so forth."
"It is said that delusion alone is the cause of the defects;

for, apart from the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), [defects] are abandoned through its abandonment. The meaning is that when the efficient cause exists, the effect exists. The collective sense is: "I shall speak of the union with Śrī Heruka, who has become the assembly of all ḍākinīs, as being of such a nature. Regarding "self-arisen" (svayambhū): some say it is "self-existent" by way of the relationship between cause and effect and so forth, yet the sense is not that it arises from cause and effect. From the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), it is not an effect produced at present, because there is no arising of what is either existent or non-existent.

Because that which already exists does not arise, since it is already present, like the entity designated as the cause. If there were to be arising again, it would follow that the entity never ceases. If, on the other hand, there is cessation, then because the prior entity has perished and a new one arises, there is no arising of that which was already existent. In that case, let it be granted that the prior perishes and the new arises; nevertheless, this is still the arising of what was existent. If you argue that it is the arising of a "new" existent, we say no; for by being new, its status as "existent" (as previously defined) is lost.

Furthermore, since that which already exists would still be present at the time of its destruction, it is illogical for it to arise as if it were non-existent; thus, there is no arising of what already exists. Nor can it be asked: "If there is no arising of the existent, how then is it existent? For things such as a rabbit's horn are not existent simply because they have not arisen. Indeed, existence is defined by causal capacity (*sāmarthya*). If eternal entities were incapable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), they would not be accepted by anyone seeking a practical result, just like a human horn.

Nor does that [origination] arise from those [causes], whether it be existent, because its arising has already been refuted; nor is it non-existent, because that is what is being negated; nor is it both existent and non-existent, because existence and non-existence are established through mutual exclusion and thus lack the nature of being either one or many; nor is there a position of neither, because that consists in the simultaneous negation of both existence and non-existence; and finally, it cannot be something other than both existent and non-existent, because such a thing is impossible as a distinct entity apart from the exclusion of existence and non-existence.

Furthermore, if that [eternal entity] were to exist as an effect produced by causes considered to be impermanent, it would necessarily follow that it possesses existence. Since the refutation of the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is the subject at hand, and because the production of what already exists is impossible, and because—given the absence of utility for causal efficiency—it will be demonstrated that all things are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) due to their lack of both unitary and manifold natures and the refutation of their production, those [eternal entities] are indeed non-existent and thus eternal by virtue of being unproduced.

To this, it is replied: Would production belong to that which exists prior to its arising, or to that which does not exist? If it belongs to that which exists, then it is not so; for that which exists has its being already established in its entirety. Nor does it belong to that which does not exist, because such a thing is itself being negated. Now, if you argue that there is production from a cause as an existing entity in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*), but as a manifest entity (*vyakti*); is that manifestation, which constitutes the nature of production, existent or non-existent? If it were existent prior to the operation of the cause, then—just like the potentiality—it would not be produced by a cause, according to the reasoning stated above.

If, on the other hand, it were non-existent [at that time], the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) would be abandoned, and the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*) would follow as a consequence. If the capacity (*śakti*) and the manifestation (*vyakti*) were of one and the same nature, the defects inherent in the positions of existence and non-existence would arise; if they were of different natures, however, the previously mentioned [objection] applies.

Now, what is this "power" (*śakti*)? Is it the essence of the cause or the essence of the effect? If it is the essence of the cause, then since that [essence] exists prior to production, the effect would already exist; thus, the doctrine of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*) would be lost. If it is the essence of the effect, then the power does not exist at the time of the effect, because it is identical with that [effect]; nor does it exist prior [to the effect]. How, then, could the effect exist within the essence of the cause by way of the essence of power? Therefore, there is no such thing as power. Nor is manifestation (*vyakti*) possible.

If power (*śakti*) were a distinct entity from both effect and cause, being inexpressible as either identical to or different from them, it would be neither power, nor effect, nor cause. And that which is neither effect nor cause cannot be the apprehender or the obstructer of anything. This is because liberation is desired for those seeking release through the non-perversion of the mind, once the objectivity of all other categories of existence is established by the negation of the relation of cause and effect, and by their being [mere] obstructions.

Furthermore, power (*śakti*) is not a distinct entity from the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), for it is not perceived as separate in its own form—unlike a jar or other objects—which would require it to meet the conditions for perception; nor can it be established as something meeting the conditions for non-perception, since its existence is inferred through its effect, such as cognition, which arises when all causes are present and the power exists, and does not arise when they are absent, just like the eye and other organs. This is because it is impossible to produce an effect that lacks the nature of existence, and thus, in the absence of such an effect, the supporting example (*dṛṣṭānta*) fails to be established.

It should be understood that even the [position] that they are inexpressible as either identical to or different from [the particular] is refuted by this very same sequence, because it follows the same logic as the universal (sāmānya). Likewise, all [such positions] should be understood as having reached the condition of non-apprehension (anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇaprāpta).

Now, if existence occurs only when there is arising, how can an entity (*bhāva*) have the nature of being existent? Or, if existence is conceived in the absence of arising, then it would follow that the non-existent (*abhāva*), which has not yet arisen prior to arising, is called "existent. For the arising of entities is intended to have the meaning of "existence" (*sattva*). And if existence were established without arising, then what would be the use of arising? If you say, "Let the entity be unarisen," we say no; because of the fault already mentioned previously and because it will be stated again later.

Furthermore, if there were some non-existent portion of that which already exists prior to its arising, then arising would not be fruitless for the sake of that [portion]; however, this position also does not hold, as it entails the consequence of the theory of pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*). This is because the coexistence of existence and non-existence is impossible, as it would lead to the absurdity of both existence and non-existence belonging to the same thing—a fault already demonstrated therein—and because the position of manifestation (*vyakti*) has already been refuted previously.

Now, if it is argued that the production of an existent is what is to be accepted, this position too is untenable. For, since its entire nature would already be established by the very first production, a second production would be redundant; moreover, the doctrine of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*) is the subject at hand. Furthermore, it is impossible for that which already exists to be produced again even by a prior production, and the position of the unproduced has already been refuted previously. Thus, in every respect, the production of an existent is not tenable.

If there is no arising of that which exists, then what will there be of that which does not exist? For instance, even though causes such as the *kalala* stage and so forth are dispersed in hundreds of ways, the body—which consists of a collection of parts such as hands and feet—is not perceived despite meeting the conditions for perception; therefore, it is simply non-existent.

For instance, among the form, light, eye, and attention, the visual consciousness appears as the aspect of a blue or other form present before one, whereas auditory consciousness does not exist as such among the ear, sound, and attention; it does not manifest as the sounds of flutes, lutes, and so forth, nor as expressive or inexpressive, pleasant or unpleasant words. Likewise, olfactory cognition manifests as the appearance of pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral odors from campaka, vakula, and other flowers, but it does not exist among the nose, the odor, and the attention.

Among the mental operations regarding tastes, the gustatory cognition that appears as tastes such as pungent, bitter, or astringent is non-existent [in the ultimate sense]. Likewise, there is no tactile consciousness appearing as touches such as soft or hard among the objects of touch for the body or the mind. Furthermore, according to the statement, "That consciousness which has passed away immediately prior is indeed the mind," there is a subsequent conceptual cognition—such as "this is blue"—which follows another cognition and has as its object the appearance of a form such as blue, which is otherwise known by the name of the immediately preceding mental operation. It is not the case that the object, such as the form blue, exists within a cognition that possesses only the non-conceptual form of blue.

Likewise, the conceptual cognitions (*vikalpaka-jñāna*) which arise subsequent to the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile perceptions—each appearing as a distinct sound, odor, taste, or touch, and determining that "this is a non-existent thing such as sound"—do not exist within the sensory cognitions of the ear and so forth that appear as non-conceptual sounds and so on. A conceptual cognition arises in the form of "this is blue," "this is yellow," and so forth.

And yet, even though the cause is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), from each preceding consciousness that manifests the form of blue and so forth present before one, there arises a subsequent, conceptual (*vikalpaka*) cognition whose object is a succession of forms—such as blue and so forth—present before one, occurring in the second and following moments and comprised within a single continuum. And yet, that [succession] does not exist in the cause. This should be understood to apply to other objects as well, wherever it is absent.

There is the possibility of a succession characterized by a single continuum of the same genus. However, where there is no such operation of a single continuum, even in that case, when one [object] is entirely absent and another is present without interruption, there arises sense-perception (*indriyajñāna*) free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*). Through the collection of objects such as sound, there subsequently arises—following the initial non-conceptual sense-perception that grasps the preceding sound and so forth—a further non-conceptual and conceptual cognition having those very objects, which bears the same form as the sound and other objects.

Furthermore, that which has been inferred regarding the cause does not exist; for according to their view, sounds proceed by way of a continuum like the ringing of a bell or like waves upon water. Consequently, from the non-conceptual auditory cognition that apprehends the preceding sound-moment, neither a subsequent non-conceptual auditory cognition apprehending the next sound-moment arises, nor does any other conceptual cognition having sound as its object arise. And at the time of explanation, from each preceding conceptual thought, a subsequent conceptual mind proceeds.

But why does conceptual cognition not arise at the very first moment, such that another subsequent conceptual cognition would arise? There is no fixed rule in this regard; it may arise from a single sensory perception, or from all of them together.

Just as for a person who is in deep sleep, there arises from the tactile sensory cognition of the body-sense (*kāyendriya-jñāna*)—produced by the contact of a staff that has suddenly fallen—[an awareness of the object]; or sometimes, during a great thunderclap, [it arises] from the auditory sensory cognition of the ear-sense (*śrotrendriya-jñāna*); or sometimes, from the olfactory sensory cognition of the nose-sense (*ghrāṇendriya-jñāna*) which has expanded within the nostrils due to the acquisition of the fragrances of aloeswood, camphor, sandalwood, and so forth, [there arises an awareness] of the domain of odor; or sometimes, [it arises] from the tongue [due to contact] with substances such as pungent, bitter, or astringent ones.

From a non-conceptual sensory cognition of taste produced through contact with its object—taste—a conceptual cognition arises at times from the visual sensory cognition of the form of elders and others when one opens one's eyes after a momentary tactile cognition; or it arises when one is again conceptualizing, following a conceptual cognition that resembles a previous mental construction or daydream, even when all other sensory cognitions have ceased. That same [conceptual cognition] may also arise simultaneously from five or six sensory cognitions.

Just as for one who has fallen asleep immediately after the six consciousnesses, how could there be the arising of something non-existent—such as a rabbit's horn—in a dream while speaking of what was previously thought, given that it would follow from this that everything could arise from everything? For the arising and so forth of the world is like an illusion.

Now, how is it determined that sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*) is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*) and not conceptual (*savikalpa*)? Regarding this, first, according to the established position of the Sautrāntikas in their view of external objects, a mere indication is being stated in accordance with memory for the sake of instructing the ignorant. In that system, two entities are established: cognition (*jñāna*) and the object of cognition (*jñeya*); no third or further entity exists, because the agent, the instrument, and so forth, are included therein.

For indeed, when these [entities] are being conceptualized, they must be conceptualized preceded by the determination of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, because the establishment of categories of things is dependent upon valid means of cognition. Otherwise, due to the absence of any comprehension of other locations and so forth—by way of excluding other locations, times, and natures such as "this is thus," "this is not this," "this is now," or "this is not now"—the world would have existed in a state of deep sleep from the very beginning, devoid of the worldly activity consisting of the avoidance of the beneficial and the harmful.

However, those things which do not perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), such as a hare’s horn and the like, are also not established externally. They are merely produced from the beginningless latencies of conceptual construction (*vikalpavāsanā*) and do not bring about any conceptual determination; they are not for the sake of another, but are simply objects of cognition (*jñeya*). Thus, there are only two entities. In that regard, there is no identity between cognition and the object of cognition. If they were identical in essence, then either cognition alone or the object of cognition alone would be non-dual. Alternatively, even that [non-duality] would not exist, because both depend upon one another. On the side of the object of cognition, the world would be blind and mute.

If knowledge were non-different [from the object], then on the view that knowledge is identical to the object of knowledge, the perception of external objects would vanish; yet this is not desired by those who maintain the existence of external objects (*bāhyārthavādins*). In that case, since the two exist in mutual exclusion, the object of knowledge cannot penetrate into the nature of knowledge; thus, it is knowledge alone that shines forth as being self-luminous (*aparaprakāśya*), and not the object, because the latter is by nature non-luminous. If it were of the same nature as knowledge, the aforementioned fault would follow. Furthermore, if knowledge itself were non-luminous, the same fault would apply to the object of knowledge.

Since it is illuminated by another, its luminosity is even greater than that of the other. Furthermore, the "other" must either be illuminable by something else or not; otherwise, the thought "this has been illuminated by another" would not occur. Nor would the state of being "illuminated" itself occur; rather, it would simply be of the nature of self-luminosity, because it is "illuminated" even when its illuminator is not apprehended. Otherwise, the cognition of its luminosity would be impossible, for one does not perceive the state of being illuminated when the illuminator is not perceived.

For if the apprehension of "being manifested" occurs first, then the cognition of the "manifestor" follows by virtue of its being otherwise inexplicable (*anyathānupapatti*), and the cognition of "being manifested" follows from that cognition of the manifestor; thus, there is the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

Furthermore, whatever entity possesses a certain intrinsic nature (svabhāva), it colors other things with that very nature. Just as a white substance becomes red through contact with a red substance, or similarly becomes black through a black substance, or green through a green one, and so forth; or just as a form becomes luminous through the light of a lamp—how could that which is itself non-luminous by nature illuminate another thing that is also non-luminous by nature? It could not.

For objects such as a jar are not manifested in darkness by a staff, which is not luminous in nature, for that would entail the absurd consequence that lamps and the like are unnecessary. If it is argued that [the staff] might manifest another object after attaining luminosity from something else, we say no; because it lacks the connection with the state of luminosity. For instance, how could that other thing, which is itself not of a luminous nature, manifest anything else?

If that [light] were to require another light for its manifestation, and that too another, there would be an infinite regress; thus, nothing would be either manifested or a manifestor, and the world would become blind and mute. Consequently, because of the absence of worldly transactions consisting of injunctions and prohibitions regarding space, time, and nature—such as "this is so" or "this is not so"—everything would have vanished. But this is not the case. By this, the other position is also refuted.

Let it be, then, that cognition is self-luminous; nevertheless, how could the object of knowledge be illuminated by it? For it has been previously established that the nature of cognition does not bring about the object of knowledge, nor does the nature of the object of knowledge bring about cognition, because of their absolute difference.

If it is argued that even though there is absolute difference [between them], just as a white substance becomes red through contact with a red substance, or as cloth and other objects situated in darkness become luminous due to proximity to a luminous substance such as a lamp, so too the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) becomes manifest through the proximity of the knower (*jñānavat*); we say no. For if there were absolute difference between knowledge and the object of knowledge, the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) would be unestablished. This is because an illustrative example is by nature an object of knowledge, not knowledge itself.

If there were an absolute difference between those two, then how could an example—which by nature is not that [consciousness]—appear while consciousness itself, which is of the nature of light, is manifesting? For an example is an object established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and it exists as distinct from that valid cognition. While that [valid cognition] is manifesting, how could that which is not its own nature manifest? Consequently, because the example would be unestablished, nothing desired would be proven; thus, the entire world, including all sentient beings, would be like the deaf and mute.

For instance, is cognition produced or unproduced? If it belongs to the category of being produced, there would have to be the existence of causes such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth; and in the absence of those, it would have to be either with-form (*sākāra*), without-form (*nirākāra*), or with the form of something else (*anyākāra*). Regarding the first position, since cognition is distinct from the object of knowledge, there can be no connection between them—either by way of identity (*tādātmya*) or causal production (*tadutpatti*)—because the object of knowledge consists of luminosity (*prakāśa*). Thus, how could there be the perception of anything at all?

Likewise, since knowledge that has not arisen from the object of cognition cannot possess its form, the perception of the object through a knowledge possessing that form cannot be established even figuratively; thus, there would be no apprehension of the object whatsoever. As for the positions regarding permanence or impermanence, existence or non-existence—since these lack identity with or production from the object, they differ from it; therefore, apart from the possession of its form, they should not be considered as factors for the apprehension of the object, as explained previously.

In the absence of identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), the postulation of another relation is not tenable; for such a relation is produced by a causal efficacy (*upakāra*), and if there is no efficacy, the aforementioned defects would follow, whereas if there is efficacy, it would entail the position of causality itself, as will be demonstrated later. Thus, in every respect, the position that [the object] has not been produced cannot be a factor in the cognition of something else.

The position that there is no [external object] is precisely the position that [the object] is produced from that [consciousness]. It is simply that in that case, there is no external object as a cause; rather, consciousness itself arises even without an object, appearing in the form of an object due to the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) conditioned by the beginningless stream of consciousness, just like dream-consciousness—so say the Vijñānavādins.

For instance, when one has closed the door and is lying within the interior of a house with eyes closed, a cognition arises in the form of elephants, horses, and so forth—whose dimensions exceed those of the house—even in the absence of actual objects such as elephants. Nor is it logical that those objects appearing in the dream, such as elephants and horses, exist [externally], because they appear despite the absence of visual activity; for there is no appearance of visible forms for one whose eyes are closed, just as there is none for a blind person.

If it is argued that the activity of the eye is also perceived there [in dreams], that is true; its perception does indeed exist. For what is being proven there is not the absence of perception, but rather the absence of the visual faculty. How could forms such as blue appear in the dream of a blind person while they are asleep? They do not exist in a dream devoid of external objects, nor elsewhere, because their bodies would have been consumed by fire.

Or how is it that within the interior of a very small house, objects such as trees, mountains, oceans, and the solar disc—occupying the vast expanse of the earth and sky—are perceived? For they have neither entered nor reside there, since they appear even during the state of sleep. Indeed, all persons whose sensory instruments are unimpaired certainly perceive the common mass of objects.

And if objects exist in a dream, how is it that teachers and others, who were perceived there while engaged in exposition, answer when questioned upon waking? If you argue that this is because they have not forgotten everything, we say no; for there is no forgetting at all [in dreams]. Even if there were indeed no objects in the state of sleep, how can consciousness devoid of objects in the waking state be established by such a mere analogy?

For if the cognition of one suffering from ophthalmia were false, then the cognition of one free from ophthalmia would also be false. Indeed, that cognition is non-erroneous and not devoid of an object, because it is non-deceptive (*avisaṃvāda*). Non-deceptiveness consists in the attainment of the object through a cognition that arises from the production of the object; otherwise, if it occurred without the object, there would be no attainment of the object from that cognition, and thus it would not have the characteristic of being non-deceptive. This [attainment] occurs for sensory cognitions such as those of a healthy person through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the production of the object.

For instance, when the eye is free from defects such as cataracts, cognition occurs; in the absence of that [freedom from defect], it does not. Furthermore, for one with eyes closed, even though form, light, and mental attention are present, [cognition] does not arise; yet when the eyes are opened, it does. Likewise, when there is light, it occurs; in the absence of that, it does not. Even when other instruments such as the eye are present, it occurs when there is illumination from a lamp or the like; similarly, it occurs when an object such as a jar is present before one, but in its removal, it does not.

Furthermore, while other factors such as light and so forth are present, [visual consciousness] occurs when that [specific factor] is present; likewise, when consciousness designated as "attention" (manaskāra) exists, it arises, and in its absence, it does not occur. Even though objects such as jars are present, it occurs again upon awakening from a state of deep sleep. In this regard, when each [factor] is individually removed, the capacity of all [factors] for the production of that specific cognition is revealed.

Likewise, the activity of that [consciousness] with respect to form occurs through the eye, not with respect to sound and so forth; nor are sound and so forth perceived by means of the eye. For if one were to postulate the existence of auditory and other sense faculties, it would follow that they are redundant, and it would also follow that deaf people and others would not exist. Furthermore, sound and so forth are not the producers of that [consciousness], such that they might appear therein. If even non-producers were to appear, then all objects would be directly perceived, and everyone would be omniscient.

In all cases, this very determination of sensory cognition occurs: visual and other consciousnesses arise bearing the form of the images of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, neither being formless nor possessing the form of something else, because through those two [latter modes], the perception of the object is impossible. For instance, just as one’s own face is always imperceptible to a person, yet its experience occurs through seeing its reflection in a mirror by means of light; so it is here.

For that person, the experience of the reflection itself is the experience of the form of his own face; there is no other direct experience of it whatsoever apart from the experience of the reflection. Likewise, for all those who maintain the reality of external objects (*arthavādins*), the object is never directly perceived by itself. The experience of that [object] is precisely the experience of its reflection in the mirror of cognition. The perception of that [reflection] is itself the perception of the object; for the object is not directly perceived in itself.

If that [object] were perceptible, then because consciousness consists of perception, consciousness itself would be nothing but consciousness and not the object, since it would follow that the object becomes knowledge by virtue of being perceived.

Alternatively, if the perception belongs to the object alone and not to the consciousness, then if that [consciousness] were imperceptible, the consequence would be that everything is imperceptible; for if a reflection is imperceptible, one's own face cannot be perceived, as it is impossible for that [face] to be perceived [without the reflection]. Therefore, the object is not perceptible. In this regard, if consciousness were of a different form than the blue form, and not of the blue form itself, then that consciousness would be merely existent in its own right [but not cognizing the object].

That cognition belongs to that [object] alone, not to blue, because it is distinguished by the form of blue; for consciousness is devoid of forms both existent and non-existent, and thus it is neither the cognition of blue nor the cognition of yellow. That which does not possess a certain form cannot be the cognition of that thing, just as the cognition of yellow is not the cognition of black. Just as in a mirror, the reflection of one's own face—which is distinct from the form of another's face—is the cognizer of one's own face alone and not of another's face, because it is devoid of the latter's form.

Likewise, a cognition possessing a different form cannot be the experience of an object having the form of blue, because that would lead to the over-extension [of the definition] to all cognitions, and because it would not be an experience [of that specific object]. Nor can a formless cognition be the experiencer of an object such as blue. For how could that—which is devoid of the forms of all objects, like a mirror-surface devoid of all reflections—be the experiencer of an object? Indeed, a surface of a mirror, when free from all reflections, is not the experiencer of one's own face and so forth, which are themselves devoid of reflections.

If that cognition were to reflect the form of some object within itself, how could it possibly fail to be a cognizer of that object? Nor is the object itself directly perceived like its own face, due to the faults previously mentioned. Therefore, the apprehension of an object is not possible through either a cognition possessing another's form or one devoid of form; enough of this digression, for only a mere indication has been shown. Hereafter, nothing more is written for fear of excessive prolixity. || 3 ||
Emerging from the form of sound within their own nature, they are the domain of the conduct of the samaya;
rare in the three worlds, they abide at the beginning, middle, and end.

"How have you come to be such as this? To this he says: "From *saṃbhava*, etc. By means of this, the deities become fully manifested (*saṃvibhajya*); thus, *saṃbhava* is the union of the vowels (*āli*) and consonants (*kāli*). To the question "Even there, from what?", he says: "From the form of *nāda*. *Nāda* is mere sound; its representative is the mere staff (*daṇḍamātra*).

Its form is its own nature (*svarūpa*): on one's own seat is the collection of vowels and consonants; above that is the syllable *HŪṂ*. From that is produced a double vajra (*viśvavajra*), upon the hub (*varaṭaka*) of which is placed the syllable *HŪṂ*. Above that, immediately without interval, is a black *HŪṂ*; above that is a red *ĀḤ*; and above that, one should meditate on a white *OṂ*. When the *praṇava* and so forth are being rendered devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvīkriyamāṇa*), that which remains as mere sound (*nādamātra*), within that mere sound and its point (*bindu*), is the *āsāra* and the half-moon (*ardhacandra*).

That [is] in the syllable Oṃ; that [is] in the two side-bindus of the syllable Āḥ; that [is] in the side-staff outside of those; that [is] in the side-staff attached to the back of the letter Ta; that [is] in the letter Ta; that [is] on its head; that [is] the mere resonance (nādamātra) of the syllable Hūṃ. That resonance [is] in the bindu; that [is] in the half-moon; that [is] on its head. Then, [it is] in the bindu; that [is] in the letter Ha; that [is] in the first half of the letter Ha; that [is] in the second half of the letter Ha; that [is] in the two side-staffs; that [is] in the letter U; that [is] the mere resonance of the syllable Hūṃ situated upon the universal vajra (viśvavajra).

That sound [is dissolved] in the *bindu*; that in the head; that in the first half of the letter *ha*; that in the second half of the letter *ha*; in the two side-staffs; that in the letter *u*; that in the central prong of the eastern side of the universal vajra; that in the left prong; that in the right prong of the southern side; that in the middle prong; that in the left prong; that in the right prong of the western side; that in the middle prong; that in the left prong; that in the right prong of the northern side; that in the middle prong; that in the left prong; [and finally] that in the eastern side.

Having reflected that he has entered the right awn of the eastern petal, then into the central pericarp which is the nature of emptiness; then again, into the right awn of the eastern petal, then the left of the northern petal, then the center, then the right, then the left of the western petal, then the center, then the right, then the left of the southern petal, then the center, then the right, then the left of the eastern petal, then the center, and finally into the one situated upon the central knob (*varaṭaka*).

From the syllable *hūṃ* comes the letter *u*; from that, the two side-sticks (*pārśvadaṇḍau*) of the latter half of the letter *ha*, by which [is formed] the former half of the letter *ha*; then on the head, the *ta*, then the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), then the bindu, then the nāda, then the mere-nāda (*nādamātra*). Then the letter *u*, then the two side-sticks of the latter half of the letter *ha*, by which [is formed] the former half; then the head, then the half-moon, then the bindu, then the nāda, then the mere-nāda.

Then the head of the letter *ta*, then the letter *ta*, then the side-staff (*pārśvadaṇḍa*), then the other side-staff, then the two dots (*bindu*), then the vowel *o*, then the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), then the dot (*bindu*), then the sound (*nāda*), and then the mere-sound (*nādamātra*).

Arising from that, rooted in the seat, situated as subtly as a lotus fiber, the deity to be meditated upon is eight cubits in measure, white, the support for the latencies of purified karma and afflictions, having the nature of Prajñāpāramitā which is the object of consciousness, and possessing the nature of Vajrasattva who is the essence of wisdom and means; she is to be meditated upon as the "Buddha-line. The phrase "in the form of sound" (*nādarūpa*) refers to the realization, born from the two [wisdom and means] through their illusory-like nature, that "I am [this]. The particle *hi* is used for emphasis.

Thus, having emerged from the pair itself through the purification of the twelvefold dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), he is primarily twelve-armed. His hand-symbols are [to be understood] from the oral instruction. Or, as he will say: "And covered with an elephant hide," and so forth. He says "I have emerged from that" not only for himself, but also [for others], stating "they have emerged," and so on. *Samaya* refers to the Gokudahanā and other [pledges]; their practice (*ācāra*) is their service (*sevā*). Those *ḍākinīs*, *lāmās*, and so forth, whose sphere of activity (*gocara*) is precisely that, are called "those whose sphere of activity is the practice of the *samaya*. *Gocara* means the domain; *samaya* means the emanation (*nirmāṇa*).

And some say that this is connected to the welfare of sentient beings. Furthermore, although the word *niṣkrānta* ends in the plural number, it should be construed with *Vajradhara* in the singular, by changing the case ending (*vibhaktivipariṇāmāt*).

Anticipating the doubt as to whether you are the very nature of the knowledge of ultimate reality (*paramārthajñāna*), he says: "Difficult to obtain," and so forth. Wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*) are two, and conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is the third; these three [arise] because conceptualization is the third due to its proximity to those two by virtue of being conceptualized. The sense is that if conceptualization does not subsequently arise, I am as easily obtained as wisdom and means. This is because, through non-attachment while practicing with those two, one directly realizes the innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*) whose nature is distinct from all afflictions (*kleśa*).

Therefore, I am of the nature of consciousness precisely because of being free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*). Hence he says: "In the worlds" (*lokeṣu*). "World" (*loka*) means seeing or perception (*darśana*, *upalambha*); and these [perceptions] arise from the apprehension of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*). From the word "world" itself, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is obtained, since perception is its primary context. Alternatively, it is difficult to find [this state] during the blisses of emission (*ānanda*) and supreme cessation (*paramavirama*), according to the statement: "The Innate (*sahaja*) does not exist in these three. The rest is as before. Therefore he says: "At the beginning," and so forth.

Because it is conceptual (*savikalpaka*), it remains divided into beginning, middle, and end, by which I am difficult to attain. Having established through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) that [I] am easily attained, [the text] speaks of [my] being difficult to attain. And this is the underlying intention: this form of mine, namely that which is called "conceptual," is not truly mine; for my true form is indeed non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), because it consists of such knowledge.

And that [state] is difficult to attain through conceptual elaboration (*vikalpa*); or rather, when moments characterized by various ripenings and suppressions have come to pass, it is "lost," meaning it has become invisible due to the absence of experience; therefore, I am difficult to attain. For it is only in a moment of distinct character (*vilakṣaṇa-kṣaṇa*) that there occurs the experience of the knowledge called the Innate (*sahaja*), which is devoid of all objective perception. || 4 ||
Just as there is the union of the churning stick and the churning base, so too is [this] joined with the recitation of mantras, meditation, and so forth;
listen to the yoga and the knowledge of the ritual procedure as declared in the Tantra. || 5 ||

Through the union of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), which is implied by the sense [of the text], [the goal] is easily attained and accomplished; nevertheless, [the author] asks "how is that so? and says: "the union of the churner and the churning. The churner is the aspect of wisdom, and the churning is the aspect of means, according to the convention of the Dharma. That in which these two are joined in a state of equal flavor (*samarasatva*) is thus described. "I am easily attained" in such a way as constitutes the union of the churner and the churning; the connection is that "he will be explained in the *Śrīherukasaṃyoga*. The Blessed One is the nature of innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*).
He asks what that very thing is like, and says: "Just as it is. This four-syllabled statement is as follows:
"Neither at the beginning, nor in the middle, nor at the end; neither existence, nor nirvāṇa.
This is that supreme great bliss—neither other, nor self."
The yogi should press the two waves together with the thumb and the ring finger of his left hand during the act of union.
Subsequently, knowledge arises, like the pleasure of a maiden in love.

Thus is the meaning of the word *yathā*. "The fourth is likewise (*tathā*)"—this is the meaning of the word *tathā*. The meaning of these two sections of the text is to be understood from the oral instruction of the Guru. Here, there is no need to analyze the meter, phonology, and so forth, because it is of *ārṣa* (sage-like) origin. This [text] is designated by the term *rahasya* (secret) along with its qualifications. Having stated the union with Śrī Heruka, he says "mantra," etc., in order to establish the yoga and other practices that constitute its very subject matter. "Mantras" refers to those of eight syllables and so forth; their *jāpa* is simply recitation, that is, repetition.

Meditation consists of contemplating the form of the deity. From the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there are included: the worship of the *Kulikā*, the female messengers (*dūtīs*), the accomplishment of desire, the worship of the drops of bodhicitta and the Bodhisattvas, liberation from all sins, the means of achieving the state of a yogi, the observance of the pledges (*samaya*), the guarding of the pledges, the consumption of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), the tasting of the five nectars in the *gaṇacakra* like the drinking of soma, the union of the two organs, divine bliss, praise, the locations such as mountains and caves, and the ten principles (*tattva*) beginning with the mandala.

The worship of the maṇḍala of the Guru, Vīra, and Vīreśvarī; the entry of the disciple into the maṇḍala; then the bestowing of initiation; the gestures (mudrās) and the worship of the Ācārya; the manifestation of the realm of the Ḍākinīs; the extraction of the mantra; the expansion of the ritual activities of the King of Vidyās; the accomplishment of the eight worldly siddhis; the procedure for secret signs (chommaka); the characteristics of the action-seal (karmamudrā); the acts of speaking, going, and coming by means of those two; the characteristics of the Ḍākinīs; the display of the seal and counter-seal (pratimudrā); the declaration of the names of the pledges (samaya); and the eight worldly and supramundane [siddhis].

The great commitments (*mahāsamaya*): the communal consumption of sacrificial food (*caru*) in one place, the offering of oblations (*balidāna*), the extraction of the *Sumbharāja* mantra, the accomplishment of its ritual applications (*karmaprasara-sādhana*), meditation on the mandala-image (*mantrabimba-dhyāna*), the cultivation of the reality free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa-tattva-bhāvanā*), the supreme supramundane [state], and thereafter the recitation (*japa*) of the mantras beginning with Cittavajrā, which are contained within the names of the Heroes (*vīra*) and Heroines (*vīreśvarī*) together with the mantra-words of the four faces; the instruction on the twenty-four sites (*sthāna*) corresponding to the ten stages (*bhūmi*) such as the sacred seats (*pīṭha*); [the rules for] dwelling at night and so forth in various directions; the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*); and thereafter—

The purification of the twenty-four elements beginning with Khaṇḍakapāla; the transformation into the forms of the goddesses, the *bhūcaras*, and the *khecaras*; the sections concerning the movement, enjoyment, and dissolution within the wheel of the thirty-seven family channels (*nāḍīcakra*); the turning of the Wheel of Dharma; and thereafter, the nature of the Emanation, Enjoyment, Dharma, and Purity bodies (*kāya*), as well as the nature of the indivisibility of emptiness and compassion—these are what are included [here]. "Yoga" refers to the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) for rites such as pacification (*śāntika*), enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), subjugation (*vaśya*), and the rite of sorcery (*abhicāra*). "Knowledge of the ritual procedure" (*vidhijñāna*) refers to this.

"Vidhi" means that which is enjoined; it refers to action such as virtuous deeds (*sukṛta*) and the like. "Knowledge" (*jñāna*) is the state of being knowable; this exists [in that action]. And this he will indicate: "Just as a vessel filled with ghee placed in the midst of fire melts, and the ghee flows out, so the time of the two vessels perishes."
In the same way, evil is destroyed by the name "Śrī Heruka."

By this statement; or alternatively, "vidhi" here refers to time (*kāla*) in its aspects of past, future, and present. "Jñāna" refers to the eight bodies of knowledge (*jñānakāya*). "Vidhijñāna" is the knowledge of that procedure. The connection [of the sentence] is: "I shall speak of the yoga, which is designated by such terms as 'the secret' (*rahasya*) and so forth. In the *Khasama* Tantra, which contains the complete compendium, that which was declared—that which is designated by the term 'secret'—[is what I shall speak of]. Therefore, "Listen to that, O Vajravārāhī! The sense is that it is because that [yoga] is the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

If the text of that tantra is abridged, what harm is there in that? [The objection] beginning with "In this way" and so forth has not been stated here because it was already explained in that very place. If it is argued: "How can this be an abridgment of a new text, since it is itself something new?"—we say no; for it lacks novelty insofar as its subject matter and connection are derived from the *Mūlatantra*. If it is argued: "Because of the statement, 'O monks, my teachings are to be compiled thus: "Thus have I heard,"' the compiler alone now possesses the authority for that connection"—we say no.

And it is a compendium because it compends the *tantra* in the form of the signifier and the signified as spoken by the Blessed One. If it is asked, "If the Blessed Lady is the teacher (*deśikā*), then how is the application of words such as 'is situated' (*sthita*) possible?", [the answer is: by means of the words beginning with "is situated," I shall speak of the union with Śrī Heruka. As to what that [union] is like, he says: "In the supreme secret," and so forth, which is to be applied. That by which the meaning is strung together is the collection of words (*śabdasandoha*). Here, the meaning is divided threefold, in the form of the fruit, the cause, and the means.

The fruit is the state of Samantabhadra, which is of the nature of the Vaipulya [extensive] teachings. It consists in the cause itself having reached a specific stage through repeated practice. The cause, however, is the assembly of deities of the maṇḍala. The means consists of the four elements, Mount Meru, the peaked pavilion, and so forth. Such is its nature as a tantra (*tantratā*). And thus it is said: "A continuum (*prabandha*) is declared to be a tantra; that continuum is threefold.
The summary of the meaning of the tantra is by means of these three: the basis, the form, and the means."

By the word "secret" (*rahasya*), the subject matter of the entire tantra has been stated in extreme brevity. Thereafter, by the passage beginning with "the union with Śrī Heruka," it was explained in detail through the mode of a commentary. Now, he speaks from the point of no further prolixity until the completion of the tantra. || 5 ||
With moderate or superior breath, together with scented water,
one should constantly worship the Kulikā and the female messengers (dūtī) according to the specific times.

He says that very thing with the words beginning with *madhyama*: "Madhyama" (the middle) and "uttama" (the supreme) are the *śvāsa* (breath), whether it be that in which one breathes or that by means of which one breathes; it refers to either the locus (*sthāna*) or the time (*kāla*). The fire is "middle" because, according to the statement "earth, water, fire, and air," it arises from the middle. Even though it arises from the middle, there is the mention of the "supreme" (*uttama*), because he will say of it: "The supreme is Māhendra, due to being the king of the gods. Thus, the meaning is that the *śvāsa*, the locus, or the time belongs to both the middle and the supreme. By this, the connection is: "one should worship Kulikā."

He asks, "By what [is she accompanied]? and replies with the words beginning with *gandha*. That which possesses fragrance (*gandha*) is "fragrant" (*gandha*); because it carries fragrance, it is the wind (*vāyu*). That which possesses water (*udaka*) is "watery" (*udaka*), namely Varuṇa. "Accompanied by fragrance and water" (*gandhodakasahita*) is a compound formed by the elision of the middle term (*madhyapadalopī samāsa*), just as a jar filled with ghee is called a "ghee-jar" (*ghṛtaghaṭa*). The word *tu* is for the purpose of completing the meter. Thus, the meaning is this: the *Kulikā* is the Yoginī; one should worship her, that is, propitiate her. "Constantly" means at all times, every single day.

Regarding "at specific times": at specific times, during the portions of half-praharas beginning with the first day of the waxing moon (*śukla-pratipad*) and so forth, according to the instruction. Starting from the first day of the waxing moon, at the morning half-prahara, one should meditate on Pracaṇḍā, born from the syllable *puṃ* (the letter *p*), on the head, generated by the mantra: *oṃ kara kara pracaṇḍe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*. On the second [day], on the crest-lock (*śikhā*), one should meditate on Caṇḍākṣī, born from the syllable *jāṃ*, generated by the mantra: *oṃ kuru kuru caṇḍākṣi hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*.

In the third, on the right ear born from the syllable Oṃ, is Prabhāvatī, born from the mantra: Oṃ bandha bandha prabhāvati hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. In the fourth, on the back of the head born from the syllable Aṃ, is Mahānāsā, born from the mantra: Oṃ trāsaya trāsaya mahānāse hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ. In the fifth, on the left ear born from the syllable Goṃ, is Vīramatī, born from the mantra: Oṃ kṣobhaya kṣobhaya vīramati hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ.

In the sixth [petal], at the center of the eyebrows, from the syllable *rāṃ*, one should visualize Kharvarī, born from the mantra *oṃ hrauṃ hrauṃ kharvarī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. In the seventh, at the two eyes, from the syllable *deṃ*, one should visualize Laṅkeśvarī, born from the mantra *oṃ hraḥ hraḥ laṅkeśvari hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*. In the eighth, at the two shoulders, from the syllable *māṃ*, one should visualize Drumacchāyā, born from the mantra *oṃ pheṃ pheṃ drumacchāye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*. This is the Mind Wheel (*cittacakra*). The seat of these goddesses is the fire-maṇḍala; such is the division for the day.

In the first half-watch of the night, one should visualize Airāvatī, born from the syllable *kāṃ*, at the two armpits, produced by the mantra: *oṃ phaṭ phaṭ airāvati hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*. In the second [watch], one should visualize Mahābhairavī, born from the syllable *oṃ*, at the two breasts, produced by the mantra: *oṃ daha daha mahābhairave hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*. In the third [watch], one should visualize Vāyuvegā, born from the syllable *triṃ*, at the navel, produced by the mantra: *oṃ paca paca vāyuvege hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*.

In the fourth, at the tip of the nose produced from the syllable *koṃ*, is Surābhakṣī, born from the mantra: *oṃ bhakṣa bhakṣa vasarudhirāntramālāvalambine surābhakṣi hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*. In the fifth, in the mouth produced from the syllable *kaṃ*, is Śyāmādevī, born from the mantra: *oṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa saptapātālagatabhujaṅgaṃ sarpaṃ vā tarjaya tarjaya śyāmādevi hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*.

In the sixth [petal], at the throat born from *laṃ*, is Subhadrā, born from the mantra: *oṃ ākaḍḍha ākaḍḍha subhadre hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*. In the seventh, at the heart born from *kāṃ*, is Hayakarṇā, born from the mantra: *oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ karakarṇe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*. In the eighth, at the genitals born from *hiṃ*, is Khagānanā, born from the mantra: *oṃ jṇauṃ jṇauṃ khagānane hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*. This is the wheel of speech (*vākcakra*). The seat of these goddesses is the Varuṇa-maṇḍala; this is the nocturnal portion.

On the second lunar day, in the morning during the first watch (*prahara*), one should meditate upon Cakravegā, born from the *liṅga* produced by the syllable *preṃ*, with the mantra: *oṃ kṣmāṃ kṣmāṃ cakravege hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*. In the second [watch], in the anus produced by the syllable *gṛṃ*, one should meditate upon Khaṇḍarohā, born from the mantra: *oṃ hāṃ hāṃ khaṇḍarohe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*. In the third [watch], in the two thighs produced by the syllable *sauṃ*, one should meditate upon Śauṇḍinī, born from the mantra: *oṃ hīṃ hīṃ śauṇḍini hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*.

In the fourth [circle], from the syllable *suṃ*, on the pair of shanks, one should place Cakravarmiṇī, born from the mantra: *oṃ hūṃ hūṃ cakravarmiṇi hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*. In the fifth, from the syllable *naṃ*, on the collection of toes, one should place Suvīrā, born from the mantra: *oṃ kili kili suvīre hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*. In the sixth, from the syllable *siṃ*, on the two backs of the feet, one should place Mahābalā, born from the mantra: *oṃ sili sili mahābale hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*.

In the seventh [petal], from the syllable *maṃ*, on the two big toes, is the one born from the mantra *cili cili* (or *hili hili*) *cakravartini hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*, namely Cakravartinī. In the eighth, from the syllable *kaṃ* (or *kuṃ*), on the two knees, is the one born from the mantra *oṃ dhili dhili mahāvīrye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*, namely Mahāvīryā. This is the Body Wheel (*kāyacakra*). The Maheśvara mandala is the seat for these goddesses; this concludes the daytime portion.

On that very night, during the first two watches, Kākāsyā, Ulūkāsyā, Śvānāsyā, and Śūkarāsyā are to be visualized in order near Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍākṣī, Prabhāvatī, and Mahānāsā. During the second two watches, Yamadāḍhī, Yamadūtī, Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī, and Yamamathinī are to be visualized in order near Vīramatī, Kharvarī, Laṅkeśvarī, and Drumacchāyā.

Likewise, on the third lunar day, a day and night [pass] by means of the mind-wheel (*citta-cakra*) and the speech-wheel (*vāk-cakra*). Then, on the fourth, it proceeds by means of the body-wheel (*kāya-cakra*) and the charnel ground-wheel (*śmaśāna-cakra*); such is the movement of the thirty-two yoginīs. This should be understood for the fifth and subsequent days as well. Śrī Heruka and the four yoginīs beginning with Ḍākinī constitute the consciousness-wheel (*vijñāna-cakra*); however, there is no movement of these because of the absence of oral instruction (*upadeśa*). Having performed meditation and recitation for six months and having attained the signs (*nimitta*), the yogin should then carry out the movement of the yoginīs for seven months.

Thus, if there is no accomplishment, one should practice in that same manner once again. It is taught that in this way, success is achieved with certainty within thirty-six months. Practice performed with devotion and without interruption for one year is followed by practice for six months and so forth; such is the sequence. The application of fire and other elements for rites such as *abhicāra* (sorcery) should likewise be understood in the same way.

Just as in the case of *abhicāra* (sorcery), one should meditate on any one of the Yoginīs during the fire-moment (*vahnikṣaṇa*) of the mind-wheel (*cittacakra*); for *śāntika* (pacification), during the water-moment (*varuṇakṣaṇa*) of the speech-wheel (*vākcakra*); for *pauṣṭika* (prosperity), during the earth-moment (*māhendrakṣaṇa*) of the body-wheel (*kāyacakra*); and for *uccāṭana* (eradication), during the wind-moment (*vāyukṣaṇa*) of the charnel-ground wheel (*śmaśānacakra*). The fire [moment] is four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), the earth [moment] is ten finger-breadths, the wind [moment] is six finger-breadths, and the water [moment] is twelve finger-breadths.

"Regarding Agni, Indra, Vāyu, and Varuṇa, there is a rule for the location of their exit based on fourteen, six, and twelve finger-breadths respectively"—so says the scriptural statement.
