Furthermore, the wind of Fire (Agni) is hot and moves upward; that of Mahendra is neither too cold nor too hot and fills the nostrils; that of Vāyu is transverse and rough; and that of Varuṇa is extremely cold and flows downward.

The mandalas beginning with that of Fire are as follows: there, the mandala of Fire is triangular, red, marked with seven flames; that of Mahendra is square, yellow, marked with a thunderbolt (*vajra*); that of Vāyu is bow-shaped, blue, marked with a banner (*patākā*); and that of Varuṇa is circular, white, marked with a bell. These are situated to the right of the Fire [mandala], starting from the exit of Vāyu. By demonstrating the worship of the *Kulikā*, the accomplishment (*siddhi*) is shown first, because she alone is primary by virtue of being the object to be attained (*sādhya*). || 6 ||
The innate siddhas of the two messengers are classified as inferior, superior, and middling;
one should contemplate the accomplishment of desire with an inward-turned mind.

He states how many *kulikās* there are with the words "the messengers" (*dūtayaḥ*) and so forth. The term "former *kulikā*" (*pūrvakulikām*) is in the singular merely by way of genus. Consequently, they are called "messengers" (*dūtayaḥ*) in the plural because they are afflicted and tormented by the suffering of sentient beings. "The *kulikās* are the messengers" is a statement of synonyms. They are the four, beginning with *Ḍākinī*, who are innate (*sahajā*) and identical in nature to the Blessed One. "They" (*tāḥ*) refers to those whose essential nature is gnosis (*jñāna*). "The accomplished ones" (*siddhāḥ*) refers to the eight yoginīs, beginning with Yamadāḍhī.

The inferior ones are those belonging to the body wheel, dwelling in the netherworld; the middling ones are those belonging to the speech wheel, moving on the earth; the superior ones are those belonging to the mind wheel, moving through the sky.

The meaning is that these thirty-six yoginīs alone are to be worshipped. It is established that Śrī Heruka is to be accomplished by means of both the body and the external maṇḍala. To the question, "What should be meditated upon by one who possesses the practice? he says: "Internal," and so forth. Desires (*kāma*) are form, sound, and so on; from them or by means of them, the accomplishment of Śrī Heruka occurs. "One should meditate" (*bhāvayet*) means one makes [the object] one's own being (*svasattvam*). This implies that the accomplishment of desires becomes real, according to the statement: "Form, sound, and so on, are desires."

To explain how this is so, he says: "by the mind. This means by consciousness (*vijñāna*), according to the statement: "Mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and then consciousness (*vijñāna*) are cognition (*vijñapti*). By the phrase "internally," the meaning is: by the mind in the form of Śrī Heruka, who is non-different from oneself. The intention is that the practitioner of Śrī Heruka attains accomplishment through the enjoyment of all sensual desires. And thus it is said: "By the enjoyment of all sensual desires, one who is pure indeed attains accomplishment."

Therefore, the word "tu" (but) has the sense of the particle "eva" (only), because there is no accomplishment of the goal through that which is devoid of [inner] manifestation. That which consists of mental activity (*bhāvanā*) is "mental" (*manomayī*); external worship is characterized by the enjoyment of objects such as form and so forth. || 7 ||
One should worship the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas with drops of one's own semen, and through seeing and touching them, as well as by hearing and remembering them. (8)

He speaks of the direct worship with the words "one should emit," and so forth. For the sake of worship within the external cognition characterized as described in other tantras, one should generate the *bodhicitta*. Having purified its union of both [parents] by means of its drops in the form of the tasting of nectar, one should worship the Buddhas—the five aggregates such as form and sensation—and the Bodhisattvas—the forms of the eyes and so forth—by means of consumption. Thus, this is to be practiced at the three junctions of the day; this is the direct worship. As it is said:
"The wide-eyed one of firm intellect should consume the secret semen.
This is the worship of body, speech, and mind for all mantras."

The secret worship (*guhyapūjā*), however, is the realization of the co-emergent (*sahaja*); the sense is that it is accomplished through the perfection of the fourfold worship. Through this yoga, because of the destruction of previously accumulated merit and demerit—which are characterized by attachment to the perceived object (*grāhya*) and so forth—there arises a merit that is unprecedented and free from such attachment. From that, accomplishment (*siddhi*) is described as beginning with "seeing" (*darśana*) and so on: seeing is apprehension by the eye; touching is by the body-faculty; hearing is by the ear-faculty; and remembering is by the mind-faculty. (8)
In this very way, one is liberated from all sins; of this there is no doubt.
This state of yoga is supremely meritorious, pure, and the destroyer of sin.

By means of these factors related to Śrī Heruka acting as instruments, even another person is liberated—that is, he is released from all sins, which consist of the misdeeds of body and so forth acting as agents. "Freedom from sin" (*niṣpāpatā*) is the state of being devoid of sin. "In this very way" (*evam eva*) means that this is stated by way of a synonym (*paryāyokta*). To the question "Is this true?", he says: "There is no doubt. This means there is no duality here. One who is liberated while being attached to the objects of perception and so forth through seeing and other senses does so through union with the moment of experiencing the secret innate (*sahaja*).

This is the secret worship (*guhyapūjā*). Regarding the phrase "and there, in this very way," the meaning is that the triple world (*traidhātuka*) itself is nothing at all. Some say "there is no doubt" because of the absence of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). He explains how this [occurs] simply through the vision of the yogin by saying "the state of a yogin" (*yogitva*), which refers to the state of being a yogin of Śrī Heruka. It is "supreme" (*parama*) because it removes all sins merely by being seen. For this very reason, it "purifies," thus it is "meritorious" (*puṇya*). It is "pure" (*pavitra*) because it is free from the stains of the afflictions (*kleśa*). It is "the destroyer of sin" (*pāpanāśana*) because it annihilates the five acts of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*) and so forth. (9)
Success is achieved through the mantra of recitation, by means of recitation and meditation; the practitioner, being well-composed, should constantly observe the rules of conduct (samayas). || 10 ||

He provides the detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*) for what was briefly indicated by "one should meditate" (*bhāvayet*), beginning with "it is accomplished" (*siddhyate*). Regarding "it is accomplished": the vowel *e* is a modification of the vowel *i*; the meaning is that [the deity] becomes manifest. Regarding "recitation" (*japa*): this is a case of the elision of the instrumental case ending (*tṛtīyā-lopa*). It is a mental activity; by means of that, one contemplates the *dharmadhātu* and protects the *lokadhātu*. Thus, the mantra of Śrī Heruka, whose nature consists of wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya-ātmaka*), is accomplished. In the phrase "by means of the mantra" (*mantreṇa*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of the nominative. Alternatively, by "recitation," the activity of speech is shown.

"By means of meditation" refers to the activity of the mind; "by means of [the body]" refers to the activity of the body, which consists of wisdom and skillful means. To the question of with what auxiliary factor recitation and so forth become fruitful, he says: "The pledges (*samaya*)," and so on. The pledges have been explained; the point is that even though they are eternal, they are nevertheless useful through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Thus it has been said: "This water of yours is hellish; it shall burn you for transgressing the pledges."

This is the explanation of the phrase "the sphere of the conduct of the *samaya*": namely, "the practitioner" (*sādhaka*). For the practitioner, while constantly performing meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), should consume at the commencement of meditation pills made from cow-products and the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). By this, indeed, freedom from obstacles arises. Regarding "well-composed" (*susamāhita*): he is thoroughly and completely benefited and nourished by the yoga consisting of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*), which is perfectly even and free from inequality. Furthermore, the *samaya* is stated elsewhere; as it is said: "The letter *na*, the letter *ga*, likewise the letter *ha*, and the beginning of the dog, and the beginning of the horse. (10)
If the commitments (samayas) are differentiated, success is not attained in the initiation mandala.
[One should offer] honey, red [substance], camphor, and mixed red sandalwood. (11)

To the question, "How is there such a secret convention even in that case? he says: "By means of distinction," and so forth. "Distinction" (*bheda*) refers to the understanding of the conventional designations (*prajñapti*) of the non-conventional (*asamaya*). The word "for" (*hi*) has the sense of "because. For, because those who do not understand the reality of things (*vastutattva*) reject [the teaching] through their sense of distinction, both faults [of the teacher and the student] arise. Consequently, there is neither accomplishment (*siddhi*) nor an adept (*sādhaka*). The intended meaning is that accomplishment occurs through the collection of the systems of Tantra and Mantra.

Regarding the reading, “*na mantramaṇḍale siddhiravāpyate*”: by means of the *mantra*—that is, by the utterance that impels the reality (*tattva*)—one takes (*lāti*) the *maṇḍala*, which is enlightenment (*bodhi*); thus it is so called. This is to be explained as the Mantra Mahāyāna. Furthermore, the *samaya* must be observed everywhere, and its violation must not be committed; this is direct worship.

He describes another form of direct worship consisting of the service of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), beginning with the word "madhu": "Madhu" is semen (*śukra*) because of its similarity to honey; it is so designated because, when combined [with the other four], it destroys the three humors (*tridoṣa*). "Rakta" (blood) is well known. "Karpūra" is that which fills the body with pleasure (*ka*); this refers to meat, established through the addition and elision of phonemes (*varṇāgama-vināśa*). "Rakta" is urine, as it is tasted (*ras-*) along with food and so forth. Vairocana is sandalwood (*candana*) because it produces delight (*āhlāda*). (11)

Established in the midst of the assembly, bearing the marks and signs of all vajras, the knower of yoga should always cause [the disciple] to taste [it] with the ring finger and thumb joined in a curved shape. 12.

"In the midst of the *gaṇa*" means in the midst of the *gaṇacakra*. The word "midst" (*madhya*) indicates a general connection. "Established" (*pratiṣṭhita*) refers to that which is established (*pratiṣṭham*). The particle "tu" has the sense of "indeed" (*eva*). To the question "Upon what support is it based?", he says: "All," and so forth. "All-vajra" (*sarvavajra*) is the universal vajra; that which has this as its mark or sign is "marked with the sign of all vajras" (*sarvavajrāṅkacihna*). That is the skull-cup (*kapāla*), and because it is held therein, it is "that [which is] thus. To the question "How should it be employed?", he says: "The ring finger," and so forth. "Licked in the mouth" (*vaktra*) is called "leham."

"He should do that" means he should cause [the disciple] to lick it. "One who knows the yoga" means one who knows the yoga of tasting the nectar (*amṛta*), or one who possesses the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) in mind-only. "Always" means that he should consume the five nectars together with the assembly of the deities of the maṇḍala. || 12 ||
Having tasted it like the drinking of Soma, one attains eternal perfection;
herein, the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) become the instigator of all accomplishments.

He says that one should not entertain doubt in this matter, beginning with the words "Soma" and so forth. At the time of sacrifice, the juice of the *kāliṅga* creeper should be placed upon the hide of a tawny cow for the Brahmins. That is Soma; its drinking bestows longevity and increases merit. Just as the Brahmins taste the Soma without any hesitation, so too the yogi, having tasted the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), attains eternal perfection. Because it consists of the nature of granting eternal fruit, the analogy is based merely on tasting without doubt, and not on the actual result. As it has been said: "One should never feel disgust toward feces, urine, semen, or blood."

"One should always consume this, born of the three secrets, according to the rite. To the question, "What is this honey and so forth called?", he says: "The five," and so on. The collection of the five nectars (*amṛta*) is *pañcāmṛta*. The collective meaning is that by means of the yoga of the deity, being free from doubt, and through the rite of tasting like nectar, all food, drink, and so forth, becomes nectar. To the question, "How does this bring about eternal accomplishment (*siddhi*)?", he says: "All," and so on. It is so because it brings forth all mundane and supramundane accomplishments. || 13 ||
The fourfold worship, as well as the heroines who are the yoginīs desired by the mind;
and the Holder of Reality (Tattvadhṛk), who has entered into the non-dual union with the heroes. 14.

He states the summary meaning of the brief indication (*uddeśa*) and the detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*) with the words beginning "four," and so forth. The meaning of "fourfold worship" (*catuṣpūjā*) is as follows: these [worships] are taught through the distinctions of external, secret, mental, and manifest [worship]. Therefore he says "likewise" (*tathā*); the meaning is that they have been specified by the manner beginning with "the middle," and so forth. Regarding "the Yoginīs": these are the four, such as Ḍākinī and the rest, and the eight, such as Kākāsyā and the rest. The meaning of the term "vīrādvayasamāpatti" is those [Yoginīs] who possess union (*samāpatti*) with the heroes (*vīra*) in a non-dual form; the case ending has been elided.

"In whatever way he has entered [meditative absorption], so it is. He is the "Bearer of Reality" (*tattvadhṛk*) because he maintains the reality that is inseparable from Vajravārāhī as his own nature. Regarding the term *tattvadhṛk*: the suffix *-tu* becomes *-ta*, and the suffix *-ka* becomes *-caṇa*. Thus, he is designated as the "Union with Śrī Heruka. (14)
Even all the happiness of gods and humans combined together is not worth a sixteenth part of that very [bliss] when compared to the tip of a vajra. (15)

That which exists in heaven is *divya*; that is bliss (*sukha*). That which belongs to this [state] is human; its nature is humanity (*mānuṣyatā*), and that is established when there is non-duality in the nature of bliss. How is bliss obtained? He says: "Bliss" (*saukhya*). Bliss is the stability of the mind; that itself is *saukhya*. And that is common to those who have gone to the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals. *Piṇḍa* means undivided. *Vajra* is stainless intellect; that itself is the *kaṇikā* (central point) because of its subtlety.

"Vajra and kaṇikā" means *vajrakaṇikā*, which signifies innate gnosis (*sahaja-jñāna*). By means of this *vajrakaṇikā*, which exists as the instrument by having unified divine and human happiness, even the sixteenth digit (*kalā*) is not worth mentioning and does not pay homage; the ellipsis implies "the afflictions" (*kleśa*). Since this method has the conquest of the afflictions as its goal, the phrase "however it may be" (*yathā tathā*) is stated as a summary of what was previously indicated. (15)
One should draw that mandala in mountain caves or thickets, on the shores of the great ocean, or in a primordial siddha cremation ground.
Thus ends the first chapter, the procedure for entering the maṇḍala, in the Herukābhidhāna. || 1 ||

Without consecration (abhiṣeka), there is no accomplishment. And that [consecration] does not exist without entry into the mandala; thus he says "on a mountain" and so forth. "Mountain" (giri) means a peak. By the word "cavern" (gahvara), the space between its two walls is meant. By the word "grove" (kuñja), a place concealed by creepers and the like is meant. "Islands" (dvīpa) are the shores of the great ocean. "Primordially accomplished" (ādisiddha) means a place where [the goal] was accomplished in the beginning. "Cemetery" (śmaśāna) is the abode of corpses. The word "there" (tatra) is used here in the locative sense of occasion. One should draw the mandala for the sake of consecration. || 16 ||

The word *iti* marks the completion of the chapter’s subject matter. That by which the Śrī Heruka, together with his limbs (*aṅga*) and sub-limbs (*upāṅga*), is expressed is the *abhidhāna*, the Tantra, the verbal body. Within that, there is the Chapter on the Ritual for Entering the Maṇḍala (*maṇḍalāvatāravidhipaṭala*). It is called *avatāra* because one enters by means of it; it is called *vidhi* because that very [entry] is prescribed. Thus, the ritual for entering the maṇḍala of Śrī Heruka and others is the first, singular chapter (*paṭala*)—a division of the text—that expresses this. Thus ends the first chapter in the *Śrī Cakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 1.
The second chapter: The Ritual Procedure for the Wheel-Worship.
Therein, one should smear the ground of the mandala with cow-dung that has not yet fallen [to the earth], combined with cremation-ground ashes and endowed with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta). (1)
He speaks of the mandala: "In that [rite], etc."—
in whatever rite one's own specific ritual injunctions do not exist,
there the wise resort to the injunctions declared in the general tantras.

This is the principle stated in the general tantras. However, since a certain common rule has been mentioned here, he says "therein" and so forth: "Therein. For the purpose of drawing the mandala, the preceptor should smear the ground—the site for the mandala—in mountain caves and other such places with cow-dung that has not fallen [to the earth], using *vairocana* (white clay), together with the disciple. Furthermore, he states that one should smear over that again with cremation-ground ashes and so forth, such that it is joined with cremation-ground ashes and endowed with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). || 1 ||
Having smeared the ground, one should then begin the mandala there;
then, having performed its meditation, one should carry out the charnel ground ritual.

The connection is that immediately after smearing with cow-dung free from insects, one should smear the ground and then begin the mandala. Immediately after smearing with cow-dung free from insects follows the smearing with cremation-ground ashes and so forth. Nevertheless, [the author] asks: "After what [should] the commencement of the mandala occur? and answers: "Then" (*tataḥ*). This means immediately after the protection-wheel (*rakṣācakra*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "one should practice the cremation ground": the sense is that if the drawing of the mandala takes place elsewhere than at a cremation ground, then one should visualize a cremation ground there. || 2 ||
With the charcoal powder of a city mixed with bricks from cremation grounds,
the preceptor should draw the divine maṇḍala possessing all the required characteristics.

The King said: "The funeral pyre's embers," and so forth. Regarding "the bricks of the cremation ground": the funeral pyre is the earth; its preparation is achieved through the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of it as being the bricks of the cremation ground. Some say that one should begin the cremation ground with the dust of the funeral pyre's embers and the bricks of the cremation ground; in this case, the brick is short. There are two types of dust: black and yellow. Because it is not within the sphere of ordinary people, it is divine (*divya*). Regarding "the Teacher" (*ācārya*):

"One who teaches the True Dharma, he who is an expounder and a giver of instruction, the one who performs the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and the performer of rituals—another [such person] is rightly called a Teacher."

Thus is its defined characteristic. Specifically, it is the Guru alone—"the Guru is designated by the term Ācārya by the learned"—so it is said. And this merit is for the sake of initiation (*abhiṣeka*). If the drawing of the mandala is for the sake of accomplishment (*siddhi*), the yogi should draw it; and he [should do so] perfectly, possessing all the required characteristics. (3)
One who possesses right knowledge, is learned in the tantras, and knows the secret mantras of Śrī Heruka;
who is free from anger, pure, skillful, a knower of yoga, and has reached the further shore of wisdom. || 4 ||

He states the definition by way of its qualifiers, beginning with "samyak" (correctly). One who possesses knowledge that is *samyak*—meaning non-erroneous and free from the [subject-object] duality of the apprehended and so forth—is a *samyagjñāna*. Such a person, being also a knower of the *tantra* of restraint (*saṃvara*) and the rest, is a *samyagjñānatantrajña*. Regarding "a knower of the *mantra* of Śrī Heruka": *Śrī Heruka* refers to [the deity] and the *mantras* such as the eight-syllable [formula], etc.; he is one who knows them according to the oral instruction, or alternatively, one who constantly recites the *mantra* of Śrī Heruka.

Anger (*krodha*) is the internal state of a mind that pursues present harm; its absence is non-anger (*akrodha*). "Pure" (*śuci*) means free from the stain of remorse (*kaukṛtya*). "Dexterous" (*dakṣa*) means one who exerts effort toward what is wholesome. "One who has reached the further shore of yoga" (*yogapāraga*) refers to one who has gone to the limit—the culmination—of yoga, such as the rites for pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth. || 4 ||

With his hair tied in a topknot using a skull, his limbs smeared with ashes, his body adorned with various ornaments, he was covered in bone-dust and remained fixed upon a skeleton, his hair cut into a single lock. || 5 ||

He whose crest is made of five skulls is *kapālakṛtamūrdhajaḥ*. He whose body is smeared with the ashes of the cremation ground that adhere to it is *bhasmānuliptāṅgaḥ*. By implication, his bodily presence is adorned with various ornaments; because they are present, he is one by whom the body is especially (*viśeṣeṇa*) adorned even without garments. "Bones" (*asthi*) are called "impurities" (*mala*); thus, *asthimālāḥ* refers to sentient beings. He who is situated, seated, among their bones is [so described].

Furthermore, some maintain that by the word *mātra* (only/merely), Amitābha mixed with Ratnasambhava is meant, and thus [the deity] has applied unguents made from that. In that regard, by the words "bones" (*asthi*) and so forth, ornaments alone are expressed. Regarding the phrase "whose hair is made into a single lock" (*ekakhaṇḍīkṛtamūrdhaja*): *khaṇḍa* means a portion. Those whose [hair] consists of a single portion are "those who are such. He by whom the hair on the head is made into a single lock is "one whose hair is made into a single lock"; the meaning is that he wears a crown fashioned from other [remaining] hair. || 5 ||
Wearing a garland of bones and holding a *khaṭvāṅga* staff in his hand, one should meditate on oneself as Śrī Heruka and then recollect Śrī Heruka. (6)

"One who wears a garland of bones" (*asthimālāvalambī*) is one who possesses a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) that hangs as a garland of bones. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include [other attributes]. "Properly situated with the left hand holding a skull-topped staff" (*khaṭvāṅgakarasaṃsthitaḥ*) means he stands correctly with his left hand grasping a *khaṭvāṅga*. Thus, he is distinguished by way of his ornaments and other features. Having thus meditated upon oneself as the glorious Heruka, together with the deities of the mandala, according to the instruction, one should recollect the glorious Heruka. (6)
Having thus demonstrated the commitment (samaya), one should place the wheel upon his heart;
having thus armored oneself, one should visualize a rampart in all directions.

"Thus" means: one should manifest such a pledge (*samaya*) consisting of the wisdom-nature of Śrī Heruka, the deity of the maṇḍala, within Śrī Heruka. "One should place the wheel in his heart" refers to "his," meaning the self who has become Heruka; "in the heart" means in the body. Therefore, the meaning is this: one should place the goddesses beginning with Pracaṇḍā, and the heroes beginning with Khaṇḍakapāla, within one's own body, and [the goddesses] Pullīramalaya and so forth upon the nails, teeth, and so on. The root *as* (in *asati*) belongs to the *bhūvādi* class and has the sense of "going. Thus, "one should lead together" (*saṃnehyet*).

Having made oneself Śrī Heruka, one should first visualize a wall in the cardinal directions outside of the dust mandala that is to be constructed. According to the method of etymology (*nirukti*), the letter *ma* is a consonant (*hal*) because it "considers" (*manute*) [reality] as being mere gnosis (*jñānamātra*). This is an attribute of the self. The meaning is: having made oneself, who is merely gnosis, into Śrī Heruka. The sense is that, in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), this is nothing but mere gnosis. || 7 ||
Having thus armored oneself, one should indeed place the weapon below;
the self is level with the discus, while the mass of arrows is above.

He explains how one should meditate on Śrī Heruka himself: "Thus, having armored oneself... The letter *ma* is as before. Having established oneself as the one who has begun [the practice] through the purification of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, the action is: "one should settle Śrī Heruka. "Below, indeed, the weapon"—one should also settle the weapon below. "Above, a net of arrows for the wheel. Then, one should settle Śrī Heruka along with the mandala deities. (8)
Having made his own body a cage for the mind-walker (the self), and being well-composed,
he thus equipped himself with armor, impenetrable even by the gods.

The connection is as follows: having created a space-faring vajra above oneself and a cage composed of that same substance, one should install Śrī Heruka. Furthermore, being "armored" refers to the ritual procedure for the armor-mantras of the Six Heroes and so forth, performed upon the completion of the generation of Śrī Heruka. || 9 ||
Having thus well protected oneself and adorned with mudrās and mantras, one should draw the formidable maṇḍala that bestows great siddhis. || 10 ||

"Thus, having well-protected oneself"—the letter *ma* is etymological (*nairukta*), as before. "Seals" (*mudrā*) refers to Vajravārāhī; "mantras" (*mantra*) refers to the root mantra and so forth. Alternatively, "seals" refers to the insignia seals (*cihnamudrā*); "mantras" refers to the components of the *karakara* mantra and others, such as *oṃ kara kara hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*, which are divided into parts. The connection is: "having thus well-protected oneself, one should draw the maṇḍala. It is "terrible" (*ghora*) because it is turned away from the worldly conventions of the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and so forth.

With the words beginning with "mahā," [the author] shows that one should also construct a mandala for the sake of attaining accomplishment (*siddhi*). The intended meaning is that one should achieve accomplishment through recitation (*jāpa*) and other practices performed day and night, preceded by the construction of a mandala, according to the previously mentioned procedure up to the limit of diligent and uninterrupted meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). || 10 ||
Then, with a thread made from a corpse or one worshipped with great blood,
one should delineate the formidable mandala, the supreme city of Heruka.
One cubit [in height], four or eight [cubits] in extent, square on all sides, provided with four doors, and adorned with four archways. || 12 ||

He states the cause for its being "terrible" (*ghora*) with the words "thereafter," and so forth. This refers to the period following the application of cow-dung paste and the construction of the vajra-fence (*vajrapañjara*). "Or worshipped with great blood" is said because its very nature is that of being draped with a corpse and a *khaṭvāṅga* staff. It is "terrible" because it is surrounded by a cremation ground, or because it generates fear in the ignorant through the revelation of the selflessness of the mandala via the explanation of the meaning of the term "Śrī Heruka. "The city of *pām*" is because it is the own-nature (*nijatva*) of Śrī Heruka. "Four and eight" means that its measurement consists of four or eight cubits; the rest is easy to understand. (11–12)
The mantra-practitioner should wander twice [the distance] and worship the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*.
Having established in its center a lotus with petals and a radiant pericarp, he should proceed.
And with lotuses possessing filaments. || 13 ||

"One should traverse it twice" means [the circumference] is two cubits, eight cubits, or sixteen cubits; this is an attribute of the thread (*sūtra*). It has been established that the thread is double the size of the wheel (*cakra*). "The Mantrin" refers to one who has recited the *vidyā*. The meaning is that one should worship the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara* in the center of that mandala. Having done what? He says: "having installed," and so forth. "With leaves of all colors" means it exists together with petals of every hue. What is that? He says: "resplendent with a pericarp (*karṇikā*)."

This is the designation for the *viśvapadma* (the universal lotus). It is characterized by *puṣkara*s, which are seed-pods; the plural number is used because of their multiplicity due to their radiation. By the word "and" (*ca*), qualities such as being fully blossomed are implied. *Kesara* means the filaments; it is so called because it is surrounded by them in a corresponding manner. The sense is that it possesses complete filaments. The remainder is easily understood. || 13 ||
Upon the pericarp, one should place the Hero, who is as terrifying as Mahābhairava,
possessing radiant energy, with limbs brilliantly aflame, and emitting the great sound of boisterous laughter.

It is "terrifying" (*bhīṣaṇa*) because it generates fear even more than the Mahāraurava and other hells, or from the *palā* (demons) and so forth. It is "radiant" (*tejaska*) because it produces radiance (*tejas*). The word "for" (*tu*) has the sense of "but" (*yasmāt*). Because it is radiant, it is "blazing" (*sudīpta*). In the reading *sudīptaṃ ca*, the particle *ca* serves to complete the meter. Regarding the phrase "with a great roar of loud laughter" (*aṭṭahāsa-mahāravam*): through his illusory manifestation, out of curiosity, he possesses a great roar in the form of loud, repeated laughter (*aṭṭāṭṭahāsa*), a resonant sound pervading the sky; thus he is so described. || 14 ||
Adorned with a garland of skulls, divine, three-eyed, and four-faced;
covered with an elephant hide, he possesses beautiful eyebrows marked by a vajra. 15.

He is called *kapālamālābharaṇa* because he bears a garland of skulls; this is the purification through the grasping of the skulls of the afflictions (*kleśa*). He is *divya* (divine) because he exists in heaven (*div*), which is the nature of bliss. He has three eyes on each face due to the purification of the three liberations (*trivimokṣa*), and four faces due to the purification of the four liberations (*caturvimokṣa*). He is also "covered with an elephant hide" because that serves as his cloak for two arms. Due to its similarity to an elephant, the mass of afflictions is the "elephant"; thus it is said: "He wears a moist garment of elephant-hide."

For even when that [elephant] is split apart, its state remains like an illusion; the "skin" is that by which it is covered, and thus the concealment (*saṃvṛti*) is like an illusion. For this very reason, it is held behind [the back] and not on the heart. Because of its insubstantiality, it is not grasped; thus there is the "covering with an elephant-hide. The word *ca* (and) clarifies that this very thing is covered. He whose two eyebrows are well-split like a diamond (*vajra*) and have attained multiplicity is "one with eyebrows beautifully split like a diamond"; the space between the eyebrows is the *varaṭaka*.

The two eyebrows and the eyes below them constitute the "three-pronged" [point]; thus the *vajra* is established. As it has been said: "The space between the eyebrows is the central hub (*varaṭaka*) of the *vajra*. (15)
The goddess Vajravārāhī, who is most terrible, stands embracing him whose hand holds a khaṭvāṅga and who is adorned with half a garland of a hundred skulls.

"Having a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) in his hand": he is "one who has performed" (*kṛta*) the benefit of sentient beings; thus, his third hand is "performed. Consequently, he is "one whose hand holds a skull-topped staff. The sense is that he bears the skull-topped staff as the purification of the performance of the welfare of sentient beings. In all instances, the accusative case is used for the verb "should place" (*nyaset*). "Adorned by half a garland" means half of a garland; half of a hundred garlands is "half-a-hundred-garland," by which he is adorned. The sense is that a garland of mantras composed of the *āli* (vowels) and *kāli* (consonants) is situated at his throat.

"Standing before her" means she stands having embraced him face-to-face. She is a goddess (*devī*) because she plays (*divyati*) together with the Blessed One. She is Vajravārāhī because she strikes (*āhanti*) the inferior afflictions (*kleśa*) with the vajra. She is "most terrible" (*sughorā*) due to her threatening of the wicked and other such acts. (16)
Having made her face the deity Śrī Heruka, she is three-eyed and of fierce form;
she holds a skull-cup filled with entrails, which drips blood from her mouth. (17)

He provides the detailed explanation for the "face-to-face embrace" that was previously mentioned: "facing Śrī Heruka. Because it is governed by the action [of facing], the accusative case is used everywhere. He qualifies the Goddess who is before him as "one whose mantra is within the skull"—that is, the "skull-mantra"—and who is "complete," meaning not inferior to her husband. And the skull-mantra belongs to the Māras. She is "flowing with blood from her mouth," which signifies the purification of passion (*rāga*). (17)
Threatening all the quarters, including the gods, asuras, and humans, there are twenty-four ḍākinīs born of the family of Vārāhī. || 18 ||

"Threatening all the directions" means [threatening] all the lords of the directions (dikpati). "Together with gods, asuras, and humans" implies the worlds (loka). In the reading "all the quarters of the directions" (diśān sarvān), it should be understood that those who possess directions are the lords of the directions. "And the twenty-four Ḍākinīs" refers to the twenty-four beginning with Pracaṇḍā. By the word "and" (ca), the twelve beginning with Kākāsyā are also included; one should worship all of them as well. "Born from the family of Vārāhī" means they are born from the families of Citta and the others along with Vārāhī. By this, the rule of the families (kulaniyama) is stated. || 18 ||
One should worship within the center of the wheel, as well as in the cardinal and intermediate directions;
likewise, one should worship the heroes who are situated here within the wheel.

Regarding the phrase "within the center of the wheel": having drawn the mandala, one should meditate upon Śrī Heruka there together with the goddesses who form his retinue, and then worship him; this is the underlying intention. As for how the deities are to be installed, he says: "in the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions. And likewise: "and the heroes here. "Here" means within the center of the wheel; the meaning is "those born of the Kula. The summary is: "one should worship the entire circle of deities. The word *cakrasaṃsthāḥ* ends in the accusative plural, due to the elision of the letter *n*.

By this, [the term] "Cakragarbha" is confirmed. The word "tu" (but/however) serves to negate [his] abiding within the body; furthermore, "one should worship again" is for the purpose of establishing the rule for worship. || 19 ||

If the seeker of accomplishment desires to attain success, he should worship the non-dual Hero; thereafter, he should prepare the ritual jars, free from the influence of the root-time and other such factors.

By this, he states whose worship [is intended]: "the non-dual Hero" (*vīramadvayam*). He is called a *vīra* because he emits (*īrayati*) dissimilar forms such as the perceived object (*grāhya*) and so forth; and that is merely mind (*cittamātra*). Therefore, he says "non-dual. The sense is that one should worship the non-dual Hero alone. Why? He says: "if one desires to be an achiever of success" (*siddhisādhaka*). [The form] *siddhi* is used with the elision of the accusative case ending. Since the practitioner (*sādhaka*) would desire success, therefore he should worship. One should know that the mandala is merely mind. The passage beginning with "and the vases" (*kalaśāṃśca*) is easy to understand.

"Free from roots, time, and so forth. "Root" refers to the portion fashioned by the potter from the wheel; "time" refers to the black portion; and by the word "and so forth," qualities such as crookedness and the like are included. (20)
[He should offer] vessels filled with pearls, gold, gems, coral, silver, copper, and all kinds of edible foods, placed upon skull-bowls (kapāla). || 21 ||

"Gold and those jewels" means gold-jewels (*hemaratnāni*). The term "jewels" (*ratna*) applies everywhere; by this, the five jewels are indicated, ending with the phrase "by means of copper. "All and edible things" means all-edible things (*sarvabhakṣyāṇi*). By the word "all," the five grains and the five medicinal herbs are meant; by the word "edible," the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) are meant. "Situated upon the skull" is an epithet of the five nectars. Therefore, the particle *tu* has the sense of specification.

The five jewels and the five medicinal herbs [should be placed] within the interior of the jar, while the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), however, should be placed in a skull-cup (kapāla) upon its mouth. Some explain this as "placed upon a skull-cup" using the instrumental case ending (*kapāloparisaṃsthitaiḥ*) to qualify the jar itself; others say it means "placed upon a skull-cup fashioned from colored powder. 21.
Having placed eight [vessels] wrapped with thread around their necks and provided with tips of sprouts at the eight gates, and having well-wrapped them with a pair of cloths; || 22 ||
Having placed the ninth pitcher in the center, wrapped in a pair of cloths, and adorned with silver or gold, as well as jewels and pearls; 23.

The neck of those jars is *tatkaṇṭhaḥ*. "Endowed with the tips of sprouts" refers to their mouths. By the words beginning with "having made," he shows the insertion of the five jewels into the ninth jar, named Vijaya—namely, "having made [it] silver or gold. Here, the nominative singular is used in the sense of the instrumental. "Jewel, pearl," etc., is an elision of the dual instrumental case. The connection is: having placed the ninth jar, adorned with silver and so forth, in the center, one should worship the excellent city. (22–23)
One should scatter all those beautiful objects made of jewels and gold within the maṇḍala and worship the delightful, excellent city; success will surely follow, there is no doubt. || 24 ||
Having sprinkled oneself and all directions with scented water, one should offer a hundred lamps if one desires the highest accomplishment. || 25 ||

By what means? He says: "One should scatter them upon the mandala with all [of these]," and so forth. "Jewels" (ratna) refers to pearls and the like. "Gold" (suvarṇa) is that which is made of gold (sauvarṇa). "Adorned by these" refers to beautiful ornaments (śobhana-bhūṣaṇa). These are both jewels and golden ornaments; thus, "with all of these" means with whatever of these is available. From where should one scatter the worship? Upon the mandala, for it is from those [ornaments] here and there that the worship arises.

The seven jewels are the jewel of the elephant, the jewel of the horse, the jewel of the gem, the jewel of the sword, the jewel of the wheel, the jewel of the counselor, and the jewel of the woman. Some say these are "golden" (*sauvarṇa*) because they exist within gold that possesses qualities. [The phrase] "the self facing in all directions" means that one should worship the self as Śrī Heruka in the center of the city; such is the connection. (24–25)
One should mentally place all the ḍākinīs in the sky above;
and those ḍākinīs who are in the earthly realm (bhūrloka), one should place them everywhere within the maṇḍala.
Whatever ḍākinīs there may be in the netherworld (pātāla), one should place them therein;
all the Mothers (mātṛs) should be assigned to the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions. || 27 ||

In the *bhūrloka*, that is, on the earth; and in the netherworld (*pātāla*), "whatever ḍākinīs there may be," meaning twenty-four. In some places, the reading is "the Mothers" (*mātaraḥ*); the meaning is the same. By the word "Mothers," the twelve [goddesses] beginning with Kākāsyā are meant. (26–27)
With flowers, perfumes, and likewise incense, one should offer a hundred lamps;
[one should worship the Lord according to the rule] if the practitioner of spiritual accomplishments desires success. 28.
One should worship the Hero-Yoginīs situated within the maṇḍala of Śrī Heruka with banners that are red, yellow, white, black, and tawny. (29)
With various garlands, diverse garments, canopies,
and beautiful cloth hangings,
as well as with foods to be chewed, eaten, licked, and drunk, one should perform [the rite] with a well-concentrated mind. (30)
Thus ends the second chapter, the ritual procedure for the worship of the wheel, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

Regarding the phrase "prior to the lamps," a hundred oil lamps were mentioned in general as "a hundred lamps. However, [the term] "great" (mahā) refers to those produced from [refined] oil; thus, the word *tu* ("but") serves to indicate a distinction. The remainder is easily understood. "Edible" (*bhakṣya*) refers to flour-cakes and the like; "food" (*bhojya*) refers to rice and the like; "chewable" (*khādya*) refers to condiments; and "drink" (*pāna*) refers to what is drunk, such as whey and so forth. "One should perform"—the word "worship" (*pūjām*) is to be supplied. Thus, the external worship has been shown. (28–30)
The wheel, its worship, the procedure for those two, the performance, and the chapter that explains them—this is the second.
This concludes the second chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. || 2 ||
The third chapter on the initiation of the fee (dakṣiṇābhiṣeka).
Then:
"First, the practitioner should satisfy the preceptor with his entire being."
One who desires accomplishment, being well-composed, should worship the Guru according to one's ability. || 1 ||

Without the instruction of the guru, there is no accomplishment of mantra whatsoever; therefore, he is the one who must be propitiated. Thus, [the author] says "then" (*tataḥ*) to indicate that worship of him takes place at the time of initiation (*sekakāla*). Since there is no success without the teacher’s instruction, there is the propitiation of the guru. The word "then" (*tataḥ*) is a separate term. He explains this very point with the words "the teacher" (*ācāryam*), etc. The word "previously" (*pūrvam*) is an adjective qualifying the teacher—one distinguished by such attributes as "possessing perfect knowledge of the Tantras," and so forth. Alternatively, it may be an adjective qualifying the time.

"First, one should satisfy the teacher"—the meaning is that one should request [instruction]. "With all one's being" means with the entirety of one's self and other constituent elements. "But one who desires accomplishment, being well-composed, should worship the Guru according to his ability. The word *tu* (but) has a restrictive sense. Therefore, in this case, the disciple should first worship the Guru alone as the teacher with all his being; afterwards comes the construction of the mandala. Therein, he should worship for the purpose of entering and so forth. "One who desires accomplishment" (*siddhikāma*) refers to one who has the desire, "I shall achieve accomplishment through the consecration and other rites obtained by me," and who is "well-composed" (*susamāhita*), having performed the recitation of mantras and other preliminary rites. || 1 ||
Relying on the resonance of the bell and adorning it with flowers and incense,
the practitioner should ring the bell with a beautiful sound, or likewise a small drum,
and cause the cry of "Hā-hā" to be uttered.

The consecration of the bell (*ghaṇṭābhiṣeka*) is established by the passage beginning with "the sound of the bell" (*ghaṇṭānādam*). The connection is that "the practitioner should ring the bell. "Adorned with flowers and incense" means it has been worshipped. By the term "possessing a beautiful tone," all the [auspicious] characteristics are indicated as a synecdoche. Having done what should he ring it? He says: "the bell," and so forth. The bell is *saṃvṛti* (conventional reality); its sound is as follows: "All phenomena are pure by nature; they are manifested through their own natures. Through sentient beings who are pure by nature, the supreme existence is brought about."
Such is the recitation of the verse and the understanding of its meaning:
"This is that wisdom of all the Buddhas, known as following the sound;
it must indeed always be maintained by you as well, for awakening is considered supreme by the Victors."

The meaning is that, by reciting this verse, one should take up and ring the bell given by the venerable Guru, relying upon the resonance of the bell. "A drum" (*paṭahikā*) refers to that which brings about auspiciousness. The word "or" (*vā*) is used to include another characteristic. Furthermore, even the practitioner (*sādhaka*), following the explicit sequence, should ring it; the word "even" (*api*) indicates that since everything has been given by the Guru, the act of giving is thereby perfected. And one should cause the cry of "Hā Hā" to be made. The "cry of Hā Hā" is the consecration (*abhiṣeka*); one should have the venerable Guru perform that for oneself.

"By such devotion alone he may perform [the rite] a hundred times"—this is the designation [of the phrase] *kārayet* (he should cause to be performed). From this, his great devotion to the Guru is indicated. As for the name *Hāhākāra*, it is so called because of the similarity between the two being essentially sound (*śabdātmaka*). Furthermore, the inclusion of the water, crown, and vajra-sovereignty consecrations is intended, since those two [consecrations] are preceded by them. Moreover, the other meaning should be understood as: "The Guru should ring the bell."

Having done what? He says: "The sounding of the bell" (*ghaṇṭānāda*) is the instruction for producing the sound of a subtle bell in the ten directions. Alternatively, as before, the practitioner should also cause the recitation of the verses, the beating of the drum (*paṭahikā*), and the cry of "Hā-hā! (*hāhākāra*). "Hāhākāra" means a resonant humming. From the word "and" (*ca*), it should be understood that there are other specific musical instruments as well as song. The "sounding of the bell" resides in its own characteristic form. It is called the "Twenty-five-fold" (*pañcaviṃśatikā*). The bell is twelve years old; the drum is sixteen years old.

The sound of the bell belongs to the Vajra family; the bell itself belongs to the Ratna family; the small drum (*paṭahikā*) belongs to the Padma family; and the cry of "hā hā" belongs to the Tathāgata family. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is implied that one may also practice with any other [sound] such as the ringing of the bell. The practitioner, who is the disciple, should cause the sound of the bell to be made—that is, he should utter the mantra "Aho sukham! (O, what bliss!). To the question "Immediately after what?", he says: "With the ring finger," and so forth.
The knower of yoga should always lick [the substance] with the curved ring finger and thumb; having tasted it like the drinking of the Soma, he attains eternal accomplishment.

Thus these verses are to be applied here. From this, there is another meaning: by means of the thumb and ring finger, the preceptor should cause the disciple to taste that which has arisen through the previously mentioned cultivation of wisdom (*prajñā*). And that disciple, having tasted it like the drinking of *soma*, attains accomplishment (*siddhi*); this is the secret consecration (*guhyābhiṣeka*). For this very reason, the master’s consecration (*ācāryābhiṣeka*) is established, because it is preceded by that. (2)
Having thus worshipped the mandala that fulfills all desires according to the prescribed rite,
he should cover the faces of those "sons" with a cloth.

To the question "Immediately after what does all this occur?", he says "In this way," and so forth. With "flowers and so forth" refers to those previously mentioned. "The mandala" refers to that previously described one made of colored powder or depicted on cloth. "Having worshipped" means having fully worshipped it, one should cause [the disciples] to enter once the obstacles have been destroyed; such is the connection. To the question "Whom?", he says "the sons" (*putrakān*). They are called "sons" because they purify (*punanti*) and protect (*trāyante*). Therefore, by virtue of the suffix *kavi* used in a sense of praise, "sons" here refers to the disciples. They are of such a nature by reason of having recited the vidyās and so forth, as well as by their noble lineage and other qualities.

Having done what? He says: "having covered," and so forth. With a cloth, that is, with a saffron-colored garment (*kāṣāya*). The plural number is used generally for those sons; in reality, however, one should cause each one to enter individually. || 3 ||
Having made a handful of flowers full, he should then scatter them properly;
then, the practitioner, being well-composed, should perform a circumambulation. || 4 ||
Having composed his mind, the wise one should cause him to enter the beautiful city;
then, taking recourse to the southern form, he should cast a handful of flowers. || 5 ||

He says this very thing in the passage beginning with "filled with flowers" (*puṣpapūrṇa*), and so forth. Immediately after entering, the practitioner should cast a handful (*añjali*) filled with flowers while turning clockwise. "Taking recourse to the southern image, he should then cast the handful of flowers"—this is the instruction that he should cast [the flowers] facing southward; or alternatively, by way of circumambulating the Blessed One clockwise according to the sequence for venerating a *caitya*. (4–5)
Wherever it should fall upon the mandala, one should indicate that person's family (kula);
the preceptor should show the sacred seats (pīṭha) of Śrī Heruka and so forth, and designate their names.
Then, on the second day, the preceptor, being well-composed, should worship the mudrā and perform the ritual correctly for the disciples.
One should apply a *tilaka* mark on him with blood over which the mantra has been recited three times;
then, having unveiled the face of the disciple, one should show him the maṇḍala.

In the phrase "the seat of Śrī Heruka and so forth," the second case ending is elided. It should be construed as: "having opened the mouth, one should then show the maṇḍala. The meaning is that immediately after showing the maṇḍala, one should show the seats and so forth characterized by Śrī Heruka and the others. By the word "then" (*tataḥ*) and so on, he demonstrates the wisdom-consecration (*prajñābhiṣeka*). "Then" means immediately after the secret consecration; "the master" (*ācārya*) refers to one who possesses qualities such as fortitude. Therein, one should apply a *tilaka* mark with the blood of a menstruating woman, over which mantras such as *karakara* have been recited.
"Of him" means of whichever one among them has been ushered in; the meaning is that he whose mouth has been opened must apply the *tilaka*. (6–8)
Whichever deity’s station belongs to whom, he should show those [deities] there;
then, having prostrated correctly, he should subsequently [show] the city together with the preceptor.

The intended meaning is that one should visualize that deity in whatever place belongs to that particular deity. One should visualize deities such as Śrī Heruka upon the seats (pīṭhas) and so forth. In the application of mindfulness of the body (kāyānusmṛtyupasthāna), one should establish the reality of the maṇḍala and the reality of the deity starting with Ḍākinī; in the application of mindfulness of sensation (vedanānusmṛtyupasthāna), Lāmā; in the application of mindfulness of phenomena (dharmānusmṛtyupasthāna), Khaṇḍarohā; and in the application of mindfulness of mind (cittānusmṛtyupasthāna), Rupiṇī. Then, having prostrated correctly, one should perform [the rite] together with the preceptor (ācārya). "In front" (puraḥ) means...
Then, after the opening of the disciple's mouth, having prostrated before the mandala and applied the tilaka, one should show the mandala to him.
Having again performed a circumambulation, and having prostrated correctly according to the rule before the mandala to the Guru from the left at the commencement, [10]
Then one should give to the guru the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) as spoken by the Tathāgata: gold of pure quality weighing a hundred thousand [units], and various kinds of jewels. || 11 ||
A hundred pairs of garments, as well as elephants, horses, and the kingdom itself; earrings, bracelets, necklaces, and finger-rings—all of these in their entirety. (12)

Having again performed a circumambulation, one should turn to the left by way of reversal; that is, having again performed a circumambulation, one should encircle the mandala by turning to the left through reversal and then by turning to the right. Having prostrated before the guru and the mandala, one should give the prescribed fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the guru as spoken by the Tathāgatas. Following the explanation of the reality (*tattva*) of the deities of the mandala, the disciple gives the fee to the guru; thereafter follow the water and other consecrations (*seka*), beginning with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and ending with the master (*ācārya*).

Then follows "the secret initiation" (*guhyābhiṣeka*). This is the collective meaning of the aforementioned text. He states the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*): "free from base metal," and so forth. "Base metal" (*jātya*) means that which exists in [inferior] types; "completely free from base metal" (*nirjātya*) means entirely devoid of such inferior types. That which is both "free from base metal" and "gold" (*suvarṇa*) is expressed as such. It refers to gold numbering one hundred thousand *palas*. The word "elephant" (*gaja*) is a term with its case-ending elided. "With finger-rings" (*aṅgulikaiḥ*) means with rings for the fingers. The third case ending is used in the sense of accompaniment. "The most excellent crown" (*samuttamaṃ makuṭam*). || 10–12 ||
Having prostrated, he should offer a golden sacred thread, or his own wife, or even his daughter, a male or female servant, or his sister. (13)

The *yajñopavīta* is golden; that is, a sacrificial thread made of gold. The word "dāsa" (servant) is used here without a case ending. All of this one should offer to the Guru—indeed, one should serve the teacher of the eternal, excellent tradition even with one's own life.
For it is said: "With things not to be given away, such as children and wife, how much more so with transient riches? (13)
The wise person should offer himself to the guru with his whole being:
"From this day forward, I am your servant; I have surrendered myself to you. (14)

"The wise one should offer himself to the guru with his whole being"—here, "whole being" refers to the activity of the body and so forth. "Buddhi" is the realization that "this is inexhaustible, such as this, and boundless. He speaks of the gift of oneself with the words beginning with "ātma"; "offered" (*samarpitā*) is used without a case ending. 14.
Having thus performed this rite with firm resolve, the ḍākinīs and the mothers of yoga will then be pleased with that practitioner. (15)

With the words "Thus," and so forth, he provides the conclusion of the inquiry: the procedure for the gift of gold and other materials mentioned immediately above has been well-ascertained, accepted as excellent, and approved by the practitioner—this is the meaning. "From that" refers to the ritual procedure. He states the fruit of the uncompleted rite with the words "The ḍākinīs," and so forth. "Ḍākinīs" refers to the various classes of ḍākinīs. He specifies them with the words "Yoga," and so forth; there are twenty-four Yoga-mothers (yogamātaraḥ). 15.
The Ḍākinīs, Lāmās, Khaṇḍarohās, and Rupiṇīs—the practitioner should wander throughout the entire world together with these Ḍākinīs. (16)
All [the goddesses] are the servants of that practitioner, without a doubt;
for them, there shall be the perfection of yoga, unimpeded throughout the three worlds. (17)
Invisibility, emergence from a hole, and the power of moving through the air, as well as foot-ointment and elixirs, arise for the practitioner at all times and eternally according to his will. (18)
She assumes many forms and travels through space;
as a ḍākinī, she especially crushes all living beings. (19)

The *ḍākinīs* are those such as Kākāsyā and others; the *lāmas* are of the *lāmā* lineage. The word *lāma* is a synonym for *lāmā*. Alternatively, this is a plural form resulting from the elision of the vowel *ā* and the substitution of the letter *ya*. Regarding the phrase "by these" and so forth: by entering such a mandala, performing worship, receiving empowerment, and following its conduct for the sake of accomplishing the siddhis, one should traverse the entire world with the *ḍākinīs* acting as the instruments. The meaning is that one makes even the inaccessible accessible.

The [mantra] beginning with "by these ḍākinīs" and so forth is to be accomplished through the addition, elision, transposition, and modification of phonemes as prescribed by *nirukta*. This is because the [mantra] of the Ṛṣis is to be accomplished primarily through those [grammatical operations]. Thus it is everywhere. Or rather, one should not suspect the presence of correct or incorrect words (*śabda*/*apaśabda*) due to the lack of faith [in such rules]. "Arise" refers to the raising of the dead; "knowledge of destruction" refers to killing (*māraṇa*); the rest is easily understood. (16–19)
Through the yoga seen but once, the state of a yogi arises in an instant;
yet he who, having not seen the maṇḍala, strives for the state of a yogi [is deluded]. (20)
He strikes at the sky with his fist and drinks the water of a mirage;
this is the most excellent yoga, the best among all yogas. (21)

"Without having seen the maṇḍala," and so forth, refers to the benefits of the maṇḍala. Just as one might strike at space with a fist, yet those functional activities characterized by striking are not accomplished; or as one might drink from a mirage, yet there is no functional activity characterized by drinking or the cessation of thirst—likewise, a practitioner who has not seen the maṇḍala yet strives for the state of a yogin will not obtain the fruit of yoga. (20–21)

Whoever desires it, having overcome those including the gods, asuras, and humans, shall go there; he who has been consecrated in this mandala is a practitioner of all the tantras as they have been taught. || 22 ||
Having performed the secret gaze, the joining of hands, the embrace, the union, and so forth, one becomes consecrated therein as the sole supreme authority over all tantras. (23)
In the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, the *Saṃvara*, the *Guhyasamāja*, or the *Vajrabhairava*, this King of Maṇḍalas has never existed before, nor will it ever exist again. (24)
Whatever has been said and whatever has not been said—all that resides within Śrī Heruka. || 25 ||
Thus ends the third chapter, the ritual procedure for the initiation of the fee (*dakṣiṇābhiṣeka*), in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. || 3 ||

"Whoever shall desire... means that whoever shall desire the boon of Śrī Heruka will go forth, having overcome the gods and others. Here, the root *gam* has the sense of "staying"; the meaning is that he will remain. The future tense is used in the expression "shall desire" (*kāṅkṣiṣyate*) and so forth, in order to show that [the result] is not merely what has been, what will be, or what is currently arisen. "And both the stated and the unstated" means that whatever has been stated or unstated elsewhere, all that—the ritual procedure for the mandala—is established within Śrī Heruka Cakrasaṃvara. (22–25)

The "Dakṣiṇā" refers to the gift given with an excess of reverence; "Abhiṣeka" is the removal of the stains of the afflictions (*kleśa*); the "Ritual" (*vidhi*) is the procedure for those two, and the chapter (*paṭala*) that explains them is the third.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 3.
The fourth chapter on the ritual procedure, titled "The Non-duality of the Hero and the Yoginī.
Thereafter, the Ḍākinīs manifest the worlds:
Mahāvīryā, Cakravartinī, Mahābalā, and Suvīrā. (1)
Cakravarmiṇī, Śauṇḍinī, Khaṇḍarohā, Cakravegā, Khagānanā, Hayakarṇā, Subhadrā, and likewise Śyāmādevī. || 2 ||
Surābhakṣī, Vāyuvegā, and likewise Mahābhairavā;
Airāvatī, Drumacchāyā, Laṅkeśvarī, and Kharvarī. (3)
Vīramatī, Mahānāsā, and Prabhāvatī,
as well as Caṇḍākṣī and Pracaṇḍā— these are the accomplished ones for the practitioner.
Indeed, beginning with Pracaṇḍā, there are twenty-four ḍākinīs in the east.
Just as it is externally, so it is within oneself, in the midst of body, speech, and mind;
the mantras consisting of the utterance of one's own name are joined with *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ* at the end. (5)

Immediately after describing the foundational maṇḍala, the fourth chapter is introduced with the words "Then," and so forth, in order to show the yoginīs who reside within it. Since those ḍākinīs said to be within the sphere of conventional practice (*samayācāra*) consist of the nature of the Body, Speech, and Mind—the Emanation, Enjoyment, and Dharma bodies—it is for that reason that the twenty-four ḍākinīs pervade (*vijṛmbhayanti*), that is, encompass, the three worlds and the wheels (*cakras*) of the body and so forth. He states who they are with the words "Mahāvīryā," and so forth.
Cakravegā, Khaṇḍarohā, Śauṇḍinī, Cakravarmiṇī, Suvīrā, Mahābalā, Cakravartinī, and Mahāvīryā—all these are white; this is the Body Wheel (kāyacakra).
Airāvatī, Mahābhairavā, Vāyuvegā, Surābhakṣī, Śyāmādevī, Subhadrā, Hayakarṇā, and Khagānanā—all these are red; this is the Speech Wheel (vākcakra).
Pracaṇḍā, Caṇḍākṣī, Prabhāvatī, Mahānāsā, Vīramatī, Kharvarī, Laṅkeśvarī, and Drumacchāyā—all these are black; this is the Mind Wheel (cittacakra).

In the previous tantra, the sequence was indeed reversed; therefore, he says: "But beginning with Pracaṇḍā. One should understand Caṇḍākṣī and the others as starting with Pracaṇḍā. The utterance of each respective name is joined with that [mantra] according to the sequence stated in the *Sādhana*; those whose mantras consist of the utterance of their own names—here the genitive case is used in the sense of the nominative (*svanāmoccāraṇamantrāḥ*). They are "joined at the end with *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*," meaning those to which the syllables *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ* are appended at the end of the names. (1–5)
Having seen this most excellent and supreme yoga, all other [practices] are like chaff to the wood-boring insect;
it is the lamp of the syllable Om, which bestows all perfections and fulfills all desires.

Regarding the term *oṃkāradīpikā*: those [mantras] for which the syllable *oṃ* is the illuminator (*dīpaka*) in the preceding [sections] by means of mantras such as *kara kara*, etc., are thus described. Therefore, the meaning is as follows: *oṃ kṣmāṃ kṣmāṃ cakravege hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*, etc., for the eight [deities] beginning with Cakravega; *oṃ phaṭ phaṭ airāvatī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*, etc., for the eight [deities] beginning with Airāvatī; *oṃ kara kara pracaṇḍe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*, etc., for the eight [deities] beginning with Pracaṇḍā. This is the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the mandala and the body.

For this very reason, there is first the mind-wheel (*cittacakra*), then the speech-wheel (*vākcakra*), and then the body-wheel (*kāyacakra*). However, in the *tantra*, there is a reversal of that order for the sake of instruction. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "joined at the end with *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*," there is another meaning. In the expression "joined at the end with *hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ* at the end of the mantra," the nominative case is used in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). Because they are included within [the mantra], Kākāsyā and the other seven are "joined at the end. The four beginning with Ḍākinī are situated in the center. These should be understood as born from these mantras according to specific times.

For whom [the mantra] begins with *oṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ kākāsyai hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ* and so forth; Pracaṇḍā and the others, ending with Drumacchāyā, reside in the mind wheel (*cittacakra*), and that [wheel] is black. Airāvatī and the others, ending with Khagānanā, reside in the speech wheel (*vākcakra*), and that [wheel] is red. Cakravegā and the others, ending with Mahāvīryā, reside in the body wheel (*kāyacakra*), and that [wheel] is white.

The four [deities], Ḍākinī and the others, are respectively black, dark green, red, and white, arranged in counter-clockwise order; Yamadāḍhī and the others have attained two colors each. "Bestowing accomplishment" and "fulfilling all desires" are the two qualifiers of this maṇḍala, which consists of these [deities] united with the Lord Śrī Heruka. (6)

Having attained heroism and become accomplished by beholding the maṇḍala in the home, one should then understand and constantly cultivate it; such is the word of the Tathāgata regarding accomplishment.
Thus ends the fourth chapter on the ritual procedure, titled "The Duality of the Hero and the Yoginī," in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 4.

"Have attained the state of heroes" (*vīratvaṃ gatāḥ*) is an epithet of the twenty-four yoginīs. This means they have attained the state of being heroes—that is, the status of being the limbs of the heroes—and are thus endowed with the embrace of the heroes (*vīrāliṅganayuktāḥ*). The heroes, however, are Khaṇḍakāpāla and the others.

They have one face, four arms, and three eyes; they wear a crown of matted hair and a cloth garment, with a tiger-skin as their lower robe. With their two left and right hands, they embrace [their consorts] while holding a vajra and a vajra-bell. Their other left and right hands hold a khaṭvāṅga and a ḍamaru drum. They stand in the ālīḍha posture and are adorned with the mudrās of the wheel, earrings, and so forth. Their colors correspond to those of the goddesses who match their respective wheels. Pracaṇḍā and the others also embrace [their consorts] with two arms, while their other left and right hands hold skull-cups filled with blood and display the tarjanī gesture.

The Ḍākinīs and others hold a khaṭvāṅga and a skull-cup with their two left arms, and hold a hand-drum (ḍamaru) and a knife (kartī) with their right hands. Kākāsyā and the others bear the same emblems as the Ḍākinīs and others. Yamadāḍhī and the others hold a hand-drum and a knife with their two left arms, and hold a khaṭvāṅga and a skull-cup with their right hands. The thirty-six yoginīs, beginning with the Ḍākinīs, have three eyes, one face, loose hair, and are naked; they stand in the ālīḍha posture, possess fierce forms, and are adorned with necklaces and other ornaments.

Furthermore, there are the vajra-garlands on the forehead, as well as the heroes and heroines. The nature of the deities is described as follows: Ḍākinī has the nature of the application of mindfulness to the body; Lāmā has the nature of the application of mindfulness to sensation; Khaṇḍarohā has the nature of the application of mindfulness to phenomena; and Rūpiṇī has the nature of the application of mindfulness to the mind—this is the wheel of gnosis.

Pracaṇḍā has the nature of the basis of psychic power consisting of zeal (*chanda-ṛddhipāda*). Caṇḍākṣī has the nature of the basis of psychic power consisting of energy (*vīrya-ṛddhipāda*). Prabhāvatī has the nature of the basis of psychic power consisting of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-ṛddhipāda*). Mahānāsā has the nature of the basis of psychic power consisting of mind (*citta-ṛddhipāda*). Vīramatī has the nature of the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*). Kharvarī has the nature of the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*). Laṅkeśvarī has the nature of the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*). Drumacchāyā has the nature of the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*); such is the wheel of mind (*cittacakra*).

Airāvatī has the nature of the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*); Mahābhairavā has the nature of the power of faith (*śraddhābala*); Vāyuvegā has the nature of the power of vigor (*vīryabala*); Surābhakṣī has the nature of the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*); Śyāmādevī has the nature of the power of concentration (*samādhibala*); Subhadrā has the nature of the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*); Hayakarṇā has the nature of the factor of enlightenment that is concentration (*samādhisambodhyaṅga*); and Khagānanā has the nature of the factor of enlightenment that is vigor (*vīryasambodhyaṅga*). Thus is the wheel of speech (*vākcakra*).

Cakravegā has the nature of the awakening factor of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*). Khaṇḍarohā has the nature of the awakening factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhisaṃbodhyaṅga*). Śauṇḍinī has the nature of the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicayasaṃbodhyaṅga*). Cakravarmiṇī has the nature of the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛtisaṃbodhyaṅga*). Suvīrā has the nature of the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣāsaṃbodhyaṅga*). Mahābalā has the nature of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). Cakravartinī has the nature of right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*). Mahāvīryā has the nature of right speech (*samyagvāk*); such is the body wheel (*kāyacakra*).

Kākāsyā has the nature of right action (*samyakkarmānta*); Ulūkāsyā has the nature of right livelihood (*samyagājīva*); Śvānāsyā has the nature of right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*); Śūkarāsyā has the nature of right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*). Yamadāḍhī has the nature of producing unarisen wholesome dharmas; Yamadūtī has the nature of protecting arisen wholesome dharmas; Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī has the nature of abandoning arisen unwholesome dharmas; and Yamamathanī has the nature of preventing the arising of unarisen unwholesome dharmas—this is the *Cakra* of the cremation ground.

Śrī Heruka has the nature of right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*). Regarding the term "the accomplished ones" (*siddhāḥ*): it means having seen the twenty-four yoginīs within the house, that is, having seen the maṇḍala within one's own body. Then, having understood accomplishment through the meditation on the maṇḍala, one should meditate; this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "according to the word of the Tathāgata": the implication is that one should meditate according to the word of the Tathāgata. (7)

The *vīrayoginīs* are the twenty-four yoginīs accompanied by heroes; the *advayas* are the twelve [yoginīs] devoid of heroes. The short vowel is due to Vedic usage (*ārṣatva*). The *nyāsa* of these [deities], its procedure, and the chapter explaining it constitute the fourth [chapter].
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 4.
The fifth chapter, on the procedure for extracting the syllables of the root mantra;
thereafter:
"In the *Sarvadharmodaya*, the universe [is located]; in the pericarp is the unstruck (*anāhata*) Śiva."
The mantra-practitioner should, according to the prescribed rule, draw that which is the sole compendium of all dharmas. || 1 ||

The accomplishment of *siddhi* is achieved not only through meditation alone, but also by means of [the extraction of mantras]; thus he says "tataḥ" and so forth. For that reason, the mantra is to be extracted. He states the method of extraction with "sarva" and so forth. It is the arising (*udaya*) of all phenomena (*dharmas*), because they arise from it. It is "universal" (*viśva*) because it possesses all colors. "Karṇikā" means by means of the pericarp. It is "unstruck" (*anāhata*) because it is attained on all sides, and "auspicious" (*śiva*) because it brings about well-being. The meaning is: such is the lotus.

Because it is qualified by the *karṇikā* (pericarp) according to the principle that "a cognition of the qualified does not arise without first grasping the qualifier. Alternatively, *dharmodaya* and *bhaga* are synonymous. "The universe" (*viśvam*) refers to that which is endowed with the universal lotus (*viśvapadma*), because of its being struck by the pericarp. The connection is that one should not merely spread [the grid] within the *dharmodaya*, nor within the universal lotus alone. Having done what? He says: "having drawn," and so forth. By this, all phenomena (*sarvadharmāḥ*)—consisting of the letters beginning with *a* and *ka*—are gathered together as a unity.
That very thing, consisting of forty-nine squares, is called both *bhuvana* and *prastāra* as synonyms. (1)
In this regard, the mantra-words are as follows:
"Having made the *āli* and *kāli* equal and transformed from the groups [of consonants], O best of sages, one should know four by four on the ritual diagram (*prastara*). (2)

"Herein are the mantra-words. Herein, in this world of forty-nine squares (*koṣṭhaka*), there are locations for mantras; these are eight, and this is the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) of the Blessed One because it will encompass all parts. The designation "mantra" is applied to the light of the syllables, just as the term "cloth" is applied to a continuous series of threads. What, then, should one spread out? He says: "The *ālī*, etc. *Ālī* is [the name] *Kālī* with the elision of the second singular case ending. "Equal" (*sama*) means that not even a single syllable is excluded.

Because it is seen [in the grammatical tradition] that [the vowels] are otherwise [arranged], excluding *ṅ, *ña, *ṇ, *na, and *m*. Having thus formed the *āli* (vowels) and the *kāli* (consonants), one should spread them out—that is, one should arrange them. "Transformed" (*pariṇāmitā*) means directly transformed. Transformation is a particular state. To the question "What is this?", he says: "from the groups" (*vargebhyaḥ*). This is the ablative case used with the elision of the suffix *-lyap* (meaning "having reached"). Having reached the eight groups, it is transformed; the meaning is that it is a particular state consisting of the form of the eight groups. Therefore, he says: "four," and so forth.

That which is to be known—that is, that which is to be understood—should be laid out exactly as it is through four groups of four. He is a sage (*muni*) because he reflects (*manana*). Between the two systems—the system of the *pāramitās* and the system of mantra—this system of mantra is the most excellent; the knower of the layout is the follower of the mantra system, the best of sages. In this regard, the sixteen vowels beginning with *a* constitute one group. There are five groups consisting of five letters each, beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*.

One group consists of the four letters *ya-ra-la-va*; another consists of *śa-ṣa-sa-ha*. Here, the letter *kṣa* is not shown because it is of no use in this context and because it is produced from the conjunction of the letters *ka* and *ṣa*. In this manner, eight groups are to be understood. || 2 ||
One should extract the Hero situated therein, which accomplishes all desires and goals:
that which is the fifth of the fourth, and also the fifth of the fifth.

"One should extract the Hero situated there" means that one should extract the eight-syllable mantra of the Hero situated within the *āli* and *kāli*, like butter from curd; the rest is self-evident. "The fifth of the fourth" means that the letter *na* is the fifth of the fourth group (*varga*), and the letter *ma* is the fifth of the fifth group as well. (3)
That which is the fourth of the fifth, that which is the third of the first, likewise the twenty-ninth, and that which is the first of the fourth. (4)

The fourth letter of the fifth [group] is *bha*. The third letter of the first [group] is *ga*. The word *tu* distinguishes [the mantra] by way of praise. It is called *bha* because one destroys (*bhanakti*) the afflictions (*kleśa*) by means of it; that is the meaning of *bhaga*. The letter *ga* is to be spoken after it. Thus it is said: "They say the letter *bha* is *bhaga*. The twenty-ninth is likewise the letter *va*. That "likewise" (*tathaiva*) demonstrates the meaning of *sattva*. One blows (*vāti*), that is, connects, wisdom and skillful means; thus it is *va*.
The first *takāra* of the fourth [group], beginning from the *ka*-group, is the initial of the fourth group. 4.
Taking the fourth of those [consonants] situated within, as well as its second, and likewise taking the thirtieth and the twenty-sixth; || 5 ||

The fourth of the semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*) is the letter *va*; the meaning is that it is labio-dental. "Taking its second" means: having taken that which is the second syllable of that very same group of semi-vowels, one should extract the Hero (*vīra*); such is the connection [of the words]. "The thirtieth," however, refers to the letter *śa*, which is palatal; and the word "tu" (but/however) signifies that it is for the purpose of pacification (*śānti*). Thus, the meaning is "that thirtieth. Likewise, "the twenty-sixth as well" refers to the twenty-sixth letter, *ya*; likewise, it serves the purpose of air (*vāyu*). || 5 ||
Having extracted all of this, then again taking half of half of fifty,
and then taking the thirty-third, one takes the first of the first.

The letter *ma* is half of half of a hundred [i.e., five]. "And likewise again" means that this is the one which establishes that all phenomena have reached death. "Then take the thirty-three" refers to the connection: having taken [the letters] immediately after *ha* and *ma*, one should extract the Hero (*vīra*). "But the first of the first" means that within the section on consonants, the *ka*-group is the first; its first is the letter *ka*.
