"Not situated anywhere" indicates the meaning of the letter *ka*; such is the sense of the word "but" (*tu*) || 6 ||
The third of the labials, the third of the first [class], the thirty-second [consonant], and that which is the fifth of the fourth [class]. (7)

"The third of those situated within" refers to the letter *la*; it establishes its earth-nature (*pārthivatva*). "The third of the first," however, is the letter *ga*. The word "but" (*tu*) signifies that its nature consists of profound dharmas and meanings. "And indeed the thirty-second" means the letter *sa* is the thirty-second; the word "indeed" (*eva*) indicates its dental nature. "The fifth of the fourth" is the letter *na*. || 7 ||
That which belongs to the fifth [vowel] is the fourth; that which belongs to the semi-vowels (*āntastha*) is the first;
that which belongs to the second [consonant class] is the third; and that which belongs to the third [class] is the first. (8)

The fourth of the fifth [group] is the letter *bha* (the "ya" in *yaś-caturtham*). The first of the semi-vowels (*āntastha*) is the letter *ya* (the "ya" in *āntasthasya yaḥ prathamam*). This group of semi-vowels is called *āntastha*; its first is *ya*. The third of the second [group] is the letter *ja* (the "ka" in *tṛtīyakam*), provided it has the sense of "muttering" (*japa*). The first of the third [group] is the letter *ṭa* (the "ṭa" in *prathamam*). || 8 ||
The fifth of the fifth, the first of the first,
as well as the eleventh and the sixteenth— thus they know them.

"The fifth of the fifth" refers to the letter *ma*. "The first of the first, however" refers to the letter *ka*. The word "tu" (however) indicates that the conjunction of the letters *ra* and *ka*, among others, serves as an illuminator of desire (*kāmadīpaka*). Likewise, "and indeed the eleventh": the word "tathā" (likewise) indicates that, by virtue of being a constituent part of the syllable *phaṭ*, it has the purpose of causing the falling away [of obstacles]. The "eleventh" is the letter *ṭa*. By the word "ca" (and), he states that the letter *pha*, which precedes it, is invariably joined with it at the end of the mantra; this is why the word "eva" (indeed) is used. "The sixteenth, they know it likewise."

"Sixteenth" (*ṣoḍaśa*) itself is "sixteenth" (*ṣoḍaśamaḥ*); the suffix *-ma* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*), as in the word *druma*. And that [sixteenth] is the letter *ta*. Because it is governed by the verb "they know" (*viduḥ*), the accusative case is employed, as in the expression "they know him. This applies not only to "the fifth of the fifth" (*pañcamasyāpi pañcamam*), but also to "that which is the fifth of the fourth" (*caturthasya yaḥ pañcamam*), and so forth. In this way, it should be understood: having taken the fifth letter of the fourth group (*varga*), and having taken the fifth of the fifth, one should extract the Hero (*vīra*). Alternatively, it means "they know [this]" (*viduḥ*). Likewise, one takes the fourth letter of the fifth group, and so on. The word "thus" (*tathā*) indicates that this [mantra] establishes the sixteen emptinesses (*ṣoḍaśa-śūnyatā*). (9)
The first of the third [group], as well as the twenty-sixth;
the third of the fourth, and also two of the sibilants (ūṣman). || 10 ||

The first *ṭa*-sound of the third [group] is the twenty-sixth, which they know to be the letter *ya*; this is the accusative case used for the action [of knowing]. This applies everywhere in this manner. There is an elision of the *ta*-sound in the twenty-sixth and the others. The word "thus" (*tathā*) indicates that this [letter] is a seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Vāyu. Regarding "the third of the fourth," this refers to the letter *da*. The word "but" (*tu*) indicates its purpose of burning away sins. Regarding "only the pair of the sibilants" (*ūṣman*): *śa*, *ṣa*, *sa*, and *ha* are the sibilants; the term "sibilants" (*ūṣman*) is used here due to the addition of a phoneme (*varṇāgama*). "The pair" means the second [sibilant], the letter *ṣa*. The phrase "and only" (*eva ca*) includes another second [sibilant] and serves the purpose of restriction. (10)
The first letter of the first [varga], likewise the twenty-seventh, then the twenty-eighth, and again the third of the first [varga]. (11)

"Of the first, the first" refers to the letter *ka*. "The twenty-seventh" refers to the letter *ra*; the word "thus" (*tathā*) indicates that this possesses the nature of the seed-syllable of fire (*agni*). "The twenty-eighth" refers to the letter *la*; the word "again" (*punar*) establishes its nature as the seed-syllable of earth (*pṛthivī*). "The third of the first, however" refers to the letter *ga*; the word "however" (*tu*) signifies emptiness (*śūnyatā*), because it moves specifically and always abides; since it denotes that, its meaning is "to go. (11)
From the fifth [chapter], one should take the thirty-first [verse] of the fourth;
likewise, the fifteenth and the twenty-fifth. (12)

The fourth letter of the fifth [group] is the letter *bha*. The word "also" (*api*) indicates the meaning previously stated. "Then one should take the thirty-first": having taken the letter *ṣa*, which is the thirty-first of *kāli*. Likewise, "and also the fifteenth": likewise means the fifteenth of *kāli*, the letter *ṇa*. "And indeed" (*eva*) serves to restrict the connection to *kāli*. "The twenty-fifth likewise" means the letter *ma*; the meaning of the word "likewise" (*tathā*) is exactly as before. (12)
The second of the first [group], and likewise the twenty-sixth;
the thirty-second syllable, and indeed the last of the sibilants (ūṣman). || 13 ||

"Of the first, the second, however": this refers to the letter *kha*. The word "however" (*tu*) indicates that its meaning is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Likewise, "the twenty-sixth, moreover": "likewise" (*tathā*) means as before, i.e., the letter *ya*; "moreover" (*punaḥ*) is a particle used for poetic ornamentation (*vākyālaṅkāra*). "And indeed the thirty-second syllable": the thirty-second syllable is *sa*; the word "and" (*ca*) suggests its nature as water; the word "indeed" (*eva*) here serves to emphasize. "And also the very end of the sibilants": this is the letter *ha*. "And also" (*eva ca*) emphasizes the connection with the end of the vowels (*kāli*). (13)
Furthermore, the thirty-second [letter], then the fourth of the fifth;
the third of the second, and indeed the fourth of the fifth. (14)

"Furthermore, the thirty-second": this refers to the letter *sa*, which consists of thirty-two syllables. "Furthermore" (*punaścaiva*) indicates that the sentence reiterates the meaning of the preceding statement. "The fourth of the fifth, however" (*pañcamasya caturthaṃ tu*): this refers to the letter *bha*. The word "however" (*tu*) demonstrates its quality of removing fear. "And the third of the second, indeed" (*dvitīyasya tṛtīyaṃ caiva*): this refers to the letter *ja*. The word "indeed" (*caiva*) emphasizes its purpose of bringing victory. "The fourth of the fifth, however" (*pañcamasya caturthaṃ tu*): this refers to the letter *bha*. The word "however" (*tu*) here indicates the meaning previously stated. (14)
The third of the sibilants (ūṣman), and the twenty-seventh which follows;
the first of the semivowels (antaḥstha), and likewise the twenty-first again. (15)

"And the third of the *ūṣman*s" refers to the letter *sa*, as before. "The twenty-seventh, the supreme" refers to the letter *ra*; it is "supreme" because it generates fire (*vahni*). "And the first of the semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*)": this is the letter *ya*. The word "and" (*caiva*) serves both to include [the previous elements] and to emphasize [this one]. Likewise, "the twenty-first again": the word "likewise" (*tathā*) indicates that this was spoken by the Tathāgata. The twenty-first is the letter *pa*. "Again, the quality (*guṇa*), without elaboration" [refers to the vowel *u*]. (15)
The second of the semivowels, and likewise the thirtieth;
the first of the fifth [class], and also the first of the sibilants (ūṣman). || 16 ||

"Of those situated within, the second"—this refers to the second syllable, *repha* (the letter *r*). "And the thirtieth likewise"—this refers to the thirtieth, the letter *śa*. The word "likewise" (*punaḥ*) indicates its recurrence. "Likewise" (*tathā*) is indicative of the meaning: that which teaches peace (*śānti*) is *śa*. "The first of the fifth" is the letter *pa*. And "the first of the sibilants (*ūṣman*) as well"—this is the letter *śa*. The particle *ca* and the particle *eva* serve to indicate the sense of peace and to restrict [the reference] to the first [of the sibilants], respectively. || 16 ||
Likewise, the first [syllable] of the fourth [group], which has the form of the letter *ya*, and also the first of the sibilants (*ūṣman*), which is the twenty-eighth [letter]. || 17 ||

"And likewise the letter *dy*": the connection is that one should extract the Hero (*vīra*) by taking the letter *dy*. The first of the fourth [class] is the letter *ta*; the first of the sibilants (*ūṣman*) is the letter *śa*; "likewise the twenty-eighth" refers to the letter *la*. The word "likewise" indicates that this possesses the same meaning as what was previously stated. || 17 ||
The second [syllable] of the first [word], the first of the third, the third of the first, and the fourth of the fourth [are to be combined]. (18)

"But the second of the first" refers to the letter *kha*, as before. "The first of the third" refers to the letter *ṭa*. "Also the third of the first" refers to the letter *ga*. "But the fourth of the fourth" refers to the letter *dha*. The word *tu* indicates that *dha* signifies "it blows away (*dhamati*) evil. || 18 ||
The second of the semi-vowels (antaḥsthā), the fifth of the third [class],
the letter *v* (vyākāra)— they call this "Vīra"— and likewise the fourth of the first [class] and the eighth. (19)

The second of those situated at the end is the letter *ra*. Regarding "the fifth of the third as well"—the word "as well" (*api*) is used for emphasis; thus it applies everywhere. The fifth is the letter *ṇa*. "They call the *vyā* the hero (*vīra*)"—it is called *vyā* because it attains distinction (*viśeṣam āpnoti*). They call that hero Śrī Heruka. The fourth of the first is the letter *gha*. And likewise, "the eighth indeed"—the word "likewise" (*tathā*) indicates the meaning of victory (*jaya*); the particle "indeed" (*eva*) is for emphasis. The eighth of the eighth is the letter *ja*. And by the phrase "and indeed," the word "eighth" indicates time (*kāla*). (19)
The fifth of the fourth, and also the fifth of the fifth;
likewise the twenty-seventh, and the fourth of the fourth.

The fifth of the fourth [group] is the letter *na*; the fifth of the fifth is the letter *ma*. "The twenty-seventh likewise" refers to the letter *ra*. The word "likewise" (*tathā*) indicates the meaning previously stated. "The fourth of the fourth, however" refers to the letter *dha*. The word "however" (*tu*) has the sense of "again. (20)
Furthermore, taking the twenty-seventh, as well as the twenty-sixth, the twenty-fifth, and indeed the thirty-third. (21)

"Furthermore, the twenty-seventh" means the twenty-seventh letter, *repha* (*r*). The word "furthermore" (*punaḥ*) has the same meaning as before. "Likewise, indeed, the twenty-sixth" means the word "likewise" (*tathā*) has the same sense as before, with the middle portion omitted; it refers to the twenty-sixth letter, *yakāra* (*y*). The phrase "and indeed" (*eva ca*) indicates that this carries the same meaning as what was previously stated. "Taking the twenty-fifth" means taking the letter *makāra* (*m*); the connection is that one should extract the Hero (*vīra*). The term "taking" (*samādāya*) also applies elsewhere, as in "the thirty-third indeed," which refers to the letter *hakāra* (*h*).
The word "and" (ca) emphasizes the meaning "indeed," [stating] that he destroys the sins of sentient beings. || 21 ||
The fourth of the fourth, the fifth of the fifth,
the fifth of the fourth as well,
the first of the first, and likewise the twenty-seventh. (22)
The fourth of the semivowels (antaḥstha), likewise the twenty-first, the second of the sibilants (ūṣman), and also the twenty-sixth. (23)

"Of the fourth, however, the fourth": this refers to the letter *dh*. The word "however" (*tu*) has the sense of "again. "Of the fifth, the fifth": this refers to the letter *m*. "Also of the fourth, the fifth": this refers to the letter *n*. The word "also" (*api*) implies that one should likewise take the first of the first in the aggregate of the fifth. "And indeed": this refers to the letter *k*. The word "and indeed" (*caiva*) indicates the meaning previously stated. "The twenty-seventh, likewise": this refers to the letter *r*. The word "likewise" (*tathā*) indicates its nature as a producer of fire. "Of the semivowels (*antaḥstha*), however, the fourth": this refers to the letter *v*.

The word *tu* indicates that it is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Varuṇa. "The twenty-first likewise" refers to the letter *pa*. The word *tathā* shows its connection with the *āli* (vowels). "And likewise of the sibilants" refers to the letter *ṣa*. The word *caiva* states the rule for its placement in this position. "And likewise the twenty-sixth indeed" refers to the letter *ya*. This is the extraction of the syllables of the root mantra. (22–23)

KARA 2 KURU 2 BANDHA 2 TRĀSAYA 2 KṢOBHAYA 2 HRĀṂ 2 HRAḤ 2 PHEṂ 2 PHAṬ 2 DAHA 3 PACA 2 BHAKṢA 3 O thou who art adorned with a garland of hanging entrails, blood, and fat! GR̥HṆA 2 the serpent dwelling in the seven nether worlds!
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the procedure for extracting the syllables of the root mantra, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 5.

Therefore, he says "having known," and so forth. That by which Śrī Heruka is accomplished is the mantra of Śrī Heruka. Having known that—that is, having realized it to be the source of accomplishment—one [should know] that any other mantra-word is like straw; this is a figurative attribution of action, because it is fruitless in view of the result to be achieved. A *ghuṇa* is a specific kind of insect.

The wood has been eaten by that wood-worm; therefore, this is the meaning: the yogi considers another collection of mantras to be devoid of causal efficacy like wood eaten by a worm, and fruitless like straw. "The root mantra is proclaimed" means it is proclaimed after being analyzed through the extraction of its syllables. || 26 ||

Regarding the "treasuries," he says: "the root-mantra. It is the root of all accomplishments (*siddhi*), and it is also a mantra; thus it is so called. The sense is that the root-mantra is other than the King of Vidyās (*vidyārāja*). And it consists of eight words through the purification of the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*). The syllables are the consonants. Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Cakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 5.
The sixth chapter: The Ritual Procedure for Extracting the Armor of the Six Heroes.

Hereafter follows the heart-mantra of twenty-two syllables and the subsidiary heart-mantra of seven syllables. The seed-syllable is the eighth from the *ya*-group (the letter *ṣa*), likewise with twelve morae (*mātrā*).

He says "therefore" (*ataḥ*) because the instruction on the mantra was condensed for the sake of those who prefer brevity. Since the teaching of the mantra was condensed for the sake of those who prefer brevity, for that reason the Heart-mantra consists of twenty-two syllables, as it is the cause of all accomplishments (*siddhi*). The prefix *upa-* signifies inferiority; this inferiority pertains to the number of syllables, not to the result. And that [result] is twofold and supreme, as will be explained hereafter—this is the meaning. Furthermore, he first states the condensed Armor-mantra (*kavaca-mantra*): "The seed-syllable eighth from the *ya*-group," and so forth.

The eighth seed-syllable after the *ya*-group is the letter *ha*. The word *ca* has the sense of *eva* (only) or signifies a specific distinction (*viśeṣa*). "By the measures" means by the *mātrās*, excluding the neuter ones; "likewise" means by those abiding in specific meanings. The third case is used here in the sense of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). || 1 ||
Having interspersed the syllables, the six-limbed Śrī Heruka is proclaimed;
through the unions with the six heroes, they are established in the single syllable. (2)

"Having made [the syllables] interspersed with other letters" means: having made that seed-syllable interspersed with other letters. "Śrī Heruka is spoken" occurs when the case ending is elided. And that consists of six limbs, meaning six parts. For example: *ha hā hi hī hu hū he hai ho hau haṃ haḥ*. The connection is: "having made [them] interspersed—that is, separated—by each letter, Śrī Heruka is spoken. For the purpose of grasping, from the letter *ha*, the *hikāra* is separated by the letter *hā*.

From that *hikāra* as well, by means of *hīkāra*, there is *hukāra*. From that *hukāra* as well, by means of *hūkāra*, there is *hekāra*. From that *hekāra* as well, by means of *haikāra*, there is *hokāra*. From that *hokāra* as well, by means of *haukāra*, there is *haṃkāra*. Thus, according to the instruction on "interposition by both," these six are grasped. These syllables are as follows: *ha, hi, hu, he, ho, haṃ*—these six. When do these become the non-dual vajra of Śrī Heruka? To this he says: "the six," and so forth.

Just as when the six hero-mantras (ṣaḍvīra-mantra) are established one by one syllable, then there is the state of the six limbs of Śrī Heruka. The term "heroes" (vīra) is used through the elision of the nominative plural ending. To explain how they are thus constituted, he says: "by means of unions" (samāyogaiḥ). "Unions" (samāyoga) refers to those yogas which are perfectly (samyak) at the beginning; the meaning is that the syllables Oṃ and so forth, along with the six heroes and so forth, precede the letter Ha and the others. || 2 ||
The practitioner should know that the heart-mantras are those joined with *oṃ*, *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vauṣaṭ*, *hūṃ*, *hūṃ*, and *phaṭ*. || 3 ||

He states the *oṃ*-syllable and the others: *oṃ namaḥ svāhā vauṣaṭ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. This is the first [mantra], with the plural number elided. It should be understood as being joined together as it occurs. "The objects of knowledge" (*jñeyāni*) refers to the heart-mantras of the six heroes. By the word "but" (*tu*), he indicates by whom they are to be known: "by the practitioner" (*sādhaka*). Here, the nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental. (3)
The first is indeed the heart, the second is remembered as the head;
one should assign the third to the crest-lock (śikhā), and the fourth shall be the armor (kavaca).
The fifth shall be the eye, and the sixth is called the weapon (astra).
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the procedure for extracting the armor of the six heroes, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

"First, however, the heart... Here, the word "however" (*tu*) includes one's own deity. The same applies in the subsequent cases as well. *Oṃ ha* is the heart; Vajrasattva is the first. The nominative case in "heart" (*hṛdayam*) is used in the sense of the locative. "The second, however, is the head, [known as] *smṛti*" means *namaḥ hi*; Vairocana is on the head. *Smṛtam* means "contemplated. "The third, however, one should apply to the crest-lock (*śikhā*)" means *svāhā hūṃ*; Padmanarteśvara. "The fourth shall be the armor (*kavaca*)"...
The word *tu* (but) indicates a continuation. *Vauṣaṭ* is for the head. It should be understood from the instruction that "the armor is Śrī Heruka on the two shoulders.

"But the fifth shall be the eye" means *hūṃ hūṃ hoḥ*; *vajrasūrya* is for the two eyes. "The weapon of the sixth is said [to be]" means *phaṭ haṃ*; *hayagrīva* is the weapon for all limbs. In the phrase "of the sixth," the genitive case is used in the sense of the nominative. In the context of the heart and so forth, the nominative is used in the sense of the locative. In all cases, the term "hearts" (*hṛdayāni*) follows the pattern of the heart-mantra. 4.

These mantras, or those produced from them, are the heroes (*vīra*) in these locations. This is the Armor of the Six Heroes (*ṣaḍvīrakavaca*), so called because it cannot be pierced by the Māras. Its extraction (*uddhāra*) is presented; the chapter that expresses it is the sixth. In the reading *ṣaṣṭham*, the letter *m* is used for the sake of the word itself (*svārthe*).
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 6.
The seventh chapter, on the procedure for extracting the mantra, follows:
[The mantra is formed] by joining the second syllable with the thirteenth of the vowels.
It is conjoined with the eleventh vowel and adorned by the sixth letter. || 1 ||

Previously, the extraction of the syllables of the eight-word mantra was performed. Now, beginning the process of joining those syllables with the vowels, he says: "Of the vowels," and so forth. In that context, the genitive case in the word *tatraiva* (in that very place) is used for the purpose of determining the extraction of the letter *a*. The thirteenth [vowel] is the letter *o*. The particle *ca* (and) indicates a specific meaning. The particle *eva* (indeed) emphasizes this point: that when visualized upon the head, forehead, and heart, [the deity] Sūryaprabha—blazing with a thousand rays—brings [beings] under control. [The phrase] "joined with the second syllable" [is explained as follows].

The second syllable is the letter *ma* following the letter *na*; joined with that, it is known as the vowel *o*. Thus, it takes the form *mo*. In this way, the sixth [syllable] indeed begins from the first letter *na*. The eleventh vowel is *e*. That which is both that [vowel] and conjoined is "that" (*sa*). Therefore, it is adorned by the sixth syllable, the letter *ta*. From that, it takes the form *te*. || 1 ||
They know the seventh syllable to be joined with the fourth vowel,
and the eighth syllable to be joined with the eleventh vowel.

The fourth of the vowels is *ī*. The particle *eva* serves to exclude the short vowel. Thus, the seventh syllable characterized by it is *va*. By that, the form would be *vī*. They know the eighth syllable to be *ra* conjoined with the eleventh vowel; by that, the form would be *re*. This rule applies everywhere. (2)
Then, taking the ninth syllable conjoined with the second vowel, the twelfth syllable is likewise conjoined with the very second of the vowels. (3)

"Then one should take the ninth"—this refers to the letter *śa*. "From that" means from the first letter *na* which has been extracted. The second vowel is *ā*; by that, it takes the form *śā*. They know the twelfth syllable to be *ha*, joined with the second vowel; by that, it takes the form *hā*. || 3 ||
Then, taking the twenty-first [letter] conjoined with the second vowel, it is considered the fourteenth syllable, which is joined with the twentieth syllable. || 4 ||
Taking the fifteenth syllable joined with the third vowel, and the fifteenth of the vowels itself, this beautiful sixteenth-syllable [mantra] is formed. (5)

"Then one should take the twenty-first": having taken the twenty-first syllable, the letter *pa*, conjoined with the second vowel, they know that the fourteenth syllable, the letter *la*, is joined with it; thus there would be the form *lpa*. "The twentieth syllable": the twentieth syllable is *na*. With that conjoined below, the fifteenth syllable is *ga*. The third of the vowels is the vowel *i*; they know it to be marked by that. Thus there would be the form *gni*. The particle *eva* serves to exclude the long vowel.
The anusvāra is the fifteenth vowel; they know that the sixteenth syllable, the letter *sa*, is honored by it. Through that, the form [of the deity] is complete. (4–5)
The seventeenth syllable is joined with the third vowel;
it is further conjoined with the eighteenth syllable by means of the second of the vowels.

They know the seventeenth letter, *na*, conjoined with the third vowel (*i*) as "the supreme benefit. Because it effects the eradication (*uccāṭana*) of those who have harmed the Guru, the Buddha, and so forth, it is such that—mounted upon the circle of wind and resembling a mass of smoke—it visualizes the heart, throat, navel, and both feet of the target and eradicates them; thus, by that letter *na*, one becomes formless (*nirūpa*). Furthermore, they know the eighteenth letter, *bha*, conjoined with the second vowel (*ā*).
The twenty-first syllable is joined with the vowel *ā* and the consonant *ka*;
joined with the fifth letter of the alphabet (*ma*), it becomes the twenty-third syllable. (7)

"Joined with the vowel-sound (ākāra) and the consonant (svara)": this refers to the twenty-first. They know the twenty-first to be the letter *ṭa*. The fifth of the Mātṛkās is the vowel *u*; joined with that, they know the twenty-third letter to be *ka*. (7)
The thirteenth of the vowels, joined with that [consonant], forms the twenty-fourth syllable;
taking the first of the first [group of consonants], it is joined with a conjunct syllable to form the twenty-fifth syllable. || 8 ||

Taking the thirteenth vowel, which is the letter *o*, and knowing that the twenty-fourth consonant, *ṭa*, is joined with it; and knowing the first letter of the first [group], which is *ka*; the letter *ca* is used for the purpose of including what has not been explicitly mentioned. [The mantra is] "the letter *ka*, possessing a splendor equal to the sun, joined with the *bindu*, when placed upon the heart, navel, and head of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), brings him under control. The particle *eva* (only/just) serves to restrict the meaning of what has been included. To the question, "Of what nature do they know that [letter *ka*]? he says: "joined with twenty-five letters."
"Pañcāvaśati" refers to the twenty-fifth letter, which is *takāra*. It is joined with that above; by that, the form *tka* arises. || 8 ||
The first [syllable] of the third [group], however, joined with the second vowel, shall consist of twenty-six syllables;
and the twenty-eighth [syllable] is indeed honored by the fifteenth.

Regarding the phrase "the first of the third, however," they know it to be the letter *ṭ*. The letter *ṭ* has a radiance equal to Indra’s bow (a rainbow); when placed upon the forehead, heart, and throat of the Sādhya, it brings them under control—this is the meaning of the word *tu* ("however"). Regarding the phrase "conjoined with the second vowel": that syllable *ṭ*, when conjoined with the second vowel, becomes the twenty-sixth syllable; the meaning is that it takes the form of *ṭā*. In an alternative reading, "the first of the third, however, would be that of the second," the meaning is that it is indeed the second *mātrā* of the second [vowel].

Through their conjunction, it is indeed the form *ṭā*. And the twenty-eighth [letter] is known as *da*. The letter *ca* is used for the purpose of including what has not been mentioned. The letter *da*, possessing a radiance equal to a cloud, when visualized upon the head of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), paralyzes him. The particle *eva* is used for emphasis. The fifteenth vowel is the *anusvāra*; they know that by it [the syllable] is honored. By means of that, it becomes the form *daṃ*. || 9 ||
The first letter of the third [varga], joined with its lower part and conjoined with fire, and likewise joined with the second vowel, shall be the twenty-ninth syllable. || 10 ||

The twenty-ninth letter is joined with the first *ṭa*-kāra of the third [group] at its lower part; it is joined below that with the fire-syllable *ra*; and likewise, by virtue of the word "ca" (and), it is conjoined with the second vowel. Thus, it takes the form *ṣṭrā*. The letter *ca* serves to indicate the conjunction of these elements. 10.
The thirty-first syllable is joined with the second vowel;
the thirty-second syllable is joined with the thirteenth vowel. || 11 ||

The thirty-first syllable is *repha* (the letter *r*). When joined with the second vowel (*ā*), it becomes the form *rā*. The thirty-second syllable is *lakāra* (the letter *l*). When joined with the thirteenth vowel (*au*), it becomes the form *lo*. || 11 ||
Joined with Bhāskara (the letter *ra*), it becomes thirty-three syllables;
joined with the fourth of the Mātṛkās (the letter *la*), it becomes thirty-four.

It should consist of thirty-three syllables joined with Bhāskara. Bhāskara is the letter *repha* (r). The thirty-third syllable is *gakāra* (g); in combination, it would take the form *gra*. The fourth [syllable] of the Mātṛkā is *īkāra* (ī). The word "eva" serves to exclude the short vowel. Regarding "catustriṃśati": the thirty-fourth syllable is *bhakāra* (bh). By that, it would take the form *bhī*. || 12 ||
The accomplishment that fulfills all desires and aims by means of the fifth *mātṛkā* alone, joined with the thirty-seven, is known as the *ḍākinī-sādhana*. 13.

The letter *u* is the fifth of the *mātṛkās*. The particle *eva* serves to exclude the long vowel. Regarding "thirty-seven": the thirty-seventh syllable is the letter *ma*. In conjunction [with the preceding], the form becomes *mu*. "The practice (*sādhana*) is the *ḍākinī*" means that the complete mantra is the practice for the *ḍākinīs*. Alternatively, the thirty-seventh letter *ma*, when meditated upon alone, shining like the sun, upon the head of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), subdues the *yakṣas* and other beings; thus it is known as the "practice" of the *ḍākinī*. It is approved by the *ḍākinīs*. (13)
And the thirty-eighth [letter], joined with the second vowel, is likewise the means for accomplishing all the gods; of this there is no doubt. (14)

"And the thirty-eighth" means that the thirty-eighth syllable is the letter *kha*. Through its conjunction with the second vowel (*ā*), it takes the form *khā*. Here, as everywhere else, the nominative case is used; "should be" (*bhavet*) is used in connection with the verb. One should know that the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is the syllable *kha*. The same applies elsewhere. "Having the radiance of an *indragopa* [insect], when visualized at the head of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the syllable *kha* brings all gods and others under control. The particle *ca* is used for conjunction, while the particle *eva* emphasizes the point. Therefore, he says: "the means of accomplishment," and so forth.
The forty-second [syllable] is indeed joined with the letter *daha* (da-ha);
the practitioner [should take] the forty-third syllable from the lower portion. 15.

"The forty-second" means the forty-second letter, which is *sa*. The word "and" (*eva*) serves to confirm the meaning previously stated. "Fire" (*dahana*) refers to the letter *ra*. The word "but" (*tu*) is used for emphasis. That [fire] is its lower part; thus it is "the lower part. The forty-second letter joined with that becomes the form *stra*. The ellipsis of the verb is supplied as "the practitioner should know that. "The forty-third" means the forty-third letter, which is *bha*. || 15 ||
The fifty-fifth [syllable] is joined with the fifth vowel, and it is also joined with the second vowel. (16)

Joined with the fifth vowel of those [consonants], it would take the form *bhu*. The particle *eva* serves to exclude the long vowel. The forty-fifth [letter] is the syllable *bha*. The word *caiva* (and indeed) is used for the purpose of emphasizing the collection of meanings previously mentioned. Joined with the second vowel, it would take the form *bhā*. || 16 ||
The forty-sixth [syllable], joined with the fifth vowel and worshipped by all heroes, as well as the forty-seventh, joined with the second vowel. (17)

"With the fifth of the vowels" is as before. "Joined with the forty-sixth": the forty-sixth syllable, *sa*, joined with the vowel *u*, becomes *su-rūpa*. "And indeed the forty-seventh": the forty-seventh syllable is the letter *ra*. The word *caiva* (and indeed) serves to emphasize the conjunction of the previously mentioned meaning. When joined with the second vowel (*ā*), it becomes *rā-rūpa*. || 17 ||
Vajrasattva is indeed that supreme fifty-first [syllable]; likewise, it is considered the most excellent when beautified by the fifth of the vowels. (18)

"Vajrasattva is indeed that supreme [syllable]. That very syllable *repha* (the letter *r*) is Vajrasattva. "The fifty-first" refers to the fiftieth-first, which is the letter *śa*. "And likewise" indicates that this possesses the same meaning as what was previously stated. Regarding "by the fifth," the word *tu* (but/however) denotes a distinction. When the letter *u*, which has a radiance equal to Indra’s bow (a rainbow), is meditated upon at the throat of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it brings them under control. Consequently, the form would be *śu*; for it is considered beautiful and supreme. (18)
The fifty-second [letter], likewise joined with the second vowel, is the means for accomplishing all the gods; of this there is no doubt. (19)

"And the fifty-second. The fifty-second syllable is the letter *pa*. The particle *caiva* (and indeed) serves to include unmentioned meanings and for emphasis. Impelled by the wind (*vāyu*), mounted upon a cloud, and smoke-colored, when meditated upon at the throat, heart, waist, and soles of the feet of the practitioner, that [letter] expelling it—the letter *pa*—effects expulsion (*uccāṭana*). When joined with the second vowel, *pā* becomes "cruel" (*rūpaṃ*). || 19 ||
Likewise, the fifty-third [letter] is joined with the thirteenth vowel;
having extracted the letter *da* from the fourth group of consonants, it is joined with the fifty-fourth [vowel]. || 20 ||

The fifty-third is the fifty-third *śakāra*. The phrase "likewise again" (*tathā punar*) indicates the previously mentioned meaning. The continuation of the action is expressed by "they know that very [letter] joined with the thirteenth vowel"; by that, the form would be *śo*. Regarding the phrase "having extracted the letter *da* from the fourth group": although one should have said "having extracted the third from the fourth group," the fact that *da* is mentioned is for the purpose of indicating that it belongs to the fourth position within the *ka*-group; otherwise, there would be doubt as to whether it was from the *a*-group or the *ka*-group.

Then, due to a confusion regarding the script, one might wonder whether this is a pair of *u*s or a pair of *d*s. "The fifty-fourth" refers to the letter *ya*. They know it to be joined with that; thus, it would take the form *dya*. || 20 ||
The fifty-six syllable [mantra], joined with the sixth vowel, is certainly the destroyer of enemies, by means of the fourth [consonant] of the semivowels (antasthā). 21.

The fifty-sixth letter is the letter *śa*. It is known to be joined with the sixth vowel, *ū*; thus it becomes the form *śū*. It is certainly "the cutter of enemies" because of the victory over the enemies that are the afflictions (*kleśa*). The fourth of the semivowels (*antaḥstha*) is the letter *va*. The third case ending is used here in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārtha*). (21)
Joined with the second vowel and likewise endowed with the fifteenth [consonant], this practice for attaining all siddhis consists of fifty-nine syllables. || 22 ||

The fifty-ninth letter, joined with the letter *va* combined with the second vowel (*u*), and further endowed with the fifteenth [consonant], becomes the means for attaining all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*). The word "viduḥ" (they know) is either a verb or the accusative case ending. Thus, it would take the form *ṭvām*. And this praise applies either to the letter *ṭa* alone or to the entire mantra. || 22 ||
The wise know it as joined with the sixty-first letter by means of the second vowel;
likewise, they know it as the sixty-second.

"One and sixty" refers to the letter *dh*. They know its form as *dhā*, conjoined with the second vowel (*i*). The word "but" (*tu*) indicates that the solitary letter *dh* expresses the previously mentioned meaning. "In this very way, the excellent ones know"—that is, the Buddhas. "Two and sixty" means they know the sixty-second letter, which is *repha* (*r*). And the phrase "in that same way" (*tathā caiva*) serves to include and confirm the manner of the previously mentioned meaning. (23)
Joined with the third vowel, it is considered the supreme [mantra] of the ḍākinīs;
furthermore, there are sixty-three [syllables] conjoined with the eleven vowels. || 24 ||

When joined with the third vowel, it takes the form *ri*. Regarding "the sixty-third": this refers to the letter *ma* (or *ṇa*). "And again" (*punaścaiva*) indicates a further extraction, used here for emphasis and inclusion. When that [same letter] is conjoined with the eleventh vowel, they know it to take the form *ṇe*. (24)
The beautiful, supreme syllable, likewise sixty-five in number, is pierced by Vajrasattva and joined with the second vowel. (25)

"Sixty-five" refers to the syllable *gha*. "Vajrasattva" is the letter *repha* (the sound *r*). "And likewise" (*tathā caiva*) is used for the purpose of conjunction and emphasis regarding the manner of the previously mentioned meaning. By that, one should know the form as *ghrā*. || 25 ||
This seed-syllable is supremely divine, bestowing accomplishment and liberation;
it consists of sixty-six syllables joined with the third vowel. (26)
The Tathāgata spoke this, which grants success in all undertakings, consisting of sixty-seven syllables and joined with the second vowel. (27)

"Sixty-six" refers to the sixty-sixth syllable, which is the letter *ja*. Thus spoke the Tathāgata. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to collect the meanings previously stated. When joined with the third vowel, it becomes the form *ji*. Regarding "the sixty-seventh syllable," he spoke of the sixty-seventh syllable, which is the letter *na*. Joined with the second vowel, it becomes the form *nā*. And that is connected with the meaning. (26–27)
In all the activities of the yoginīs, it is exactly thus; there is no doubt.
Furthermore, one should join the letter *ba* there sixty-eight times.
With this seed-syllable, one should fashion [the foundation] in the lower part;
it consists of seventy-one syllables and is joined with the second vowel.

"Sixty-eighth": he stated that the sixty-eighth syllable is the letter *ma*. "And again" (*punaścaiva*) is used for the purpose of collecting and emphasizing the previously mentioned meaning. "One should join the letter *ba* there" means one should arrange it below the letter *ma*; by this, the form *mba* would result. "Seventy-first": he stated that the seventy-first syllable is the letter *ra*. The word "and" (*caiva*) is used for the purpose of collecting and emphasizing the previously mentioned meaning. Through its conjunction with the second vowel (*ā*), the form *rā* would result. (28–29)
This is indeed auspicious for all castes; there is no doubt about this.
It is the seventy-fourth [letter], joined with the second vowel. (30)
"Seventy-four": he spoke of the seventy-fourth letter, the syllable *ha*. The word "and" (*ca*) is as before. When joined with the second vowel, it takes the form *hā*. || 30 ||
This bestows primordial accomplishment, having issued from the mouth of the Tathāgata;
it is the seventy-fifth [chapter] and indeed the sixth [section] on the Mātrikās.

"Seventy-five": he spoke of the seventy-fifth letter as the syllable *dh*. And this is just as before. When joined with the sixth vowel-matrix (*mātrikā*), that [syllable] would take the form of *dhū*. || 31 ||
This is the most excellent yoga, the best among all yogas;
it consists of seventy-six [syllables] with the second letter of the Mātṛkā.
One should split the seventy-sixth syllable, the letter *ma*, with the second vowel (*ā*). The word *ca* (and) is as before. || 32 ||
One should indeed split it with the Sun (Sūrya) and join the syllable *va* there;
there is nothing else more auspicious than this mantra, which consists of seventy-seven syllables.

One should indeed split the letter *va* with the sun (*sūrya*); one should join the form of those two [letters] there between the lower ones. By that, the form *mvrā* arises. "There is nothing else more supremely beautiful" refers to the seed-syllable *mvrā*. Regarding the phrase "the seventy-seventh syllable," he spoke of the seventy-seventh syllable, the letter *na*, as being joined according to the meaning previously stated. (33)
One should join the letter *dhakāra* there; it is beautiful and the doctrine of the Ḍākinīs.
Furthermore, the seventy-eighth [letter] is joined with the second vowel. (34)

Through the conjunction of the letter *dha* with the lower part [the vowel *u*], the form *ndha* arises. Regarding "seventy-eight," the seventy-eighth syllable is the letter *ka*; and as before, through its conjunction with the second vowel, the form *kā* arises. || 34 ||
This supreme, divine seed-syllable is considered the highest cause;
it consists of eighty-one syllables and is differentiated by the vowel at the end of the fourth [group]. (35)
The eighty-first syllable is my syllable *pa*; in the division of the fourth vowel, it becomes the syllable *pu*. And this is just as before. || 35 ||
For this brings about primordial accomplishment and sets all accomplishments in motion;
it consists of eighty-two syllables and is likewise joined with the second vowel. (36)
The excellent ones know this supreme divine root-mantra to be the abode of all accomplishments and the crusher of the hearts of the ḍākinīs. (37)

"Eighty-two syllables of mine"—the eighty-second syllable is the letter *ṣa*, as before. When joined with the second vowel, it takes the form *ṣā*. This is the root mantra consisting of eight words; therefore it is said: "The excellent ones know this as the root mantra. (36–37)

This is the root mantra of the deity Śrī Heruka, the King of Vidyās, which achieves success through recitation. Joined with the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning and ending with *hūṃ* twice followed by *phaṭ*, this root mantra accomplishes all desired aims. (38)
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the procedure for extracting the mantras, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

The Lord Śrī Heruka is so called because he sports with Śrī Heruka. His King of Vidyās (vidyārāja) mantra begins with *karakara* and so forth. The phrase "joined with the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning and ending with *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*" refers to its recitation as a single, indivisible, and protracted utterance. This qualification applies both to the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) and to the King of Vidyās, as seen in the *Mantraprabhāvalocana*. Therefore, it says: "this mantra. The meaning is that not only is the root mantra distinguished by the word *om* and so forth, but this King of Vidyās is likewise so distinguished. [The phrase] "devoid of all ritual means" (*sarvasādhanavarjitā*)...
The heart-mantra, the upahr̥daya-mantra, the armor-mantra, the root-mantra, and the king of vidyās are all devoid of ritual procedures such as writing and other means of accomplishment. || 38 ||
The extraction of the root mantra by means of its entirety and of the King of Vidyās by means of a portion, as well as the chapter that explains the procedure for those, is thus the seventh.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 7.
The eighth chapter: The Ritual for Extracting the Mantra of the Six Yoginīs of the Inverted Heart.
Then, [one should contemplate] oneself as the union with all heroes, the bringer of all accomplishments, the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*.

The *hṛdaya* and *upahṛdaya* mantras have been previously indicated; the *ṣaḍyoginīkavaca* mantra and the *hṛdaya* mantra of Vajravārāhī have now been indicated. To the question "What are all of them?", he says "Then," and so forth. It should be understood from the words beginning with "all" (*sarva*) that one should extract the *Sarvavīrasamāyoga-Ḍākinījālasaṃvara* from that very collection of vowels and consonants (*ālikāli*).

Śrī Heruka and his mantra are also described in that same way; just as these syllables, beginning with *hā*, *s*, and *ā*, are shown to be established within the mantra, so too are they extracted individually from *Āli* and *Kāli*. This is the extraction (*samuddhāra*), because they are drawn out from the cow (*go*) in reverse order. To the question "Of what nature is it?", he says: "One's own self" (*svātmānam*). This means one's own mind (*nijaṃ cittam*). || 1 ||
Hā svā raṃ va saṃ la jā nī ki ḍā ṭpha hūṃ hūṃ kaṃ ru ru he he jrava śrī oṃ || 2 ||
The heart of the King of Vidyās has neither been, nor will it ever be. || 3 ||

*Oṃ śrīvajra he he ru ru kaṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ ḍākinījālasaṃvara svāhā*. Writing [this] in direct order (*anuloma*) is the extraction (*samuddhāra*). This heart-mantra consists of twenty-two syllables. To the question "Whose heart [is this]?", he says: "The Vidyā," and so forth. *Oṃ kara kare*, etc., is called the concise heart of the eight-line heart of the King of Vidyās. He states its power with the words "Not by any being," and so forth. The meaning is that in the past and future times, this mantra has not been told by me to anyone, nor will it be told. (2–3)
ṬPHA HŪṂ 2 HA HA HRĪḤ OṂ | ṬPHA HŪṂ HREṂ HRĪṂ HĀṂ OṂ || 4 ||

He states the extraction of the mantra for the Armor of the Six Yoginīs (Ṣaḍyoginīkavaca), beginning with "ṭpha" and so forth: "Oṃ hāṃ hrīṃ hreṃ hūṃ phaṭ"—this collection of syllables, namely ṭpha hūṃ hreṃ hrīṃ hāṃ oṃ, has been thus properly arranged. || 4 ||
The syllable VAṂ, the syllable YOṂ, the syllable MOṂ, and likewise the syllable HRĪṂ;
the syllable HŪṂ and the syllable PHAṬ—these are proclaimed as the six Yoginīs. || 5 ||

The syllable *vaṃ*, the syllable *yoṃ*, the syllable *moṃ*, the syllable *hrīṃ*, the syllable *hūṃ*, and likewise the syllable *phaṭ*. The syllables beginning with *oṃ* are to be joined at the beginning of those beginning with *vaṃ*. *Oṃ vaṃ Vajravārāhī* at the navel; *hāṃ yoṃ Yāminī* at the heart; *hrīṃ moṃ Mohanī* at the mouth; *hreṃ hrīṃ Saṃcāriṇī* at the head; *hūṃ hūṃ Trāsanī* at the crest-lock (*śikhā*); *phaṭ phaṭ Caṇḍikā* as the weapon (*astra*) for all limbs. The particle *ca* (and) is used everywhere to indicate mutual dependence.
The particle *eva* serves to restrict the meaning to its own specific sense. "The six yoginīs are proclaimed" refers to Vajravārāhī and the others. (5)
Hā svā ye nī ca ro vai jra va oṃ!
This great vidyā of the ḍākinīs has not existed, nor will it ever exist. || 6 ||

This armor-mantra (*kavaca-mantra*) of the six yoginīs has been extracted: *oṃ vajravairocanīye svāhā*. This subsidiary heart-mantra (*upahṛdaya-mantra*) of Vajravārāhī has been extracted from the secret place (*gopa*). For while [the mantra] stands as *oṃ vajravairocanīye svāhā*, the syllables *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ* have been concealed; and these two are placed before the word *svāhā*. Regarding the term "ḍākinī": the mantra of Vajravārāhī and the others is the ḍākinī. The particle *tu* is used to demonstrate her majesty. Regarding the phrase "not a ghost" (*na bhūta*): because it is an adjective qualifying the mantra, the singular number is used for the genus (*jāti*). (6)
On this earth, there are four jewels: the mantra-garland is the most excellent;
the Ḍākinī is the great vidyā, and Heruka is the king of vidyās.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, the procedure for extracting the mantras of the six Yoginīs of the "Inverted Heart," from the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

"Upon the earth," and so forth. "As many world-systems as there are, in all those [worlds], whatever earths there are"—this is the singular number used for the genus (*jāti*). "The four jewels" means the four precious things; they are called such because they extend delight (*rati*). To ask what these are, he says: "The mantra-garland," and so forth. The "mantra-garland" is the *mālā-mantra*, and it consists of eight words. Therefore, the word *tu* is explained as signifying a distinction, and the letter *ma* is explained as signifying the supreme. "The *ḍākinī* is the knowledge of *majā*" refers to the mantra of Vajravārāhī and others. The word *tu* is used here for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).

The King of Knowledge (vidyārāja) begins with "oṃ kara kare" and so forth. The word "ca" (and) serves as a conjunction. [This refers to] Śrī Heruka; and the knowledge of this meaning consists of his forms, such as his arms and faces. (7)
The eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Extracting the Mantra of Vajravārāhī, the Six Yoginīs of the Inverted Heart. This is the summary of this chapter.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*.
The ninth chapter on the ritual procedures for the root mantra.
Now, therefore, I shall explain the supreme rites of the root mantra correctly and in due order;
whatever exists within the three worlds, all that one shall accomplish in an instant.

Since there is no application of a mantra without hearing its efficacy, he speaks the ninth chapter in order to explain that, beginning with "atha" and so forth. "Atha" means immediately after the extraction of the mantra. The connection is: "I shall declare the ritual action (*karma*). And that [action] is the desired boon. Why? He says: "Because of this. For there is no engagement in a means without seeing the fruit, and because the root-mantra was mentioned first. The word "karma" refers to what is to be performed. Furthermore, the Blessed One has himself declared this correctly through the accumulation [of the teachings].

"Successively" means in due order. He states the agency of the mantra: "Whatever exists or is found in the three worlds, all that, without exception, one shall accomplish in an instant," that is, immediately after the recitation characterized by its specific marks. || 1 ||
It performs all rites; by remembering it but once, one slays all nāgas, all gods, all yakṣas, and all gandharvas, as well as those of every birth.

It terrifies the clouds, causes them to rain, and stops them; it dries up the oceans and drives rivers onto their banks. It restrains Indra. By reciting this mantra one hundred thousand times, one shakes the earth. Having climbed a tree, one goes wherever one desires. It takes away all mantras and takes away all supernatural powers (siddhi). One may summon whatever is desired and release it again.

He creates many thousands of forms; by his will he is seen, and by his will he is not seen. He pulverizes palaces, tree-tops, and the like. He turns poison into nectar, and nectar into poison. He turns the *soma* plant into milk, and milk into *soma*. He removes all fragrances. He transmigrates wherever he desires. With the face of Garuḍa, he effects the creation of vehicles. That best of men who practices this during the conjunction of the moon with women—therein, the Goddess of Fortune (*Lakṣmī*) comes into his hand and cannot be thwarted by anyone.

One who is thus endowed with this procedure shall partake in the fruit of all accomplishments (*siddhi*). By mere recollection, one causes death; one produces fire; one splits open the underworld (*pātāla*) and causes a thunderbolt (*aśani*) to fall, and then restrains it again; by recollection, one produces lightning; one makes the images of all the gods dance. For whomever the accomplishment belongs, by merely uttering their name once and reciting [the mantra], that person dies at that very moment. One becomes the enjoyer of all worlds without exception. This Blessed One gathers [all things] according to his will; no vow, no conduct, and no fasting are prescribed.
By means of this ritual application, one should perform whatever action is desired.

He describes the activity of the practitioner with the words beginning "all" (*sarvam*), etc. The particle *vai* is used for emphasis. He states the ritual action (*karman*) with the words beginning "all," etc. "All nāgas" refers to those who cause harm, such as those whose gaze is poisonous; they are mentioned because they were previously described. "All gods" refers to Hari, Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, and so forth. "All yakṣas" refers to Ojo-hāras and others. Regarding "all origins" (*sarvayonayaḥ*): cruel humans are meant here; the nominative case is used in the sense of the object. By means of taking life and so forth, the practitioner kills the gods—those who act as gods—and deprives them of their lives.

The capacity regarding those who are neutral or cruel has already been stated; furthermore, the capacity for their rebirth should also be inferred, otherwise it would follow that the Compassionate One lacks such power.

Now he states the efficacy [of the mantra] with respect to insentient things, beginning with "the clouds" (*meghān*), etc. It "terrifies" means it agitates; the meaning is that it breaks them into pieces. "One who obtains rain" is *varṣāpaḥ*; one who causes rain to fall is "one who makes rain-fall," i.e., he causes the clouds to rain. The rest is easily understood. Regarding "the river": she is possessed of great velocity. He asks, "What does this effect? and answers: "It wards off Indra. "Indra" is used here in the singular to denote the class; thus, "those who are Indras" (*indrāḥ*). The meaning is that it prohibits those who are lords over sentient and insentient beings from performing their respective functions. "It agitates" means it shatters [them].

By the words "a tree," and so forth, he shows that one makes the insentient appear as if sentient. "All mantras" means that one even steals those that have been brought down; thus, the theft of speech is demonstrated. "The accomplishment of all things" (*sarvasiddhi*) refers to the attainment or completion of all [substances] such as elixirs (*rasa*); the sense is that one steals even the accomplishment, such as medicinal substances and the like. "One removes the desired food" means that one takes what is desired or liked from elsewhere and then releases it again—referring here to mantras and so forth.

He explains the power of mantra residing in the body with the words beginning "rūpa" (form), etc. By this, the possession of many arms, faces, and so forth is demonstrated. Regarding the phrase "by desire": through the desire of the yogin, the yogin is seen and not seen; thus, the accomplishment of invisibility is the power of concealment. Alternatively, having known that whatever form the observer of the yogin shall see is to be brought [to him], he shows it; this is "seeing by desire. By the words beginning "prāsāda" (palace), the disintegration even of that which is well-constructed is demonstrated.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), stones, mountains, walls, and so forth are indicated; thus, the capacity to dismantle even that which is well-constructed is shown. By the phrase beginning with "poison" (*viṣa*), the capacity to alter the very nature of things is shown. "Soma" refers to wine; "payas" refers to water. By the phrase beginning with "all," the removal of the odors of wine and other substances is demonstrated. By this yoga, it is indicated that one should demonstrate to the disciple their own capacity regarding those [substances].

There is another explanation: "all nāgas" refers to all afflictions (*kleśas*). "All gods" (*sarvadeva*) refers to the objects such as forms and so forth, because they sport (*divyanti*) by means of these. "All yakṣas" refers to those by which one conquers in every way; here the letter *ya* is substituted for *ja* according to etymological rules (*nairukta*). These are the sense faculties (*indriyas*) of all beings. "All sources" (*sarvayoni*) refers to the causes of birth and all ritual actions for attaining accomplishments (*siddhi*). Through "recollection"—that is, through the contemplation of the mantra—there is "slaying," which is purification.

It terrifies, dissolves, and causes rain to fall upon the clouds—the junctions of the *ḍākinī*-channels. It causes the *bodhicitta* to descend; it restrains it and makes it firm again within them. [It restrains] the oceans of sins. It causes the river-seed to rise upward. "Indra" refers to the mind; it restrains it from all sovereignty and establishes it therein. Regarding the phrase "by the recitation of one hundred thousand of this mantra": the genitive case in "of the mantra" (*mantrasya*) is elided. "Lakṣa" means Śrī Heruka; it is derived from the root *lakṣ* with the suffix *ac*.

The meaning is that his mental activity of recitation (*japa*) is "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*). The point is that all this is accomplished through the recitation of the mantra and the cultivation of Śrī Heruka. At the time of drawing the mandala, the entreaty to the Earth results in the shaking of the Earth. Having ascended the tree—the fivefold yoga—one obtains whatever one desires to obtain wherever one wishes. Here, it is said that the desired one is Śrī Heruka himself who has been summoned.

The method for rendering the *praṇava* and the rest devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvīkaraṇa*) through the entry of the *nāda* and so forth into the *bindu* and so forth has been established by the passage beginning with "all" (*sarva*). Furthermore, by the passage beginning again with "all," the accomplishment of the entry of the *nāda* and so forth is shown; from the exit of the *nāda* and so forth, there is the offering of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*). By the passage beginning with "as desired" (*rucita*), the radiating forth (*spharaṇa*) and so forth are indicated. By the passage beginning with "form" (*rūpa*) and "om kara kare," the division of the mantra is shown. By the passage beginning with "by will" (*icchayā*), the formal resolve (*praṇidhi*) is indicated. It is "not" (*na*) because of the absence of dogmatic attachment (*anabhiniveśa*). Because the mind becomes serene (*prasīdati*) in this, it is the "palace" (*prāsāda*), which is the body.

It flows, thus it is *dru*; because the rules of grammatical augment (*āgama*) are not always mandatory, there is no *tuk* suffix. *Dru* itself is *druma*, which is sensation (*vedanā*). The peak is the mind (*citta*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the mental factors (*dharmas*) are included. It is pulverized—that is, analyzed—by the weapon of wisdom (*prajñā*). Thus, the four recollections (*anusmṛtis*) have been stated, and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) has been shown. Poison is the sense object (*viṣaya*); nectar is that which resembles nectar. One makes the nectar an object of non-serenity and partakes of it.

"Amṛtam" (nectar) refers to the liberation of his mind, like the extinguishing of a lamp; he treats *nirvāṇa* as if it were poison because it is not to be indulged in. The sense is that he enjoys [the senses] after purifying form (*rūpa*) and the rest. Regarding "Soma": it exists together with the two *umā*s, thus it is *soma*, the syllable *oṃ*. *U* and *ma* are the two; their combination is in reverse order (*vilomena*), because of the instruction regarding the half-moon and the nasal sound (*nāda*). The letter *pa* is water because it belongs to Varuṇa. He "makes" (*karoti*) both of these. Again, "milk-Soma" is as before. Therefore, this is the mantra: [The mantra follows: *om hrīṃ śrīṃ klīṃ aiṃ paṃ haṃ saḥ amṛte amṛtodbhave amṛtavarṣiṇi amṛtaśīkari amṛtahṛdaye amṛtavarcase amṛtasambhave amṛtagarbhe amṛtodbhave amṛtahṛdaye amṛtavarcase amṛtasambhave amṛtagarbhe amṛtodbhave amṛtavarṣiṇi amṛtaśīkari amṛtahṛdaye amṛtavarcase amṛtasambhave amṛtagarbhe amṛtodbhave amṛtavarṣiṇi amṛtaśīkari amṛtahṛdaye amṛtavarcase amṛtavarṣiṇi amṛtaśīkari amṛtahṛdaye amṛtavarcase amṛtasambhave amṛtagarbhe amṛtodbhave amṛtavarṣiṇi amṛtaśīkari amṛtahṛdaye amṛtavarcase amṛtasambhave amṛtagarbhe amṛtodbhave amṛtavarṣiṇi amṛtaśīkari amṛtahṛdaye amṛtavarcase amṛtasambhave amṛtagarbhe amṛtodbhave amṛtavarṣiṇi amṛtaśīkari amṛtahṛdaye amṛtavarcase amṛtasambhave amṛtagarbhe amṛtodbhave amṛtavarṣiṇi amṛtaśīkari amṛtahṛdaye amṛtavarcase amṛtavarṣiṇi amṛtaśīkari amṛtahṛdaye amṛtavarcase amṛtasambhave amṛtagarbhe amṛtodbhave amṛtavarṣiṇi amṛtaśīkari amṛtah

Saying "Oṃ va va oṃ," one should visualize within a Varuṇa mandala—white as a jasmine flower or the moon—the four mantras in the four directions; if there is a person to be accomplished (sādhya), one should imagine them adorned with pure garments and so forth in the center of that [mandala], and recite the mantra while sprinkling them from the front with dripping drops of nectar. One should perform the recitation (*japa*).

To the question "What is that?", he says "all," and so forth. "Gandha" refers to diseases, poisons, and the like; the remainder is easily understood. "Mukha" (mouth), "dvāra" (door), and "upāya" (means) are synonyms. Because he moves by means of two mouths as if by two wings, he is "Mukhagaruḍa" (the Garuḍa of the mouth). Alternatively, the term "mukha" [is used] with the elision of the third case ending (*tṛtīyā-lopa*); he is "Garuḍa" because his two arms move like wings. He is the "Yānasṛṣṭikṛt" (the creator of the vehicle's movement), meaning he effects the production or accomplishment of the vehicle's motion. Thus he is the Yogin.

He practices that union of the two *somayas*—the bodhicittas arising from wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*). Because he is discerning, the man who [unites] with women who possess the flow of flowers (menstruation) is "supreme," meaning uncommon. By this, having taken that bodhicitta with his mouth and raising both wings like a *garuḍa*, he should place it in the mouth of wisdom and consume the remainder himself. And this is to be accomplished as equal to the recitation of the eight-limbed mantra performed one hundred thousand times.

Having gone there, the Goddess Lakṣmī remains as sovereign power (*vibhūti*); she is not obstructed by any son of the gods or by Māra—that is to say, she is free from impediments. The instruction here is as follows: "By the application of the loss of the two *kūṭas*, it is remembered as *murmukuṭa*. Thus, *mu* is the root, purified by the knowledge of the two faces; *ga* is the northern [face], purified by the emptiness of causes and so forth; *ru* is the western [face], purified by the liberation of aspiration; *ḍo* is the southern [face], purified by non-abiding anywhere.

In its collective sense, he who possesses faces and garuḍas is the Face-Garuḍa, Śrī Heruka. He who practices the union with Soma (the Moon) is the Face-Garuḍa; thus it should be construed. To the question "Of what nature is he?", he says: "The creator of the emanation through the vehicle" (*yānasṛṣṭikṛt*). "Vehicle" (*yāna*) refers to the knowledge of wisdom and means; by that, "emanation" (*sṛṣṭi*) means production, and he is the "creator" (*kṛt*) of that. Of whom? He says: "of women," meaning of the yoginīs. The letter *sa* is the half-moon because it is the seed-syllable of nectar (*amṛta*). From that comes the letter *u*. From that comes the fragment, the letter *a*, which denotes the anusvāra.

The letter *a* denotes the lower horizontal staff (*adhaḥ-pārśva-daṇḍa*). The letter *ha* is the "union with Soma" (*somasaṅgama*), meaning it joins with the *soma*s (the vowels). By the combination [of *a* and *ha*], there is the syllable *hūṃ*. The *nāda* is [included] by virtue of oral instruction (*upadeśa*). One who practices that—meaning one who knows or meditates upon it—is called *nara*. Regarding the word *nara*: the root *nṛ* (as in *nṛ naye*) belongs to the *bhvādi* class; since he moves (*narati*) by beholding the Goddess in her proper place, he is *nara*, formed with the suffix *ac* according to Pāṇini 3.1.134. He is "excellent" (*śreṣṭha*) because of his leadership (*nāyakatva*). Śrī Heruka is born from that *vajra* consisting of the syllable *hūṃ* which resides within the *varaṭaka* (the central seed-syllable).
"Creator of emanation" is the collective meaning. In that regard, the Fortune held in the hand—Vajravārāhī—is not struck down by anyone between the two armors; she cannot be reached by any limb.

Thus, by being endowed with the previously mentioned procedure, one shall become a partaker of the fruit of all accomplishments (*siddhi*). By the words "from remembrance," etc., [it refers to] the power [to act] upon those situated in the human, animal, and hellish realms. Having visualized the fire—the letter *ra*—as a triangle within the fiery mandala, one generates fire through the impelling of the wind-mandala, or even spontaneously, because the power of mantra is inconceivable. Thus, it "tears asunder the underworld" (*pātāla*).

The meaning is that he mocks the multitude of serpents dwelling in the netherworld (*pātāla*), saying, "You are powerless, for he rends asunder the netherworld itself. Alternatively, it means he terrifies them. He also causes lightning (*aśani*) to fall; by the word "and" (*ca*), other specific weapons are implied. Another interpretation is that he brings down the "thunderbolt" (*aśani*)—meaning food—from somewhere at will. Regarding the word "lightning" (*vidyut*): it is in the nominative case. The emergence of lightning occurs even without clouds. It refers to the splendor or brilliance of lightning. [He does so] from remembrance—that is, from contemplation—or he produces it.

"Lightning and the shower of wealth"—the meaning is that one produces that [shower] from the syllable *HŪṂ* through recollection. The rest is easily understood. "He whose success comes from the utterance of his name": this means that for whom there is success in mantra and so forth through the mere mention of his name; the sense is that he is one who has attained extraordinary mastery over mantras. The collective meaning is that by the utterance of his name, there is success in mantra. Even such a person dies by means of the mantra recited but once; this refers to the power of the extraordinary mantras of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).

He is the enjoyer and protector of the worlds, such as the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and others; or alternatively, he is the one who expands or creates the worlds. Therefore, it says "by mere wish" and so forth. It says "this [mantra]" and so forth to show that it is accomplished even without observances (*niyama*) and the like. The connection is that this eight-syllable mantra here performs whatever action is desired. *Vrata* refers to the Great Vow (*mahāvrata*) and so on. *Caryā* refers to the state of being an Avadhūta and so forth. *Upavāsa* (fasting) is remaining for a day and night without food. For this very reason, it is said to be "accomplished by mere recitation."
The Kalpa-śāstra; therein described is the ritual procedure (upacāra), the method of performance (vidhāna), and the wandering at will (yatheṣṭavihāra). || 2 ||

If one recites it once while angry, it kills ten million; if recited with a peaceful mind, it restores them to life. If one strikes Yama with charcoal from a cremation ground over which the mantra has been recited once, he falls down at that very moment. If one strikes Yama with ashes over which the mantra has been recited, he is seized by a *piśāca* at that very moment. If one writes someone's name at night on a wooden board or a wall using charcoal from a cremation ground, that person is seized by a great spirit (*mahāgraha*).

If one strikes someone with a creeper of *atimuktaka* after reciting [the mantra] once over it, that person arrives at that very moment with the speed of the wind. If one strikes someone with sugar after reciting [the mantra] once over it, that person becomes paralyzed; he can then transfer himself wherever he desires. Having recited [the mantra] once over *guggulu* resin, if one employs it as incense, he causes all beings to enter into a state of possession (*āveśa*). Having recited [the mantra] once over his hand and covered his own mouth, he raises up one who has been bitten by a deadly snake.

By sprinkling water over which [the mantra] has been recited once while it is sealed with the ḍākinī-mudrā, one paralyzes. By means of a karavīra creeper over which [the mantra] has been recited once, one causes the embryo to be transferred to wherever one desires. || 3 ||

Now he explains the efficacy of the mantra that acts as a medicinal aid, beginning with "If," and so forth. Chewing iron dross [and saying] "I eat the head of so-and-so," while reciting the mantra once with an angry mind, one kills ten million beings. With a peaceful, non-angry mind, by wrapping [the victim's] living head [in the cloth] and unwrapping it, there is a bringing back; "jīvāpa" means the obtaining of water for life (the water of life), and to cause that is "to restore to life" (*jīvāpayati*).

On the night of the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should take a branch of the *ariṣṭa* tree located to the south that has been cut by the axe of a *caṇḍāla* or similar person; having burned it in a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*), one should extinguish the embers with the juice of its leaves and collect the ashes. Alternatively, regarding the word "cremation ground" (*śmaśāna*): it refers to ashes found in a cremation ground, the third case ending being elided. Regarding the phrase "with the embers" (*aṅgāreṇa*): this procedure is to be performed on a Tuesday using those ashes collected on a Tuesday. This is the collective meaning.

After reciting the mantra one hundred thousand times, having entered the circle of *atimuktaka* creepers, one should take a thread spun by a maiden, triple it, and wrap it around a branch of that [creeping plant] located in the western direction, which has been dyed with the juice of turmeric. Then, naked and with disheveled hair, during a lunar eclipse, one should hold it with the left hand until its release and recite the mantra continuously. Thereafter, it should be seized. It moves forward with the *agreṇa* [mantra] and returns with the *mūla* [mantra]. The suffix *-kta* in "once recited" (*sakṛjjaptena*) is used in the sense of the action itself (*bhāve*).
It is "paralyzed" through the visualization of it being yellow. The rest is easily understood. || 3 ||
He who desires the accomplishment of the knowledge of Śrī Heruka without knowing it, is like one who threshes husks while being devoid of this mantra. (4)

He says that cultivation is indeed permeated by selflessness: "Having known," and so forth. Knowledge such as "the syllable Śrī is non-dual knowledge" is the knowledge of Śrī Heruka. The word "siddhi" (attainment) is used in the nominative case for the sake of the accusative. The particle *tu* signifies excellence. The meaning is: "he who desires a distinguished, desired attainment. As for the phrase "he who threshes husks": for him, it is merely the threshing of what is pithless; for by threshing the pith, one abandons the pithless and remains in the state of the pith.

The meaning is that because he has grasped the essence from the very beginning, there is no further need for its accomplishment. He states that accomplishment occurs even without the mantra of selflessness: "devoid of this mantra," and so forth. This refers to the root mantra. Therefore, the unique nature of the mantra has been explained. (4)
A person does not attain accomplishment nor happiness if, without knowing this mantra, he desires the state of a yogin. || 5 ||

*Siddhi* means that which is accomplished or manifested directly; it is *samyaksaṃbodhi*. *Saukhya* is the bliss of the supramundane and so forth. Even one who abides in the *naya* (the method) is called a "man" (*nara*). He says, "without knowing," and so forth, because accomplishment is not achieved without the non-dual yoga of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*). *Mantra* refers to the yoga of wisdom and means. (5)
His labor will be in vain, and he shall not obtain its fruit;
this mantra, which grants all accomplishments, is for one who acts according to his own desire.
[The practitioner] need not observe vows, nor asceticism, meditation, mantras, or mudrās;

for once he has understood that which was praised by the Sugata, the practitioner indeed attains all accomplishments, including food and drink, sacrificial offerings (caru), various edibles, and the essential flavors. || 7 ||
Thus ends the ninth chapter, on the ritual procedures for the root mantra, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

His exertion, characterized by meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth, is thus in vain; such is his activity. This mantra is one of unrestrained conduct (*kāmācāra*); it is perfected through the enjoyment of the five objects of desire. For this very reason it is said: "There is no vow," and so forth. As for what that mantra is, he says: "The Sugata," and so forth. It is described and determined by the Sugatas. Having known such [a mantra], the practitioner becomes a master of the deities born of mantra, mudrā, and mantra. Regarding "khāna" and so forth: *khāna* means eating, and *pāna* means drinking, including intoxicants and what is to be drunk.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), things such as the lickable (*lehya*) and the suckable (*coṣya*) are included. *Caru* refers to what has been offered. *Bhojya* means that which is to be eaten; its enjoyment is *bhoga*. *Rasa* here means sound. By the first word "etcetera," form, smell, taste, and touch are to be understood. Having recognized these as the worship of the Self (*ātman*), the practitioner attains all accomplishments (*siddhi*). He is "one from whom all accomplishments arise. By this, neither the acting according to one's own will nor the enjoyment of sense objects is excluded; rather, the knowledge of selflessness (*nairātmyajñāna*) is thereby adorned. (6–7)
The ninth chapter, which explains the ritual procedures for the root mantra.
Thus ends the ninth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 9.
The tenth chapter on the ritual procedures for the heart-mantra of the accomplishment of the three bodies.
Now I shall explain the three bodies through the non-dual yoga of Śrī Heruka;
by the mere knowledge of which, accomplishments are attained—of this there is no doubt.

If Śrī Heruka consists of the three bodies (*kāyatraya*), then what are those three bodies? This is the question posed by [the author] himself; the word *atha* (now/then) serves this purpose. Therefore, the meaning is as follows: if you ask, "What are those three bodies?", the answer is that he will explain the three bodies. To the question "Of what nature are they?", he says: "Through the non-dual yoga with Śrī Heruka. That [three-body nature] is such that Śrī Heruka is joined (*yujyate*) with it without doubt; thus, the three bodies are so described. The suffix *-tasil* is used here from a word ending in the nominative case.

He shows that the three bodies—the three distinguished bodies themselves—are what must be accomplished here, by means of the words beginning with "by which" (*yena*). "Merely known" (*vijñātamātreṇa*) means merely understood, that is to say, directly realized; the word *mātra* is used for emphasis. "Are accomplished" (*siddhyante*) means they are perfected; the sense is that the yogis obtain the Dharmakāya and so forth as they desire. "Not here" (*nātra*) means that regarding this accomplishment, there is no doubt as to whether it occurs or does not occur. || 1 ||
When one becomes an adept regarding the bodies of the Dharmakāya—[for those who possess such excellent discernment]—then I shall proclaim that knowledge. (2)

He speaks of the means of accomplishing the *dharmakāya* with the words beginning "Dharma... and so forth. That which is both *dharma* (phenomenon) and *kāya* (body) is the *dharmakāya*; those whose body is thus are the *jinās* (Victors). When one becomes their accomplisher—that is, when one brings them to perfection—then I shall proclaim the *jñāna* (gnosis). I shall analyze and determine that *jñāna*, the *dharmakāya*, which is devoid of unity and plurality, is the domain of the Tathāgatas, is eternal by nature, and is luminous by nature. And that *dharmakāya* is the very essence of the Victor; such is the summary. Thus it has been said: "That which is neither one nor many, which serves as the foundation for the great prosperity of the welfare of oneself and others..."
Neither non-existence nor existence, like space, it is of equal flavor, its nature difficult to discern;

unstained, changeless, auspicious, peerless yet equal to all, all-pervading, free from conceptual proliferation—I bow to that incomparable Dharmakāya of the Victors, which is to be realized within oneself. (2)
When the practitioner becomes one with the bodies of the saṃbhogakāya, then I shall proclaim the enjoyment (saṃbhoga) of those who are in meditative equipoise. (3)

He speaks of the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) with the words beginning "In enjoyment," and so forth. When [the Buddha], endowed with a form that is never-tiring to behold and other such qualities, performs the teaching of the Dharma, then the Enjoyment Body is the domain of the Bodhisattvas. It is called "Enjoyment" because it is eternal by way of its continuous flow (*pravāha*). It is such because it is enjoyed—that is, taken into oneself—by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas through correct practice. And thus it has been said:

"He who, in the midst of the assembly, displays his own great and manifold majesty—which transcends the world, is inconceivable, and is the fruit of well-performed deeds—for the sake of bringing joy to the wise."

I pay homage here to that Saṃbhogakāya of the Buddhas, which is established in this great kingdom of Dharma and whose sound of the true Dharma—constantly being extracted—is spread throughout all worlds. Thus, [verse 3].
When the practitioner becomes one with the bodies of the nirmāṇakāya, then I declare that single-pointedness of mind is the nirmāṇakāya. (4)
He speaks of the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*): "The emanation [body]," and so forth. The emanation body is common to all sentient beings and is eternal by way of its continuity. Thus it is said:

"For the sake of maturing sentient beings, he appears in some places like fire while blazing in perfect enlightenment; and in other places, he is seen again as utterly peaceful within the wheel of Dharma."

I pay homage to that Emanation Body (nirmāṇakāya) of the Munis, which proceeds in manifold forms, removes the fear of the three realms of existence, reaches throughout the ten directions, and accomplishes the great purpose of beings through various means and universal manifestations. Thus, [verse 4].
One attains the wisdom, enjoyment, and emanation bodies; of this there is no doubt.
One accomplishes one's own self as Śrī Heruka; of this there is no doubt. (5)
I shall declare the heart of this mantra; listen, O secret practitioner! (6)

[The three bodies are indeed established because they are that which is to be accomplished. To explain what is meant by this, he says "knowledge," and so forth. Regarding "the venerable Heruka’s own self": the connection is that the venerable Heruka attains his very own self. How is that? He says "knowledge, enjoyment, and emanation," and so forth; here "knowledge" refers to the *dharmakāya*, and the singular number is used for the sake of conjunction (*samuccaya*). This, then, is the perfection of that which is to be attained. Furthermore, of what nature is it? He says: "the self. The maintenance of the self is called "bliss" as well, because it is the cause.

The meaning is that it has the nature of bliss (*sukharūpa*). Regarding the phrase "they succeed": this is the conclusion that those who possess the yoga of the three bodies succeed. He says "of this," and so forth, to show that the mantra of such Śrī Heruka is also of that same nature.
