The heart-mantra consists of twenty-two syllables; its purpose is also called the "heart," just as one says "clarified butter is life. To the question of what kind of person he will proclaim it, he says: "the secret practitioner" (*guhyasādhaka*).

He is so called because he accomplishes—that is, brings to perfection within practitioners—the secret three bodies (*kāyatraya*), which are the true nature of mind and so forth. You, being such as that, listen. (5–6)

By reciting the heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*), one flies up to ten million *yojanas*; one goes and comes; one assumes many thousands of forms. Having ascended palaces, trees, and celestial realms, one travels with a *ḍākinī* for ten million *yojanas*. Having gone into the sky, one returns again. By will, one is seen; by will, one is not seen. By will, one assumes the form of a child, an old man, or a youth. By will, one assumes the form of an elephant, buffalo, gayal, tiger, lion, bull, rabbit, cat, or camel.

By his will, he assumes the form of a peacock, a cock, a swan, a cakravāka, a crane, an owl, a hawk, a vulture, or a crow. He takes on whatever form he desires. He steals speech, he steals hearing, he steals sight, he steals the sense of smell, and he steals the tongue. He draws out the blood of whomever he wishes, or he causes it to be paralyzed.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, the ritual procedure for the action-mantra of the Heart of the Three Bodies, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

"Utpati" means she goes upward. "Gacchatyāgacchati" (goes and comes) means that she goes and returns from ten million *yojanas* in a mere instant; this indicates the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the speed of mind (*manojava*). Regarding "prāsādadruma": the second case ending is elided in the dual. "Bhuvaneṣu" refers to the three worlds, such as the heavenly realms (*svarga*). "Yojanakoṭī" has the second case ending elided. "Ḍākinī" indicates her delight (*rati*). In that very same way, having gone through the sky, she returns again. The remainder is easily understood.

[Regarding the passage beginning with "rūpam" (form), he provides the explanation for the ninth section indicated—namely, "by will, a child," and so forth. A "yauvana" (youthful) person is one who possesses youth, or one who is simply young. This refers to the capacity [of the mantra] according to age. By the phrase "by will, an elephant," and so forth, the form of an animal is assumed. By "by will, a peacock," and so forth, the form of a bird is assumed. Thus, its capacity as a being of the animal realm has been stated. By the phrase "of whom," and so forth, its capacity to assume a general form is indicated. The remainder is easily understood. Regarding the phrase "he causes to stiffen": it means that passion and the like are paralyzed. Or, the word "vā" (or) is used to include what has not been explicitly mentioned. || 7 ||
The tenth chapter, which explains the accomplishment of the three bodies and the ritual procedures for the activities of the heart-mantra.
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*.
The eleventh chapter, on the ritual procedure for the characteristics of seven births.
Now I shall describe another [method] by which a practitioner may attain success;
by merely consuming it, swift accomplishment proceeds. (1)

Now he speaks of the power of the heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*), which acts as a companion through seven births, beginning with the words "atha" and so forth. "Atha" (now/then) signifies a conjunction. "I shall explain another application of the heart-mantra for seven births. Alternatively, the meaning of the word "atha" is that it follows the inquiry of the petitioner: "What are the medicinal applications of the heart-mantra? To the question "Of what nature is this application?", he says "the practitioner" (*sādhaka*) and so forth. The connection is: "I shall explain that application by which one attains accomplishment (*siddhi*)."

By merely smelling it—that is, by the mere act of olfactory perception—the accomplishment of knowing seven lifetimes arises quickly. The sense is that, in brief, the accomplishment of that knowledge occurs. || 1 ||

That person from whose perspiration a fragrant scent emanates, who speaks the truth, blinks slowly, is free from anger, and whose breath is sweet-smelling, will be born as a human being for seven lifetimes. Having consumed him, *rocanā* (yellow pigment) appears in his heart. Taking that, one makes a *tilaka* mark with the heart-mantra of Śrī Heruka recited one hundred and eight times; [by doing so], one flies upward.

One hundred thousand recitations of the mantra should be performed; by this, one travels for ten million *yojanas*. By merely consuming that [substance], one becomes a knower of the three worlds. Having traveled fifty million *yojanas*, one returns within a single day and night and attains a divine body. Whoever knows the heart-mantra of Śrī Heruka obtains whatever desires he may wish for. || 2 ||
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the procedure for the characteristics of one who has seven births, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 11.

"Of which person" means that the mass of merit exists in the form of that person. "Sugandhagandha" refers to the perspiration whose scent is like that of incense, *kaśa*, *tūrya*, and so forth. The rest is easily understood. It should be known that he who speaks the truth and remains free from anger for a long time [is such a person]. The phrase "his breath is endowed with fragrance" uses the neuter gender (*niśvāsam*). He whose breath possesses fragrance is born from seven births as a human being.

"Born in human form through seven successive births" means born as the best among humans; or, it may mean "born in the human [realm]. He states the purpose for using the sign of the scent in the passage beginning with "it is brought," and so on. It should be understood that "having smelled it, it is to be known. To the question "What is that?", he says: "Of that," and so on. For by its fragrance, *rocanā* (yellow pigment) is inferred, since it is produced from it; this is because it does not belong to another birth. With the words beginning with "that," he states the purpose of the *rocanā*: "A recitation of one hundred thousand times is to be performed."

"It travels ten million yojanas" means that it ascends a path measuring ten million yojanas. "Fifty crores" refers to yojanas. Because the heart is a divine body, it is called the "divine-body heart. Whatever desires the practitioner wishes to bestow, those it bestows. (2)
The eleventh chapter, which explains the characteristics and the ritual procedure for [attaining] seven births.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 11.
The twelfth chapter: The Ritual Procedure for the Upahṛdaya.
Now I shall declare the Upahṛdaya mantra, which accomplishes all siddhis;
whatever may exist in the three worlds, it shall accomplish all that in an instant.
"Then," and so forth. "Then" means immediately after the explanation of the procedure for the heart-rite (*hṛdayakarma*). The remainder is easily understood. || 1 ||

*ṭpha hūṃ hūṃ ha ha hrīḥ oṃ*. This is the *upahṛdaya* (near-heart) of the heart-mantra. By reciting this mantra one hundred thousand times, one causes even the three worlds to tremble; one attracts gods, dānavas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, nāgas, gandharvas, and kinnaras; and one dries up and paralyzes rivers, oceans, ponds, and the like. In whatever place one recites it, all the ḍākinīs become the servants of the practitioner.

Having consecrated water with this mantra, one washes one's own eyes; then one knows seven lifetimes. One sees even those whose life-span has ended as if they were dead, and one sees those with long lives as being alive. Having empowered the eye with this mantra, whomever one looks upon becomes paralyzed. || 2 ||

*ṭpha hūṃ hūṃ ha ha hrīḥ oṃ*. *Oṃ hrīḥ ha ha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—this is the mantra that has been made straight. This is the "sub-heart" (*upahṛdaya*) of the Heart [mantra]. The prefix *upa-* signifies "inferiority. It is inferior to the Heart mantra by way of its syllables, but not in terms of its efficacy. Or, it means "proximity. "Of this" refers to the recitation of the syllables of the sub-heart; and that recitation consists of one hundred thousand [repetitions]. By the words beginning with "O God," the capacity for summoning is stated. A "pond" (*taḍāga*) is a lake; and [the mantra] "paralyzes" it.

The immobilization of water (*jalastambhana*). Regarding the phrase "in that place": it refers to where one recites the mantra seven hundred thousand times. "They become servants" means they do not create obstacles; this is due to the power inherent in the mere act of recitation (*jāpa*). "By this" refers to the seven-syllable mantra-vidyā. "Water" refers to the efficacy of water acting as a cooperative factor for medicinal herbs. "Seven births" refers to seven past and future lifetimes. From the point "having consecrated the eyes," the word "water" is no longer applicable. || 2 ||

Taking the skin from the sole of the foot of a hero who has died a natural death, grind it with human blood; place *srotoñjana* in the middle of a ball [of that mixture] and saturate it with *manaḥśilā*, *gorocanā*, saffron, and blood. Drying it in the shade, wrap it in the three metals (*triloha*), perform the consecration (*adhivāsana*) again, and prepare it under the asterism of Puṣya. Having placed it in the mouth of Śrī Heruka and covered the mouth with the left hand, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times more. At that very moment, he becomes invisible and his shadow vanishes.

It is not seen even by the gods, much less by insignificant humans; thus, it is seen when removed from the mouth. In this tantra, this pill for the accomplishment of moving through the sky (*khecarīsiddhi*) was spoken by Vīra himself. It is the heart and near-heart mantra of Śrī Heruka. (3)

He speaks of the efficacy for accomplishing the pill (*gulikā*) with the words beginning "vīra... and so forth. "The skin from the sole of the foot of a *vīra* [corpse]" means that one should grind it with the blood of that human; having ground it, [one places it] "in the middle of a *gokala*"—the sense is that it should be made into a ball (*piṇḍī*). "Srotāñjana" means "stream-born collyrium. "Manaḥśilā, rocanā, and kuṅkuma"—this is a case of the elision of the second case ending.

The collective meaning is as follows: having impregnated realgar (*strotāñjana*), red arsenic (*manaḥśilā*), and so forth with blood, one should place them inside that ball (*golaka*), dry it in the shade, enclose it within the three metals (*triloha*), and then cause it to be prepared—that is, accomplished. Furthermore, "he" refers to the yogi who has recited the mantra seven hundred thousand times. Regarding "having consecrated" (*adhivāsya*): having visualized the wheel-bearer of the Heruka maṇḍala within that ball encased in the three metals, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times at twilight; this is the consecration (*adhivāsanā*). And "by Puṣya" means:

It may also be done by means of other auspicious constellations and so forth. He states the method of accomplishment: "Of Śrī Heruka," and so on. The practitioner of Śrī Heruka yoga, having placed that pill—which contains the mandala-circle—within his own mouth, should recite the mantra as prescribed. Then it will be as stated:
"The māṣas for gold, the moon, and the sun are measured at four, three, and four [units] respectively;
the sequence for binding the pill is increased by twenty-seven raktikās."

Thus is the rule for the three metals (*triloha*). The remainder is well-established. To the question, "Of whom is that which is this *upahṛdaya* (near-heart mantra) the *hṛdaya* (heart mantra)? he says: "Of Śrī Heruka," and so forth. "Of Śrī Heruka" refers to *oṃ kara kare*, etc. (3).

With this mantra, using the tip of the index finger, one should scrape the skull of the head until it is free of flesh and impurities; thus one extracts its blood. By rubbing with the left hand (the reverse direction), it enters back again.

Having consecrated it, a blow of the fist should be dealt upon the skull. For whomever one performs this by name, that person suffers a headache. Recalling the mantra, one should fill the skull with milk; it brings about pacification.

Having recited the mantra over *gorocanā* (cow-gallstone), one should apply it as a forehead mark (*tilaka*); whoever one looks upon becomes sealed [paralyzed]. Having recited the mantra over the index finger, whomsoever one threatens with it, he falls down at that very instant. Having recited the mantra, if one strikes the ground with one's foot while uttering someone's name, that person dies at that very instant. Having consecrated water with the mantra, if one sprinkles the ground, one brings them back to life again.
With the tip of the index finger over which the mantra has been recited, one may threaten even a thousand people; all who see this become paralyzed, yet one releases them by means of speech.

Having consecrated the ashes of a Caṇḍāla by reciting [the mantra] one hundred times, if one strikes someone while recollecting [the deity] Yama, that person becomes possessed by his form. Having consecrated the ashes from a sacrificial fire by reciting [the mantra] one hundred times, if one strikes someone, that person cannot even be seen by the gods. One should strike with water over which the mantra has been recited seven times; then the person is seen again.

Having formed the *kapāla-mudrā* (skull-seal) and joined it together, one should recite the mantra without breathing, while enraged, in the name of whomever [one intends]; that person becomes insane at that very moment. Even a thousand people may be made insane. One releases them by means of the mind alone.

Having consecrated a lock of hair ten times with the name of whomever one desires, if one binds it [to that person's head], all the ḍākinīs will come. Having gone to a deserted place, one should bind the lock of hair after reciting [the mantra] a hundred times. Without opening the eyes, one should continue reciting until one becomes invisible; when the lock is released, one is seen again.

Having consecrated a sugar-cake (*śarkaroṭā*), one should throw it upward, downward, in the cardinal directions, and in the intermediate directions; all gods, asuras, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, kinnaras, and mahoragas will then be bound. It takes away the yoga of all *ḍākinīs*. Having seen a woman or a man on a bed, seat, or couch, one should recite the mantra one hundred times; it causes them to become attached. Liberation occurs through the mind. Having recited over a sugar-cake and thrown it into rivers, it causes them to flow against the current.
With that very same sugar-cake, one arrests the waves. One should revolve the mantra with the mind.
Looking upwards, one should recite it a thousand times; this wards off heavy rain.

Having performed the recitation a thousand times while facing an enemy army, one may enter into battle. Even when being struck by hundreds of weapons, no pain arises, nor is one pierced even by thousands of weapons; one’s body becomes like adamant. 4.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, concerning the ritual procedures for the subsidiary heart-mantra, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 12.

"By this," and so forth. "Head-skull" (*śiraḥkapāla*) is a word without a case ending; and that is indeed a skull. "Fleshless" (*nirmāṃsa*) means that its flesh has been pierced away due to the piercing of the veins. "Upādhi" refers to the body; thus, it is "fleshless" and it is also the "body" (*upadhi*), hence it is "fleshless-body. Having made or caused the body of the target (*sādhya*) to become such, one "grinds" or "crushes" it. How? He says: "with the index finger. With the right [hand], and with its tip. And this is to be understood through meditative visualization (*bhāvanā*).

Taking a human skull-cup, the practitioner in the yoga of Vajrarudra emanates Khaṇḍarohā, who holds a weapon in her hand, from within his own right nostril through the utterance of the syllable *hūṃ*. Having caused her to pierce the five heads of the victim by calling upon his name, he visualizes the skull-cup being filled with that person’s blood. Then, with the tip of his index finger and the mantra recited seven times, he draws out all the fleshless blood from within the victim’s body; this is the collective meaning. He explains the method of bringing [the victim] back with the words beginning with *ava* and so forth.

By means of the tip of the left index finger, through the state of a peaceful mind, because of the churning of the interior of that body, the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*) becomes one whose body is completely filled. Why? He says: "it enters. Because of the entry of that very blood. "Having consecrated" refers to the head of the one to be accomplished. A blow with the fist should be administered with the visualization (*bhāvanā*) of a skull-cup. This is because, through the visualization of a skull-cup, there is the filling of the skull-cup along with its contents, and because of the direct filling of the interior of the skull-cup. "Chanted with mantra" is an adverbial modifier. The rest is easy to understand.

"‘All the ḍākinīs come’—here, ‘ḍākinī’ is used with the elision of the nominative plural ending. ‘Śarkaroṭā’—here, ‘śarkarā’ is used with the elision of the accusative ending. ‘She removes all the yoga of the ḍākinīs’—by means of that very *śarkarā* (sugar/gravel) cast in the cardinal and intermediate directions. ‘Bed’ (*śayana*) means sexual intercourse. For that purpose, she has gone to or stays upon a seat or a bed; thus she has come even to the ‘bed-seat’ (*śayanāsana*). The word ‘or’ (*vā*) in ‘that woman or’ is a conjunction. Regarding ‘or in battle,’ the word ‘or’ (*vā*) carries over from ‘*śarkaroṭā*’. (4)

The "Upahṛdaya" refers to the Upahṛdaya mantra; the chapter that explains its ritual procedure is the twelfth chapter on the ritual procedure for the Upahṛdaya. Thus ends the twelfth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 12.
The thirteenth chapter: The Ritual Procedure for the Application of the Armor-Mantra (Kavaca-mantra).
Now, I shall describe the ritual application of this armor exactly and in due order:
whatever exists in the three worlds, and whatever may be desired by the mind—[all that].

Now, immediately after the explanation of the *upahṛdaya* mantra and its ritual procedure, the ritual application (*karma*) of the *kavaca*, that is, the *kavaca* mantra, will be described. The mantra is: "Oṃ ha, namaḥ hi, svāhā hūṃ, vauṣaṭ he, hūṃ hūṃ hoḥ, phaṭ haṃ. Regarding the phrase "in due order" (*anupūrvaśaḥ*): it refers to the sequence for demonstrating the efficacy of recitation (*japa*), medicinal herbs (*oṣadhi*), and so forth. To the question "What is that?", he says: "The three worlds," and so on. "All that which is desired by the mind" means whatever is longed for by the mind. (1)
In that regard, while reciting the *kavaca*, one may travel on the road; there shall be no fear from thieves, tigers, and the like.
While reciting the *kavaca*, upon entering a royal court or a place inhabited by women, one remains unseen; having taken whatever one desires, one departs, and even by the gods one is not seen.

Whomever one touches with a hand that has recited the *kavaca* becomes paralyzed as if by a stake (*śūla*); even by the thirty-three gods (*tridaśa*), he cannot be moved. Having recited the mantra, if one strikes [the victim] with the foot, there is liberation.

Having applied a forehead mark (*tilaka*) made of one's own blood or one's own semen over which the mantra has been recited three times, one draws out the blood of everyone with whom one speaks, whom one looks at, and those who look at him.

If one recites it a thousand times while possessed by anger in someone's house, a fever arises for everyone there. If one throws water over which the mantra has been recited five times, it brings them back to health.
By looking into someone's face and reciting the mantra, one steals their speech.

Standing by a river or a pond, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times; then one may walk upon the water. Just as on dry land, so too does one move upon the water. Having entered the water, one remains even in a river or the ocean. Reciting it a thousand times while rising up with both hands, the *yoginīs* become submissive. || 2 ||

The meaning of the passage beginning with "the armor" (*kavaca*) is as follows: for one who travels on a road while reciting the *kavaca*, there is no fear from thieves and the like. One may enter the royal court, that is, the king’s palace; and yet, one is not seen. Where is one not seen? He says: "in the precincts of the courtyards" (*aṅganādhiṣṭhāne*), which means in the inner apartments (*antaḥpura*). For here, indeed, others employ subtle scrutiny toward men; even there, one is not seen—this is the power of the mantra.

"Taking whatever pleases him, he goes out"—the connection is that as he goes out taking whatever object from the treasury that pleases him, he is not seen. Here too, because of his ability to perceive many subtle things, it is impossible for him to be perceived; such is the power of the mantra. "He is not seen even by the gods"—for although the vision of the gods is unimpeded even with their physical eyes (*māṃsacakṣus*), since he is not seen even by them, this is due to the power of the mantra. "Like a stake" means like something driven into the ground.

Because of its entry into the distance, it becomes motionless. "One's own blood," and so forth, is easy to understand. In the phrase "whose house," the word "there" (tatra) is to be supplied. "Yoginīs" is a case of the elision of the nominative plural ending. || 2 ||
And the Yoginīs of various forms, as well as the Ḍākinīs, Lāmās, and those with the forms of Khaṇḍarohā and others, are thus proclaimed. (3)

All become submissive and follow his will. Having prepared a cloth-painting during the conjunction of Puṣya, one who has covered his body with it and entered into union with the Yoginīs should recite the mantra ten thousand times; then he becomes accomplished. With his body covered by that, he becomes invisible in the sky for a thousand *yojanas*. He goes wherever he desires; he wanders over the earth as far as the oceans, or he travels upwards against the current. || 4 ||

The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and indeed the *yoginīs*" is used in the sense of the first case (nominative). The particle "and" (*cakāra*) serves to aggregate the various divisions; "indeed" (*eva*) is for emphasis. He states their manifold forms with the words "Ḍākinī," and so forth. "Ḍākinī" refers to the classes of Ḍākinīs; "Lāmā" refers to the classes of Lāmās; "Rupiṇī" refers to the classes of Rupiṇīs. Regarding the term "ūrdhvastrota": etymologically, it means "those who go by the upward stream. There is an elision of the letter *s*. The meaning is that they come by not transgressing the flow of the river in reverse order.

Alternatively, another interpretation is that when the bodhicitta is stabilized within the jewel [of the secret organ], the yogi directly arrives at and realizes the innate (*sahaja*) state by way of the upward stream. (3–4)
Whatever sense faculty should enter the path, each and every one, by its very nature,
should carry forth everything as consisting of the Buddha through the yoga of supreme absorption.

Pointing out the enjoyment of the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañcakāmaguṇa*), he says "that which," and so forth. One should go—that is, enter—the path or domain of the sense faculties, such as the eye and the rest. Whatever [practice] there may be, such as recitation (*jāpa*) and so on, one should carry—that is, experience—all of that as being composed of the Buddha, consisting of Vairocana and the others. To the question of how one experiences it through action by way of its intrinsic nature, he says: "by means of the yoga of supreme absorption" (*paramāhitayogena*). This refers to the yoga, namely meditative absorption (*samādhi*), which is applied or directed toward the Supreme, Śrī Heruka.

Vairocana is in form, Akṣobhya in sound, Ratnasaṃbhava in smell, Amitābha in taste, and Amoghasiddhi in touch; thus, one possesses the nature of all Buddhas. The intended meaning is that the mantra should be recited through the enjoyment of the five qualities of sensual pleasure. || 5 ||

Taking the juice of the *pārijāta* tree in one's hand and having recited [the mantra] a thousand times, if one applies it as a tilaka-mark on someone, that person becomes a tree. If one sprinkles [someone] with water over which the mantra has been recited seven times, this is the method for restoration. Taking dust from the sole of an elephant’s foot and having recited [the mantra] a thousand times, if one strikes someone with it, that person becomes an elephant. || 6 ||
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, the ritual procedure for the armor-mantra, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 13.
Regarding "pārijāta," *pārijāta* refers to *bhadradala* and so forth; the remainder is easily understood. || 6 ||

The "application of the armor-mantra" (*kavacamantrayoga*) is the application [of mantras] by dividing the armor-mantra. That which prescribes this very [application] is the chapter (*paṭala*); thus, it is "the thirteenth chapter.
This concludes the thirteenth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 13.
The fourteenth chapter: The procedure for the transformation into Śrī Herukī through the yoga of the donkey-form.
Now I shall explain that sādhana by which practitioners achieve success—the self-nature of the yoga of the donkey-form, for the sake of bringing the impulse of the mind to rest. (1)

The word *atha* has the sense of "furthermore. The connection is: "I shall again state the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) for the heart-mantra. To the question "What is that?", he says: "By which," and so forth. The meaning is: that by which practitioners achieve success is the means of accomplishment. To the question "For what purpose?", he says: "The speed of the mind," and so forth. The "speed of the mind" refers to the kingdom of the mind (*manorājya*); its cessation occurs because [the goal] has been accomplished. To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of the yoga of the form of a donkey. This means: because of the yoga of the form of a donkey. (1)

The Yoginīs Lāmā, Rupiṇī, Ḍākinī, and Khaṇḍarohā, as well as the Yoginīs who can assume any form at will, Gardabhākā, Rudhiravaktrā, and the Ḍākinīs encircled by tridents, have been accomplished. One may see even one whose life has ended as long-lived, yet in this case, the yogi sees a fine donkey. Then, he sees the donkey and the elephant; whichever form one brought forth in a previous birth, that very form is seen here by the yogi.
That man shall be a bestower of success; he is a human being who has reached the seventh birth. By him, the bali-offering and homa must be performed, and thus the practitioner attains accomplishment.

With the words "the Yoginīs" and so forth, he speaks of the deities of the maṇḍala: "The Yoginīs" refers to those who abide in the three wheels (*tricakravartinī*). "Those who take on forms at will" (*kāmarūpiṇyaḥ*): because they have faces like those of donkeys and blood-red in color. Therefore it says, "and those with donkey-shaped blood-red faces," due to the elision of the nominative plural ending. Likewise, regarding "the Ḍākinīs": apart from the four-faced ones beginning with Kākāsyā, all the Ḍākinīs are characterized by having donkey-shaped [faces]. "Encircled by tridents in their hands."

Having discarded the *khaṭvāṅga*, in its place there are thirty-six divine yoginīs bearing tridents; their colors follow the sequence of the sādhana itself. One is oneself possessed of the yoga of Śrī Heruka, who has a donkey face and from which blood flows. By this it is stated that the distinction lies in having a donkey face from which blood flows. All else is exactly as described in the sādhana. When is this so? He says: "when accomplished" (*sādhitā*). The meaning is that this sādhana is to be performed when the heart-mantra has been recited seven hundred thousand times.

It is stated according to the oral instruction (*upadeśa*): having drawn the mandala of the support (*ādhāramaṇḍala*) with red powder (*rajas*), one should meditate upon the syllable *hūṃ*, surrounded by the fifty letters, in the center of its eight-petaled lotus. On the four petals in the cardinal directions are the heart and near-heart mantras of the Blessed Lord and the Blessed Lady. On the petals in the corners are four skull-cups (*kapāla*) filled with blood. On the twenty-four spokes are the twenty-four mantras beginning with *oṃ khaṇḍakapālini hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*.
"Oṃ kara kara pracaṇḍe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ," and so forth; thus, when combined with those of Khaṇḍakapāla and the others, as well as Pracaṇḍa and the others, there are forty-eight mantras in total.

Within the root mandala, there are the eight [deities] beginning with Kākāsyā; above that, at the four gates, are the four mantra-words of Sumbha; outside the enclosure wall, above the gates and at the junctions of the *niryūha* (turrets), are the two *kavaca* mantras; in the circular wind-rim (*cakravāta*), the heart-mantra of the Bhagavatī is placed; and externally, one should visualize an encircling of the seed-syllables of Pullīramalaya and so forth, such as *puṃ* and the rest. Inside the circle, having placed an image made of rice-flour in the form of a donkey, smeared with oil and lac, and anointed with clarified butter—

Possessing the yoga of Heruka with a donkey’s face and flowing blood, having lit lamps in the four corners and reciting the heart-mantra with one-pointed concentration, one should gaze at the effigy. Then, regarding the instruction "one should see it as described," he says: "one whose life has departed," and so forth. The word *api* (even/also) is used in the sense of possibility. Regarding the phrase *asmin tu*: the word *tu* is for the purpose of restriction; it means when this very procedure has been performed. Regarding the term *sugadarbha*.

If the donkey were previously a yogin, then he would perceive himself as a donkey. The word *hasti* ends in the vowel *i*. He says "of whom," etc., to show that [the yogin] perceives even the genus (*jāti*) of another; here, "of whom" refers to a human being or similar creature, which is the "being" (*sattva*). The genitive case in "of the yogin" (*yoginaḥ*) is used in the sense of the instrumental. By this, he states that the perception of seven births is easily attained—starting with "he," etc. The *balihoma* (oblation) is to be performed; intending to perform it, by that very act, the yogin becomes one who performs the *balihoma*.

He asks "Why? and says: "It succeeds for the practitioner. Wherein [the practice] succeeds for the practitioner who has seven births remaining, according to the stated sequence. "Yoga" is without a case-ending; the meaning is that this is the *gardabhayoga* (donkey-yoga). || 2 ||
Likewise, he ascends a hundred thousand yojanas upward in an instant;
this is the supreme yoga of the excellent mantra, the practitioner of which accomplishes the yoga of the ḍākinīs. (3)
Whoever recites the sign of yoga for one month attains success;
this is the secret of the tantra, the supreme heart of the mantra.
He who knows this in its true essence is a yogi; of this there is no doubt.
This is the Heruka hero for you, the *Saṃvara* of the *Ḍākinījāla*. 5.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, the procedure for the transformation into Śrī Herukī through the yoga of the donkey-form, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

"Mantravara" means the supreme mantra; it is the yoga because it acts in conjunction with the heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*). It is the same even when the reading is "mantradhara. It is "excellent" (*śreṣṭha*) because it accomplishes what is desired. "Ḍākinī" refers to Vajravārāhī. Yoga with her is the means for accomplishing the vision of previous births; the sense is that one has attained union with her. The passage beginning with "yoga" is easy to understand. Regarding "the secret" (*rahasyam*): it is the essence of this tantra. To the question "What is it?", he says: "the heart" (*hṛdayam*), which is the heart-mantra.

To whom does the "heart" belong? He says: "of the mantra," that is, of the King of Vidyās (vidyārāja). That one who knows it in its true essence as non-different from Śrī Heruka, the King of Vidyās, is the yogin. In the reading "of knowledge" (jñānasya), he is the yogin of mere knowledge who knows the heart. "This is the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*" refers to Śrī Heruka, since the gender [of the word] is not restrictive. This very thing is joined; by means of this, the state [of being] is concentrated (samādhīyate) in the mind. In the reading "eṣate," the verbal root *eṣ* has the sense of "going. It should be explained as: "he attains (*eṣate*), he reaches, the knowledge of the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*. (3–5)

That by which one becomes Śrī Heruka is "becoming Śrī Heruka" (*śrīherukīkaraṇa*); the ritual procedure for becoming Śrī Heruka through the yoga of the donkey-form is the "means of accomplishment" (*sādhana*), and the chapter explaining that is the fourteenth.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 14.
The fifteenth chapter: The Ritual of the Code of Syllables (*Akṣarachomma*).
Now, therefore, I shall explain the secret signs (*chommaka*) within all the vows;
he who knows them in their true essence attains accomplishment, without a doubt. (1)

The word *atha* signifies a conjunction (*samuccaya*). The word *ataḥ* signifies a reason (*hetu*). It is not only he who knows the heart who is a yogin; what then? He is also one who knows the *chommakas*. Since one might ask for what purpose the procedure of the *chommakas* connected with yoga is intended, he says: "In all the *saṃvaras*. This means: for the sake of those *saṃvaras*, which are the protections (*rakṣaṇa*) of all [beings] such as men and others that are to be concealed from the Śrāvakas and so forth. || 1 ||
The syllable *ḍā* is known as the male, and *ḍī* is therefore [the seed] of women;
*ṣu* signifies immobilization, and *su* signifies devouring. || 2 ||

By what means is the apprehension of the connection [established]? He states those very [means] with "Ḍā" and so forth. "Smṛtaḥ" (remembered) means: it was conventionally designated by infinite Tathāgatas. Regarding "Ḍī," it refers to women; this is the application of the verbal root *ḍīṅ* in the sense of "moving through the sky. "Tataḥ" means from that, because in reality there is a connection (*anvaya*). The form *ḍī* is established by the elision of the suffix (*kvip*). It is said that "it flies" (*ḍīyate*), meaning it pervades everything. Regarding "Ṣu," this word is conventionally designated for "stiffening" (*stambhana*); it is like the word *ḍitha* (or *ḍittha*) used for a particular type of tree.
The word "su" signifies both eating and so forth; its conventional meaning is joined by the two words "ca" and "eva," and is thus distinguished. || 2 ||
*Mā* is known as the mother; *ye* is indeed the wife;
*bhī* is likewise the sister; and *vī* is proclaimed to be the female friend. || 3 ||

*Mā* is known as the mother; the meaning is "like a mother. *Ye* refers to the wife; the meaning is that she is indeed a distinguished consort (*kalatra*). *Bhī* is known as the sister; this is according to the literal sense. *Vī* is celebrated as the female friend (*sakhī*); that is, the beloved one (*preyasī*). || 3 ||
*Lu* is to be known as the daughter, *strī* as blood;
*so* is the drinking of *sīmā*, and *pe* is likewise that which is to be drunk. || 4 ||

*Lu* means "daughter," that is, one's own offspring. *Strī* (woman) is to be understood as blood, that is, *rakta*. *So* means "drinking soma," that is, drinking nectar (*amṛta*). *Pe* means "drinkable," and *tathā* (thus) means "that which is to be drunk," namely a liquid substance; the word *tathā* indicates that it is a convention established by way of a partial expression. || 4 ||
*Hī* indeed refers to meat; *bha* refers to eating;
*bhū* refers to the gathering (*melāpaka*); and *pī* likewise refers to the cremation ground (*śmaśāna*). || 5 ||

*Hī* means "flesh," that is, meat itself; *bha* means "eating," that is, consuming; *bhū* means "meeting place" (*melāpaka*), which is a specific location for the assembly of yoginīs; and *pī* means "it would be a cremation ground" (*śmaśāna*), that is, the abode of corpses. || 5 ||
"Hū" is known as Mṛtakā; "dhī" is remembered as Yoginī;
"ga" is likewise Lāmā; and "trī" is indeed Rupiṇī.

"Hū" is known as the corpse; the Yoginīs know it as the dead body. "Dhī" is remembered as the Yoginī, because she possesses meditative absorption (samādhi) due to her non-dual nature. "Ga" is likewise [known as] Lāmā; the various classes of Lāmās are thus designated by this convention. "Trī" is indeed Rupiṇī; the meaning is that the various classes of Rupiṇīs are likewise designated by this convention. || 6 ||
*Ku* is known as Ḍākinī; *hā* is indeed Khaṇḍarohā.
*Ja* is the pair of shanks, and *ka* is the pair of arms. (7)

*Ku* refers to *ḍākinī*; thus it is said, "so be it," because the various classes of *ḍākinīs* are likewise designated by that convention. *Ḍā* refers to Khaṇḍarohā; *vāyi* refers specifically to the classes of Khaṇḍarohās. The word *ḍā* also has a double meaning. *Ja* refers to the pair of shanks; it denotes the two shanks. This is a convention based on a single part [of the whole]. (7)
"Bha" is the salutation; "su" is the act of welcoming.
These single-syllable secret signs (*chommaka*) are to be known as belonging to the Hero's Sisters (*vīrabhaginī*). || 8 ||
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, the Chapter on the Ritual of the Syllable Gesture (*akṣarachoma*), in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 15.

"Bha" is the greeting; it is a salutation. The word "bha" has two meanings. "Su" is the act of welcoming; it means performing a welcome. All these syllables are used without case endings and so forth. And these are the *chommakas* consisting of single syllables; that is, those which have one syllable each. "But she is to be known as the Hero’s Sister (*vīrabhaginī*). The "heroes" (*vīra*) are the yogins; the "sisters" (*bhaginī*) are the yoginīs. The particle "tu" (but) is for emphasis. "She" (*sā*) refers to those *chommakas*, because they are established as a convention in their plurality.

The nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental. They are to be known by the heroes (vīras) and the yoginīs, because they are members of that secret linguistic convention (*saṃketa*). Alternatively, the *chommakas* are twenty-four syllables, corresponding to the purification of the twenty-four yoginīs. || 8 ||

The *akṣarachommakāḥ* are the secret signs (*chommakāḥ*) consisting of single syllables. The method for explaining them is the "method of the *akṣarachommakāḥ*. The fifteenth chapter, which expresses that [method], is the fifteenth.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 15.
The sixteenth chapter: The Procedure for Examining the Characteristics of the Seven Yoginīs.
Now, O practitioner, I shall proclaim the secret great accomplishment;
those who abide in the supreme commitment are worthy and provide pleasing assistance.

Now, immediately following the syllable *atha*, I shall explain the "Great Secret Siddhi"—the great accomplishment of certainty (*mahāniścayasiddhi*) for the secret yoginīs. The meaning is that I shall explain it by way of its varieties and distinctions. The word *ha* is a poetic ornament (*vākyālaṅkāra*), since indeclinables have multiple meanings. Regarding the phrase "for the practitioner" (*sādhaka iti*), this is the dative case expressed in the nominative. To the question "Which are the yoginīs denoted by the word 'secret'?", he says: "The supreme," and so forth. The "supreme commitment" (*paramasamaya*) consists of color, fragrance, and other such qualities.

"Abiding" means having remained for a long time. To the question "Of what nature are they?", he says: those from whom pleasing assistance arises for practitioners are the "Yoginīs who provide pleasing assistance. (1)
This should be given to a devoted disciple by the non-dual yogi who has mastered the distinctions between the castes;
by the mere knowledge of which the practitioner shall attain perfection. || 2 ||

To explain for whose sake this is so, he says: "for the devotee" (*bhaktāya*). This means for those characterized by service (*sevā*). Therefore, the sense is that one must exert effort to know them. Expounding upon the *samaya*, he says: "the letters" (*varṇa*), etc. The particle "tu" is for the purpose of restriction. Establishing that restriction, he says: "the heroes" (*vīra*), etc. The connection is as follows: I shall proclaim that knowledge of the letters and so forth, without which the two types of heroes cannot attain the direct realization of *siddhi* among the hosts of Yoginīs.
The sense is that when known by an external practitioner, they bestow such a *siddhi*. || 2 ||
But that woman who is as pale-white as a lotus stalk, whose eyes are as long as lotus petals, who always delights in white garments, and who possesses the fragrance of fresh sandalwood; (3)

He states the defining characteristic with the words beginning "mṛṇāla" and so forth; it is easy to understand. "Nava" refers to the well-known *gośīrṣa* sandalwood. She possesses the fragrance of fresh sandalwood, thus she is called "navacandanagandhinī. || 3 ||
She who delights in the assemblies of the Sugatas should be known as one born of a noble family and lineage;
she is a woman with the luster of molten gold, who is fond of red and yellow garments. (4)
Possessing birth and a singular fragrance, she follows the heroes;
she is dark as a blue lotus and fond of one who wears blue garments. (5)
She who possesses the beautiful fragrance of a blue lotus and follows Śrī Heruka is indeed that woman who is truly beautiful and has a complexion like the petal of a white lotus. (6)
Mṛṇālagandhā and likewise Vīramatī are always present;
as is the woman who is reddish-fair, with a red face and a beautiful form.
She possesses the fragrance of jasmine and blue lotus and is born of the Vajra family;
she is a woman of yellowish-dark complexion who is fond of wearing white garments. (8)
She who has the fragrance of *śirīṣa* flowers on her head and follows the lineage of the Tathāgatas, and that woman who is reddish in color and wears garments of that same color— (9).
Karpūragandhā always follows the Vairocana family.
These seven families of yoginīs have been described by me. (10)

And she delights in the assemblies of the Sugatas (*saugata*). She whose family (*kula*) and lineage (*gotra*) are those of Hayagrīva is *śauṇḍinīkulagotrā*; because she is born from her, there is the form *kulagotrajā* with the short vowel. Vīra is Ākāśagarbha; his follower is Cakravarmiṇī, who is so called because she is born from that family. "Followed by Śrī Heruka" means followed by the Suvīrā family. "Vīramatī" means followed by the Vīramatī family. The Vajra family is the Vārāhī family.

The Tathāgata is Padyanarteśvara; because one is born from him, there is the "Tathāgata family" (tathāgatakula), which is the Great Power (mahābala) that follows it. "By me" means by myself. "For the sake of firm conviction" (*abhisaṃpratyayāya*): the particle *tu* indicates immediate succession. (4-10)
Those who are constantly devoted to the left-hand practice (vāmācāra) are indeed filled with their own mudrās and colors;
for the syllables of the family-mantra (kulavidyā) consist of six letters. || 11 ||

The women are beautiful; their conduct consists of extreme anger, egoism, and so forth. The word *hi* is used as a conjunction. These are the people of the Yoginīs. Again, asking what they are like, he says: "By their own mudrās"—meaning color, such as white and so on—and "by their complexion," such as being as pale-white as a lotus stalk (*mṛṇāla*); they are "crowded with" or connected to these two. And "the syllables of the family-vidyā": the family is the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and his vidyās are themselves the syllables; because of their firm resolve (*adhimokṣa*), they are the Yoginīs. The sense is that these goddesses possess an immovable form.
"There are six colors" means that the six types of colors of the Yoginīs are to be known; "hi" (indeed) is used as a particle of conjunction. || 11 ||
For she binds her own mudrā and speaks speech born of her own lineage;
that woman who goes on the left, the Yoginīs always [follow] from the left. 12.
He who speaks with great eloquence, gazes with a leftward glance,
and laughs joyfully at women— he is called a *samayin*.

He says to them: "binds," and so forth. He describes the binding of the mudrā: "with the left," and so forth. [This means] with the left hand of the yoginīs; that is, the yoginīs are on the left. Regarding the speech born of her own lineage, he says: "speech," and so forth. One who speaks greatly—that is, one whose nature is excellent speech—is a *prabhāṣī*. The particle *vai* is used in the sense of *vā*, meaning "or" or as a conjunction. Because his nature is to laugh joyfully, he is a *hṛṣṭaprahāsī*. The particle *ca* is as before.

*Samaya* is the rule that must not be transgressed; one who possesses this is called a *samayin*. Although the term refers to a man in relation to the community of *yoginīs*, it may also be used out of disregard for gender distinctions, as this is merely one way of classifying them. (12–13)
She who fulfills the desires of women is proclaimed as one of noble lineage;
she does not abandon the family traditions nor does she forsake that which is taught in her own scriptures. || 14 ||
He who recites the vidyā of his own family is called a *samayin*;
for he who, having performed a salutation, always bows with his left side bent. (15)
He should engage in conversation with women; indeed, they [respond] to him with their true feelings.
With her left big toe, she draws upon the good ground, tracing a footprint with her foot.
One should scratch the head with the left hand while looking askance;
for that practitioner, the recollection of one's own vidyā is beneficial in this regard. (17)
Placing a finger on the cheek, the chin, or the nose, and reciting the mantra once while casting a sidelong glance, one should gaze upon the Vidyā;
thus the Yoginīs truly attain a state of sincere devotion toward those who observe the pledges (samayins). 18.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, the procedure for examining the characteristics of the seven yoginīs, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

The genitive case in "strīṇām" (of women) is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). "Families" (*kulāni*) refers to the practitioners (*sādhakāḥ*); these very families are the "seeds" (*bījāni*), meaning the causes for proclamation. By means of them, [the teaching] is spoken after having been analyzed. "Family-activity" (*kulakriyā*) is the conduct of the observance (*samayācāra*). "Family-knowledge" (*kulavidyā*) is the family-deity. That which is taught in one's own scripture—that is, taught in the system of Mantra—is what is being designated; this is the second [point]. Regarding the phrase beginning with "namaskāram" (homage), it says: "by means of true states, they indeed... (*sadbhāvaistastā tāḥ khalu*).

By recognizing these characteristics, the practitioner should indeed show true devotion toward such yoginīs through prostrations and other such acts; this is the third [point]. "With the left thumb" means with the foot. "Drawing" means that which is drawn again and again should be understood as the manner of the class of yoginīs; this is the fourth [point]. "One should scratch one's head" means it should be done with the hand; that should be known as the manner of the class of yoginīs.

"Always following": this means it is beneficial for the practitioner (*sādhaka*) within his sphere. Having seen her who is thus constituted, it is appropriate for that practitioner to remember the *vidyā*; the sense is that he should regard her as his own *vidyā*, like his own chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). Why? He says: "beneficial in the sphere. For such a sphere leads to dignity. The locative case is used in the sense of the nominative; such is the fifth [explanation], the aggregate of meanings. Or, *gaṇḍa* refers to the mandala, or it is used in the sense of conjunction. The particle *api* expresses possibility. "A sidelong glance" (*tiryagdṛṣṭi*).

The sixth [point] is that a woman who casts a sideways glance with her fingers placed upon her chin and other such parts should be known as belonging to the class of *yoginīs*. Having seen them thus, what should be done? He says: "Reciting the mantra once, one should cause the *vidyā* to gaze. The "mantra" is the King of Vidyās (*vidyārāja*). To the question "What is accomplished by this?", he says: "The true state," and so forth; this is easy to understand. (15–18)

"Saptayoginī" (the seven yoginīs) is an elliptical designation; it refers to the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all six as well. There are thirteen yoginīs. "Lakṣaṇa" means a mark or sign. The examination of the characteristics of the seven and six yoginīs is called "Saptayoginīlakṣaṇaparīkṣā," which is a compound formed by the elision of the middle term (*madhyapadalopī-samāsa*). The sixteenth chapter (*paṭala*) is that which sets forth the procedure for this.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 16.
The seventeenth chapter, on the ritual of signs and mudrās, in the section concerning the forms of all Yoginīs; following that:
"Yoginīs as well as Ḍākinīs are indeed difficult to find."
Because of the true presence of the five nectars, she is Yāminī and Trāsanī. || 1 ||
The seven Ḍākinīs—Kāminī, Bhīmā, Rupā, Sañcārā, and Bhāsurā, along with the others—are here subsumed; their own specific characteristics are now stated. (2)

Immediately following the description of the characteristics, he speaks the seventeenth chapter, beginning with the words "Then they are difficult to find" (*tato durlabhā*). In the phrase "of the yoginīs, [namely] the ḍākinīs," the genitive case is used in the sense of the nominative. Thus, the yoginīs are the goddesses. The particle *tu* (but/then) serves to indicate a distinction. Regarding the term "yoginīs": ḍākinīs, māniṣīs, and yoginīs are those who follow the qualities of a yoginī; this is the meaning. Therefore, there is the phrase "and likewise. To the question "Why?", he says: "Because they are difficult to find."

The meaning is that because they possess the qualities of goddesses, these *ḍākinīs* are difficult to encounter. If this is so, how are they encountered? He says: "Because of the true presence of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). The meaning is that they remain present for the practitioner who makes use of them.

He states the characteristics of the ḍākinīs: "The seven ḍākinīs—Yāminī, Trāsinī, Kāminī, Bhīmā, Rupā, Sañcārā, and Bhāsurā—are subsumed. The meaning is that these [ḍākinīs] beginning with Yāminī are "subsumed," which is to say they are briefly declared as seven. "Their own characteristics are stated here" means that their names are stated by way of explaining these characteristics through positive concomitance (anvaya). || 1–2 ||
Rūpikā, Cumbikā, Lāmā, Parāvṛttā, Sabālikā, Anirvṛttikā, and Aihikī—these are known as the seven Ḍākinīs. || 3 ||
One should observe her who is not dispassionate and who raises her eyebrows;
she first withdraws her form and afterwards brings about destruction.
She should be known as Rūpikā, who, when served by a hero,
kisses the boy while embracing him, whether he is pleasing or displeasing.
She should be known as Cumbikā, a ḍākinī who destroys all evil;
she glances askance with a frowning face and threatens with a knitting of her brows.
Otherwise, Niḥśvāsa Bhairava has designated Lāmā as follows:
the boar, the śarabha, the cat, the jackal, and so forth; the goat and the horse. (7)
Then she should terrify them all; for when she has turned away, she is said to be "Parāvṛttā" (the Averted).
When she has gone away delighted and laughs, she does not return again. || 8 ||
She who laughs clearly when [her lover] is attached is indeed known as Khaṇḍarohā;
she whose mind is agitated [uses] a hand, a clod of earth, or a foot [to strike him].
If he is touched by her with the edge of her garment, or with a piece of wood, he does not survive;
one should know him to be beyond recovery, for she is declared incurable.

He also states their alternative names along with their lineages: "Rupikā, Cumbikā, Lāmā, Parāvṛttā, Sabālikā, Anirvṛttikā, and Aihikī—the goddesses, the Ḍākinīs, are remembered as sevenfold. He states the definition of Rupā, whose other name is Rupikā, beginning with "aviraktām" (one who is not detached), etc. "Vīrādvayasevitum" means one who serves the non-duality of the Hero (vīra).

He states the definition of *Yāminī*, whose other name is *Cumbikā*—beginning with "or desired" (*iṣṭaṃ vā*) and so forth. And as for *Ḍākinī*: the sense is that she is the destroyer of the multitude of *ḍākinīs*. For this very reason, *yama* means restraint; *yāma* is derived from that by adding the suffix *aṇ* in its own sense. She who possesses that is *Yāminī*, because she effects destruction. He states the definition of *Bhīmā*, whose other name is *Lāmā*—beginning with "sidelong glance" (*tiryagdṛṣṭi*) and so forth. Regarding "they threaten" (*tarjayanti*): the plural is used for the singular; the meaning is exactly that.

Otherwise, even Bhairava, though attached to desire, would [only] breathe with great effort; *tu* here denotes a distinction. Therefore, she who delights especially (*viśeṣeṇa ramate*) is a *rāmā*. Because of the substitution of *la* for *ra*, she is a *lāmā*. Due to the conjunction of these two characteristics, she is indeed a *bhīmā-lāmā*. He states the definition of the *trāsanī*, also known by the name *parāvṛttā*: "the boar," and so forth. A *śarabha* is a specific kind of beast. In the reading *śarabhā*, however, it means a dog. "She should terrify them all" means that they are afraid at the sight of her; therefore, she is the *parāvṛttā*.

The word *hi* is used in the sense of "because. That [movement] from which others turn back is thus described; because of this, he states the definition of *sañcārā*, who is also known by the name *sabālikā*: "exultant," and so forth. It is called *sañcārā* because she does not return again. He states the definition of *kāminī*, who is also known by the name *aihikī*: "spoken to with affection," and so forth. She is *khaṇḍarohā* because she ascends—that is, stands—again and again upon a *khaṇḍa*, meaning an unbroken spot. Because of this, she is *aihikī*, as she remains for a long time in this particular place.

He states the definition of the *bhāsurā*, which is also known by the name *anivartikā*: "distressed in mind," and so forth. That which is called *bhāsurā* or *anivartikā* becomes distressed in mind; and a sentient being touched by such [a spirit] with a clod of earth or the like does not live. It is "irreversible" (*anivartyā*) because it is impossible to turn back. Why? He says: "for it is incurable" (*asādhyā hi*). The word "hi" (for) indicates the reason. (3-10)
She laughs, speaks, or weeps, and becomes angry without cause;
she is known as the goddess Aihikā, who speaks first.
She who delights in the assemblies of the Sugatas is born from the Vajra family;
one should recognize the families of the Ḍākinīs here as being great speakers. (12)
The skull, the axe, the fangs, the saw-banner, and the sword-terrorizer,
along with the conch as the eighth— these are remembered and proclaimed as the family mudrās.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, the section on the ritual of the insignia and mudrās, in the transformation of the forms of all yoginīs within the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 17.

"One should recognize the families of the ḍākinīs here as the great heroes" means that the yoginīs beginning with Vāyuvegā and ending with Mahāvīryā are the families of those beginning with Yāminī and ending with Aihikā. *Ḍākinī* and *yoginī* have the same meaning. In the alternative reading, "one should recognize the families of the ḍākinīs as the seals (mudrās) to be served by the heroes," it means that the families of the aforementioned ḍākinīs are indeed the mudrās; the yoginīs themselves are Vāyuvegā and the others. One should recognize them, that is, know them. "To be served by the heroes" means "those who serve the heroes"; the second case ending is used here due to the elision of the plural number.

"Skull, axe, fangs, discus, saw, banner, sword, and the terrifying [mudrā]—these are the eight. The word "and" (ca) serves as a conjunction. "Fangs" refers to boar-teeth. "Saw-banner" refers to having disheveled hair. The eighth is the eighth mudrā. Among these mudrās, whichever one belongs to any particular ḍākinī; in another reading, it is "skull, axe, fangs, sword, and the terrifying [mudrā]. Here, "sword" is without a case ending, and "terrifying" refers to the knife (*kartī*). Thus, there are exactly five mudrās.

And this—namely, the transformation of the yoginīs' forms, the gazing with undimmed passion and so forth, the mudrās such as the skull-bowl, the ritual procedure, the purpose, the knowledge of the yoginīs, and their characteristics—is [the subject matter].
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 17.
This is the eighteenth chapter, the procedure for the colors, characteristics, and symbols of all the yoginīs.
Now, furthermore, I shall proclaim another supreme state of the ḍākinīs.
By means of which one correctly understands the ḍākinīs who abide in the commitment (samaya). || 1 ||

Regarding the word *atha*: the connection is that immediately after the description of the transformation of form and so forth, I shall next explain the "pada," which means the sign (*cihna*). It is called a *pada* because by it the *ḍākinī* is reached or understood. To the question "Of what kind?", he says "by which" and so forth. The nominative case in *ḍākinyaḥ* is used in the sense of the accusative. || 1 ||
For that woman who is reddish-fair in complexion, who emits the fragrance of a lotus, who possesses a gentle gaze, and whose very nature is one of affectionate appearance; || 2 ||

He states the verse beginning with "raktā" and so forth. "Padyagandhagātrā" means one whose body emits the fragrance of a lotus (*padya*). "Saumyadṛṣṭiḥ" means because she is free from frowning and the like. "Saṃraktadarśanā tu yā" means because she is characterized by extreme affection. In the reading "saṃraktanayanānugatā," it means one who is endowed with reddened eyes. || 2 ||
For that woman whose nails and eyes are likewise reddened,
and who has the verse inscribed in her home, she is born of the lineage of Padyanarteśvara.

Regarding the phrase "The nails indeed" (*nakhā hi*): the particle *hi* is used in the sense of emphasis (*adhikārtha*). The meaning is that the nails are exceedingly red. Because this occurs in the context of passionate attachment (*saṃrāga*), the reading "a lotus design has been drawn" (*cihnaṃ padyaṃ likhitaṃ padyam*) is easily understood. It should be known that the Lord of the Dance of the Lotus (*padyanartteśvara*) is Amitābha, and [these women] are born from his family (*tatkulodbhavā*). || 3 ||

One should always worship the trident located between the eyebrows, which is dark blue with a white body, as it is constantly meditated upon in the Vajra family; indeed, one should always worship the vajra drawn in the house.
She from whom a trident and indeed a spear are seen upon the forehead should be known as Vajraḍākinī, born from the family of Śrī Heruka. (5)
Red-eyed, reddish-white, and likewise with red feet and hands,
she who is constantly cultivated always delights in goats or even in cocks.
One should constantly worship the vajra, her sign, in that house;
there is no doubt that the ḍākinīs born of the Śrī Heruka family [reside] there. (7)
She whose discus is seen on her forehead and also in her hand, who is dark-complexioned like a rain cloud, and always wears a turban upon her forehead; || 8 ||
She who is endowed with great good fortune, virtuous, and most excellent—
she indeed in whose house the drawn wheel is always worshipped.
Born from the family of Vajravārāhī, this ḍākinī is proud of her strength;
she is dark as black collyrium and possesses high, white teeth. (10)
She who is both cruel and constantly perverse, yet endowed with inner strength;
she who is always devoted to bathing and does not speak excessively. || 11 ||
The auspicious vajra, when inscribed, is constantly worshipped in the home;
fifteen thousand [beings] born from the family of Vajravārāhī [are thereby honored]. 12.

The trident located between the eyebrows is a limb having the form of a trident; she is dark-complexioned with a pale-white body—that is, one whose body is both dark and pale. A vajra is drawn in her own house; one should worship that house. "Tu" signifies certainty. She is to be known as necessarily born from the family of Śrī Heruka. "Vai" is a particle used for emphasis or as an alternative. "Api" expresses possibility. "Hi" indicates excellence. "Rakta" and so forth: *chāgala* is simply *chagala* (goat). *Satatatā* means continuity or uninterruptedness.

"Ḍākinī" means ḍākinī. "On the forehead" (lalāṭa) means "in the middle of the forehead," as is to be understood from the word "tu. The particle "hi" is used for emphasis. By the word "forehead" (lalāṭa), the hero's cloth (vīrapaṭa) is meant. "Sādhvī" means a woman with one husband. "Paratarā" means most excellent. "Daśanonnatā" means having prominent teeth. "Vāmā" means she who delights in the wrong path. She is born from the family of Vajravārāhī. As to how many there are, he says: "ten times five thousand," meaning fifteen thousand yoginīs. (4–12)
A woman who is fair-complexioned like gold, as well as one with fixed eyes and hairy [brows], or one on whose forehead or even in whose hand a thunderbolt is seen; || 13 ||
Having ascended the throne, she was ever proud and truthful;
she possessed the fragrance of jasmine, and the great thunderbolt inscribed upon her was constantly worshipped. (14)
Khaṇḍarohā, born of the Kula, is the supreme Great Mistress of Yoga;
she who is eternally fond of meat, thirsty, and has the luster of black collyrium. (15)
She whose forehead has the shape of a trident, who is devoted to cruel deeds, and who constantly goes to the cremation ground, fearless and pitiless; (16)
She upon whose forehead a trident and a skull are drawn, who is worshipped in the home—that ḍākinī is born of the family of the god Śrī Heruka. (17)
A woman who has the color of a cloud, whose teeth are unevenly set, who is constantly engaged in cruel deeds, and whose left canine tooth is prominent; || 18 ||
She in whose house an axe is kept and constantly worshipped is undoubtedly a Ḍākinī born from the lineage of Vināyaka. (19)

From the words beginning with *gaurī* up to *vare*, the characteristics of her who has arisen from the *Khaṇḍarohā*-family are described. She whose fragrance is like the scent of a jasmine flower is "jasmine-scented" (*mallikāmoda*). From the words beginning with *māṃsapriyā* up to *ḍākinī sā kulodbhavā*, the characteristics of her who has arisen from the *Śrīheruka*-family are described. From the words beginning with *jīmūta* up to *na saṃśayaḥ*, the characteristics of her who has arisen from the *Vināyaka*-family are described. "With teeth set unevenly" means having irregular teeth. *Vināyaka* is the enemy of obstacles (*vighnāri*). (13–19)
This characteristic, arising from the family of Śrī Heruka, has been proclaimed for the benefit of practitioners as a sign belonging to the host of Ḍākinīs. (20)
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, the procedure for the colors, characteristics, and signs of all yoginīs, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

This has been proclaimed as the defining characteristic of the host of ḍākinīs, for the benefit of practitioners born from the family (*kula*) of Śrī Heruka. This characteristic pertains to the host of ḍākinīs. To the question "Of what kind [of practitioners]? he says: "born from the family of Śrī Heruka," which is a form without case endings (*nirvibhaktika*). The family is Śrī Heruka himself; it refers to those who have arisen from that. There is a protracted pronunciation (*pluta*). Words such as *ca* (and) and so forth should be understood as having the sense of conjunction and the like.

The characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and families (*kula*) are not mixed; rather, as they were correctly brought down by the mind in the sixteenth [chapter], the seven yoginīs are described by means of color, scent, and so forth, along with their families. By means of ritual action alone, there are six. In the seventeenth [chapter], there are seven by means of the utterance of names and so forth, and by signs such as the skull-bowl (*kapāla*). Here, however, there are eight by means of color, scent, and so forth, along with the signs and the associated families. In total, there are twenty-eight. The word "all" (*sarva*) refers to the entirety of the section. (20)

That which prescribes and explains the colors, characteristics, and symbols of all eight Yoginīs is the "Chapter on the Rules for the Colors, Characteristics, and Symbols of All Yoginīs"; thus ends the eighteenth chapter.
This concludes the eighteenth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*.
The nineteenth chapter: The Procedure for Teaching the Mudrās and Counter-Mudrās of All Yoginīs.
Now I shall further explain specifically regarding the Lāmās, so that the practitioner may correctly understand their bodily limbs and parts. 1.

*atha* (now) signifies a collection of characteristics. *aparam* (another) refers to the characteristic of the *lāmās*, meaning the yoginīs belonging to the *lāmā* class. *tu* is a particle used for poetic ornamentation (*vākyālaṅkāra*). *viśeṣataḥ* (specifically): the general characteristic of those born from the families of *lāmā* and so forth has been stated; now, that which belongs specifically to those of the *lāmā* class is being declared—this is the distinction (*viśeṣa*). Because it exists as a constituent part, it is a "limb-characteristic" (*avayavalakṣaṇa*); the connection is: "I shall correctly proclaim that.
In the reading *sādhaka* (the practitioner), although the dative case is elided, because it serves that purpose, even when the nominative is used, it carries the sense of the dative. || 1 ||
Her face is seen to be broad and circular;
there is always a beard upon her face, and her eyebrows are long and hairy.
Clad in white garments, pure, gentle, unshakeable, and speaking with courage—she who is ever devoted to the true Dharma is to be known as the Heroic Sister (Vīrabhaṭṭārikā). || 3 ||

He states the defining characteristics, beginning with "the face" and so forth. "Circular" means round. "Hairy" means having abundant hair. "With a bright garment" means wearing a stainless cloth. "Pure" means stainless. "Unshakeable" means possessing firm resolve. "Sister of the heroes" means a *yoginī*. In the alternative reading "sisters of the heroes," the plural number is used despite the singular sense. (2–3)
The Padya-mudrā or alternatively the Kūrma-mudrā should be presented;
likewise, the deer-skin and the water-pot are prescribed as the counter-gestures (pratimudrā). || 4 ||

Having seen her, he says that the *mudrā* should be offered: "The lotus," and so forth. The *padya-mudrā* (lotus gesture) arises from the contraction of the fingers held in the *añjali* position. Or else (*athavā*), which indicates an alternative; furthermore, it serves as a poetic ornament (*vākya-alaṅkāra*). Having extended the right hand and raised it up, one should place the left hand, which is contracted, upon it; this is the *kūrma-mudrā* (tortoise gesture). Regarding "the deer skin and the water-pot": the deer skin is represented by the gesture of holding with the left hand the hem of the garment draped over the left shoulder.

Some say [the gesture of] the sacred thread is from the gesture of wearing it; the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) is from the gesture of holding a water-pot. *Ca* is used for certainty and emphasis. One should show the deer-skin (*ajina*) to the one who takes the lotus-gesture (*padya-mudrā*), and the water-pot to the one who takes the tortoise-gesture (*kūrma-mudrā*). From showing the gestures of a Yoginī, the gestures of a Yogin are the counter-gestures (*pratimudrā*). || 4 ||
The tenth lunar day is her festival, and a verse concerning her is written in her home;
this is the characteristic mark of those who have attained prosperity.
Long-lipped and large-eyed, with reddish-brown eyes,
she is wealthy, fortunate, blessed, fair-complexioned, and resembles the campaka flower.
Neither short nor excessively long, she is fond of variegated garments;
and there are three lines on her forehead extending to the upper hairline.
He laughs and indeed takes delight, remaining fixed upon the path;
he always delights in stories of those who have died in battle.
Having seen such a young woman, one should cause the Śūṣma-mudrā to be presented;
moreover, one should display it while dancing with the left foot contracted. || 9 ||
The reversal is performed with the left hand, and the counter-seal (pratimudrā) is prescribed;
the fourteenth and eighth days of the lunar fortnight are prescribed as her festivals (parvan).

Regarding the term *śriyāṇām*, it is due to the addition of a phoneme (*varṇāgama*). *Śrī* refers to Vajravārāhī; *Śrīheruka* is joined with her, and the yoginīs born from him are the *śriyas*. "Lamboṣṭhī" and so forth. Another [author] says: "with the left foot contracted"—the meaning is that one should display the *ardhaparyaṅka* dance posture. "Turning away" means becoming averted. These two constitute the counter-seal (*pratimudrā*). "Parvan" is an auspicious time; on such parvans as the fourteenth day, one performs worship to the Tathāgatas, the Ācāryas, and others. (5–10)
One should constantly worship her, or have her trident depicted in the house;
this is the characteristic mark of the Lāmās, the mistresses of the world (lokeśvarīs). || 11 ||
She whose two dimples are always visible on her cheeks, who is perpetually reddish-fair in complexion, and whose eyes are greenish-brown; || 12 ||
Likewise, his hair is curled, his head is bound with a silk cloth, and a single line is clearly visible established upon his forehead. || 13 ||
She has a long neck and is likewise tall; she is constantly fond of red garments;
she laughs and sings, and she becomes angry for no apparent reason. (14)
Her mind is especially fickle and she takes delight in quarrels;
seeing such a woman, one should display the Śaktimudrā. || 15 ||
The bell-mudrā should be offered with effort as the second;
however, the counter-mudrā is prescribed by means of the left hand in its reversal.
She has short and thick calves;
she always loves yellow garments and wears her cloth draped over her shoulders. (17)
Upon seeing such a woman, one should display the face-mudrā;
the conch-mudrā should also be offered with effort as the second. (18)
A reversal is performed with the left hand, and the counter-seal (pratimudrā) is prescribed;
on the fourteenth lunar day, which is a festival, a vajra is to be drawn in his house.
This is the characteristic of those who possess the essence of Śrī Heruka:
she is hairy on all her limbs and has dark-brown eyes. (20)
Karālī, Vikṛtā, Ghorā, Sthūlāsyā, Sthūlavaktrā, Lamboṣṭhī, Kṛṣṇavarṇā, Koṭarākṣī, and Bhagnanāsikā. || 21 ||
One who is constantly skilled in the arts of music, cloud-colored, and captivating—having seen such a woman, one should cause the seal of the Naga to be bestowed upon her. || 22 ||
The Śakti-mudrā should be offered with effort, and indeed the second [mudrā] as well;
furthermore, the counter-mudrā (pratimudrā) is prescribed by means of the left hand.
The eleventh day (Ekādaśī) is her festival, and her fang is drawn in the house;
this is the characteristic mark of the Lāmās of Vajravārāhī. (24)
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, the procedure for the instruction on the seals (*mudrā*) and counter-seals (*pratimudrā*) of all yoginīs, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

[This refers to] the *lokeśvarīs* of the Amitābha family. "The hollows at the junction of the cheeks" means the depressions on both the temples (*kapola*). In some readings, it appears as *kapolagaṇḍa*; in that case, *kapolagaṇḍa* simply means the temple. One should hold the index finger raised by pressing all the other fingers together with the thumb; this is the *śaktimudrā*. The *ghaṇṭāmudrā* is performed by the gesture of ringing a bell. Of these two mudrās, one should be displayed.

With the words beginning with *hrasva*, he states another [mudrā]: she whose nature it is to hang a corner of her garment from one shoulder is the *skandhavastrāvalambinī*. Having formed the vajra-añjali, having raised the two middle fingers, having encircled the two ring fingers with the two index fingers, and having straightened the two thumbs, one should hold that near the face; this is the *mukhamudrā*. Having contracted the three fingers beginning with the little finger of the upturned left hand, and having joined the index finger and thumb, one should extend them; this is the *śaṅkhamudrā*.

Raising the left hand and placing the right elbow upon it, one should hold the right hand with the three fingers [middle, ring, and little] contracted and the thumb and index finger extended; this is the *nāga-mudrā*. The second is the *pratimudrā* (counter-seal). Therefore, it is said: "The second is the *pratimudrā*; 'second' and 'counter-seal' (*pratimudrā*) are synonyms. Thus, the characteristics of the five *yoginīs* belonging to the *lāmā* family have been described. By means of the totality, the characteristics of the thirty-two *yoginīs* are established through the observation of their respective characteristics and mudrās.

The specific distinction is that "the counter-seal (pratimudrā) should be given. The meaning of the words beginning with "tu" (*but/however*), which has not been explicitly stated, is to be inferred by oneself. || 11-24 ||

By means of the mudrās and counter-mudrās (pratimudrā), he states the summary meaning of the chapter, beginning with "sarva" and so forth. The word "sarva" is as before. The mudrās of all five yoginīs and the counter-mudrās of the yogins toward them—their instruction, that is, their exposition—is that by which this chapter is established; thus it is so called. It is the nineteenth, provided the letter *ta* is elided. 19.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. || 19 ||
The twentieth chapter: the ritual procedure for the hand-gestures and secret signs of all the Yoginīs.
Now I shall explain another [matter], the secret sign (*chommaka*) of the left hand, by which one correctly recognizes a brother as well as a sister.

In the fifteenth [chapter], the code of syllables (*akṣarachommaka*) was taught; here, however, he speaks of the code of hand gestures (*hastachommaka*), beginning with "Now" (*atha*) and so forth. "Now" (*atha*) means immediately after the explanation of the seals (*mudrā*) and counter-seals (*pratimudrā*). "Another" (*anyatama*) refers to the connection: "I shall explain another code, namely the code of hand gestures, following the code of syllables. Regarding "the left hand" (*vāmahasta*): it is called the "code of the left hand" because it is accomplished by means of the left hand. By the word "and" (*tu*), it should be understood that he will also explain the code accomplished by the right hand. The alternative reading, "Henceforth I shall proclaim the characteristics of the *ḍākinīs*," is easily understood. || 1 ||
She who shows her left hand has said, "I salute you. She who shows her ring finger has said, "I return the salutation. || 2 ||
She who strikes her belly signifies, "We are hungry";
she who shows her forehead signifies, "I have come from the sky. || 3 ||
She who inserts her finger into her mouth has said, "I am eating";
she who licks her tongue has said, "I have eaten. || 4 ||
She who touches the knee has said, "I am weary";
she who touches the tip of a finger has said, "I have rested. || 5 ||
She who makes her teeth grind together has said, "I shall devour you";
she who displays a frown has said, "I am bound. || 6 ||
She who shows the "teacher" (guru) gesture has said, "I am liberated. She who shows a fist, to her one should show the *paṭṭiśa* weapon.
She who shows her hair, or looks at something deformed, or shows her nail—him he should show a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga). || 8 ||
To her who shakes a limb, one should show two teeth;
to her who makes a sound with hand against hand, it is said that the offering (bali) should be eaten. || 9 ||

He states the secret sign (*chommaka*): "The left hand," and so forth. The particle *tu* is used for emphasis. "I salute" means "I pay homage"—this is what is being said by her. Regarding "the ring finger": it refers specifically to the left hand; the particle *tu* here serves to distinguish it. "She with whom one should strike" implies both the belly and the tongue—this is the meaning of the word *tu*. It should also be understood that "one should show [it]" applies everywhere as something she says. "Come from space"—the phrase "is said" is to be supplied here. "One should insert a finger."

The meaning of the word *tu* (but/however) is that it should be understood as "in the mouth. Regarding the phrase "she who touches the knee": *tu* here denotes a distinction. Because she has come from somewhere and touched the knee, she says, "I am weary"; this is what is expressed by the statement "I am weary," which is based on the mention of a specific location. And likewise, in the case of feminine and masculine genders, there is generally a common expression regarding the private parts and so forth. Regarding "the tip of the finger": where one touches the tip of a finger with a finger, the meaning of the word *tu* is stated specifically; therefore, in this context, that same meaning applies.

"Garuda" refers to the tip of the nose. "Paṭṭiśa" refers to the left hand in the shape of a hero's turban-band; one should display this at the forehead. "Hair" refers to that [forehead] because of the activity of the left hand there. "Deformed" refers to the deformity of the gaze with a frown. By the word "and" (ca), the syllable *hūṃ* is to be understood. "Displaying a khaṭvāṅga" is the symbolic gesture (*abhinaya*) of holding a khaṭvāṅga staff. This is the convention for shaking a limb; here, there is an absence of activity of the left hand.

Having formed two small fists with the two little fingers, one should place the two vajra-fists upon the two mouth-bindings; this is the *dvidaṃṣṭrā* (two-fang) mudrā, so called because it possesses two fangs. "The offering (*bali*) is to be consumed" means that the offering is the worship itself; the meaning is that the offering is to be enjoyed. In all instances, the activity belongs solely to the left hand. (2–9)
She who displays her right hand means "Do exactly so";
she who touches her ear means "It must be brought under control. || 10 ||
