She who scratches her nails with her nails means it is said: "I am being led away as one dead. She who scratches the ground means it is said: "Today I enter the maṇḍala. || 11 ||
She who touches her chin has said, "My son must be protected";
she who scratches the ground with her left big toe has said, "My elders must be protected. || 12 ||
She who opens her eyes means "do exactly so";
she who licks her lips means "sleep well. || 13 ||
One should display all those [mudrās] which belong to the female messengers (dūtīs). || 14 ||
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, the procedure for the conventions of the hand-gestures (*hasta-mudrā*) of all the yoginīs, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

He explains the *chommaka* (secret sign) of the right hand—“the right,” and so forth, which is easy to understand. “The left,” and so forth: with the thumb of the left hand. “The eyes” is the convention (*saṅketa*). Their activity may be performed in any manner whatsoever. Regarding the phrase “those which,” etc.: certain characteristics of the female messengers (*dūtī*) in the form of *mudrās* have been described; the meaning is that when these are displayed by the Yoginīs, the practitioners (*yogins*) should offer the counter-seal (*pratimudrā*). [“One should show them all”—this means the counter-seals. Since this statement is permeated by the underlying intention (*bhāva*), it must be understood specifically. (10–14)

The word *sarva* (all) is a term denoting generality. That which prescribes these hand-gestures (*hasta-mudrā*) and secret signs (*saṅketa*) for all the Yoginīs, and which is a chapter (*paṭala*), is the "Chapter on the Procedure for the Hand-Gestures and Secret Signs of All Yoginīs," the twentieth, the very twentieth.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the *Śrī Cakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 20.
The twenty-first chapter on the procedure for the characteristics of the mudrās of the limbs of vision.
Now, I shall proclaim the characteristic of the great secret of vision:
when a woman touches the crown-lock (śikhā), one should show her one’s own head.
To her who shows her forehead, one should show the cheek;
to her who shows her tooth, one should show the tongue.
To her who shows her lips, one should show the chin;
to her who touches the neck, one should show the belly. (3)
To her who shows her two hands, one should show the arm;
to her who shows the three joints of the neck, one should show the earth. || 4 ||
To her who shows her breasts, one should show the chin;
to her who shows her belly, one should show the navel. || 5 ||
To her who shows the secret [organ], one should show the male organ;
to her who shows the thigh, one should show the anus. || 6 ||
To her who shows her knee, one should show her shank;
to her who shows her feet, one should show her sole.

Regarding the word *atha*: the connection is that immediately after the hand-seals (*hastamudrā*), "I shall proclaim the characteristics. He asks what kind of thing those [characteristics] are for the Yoginīs, and says: "the great secret of vision" (*darśanamahāguhya*). It is so called because the Yoginīs are great secrets for the sake of being seen. The "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is the nature of touching the crest-lock (*śikhā*) and other parts. Regarding the reading *athāto hyaṅgamudrāṇām* found in some manuscripts: *atha* is as before; the meaning of the word *ataḥ* is "because the Yoginīs are known by means of the characteristic."

The word *hi* is used for emphasis. Those [deities] whose limbs are touched and so forth are the *Aṅgamudrā-yoginīs*. As for "she who touches the crest" (*śikhām*), the defining characteristic is merely the touching of the crest or tuft of hair. Regarding "the head": the demonstration is simply the touching with the hand. The same applies elsewhere. "She should show what has been shown" means she should show [her teeth] by opening her lips with her hand. Regarding "the tongue": the tongue is likewise [to be shown]. Regarding "the triple-junction" (*trikaṭikā*): it is the knot connecting the two buttocks. Regarding "the earth": [it refers to the ground].

The meaning is that one should display the earth-touching mudrā (*bhūsparśamudrā*). "Secret" (*guhya*) refers to the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*). "Apāna" refers to the downward path. "Tala" means the sole of the foot; this is easily understood. (1–7)
To her who shows a finger, one should show a fingernail;
to her who shows the earth, one should show the sky. (8)
To her who shows the sky, one should show the sun;
to her who shows a river, one should show the ocean. || 9 ||
These are the limb-mudrās of the ḍākinīs; there is no doubt about this.
By displaying these, one should always cause the secret ones (guhyakas) to attain perfect vision. 10.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, the procedure for the characteristics of the mudrās of the limbs of vision, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

One should display the earth with the earth-touching mudrā alone; its indication in the sky is by means of a downward circling motion. [The sun is indicated] by looking upward. The river mudrā is the gesture of drawing a line in the sky with the hand in the shape of a river. The ocean mudrā is made by both hands trembling in the sky. (8–10)

The *darśanāṅgamudrālakṣaṇa* refers to the characteristics of the limb-seals (*aṅgamudrā*) as seen [in this context]. That by which these are prescribed is the chapter (*paṭala*), and thus it is the twenty-first chapter on the procedure for the characteristics of the limb-seals as seen.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 21.
The twenty-second chapter on the rules for the characteristics of the special mudrās.
Hereafter, I shall explain the limb-mudrās according to the ritual procedure,
by which one may specifically recognize a brother or a sister.
If one shows a single finger, it means "Welcome";
if one shows two fingers, it means "A very warm welcome. || 2 ||
These are proclaimed as the limb-mudrās (aṅgamudrā) of all the yoginīs.
One should know the eye-mudrā (netramudrā) by means of two fingers forming a needle.
The practitioner of mantra should display that [mudrā] with the index finger slightly curled;
at that very moment, O Guhyaka, she comes under control for as long as life lasts.

"Beyond this" means: after the description of the mudrās such as the touching of the crest-lock (*śikhā*), the connection is "I shall explain the limb-mudrās (*aṅgamudrāḥ*). To the question, "Since those [other mudrās] have already been explained, what is the use of these?", he says: "Specifically. The meaning is that they are the limb-mudrās specifically. This remains true even with the alternative reading: *athātaḥ saṃpravakṣyāmyaṅgamudrā yathāvidhi*. Here, *atha* is used in the sense of conjunction; *ataḥ* means "specifically. "A very welcome [gesture] with two fingers" refers to the showing of the index finger (*tarjanī*) and the middle finger (*madhyamā*).

"These are proclaimed as the limb-seals (*aṅgamudrā*) of all yoginīs. The meaning is that the limb-seals are common to all yoginīs. In an alternative reading—"The seals named Potaṅginī are proclaimed as the limb-seals"—he describes those seals called Potaṅginī: "One should know the eye-seal (*netramudrā*): with two fingers [forming] a needle, and slightly bending the index finger; when the yogī displays this, the Guhyakas come under his control at that very moment."

Having formed a needle by means of the two index fingers (*tarjanī*) located on both hands, that mudrā in which the remaining fingers are contracted and the index finger is slightly bent should be known as the Eye Mudrā (*netramudrā*). "Of whom" means of whichever yogi one should display this mudrā; "he" means that those secret *yoginīs* come under his control—this is the meaning. (1–4)
The mudrā named Potanginī lasts for as long as one lives, without a doubt; one should display the middle finger and likewise display the index finger of that [hand]. (5)
To her who displays the ring finger, one should display the tongue;
to her who displays the *paṭṭiśa* weapon, one should display the trident.
To her who shows the head, one should show the earth;
to her who shows the earth, one should show the sky. || 7 ||
To her who displays a frown, one should show the hairline;
to her who shows her teeth, one should show the lip. || 8 ||
To her who shows her neck, one should show one's face;
to her who shows her forehead, one should show one's eyes. || 9 ||
These are all the yoginīs, whose limb-seals (aṅgamudrā) have been taught in sequence.
By displaying these correctly, the Guhyakas come to behold [the truth]. (10)
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, the procedure for the characteristics of the special mudrās, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

"The mudrā named *potaṅginī* [is to be held] for as long as one lives; of this there is no doubt. This is the eye-mudrā known as *potaṅginī*. The plural designation in the phrase "these [mudrās]" and so forth is due to the connection with the various limbs of each individual Yoginī. The *paṭṭiśa* is as before. "One should show the head" means merely showing the head. "The earth" has already been explained. "Face" refers to the face-mudrās. "These are all the Yoginīs; the limb-mudrās have been taught" means that all the Yoginīs are indeed limb-mudrās, because there is no difference between them.

And the meaning is "of all [these] indeed. "By these" refers to the counter-seals (*pratimudrā*). The third case ending is used in the sense of the object (*karman*), and there is also a change in gender. (5–10)

That which specifically prescribes the characteristics of the limb-seals (aṅgamudrā) is the chapter on the specific procedure for the characteristics of the limb-seals; thus it is the twenty-second chapter.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 22.
The twenty-third chapter, on the ritual procedure for the characteristics of the specific signs and mudrās of the ḍākinīs.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the ḍākinīs,
by which the heroic sister of the heroes is recognized even from afar.

Regarding the word *atha*: it means immediately after the description of the characteristics of the limb-mudrās (*aṅgamudrā*). In the phrase "I shall fully explain" (*saṃpravakṣyāmi*), the word *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic) is to be understood as continuing from the previous context, yet it is distinguished from what came before; this is because the word *ataḥ* (therefore/here) carries a sense of distinction. What is that specific characteristic? He says: "It is known," and so forth. "Not far away" (*adūrataḥ*) means without delay. "Of the heroes" (*vīrāṇām*) means by the heroes (*vīraiḥ*). It is called "the sister of the heroes" (*vīrabhaginī*) because she can be known only by heroes, or because she bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*) upon heroes, or because she shares the same commitment (*samaya*) with them.
Henceforth, I shall explain the characteristics of the ḍākinīs; this reading is easy to understand. || 1 ||
He whose devoted consort is to be enjoyed by the heroes,
having made the earth his support, should indeed worship the Yoga-saṃvara.

He explains how these [mantras], when practiced, bestow accomplishment: "Anuraktā" and so forth. For that yogin whose *samayinī*—a yoginī of equal commitment (*samaya*)—is satisfied, the earth shall become the enjoyment of heroes (*vīrabhogyā*). A hero is a great warrior; she is his enjoyment, thus "the enjoyment of heroes. She holds treasures (*vasu*), hence she is "Vasundharā" (the Earth). The sense is that, having conquered her, he enjoys the earth filled with jewels. Furthermore, he says "Ādhāram" and so forth.

That by which happiness is supported is the *ādhāra* (support). *Medas* is fat; it is *sneha* (moisture/lubrication). If she (*sā*) should be *snigdha* (moist/greasy), then having made that *ḍākinī* the *ādhāra*, the fixed place, one should worship the *yogasaṃvara*; such is the connection. *Yoga* refers to wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*); it is so called because by this one restrains (*saṃvṛṇoti*) the nature of duality. *Saṃ* is happiness; the restraint (*saṃvara*) of yoga is *yogasaṃvara*, and one should worship—that is, take up—that.

When, immediately after supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), the collection of sense-faculties withdraws from objects and the mind (*manas*) takes as its sole support mere happiness (*sukha-mātra*), that is the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*). Furthermore, "cessation" (*virama*) refers to the withdrawal of the senses from objects. That which constitutes the ultimate limit of this very process—consisting of non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), filled with unsurpassed bliss, and arising therefrom—is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*); it is this that one "takes hold of. This is the collective meaning.

And although that [innate bliss] is perceived through the stabilization of the bodhicitta within the jewel, it requires great instruction for its own realization. For that purpose, one must propitiate the lotus feet of the venerable true guru alone. Therefore, because he conceals (saṃvṛṇoti) the nature of conceptualization, innate bliss is called *saṃvara*. Through the union of wisdom and means, such knowledge arises from those two alone. It should be understood that wisdom and means are like jewels, for from them this priceless knowledge is born. || 2 ||
For these ḍākinīs, there is a gaze that is contrary [to the norm], a deformity of the face, and the eternal bliss of the constant knitting of the eyebrows. (3)

He states the characteristics of the ḍākinī with the words "in reverse order" (*vilomena*). Looking behind instead of looking forward is "looking in reverse order. He clarifies the deformity of her face itself: "perpetual frowning of the eyebrows" (*bhrūbhaṅgaśāśvatam sukham*), which means she has a constant frown on her brows. || 3 ||
The various [signs] emerging from the ḍākinīs should be known quickly;
they are to be recognized as circular, distorted, or consisting of three lines. (4)

"Various, swift, to be known, and likewise emerged from the *ḍākinī*. "Various" means manifold; "swiftly" means quickly; "emerged from the *ḍākinī*" refers to a movement that is free from intention (*nirabhiprāya*). "Likewise" means being of such a nature, beyond the sphere of speech—this is the meaning. He states its variousness with the words "whirlpool," and so forth. Because she goes in one way and then returns again and again by another way, there are whirlpools (*āvarta*), which are circular movements. Therefore, they are distorted. Those three lines consisting of coming and going are likewise the whirlpools. Furthermore, he asks, "Of what kind? and says: "Circular," because of their coiled shape. (4)
One should observe all the signs of a ḍākinī as she departs;
suddenly she turns back, her speech interrupted by broken words.

"She is surely departing"—this is indeed the observation of all the signs by one who is skillful; thus it is said: "one should observe every mark. "They turn back suddenly" means that even when the purpose for which they had set out is still present, they turn back specifically because of receiving a command; this is the characteristic of departure. "Broken by the speech of the past" means the breaking or interruption of the utterance of former words; this is the characteristic of speech, namely, the lack of connection between preceding and succeeding statements. The reading "broken by meaningless speech" is easily understood. || 5 ||
In that very same way, her voice was clearly manifest as having the form of a thunderbolt, yet her sound was always distinctly like the cry of a cuckoo.
And in her house there shall be a sign: a mirror in the shape of a vajra;
and another form shall be a sword together with a mirror.
The banner and the spear are known eternally, as is the casket by means of the mirror;
these are the signs of that which is to be known, for he who has assumed form is indeed subtle.
One who is endowed with these characteristics should be known as a supreme ḍākinī. || 9 ||
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, the procedure for the characteristics of the special signs and mudrās of the ḍākinīs, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

"The shape of her [forehead] is clearly that of a vajra"—this is the characteristic of the forehead (*lalāṭa*). "Her voice is clearly like the song of the cuckoo"—this is the characteristic of speech (*vāc*). "And in her house," and so forth, describes the characteristic of the house (*gṛha*). "The banner and the power are known to be constant" means that she possesses a banner, which is the *liṅga*, and that power. The characteristic of the mirror (*darpaṇa*) is "the casket by means of the mirror"; the meaning of being a "casket" is the constant gazing with a mirror. This is the characteristic of the mirror. These signs are to be known.

Thus he concludes. Therefore he says: "By these," and so forth. How does the yogi know those beings to be such? He says: "For one who has assumed a form. Since he has practiced the specific characteristics (*cihna*) and essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the Ḍākinīs, he therefore says: "By these," and so forth. This is because of the rule of conjunction (*yukta*). She is called the "Supreme Ḍākinī" due to her possession of the specific characteristics. These are the characteristics of whichever single [Ḍākinī] it may be. (6–9)

The specific signs, such as the arrival of the ḍākinīs and so forth, are indeed characterized by the features of the mirror and other items in the house of the mudrā. Because they are characterized by these [signs], and because that by which they are established is this chapter, it is called the twenty-third chapter on the procedure for the characteristics of the ḍākinī-sign mudrās.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 23.
The twenty-fourth chapter: The Ritual of All the Conventional Languages of the Four Aims.
Now, I shall further explain the secret signs (*chommaka*) in another language, by which a practitioner is recognized as a brother or a sister, without a doubt.

The word *atha* (now) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*). The syntactical connection is: "And I shall explain the secret signs (*chommaka*) in another language. Since the secret signs of syllables (*akṣarachommaka*) have already been taught in the fifteenth [chapter], the particle *tu* serves as an ornament for the sentence. By which secret sign the practitioner (*sādhaka*) is recognized—as a "brother" (*bhrātā*)—this qualifies the practitioner; and as a "sister" (*bhaginī*), it refers to the Yoginī. Otherwise, there are secret signs in other languages; this alternative reading is easily understood. || 1 ||

The salutation is *potaṅgī*, and the return salutation is *pratipotaṅgī*. *Gamu* means "I am going"; *lumu* means "I am coming. *Dehaṃ* means "the city"; *vaṭuka* means "of the houses. *Hṛdaya* is the cause of the heroes (*vīrāṇām*). *Māraṇa* refers to the Kauravas; *ghaṇṭā* is the pericarp (*karṇikā*). *Śiraḥ* is the bee (*ali*); *karaṇa* is the hair of Varāha. *Śravaṇau* are the ears; *amṛtasthāna* is the churning-stick (*manthāna*). *Samāgama* is the man (*nara*).

The *tilakas* are the *ḍākinīs*. Hell is the maṇḍala. Such-and-such is the cremation ground. Kāmpilyā is the gate. The Brahmin is the wind. The Kṣatriya is the enclosure. The Vaiśya is detachment. The Śūdra is the cruel one. The Caṇḍāla is the end. The house is the finger. The *ḍākinī* is the sister. Fat is water. "Housewife" refers to the mudrās. "She touches her teeth with her tongue" means she is hungry. "Thirst is the carrier of fragrance. "From where have you come? means from such-and-such a place. "Ray" means flower.

"Hāsya" means "lamba. "Dara" means "tooth. "Nirodha" means the obstruction of rain. "Vijñapti" means satisfaction. "Bahiḥ" means the shoulder-yoke. "Meghā" means one who is fond of incense (*dhūpa*). "Sānu" means a mountain. "Saritaḥ" means rivers. "Aṅguli" means a limb or finger. "Vadana" means the face. "Rājikā" means the tongue. "Adanā" means the teeth. "Paṅkti" means a banner. "Chandaḥ" means a garland. "Calaḥ" means the wind. "Pravāhaḥ" means a boat. "Paśu" means a deer. "Yānti" means a circle. "Sama" means a crossroads. "Janaḥ" means worthless or trivial.

*Mahāśava* means the Great Letter. *Mahāpaśu* means a goat. *Nā* means a man. *Go* means a bull. *Ma* means a buffalo. *Bhā* means eating. *Hā* are synonyms. *Appakā* means a royal attendant or a king’s officer. *Vana* means standing still. Touching the mouth signifies "it has been eaten. Touching the teeth signifies "one is satiated. *Ho* is sometimes used as a synonym. *Hrī* means shame. Touching the void signifies "it does not exist. Touching the thighs signifies "engage in sexual intercourse."

Likewise with the upward [gesture]. Thus, "there is nothing below" refers to the mudrā, the counter-mudrā (pratimudrā), the secret signs (chommaka), and that which is called the hero (vīra); these are the characteristics of the fourfold group. || 2 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, the procedure for the language of all conventions regarding the four aims, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. || 24 ||

"Potaṅgy-abhivādana" means that the word *potaṅgī* is a designation for salutation (*abhivādana*). "Pratipotaṅgī" means a return salutation (*pratyabhivādana*), which is a specific form of greeting once again. In the utterance of the sound *gamu*, one indicates "I am going. In the utterance of the sound *lumu*, it signifies "coming. Some say it is *lumbur*. It has been stated that "deha" means "city"; thus, it is a name for the body. It has been stated that "vaṭuka" means "household"; thus, *vaṭuka* is a designation for a house.

Regarding the reading *gṛhāṇam* found in some manuscripts: *gṛhāṇam* is a technical term (*saṃjñā*) for a vessel. The phrase "from the east" (*pūrvataḥ*), as previously stated, applies everywhere. "The heart of the heroes" (*vīrāṇāṃ hṛdayam*): "heart" (*hṛdayam*) is a technical term for the heroes. In the reading where it says "the cause is the heart" (*kāraṇaṃ hṛdayam*), "heart" refers to the cause. The two particles *ca* and *eva* are used for conjunction and restriction, respectively. "The Kauravas are the slaying" (*kauravā māraṇam*): "Kauravas" is the name for the act of slaying. The word *kauravā* is feminine. And [the terms] "bell" (*ghaṇṭā*) and "pericarp" (*karṇikā*).

*Karṇikā* is the name for the bell. *Śiro’li* means the bee known as the head. *Karaṇa* refers to the hair of a boar; it is the technical name for the bristles of a boar. *Śravaṇau* (the two hearers) is the literal meaning of *karṇau* (the ears). *Manthāna* is the place of nectar; the churning-stick is called the locus for the extraction of nectar. *Samāgama* is a feminine word used as a designation for a man. *Tilakāḥ* refers to the *ḍākinīs*; they are called *tilakās*. *Naraka* is the *maṇḍala*.

The designation of the maṇḍala is "hell" (naraka). "Such-and-such a cremation ground" (śmaśāna) is the name for a cemetery. "Kampilyā" is a word in the feminine gender; it is the name for the gate. "The Śvasana is a Brāhmaṇa" is the designation for a Brāhmaṇa. "The Paridhi is a Kṣatriya" is the designation for a Kṣatriya. "Virati is a Vaiśya" is the designation for a Vaiśya. "The Krūra is a Śūdra" is according to the literal meaning. "Anta is a Caṇḍāla" is the name for a Caṇḍāla. "Gṛha is Aṅgulikā" is the designation for a house.

*Ḍākinī* and *bhaginī* are easily understood. *Medaka* and *udaka*: these are names for water. *Gṛhiṇī* refers to the *mudrās*; that is, *gṛhiṇī* is a designation for the *mudrās*. "She touches her tooth with her tongue" means she is hungry for food; the meaning is that she asks for food due to hunger. *Tṛṣṇā* and *gandhavāhinī* are designations for thirst. "From where is the arrival?"—this is the giving of a *chommaka* (secret sign). "From such-and-such a place" is a word ending in the ablative case (*pañcamyanta*), established by its own nature. This is the designation for the giving of a counter-sign (*pratichommaka*).

*Kiraṇa* means *puṣpa*; this is a name for a ray (*kiraṇa*). *Hāsya* means *lamba*; *hāsya* signifies laughing, laughter, or the act of laughing. The particle *tu* is used in the sense of conjunction. *Dara* means *danta*; this is a name for a tooth. *Vṛṣṭinirodhana* means obstruction; this is a name for an obstruction. *Tṛpti* means *vijñapti*; this is a name for satisfaction. *Dhuryu* means *bahiḥ*; this is a name for the exterior location. *Meghā* means *dhūpamapriyā*; this is easily understood. *Sānu* is a name for a mountain. *Saritaḥ* means rivers.

"Part of a finger" (*aṅgulyavayava*) is a designation for a finger (*aṅgulī*). "Face" (*vadana*) is "mouth" (*mukha*); this is according to their actual meaning. "Black mustard" (*rājikā*) is a designation for the tongue (*jihvā*). "Eating" (*adanā*) and "teeth" (*dara*) are both designations for teeth (*danta*). "Line" (*paṅkti*) is a designation for a banner (*dhvaja*). "Meter" (*chandaḥ*) is a designation for a garland (*mālā*). "Moving" (*calaḥ*) is a designation for wind (*vāyu*). [A current (*pravāhaḥ*) is a designation for a boat (*nau*)]. "Beasts" (*paśu*) and "wild animals" (*mṛga*) are designations for wild animals (*mṛga*); here, there is an elision of the nominative plural ending from the word *paśu*. "Going" (*yānti*) is a designation for a circle (*maṇḍala*), as is "hell" (*naraka*).

"Even crossroads" (*samaṃ catuṣpatham*) is a designation for a crossroads. "Phalguṣa person" (*janaṃ phalguṣam*) is a designation for a person; the gender [of the word] is not restrictive. "Great corpse" (*mahāśavam*) and "great syllable" (*mahākṣaram*) are designations for a human corpse. "Great beast" (*mahāpaśu*) and "goat" (*chāgalam*): *chāgala* is simply *chagala*, and that is a human. In all cases, the accusative case is used due to the ellipsis of the verb *āhuḥ* ("they say"). "Nā" means "man" (*naram*); the word *nā* is feminine in gender but denotes a male person. Some say it is the word *nṛ*. "Go" means "bull" (*valīvardam*).

Nor, however, is the meaning of the word *gāvī*. *Ma* means "buffalo" (*mahiṣam*); it is a partial form of the word *mahiṣa*. *Bhā* means "eating" (*bhakṣaṇam*); this too is feminine in gender, because of the statement that [the buffalo] is "devoured as food. *Hā* refers to synonyms; in some places it appears as *yā*. The word *rā* is also a synonym for eating and is feminine in gender, because of the statement "to be seized by power" (*hāryāḥ prabhāvāt*). *Appakā* means "in the king's presence"; the meaning is "acting as a spy among the king's men."

"Those settled in a small body"—from such a vision [one understands]. "He stands in the forest": this is without a case-ending; it is a designation for the act of standing. "The touch of the mouth has been experienced": the meaning is that he conveys [the sense] that "he has eaten the touch of the mouth. "Satiated by the touch of the teeth" is easy to understand. *Ho* is a synonym; in some contexts, it is a synonym for "satiated. *Hrī* means "shame"; the designation *hrī* occurs upon the touch of emptiness. "Engage in sexual intercourse" is easy to understand. "Upon the touch of the thighs": "upwards, thus"—the sense is, "perform it in this manner from the very beginning."
"Below," and so forth; the meaning is that from this point onward, there are no mudrās, counter-mudrās (pratimudrās), nor secret signs (chommakas) by name. || 2 ||

The Ḍākinī, as well as the Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rupiṇī—these are the four classes (*caturvarga*). Their "all-conventional language" (*sarvasaṅketabhāṣā*) consists of the *chommakas* (secret signs) such as "ḍā," which is traditionally said to mean "man," and so forth; that collection of letters and so on, of which these are the primary elements, is the "all-conventional language and *chommakas* of the four classes. That very thing is prescribed, hence they are "prescriptions" (*vidhi*); those nine chapters in which these are prescribed are the "prescriptions concerning the all-conventional language and *chommakas* of the four classes. This chapter is included within them.

In relation to the first chapter, this is the twenty-fourth; in relation to the fifteenth, it is also the tenth. Thus, setting aside the chapter on the procedure for transforming into Heruka through the yoga of the donkey-form (*gardabhākāra*), the summarized meaning of the ten chapters has been shown. Regarding the phrase "in direct and reverse order" (*anulomavilomena*), there is another meaning: it refers to the meditation on the yoginīs of the three wheels in their respective places according to the sequence beginning with the first day of the bright fortnight (*śuklapratipad*), as well as the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the yoginīs rotating to the left and right.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 24.
The twenty-fifth chapter: The Procedure for Concealing All Root Mantras.
Now, all desired objects are joined with the end of the eightfold concealment for those beings of inferior inclination whose minds are shrouded by delusion and ignorance. (1)

Regarding the doubt raised by the question itself—“What is the root mantra extracted previously like, and for what purpose was it concealed?”—the word *atha* (now) is used. Therefore, he says: “*Sarva-ityādi*. The connection there is: “these mantras were concealed. To the question, “For whose sake were they concealed? he replies: “*Sarvathā'rtheṣu viṣayeṣu kāma icchā yasya sa tathā*,” meaning “for one who has desire—that is, longing—for objects (*viṣaya*) in all matters (*sarvathā*). The sense is: for the sake of one who seeks objects. For by that [mantra], it is impossible to achieve success; on the contrary, it results in being presided over by Māra. This is the intended meaning.

As to how many there are, he says: "Eight. Because they consist of eight words, there are eight mantras. The nominative plural ending is elided due to the word being concealed (*gopita*). They are joined with the final [word] in its true form. "One whose disposition is for beings of inferior inclination" means one who has such an intention; that is to say, even for the sake of a *śrāvaka*. For he is of inferior inclination because he seeks only his own self-restraint and tranquility. "For the sake of the ignorance of those belonging to other sects" refers to the mind or intellect directed toward that [ignorance]. By this, the underlying intention is that they were concealed for the purpose of protecting them from the wicked. (1)

There, this mantra was clearly spoken by the heroes and yoginīs: *Oṃ namo bhagavate vīreśāya | mahākalpāgnisaṃnibhāya | jaṭāmakuṭotkaṭāya | daṃṣṭrākarālograbhīṣaṇamukhāya | sahasrabhujabhāsurāya | paraśupāśodyataśūlakhaṭvāṅgadhāriṇe | vyāghrājināmbaradharāya | mahādhūmrāndhakāravapuṣe ||* "Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One, the Lord of Heroes! To him who resembles the fire at the end of a great aeon; to him who is fierce with his crown of matted locks; to him whose face is terrifyingly formidable with fangs as sharp as saws; to him resplendent with a thousand arms; to him who bears an axe, a noose, a raised trident, and a *khaṭvāṅga*; to him who wears a garment of tiger-skin; to him whose body is like a great smoky darkness."

Kara kara! Kuru kuru! Bandha bandha! Trāsaya trāsaya! Kṣobhaya kṣobhaya! Hrauṃ hrauṃ hraḥ hraḥ pheṃ pheṃ phaṭ phaṭ! Daha daha! Paca paca! Bhakṣa bhakṣa! O you who hang from a garland of entrails, blood, and fat—graha graha! Seize the serpent or snake dwelling in the seven netherworlds! Tarjaya tarjaya! Threaten it! Ākaḍḍha ākaḍḍha! Drag it forth! Hrīṃ hrīṃ jñauṃ jñauṃ (jṇauṃ jṇauṃ) kṣmāṃ kṣmāṃ hāṃ hāṃ hīṃ hīṃ hūṃ hūṃ kili kili sili sili hili hili dhili dhili hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! || 2 ||
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, the Chapter on the Procedure for the All-Secret Root Mantra, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 25.

Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): it refers to [the context of] one's own doubt. As for the question, "How is it known that these eight words are concealed? he says: "clearly," and so forth. Although they were spoken by the *vīras* and *yoginīs*, they are "not spoken" (*abhāṣitāḥ*) [to others], meaning they have not been disclosed. For indeed, a ritual procedure (*vidhāna*) that lacks a teacher (*anācāryaka*) results only in the loss of accomplishment in the Mantra system. He states the mantras: "Oṃ namaḥ," and so forth. Because of their being mixed with the King of Mantras, there is concealment here of both parts of the Root Mantra. Regarding the application of the two *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* syllables, he says "of both": *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*. (2)

Therefore, he says: "The root-mantra," and so forth. "The root-mantra-sarvātman" means that which has the nature of the entire root-mantra; its "gopya" (to be hidden) refers to concealment (*gopana*). The suffix *ṇyat* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). For in the extraction [of the mantra], there is the concealment of each individual syllable; that by which or wherein this is prescribed is the "chapter on the procedure for the concealment of all [syllables] of the root-mantra" (*mūlamantrasarvagopyavidhipaṭalaḥ*). This is due to the elision of the middle term (*madhyapadalopa*). It is the twenty-fifth. Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. || 25 ||
The *Cakrasaṃvaratantra*, Volume 2:
The Twenty-sixth Chapter on the Examination of Disciples and the Ritual for the Vow.
Beyond this, such a mantra-word is not found in the three worlds.
Having known the mantra of Śrī Heruka, one should abandon all other mantras. || 1 ||

Now he speaks of the benefits of the mantra, beginning with "ataḥ" (therefore): "Therefore" refers to the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). "Vidyatā" means Vajravārāhī; it is her vocative address, or it is a designation for that which does not exist [independently]. "Mantra" refers to the root mantra and so forth. Having understood [this], one should abandon all other mantras. Even the mantra of Śrī Heruka is Śrī Heruka himself.
Because there is no difference between those two.
The Yoginīs are established in both direct and reverse order;
bestowing accomplishment eternally above and below, they are all-pervading as the messenger of the Self.
He explains the sequential placement (*kramanyāsa*) of the Yoginīs, such as Mahāvīryā and others, who were mentioned in the fourth chapter—beginning with the words "anuloma" and so forth.
*Anuloma* (direct order) is the opposite of *viloma* (reverse order), which is the non-sequential; by that [reverse order], the Yoginīs were previously established and shown.
Now, showing that they are to be placed in direct order (*anuloma*), he says: "below and above. Below itself is above. One should perform it thus.

This is the meaning. The intention is that one should place those well-known goddesses, Pracaṇḍā and the others, above the Citta-cakra and so forth. To the question "Why is that?", he says: "They grant success eternally. The meaning is that when they are meditated upon in such a manner, they become efficacious. Therefore, he says: "But the self-messenger (ātmadūtī) is omnipresent. "Self" (ātmā) means the mind (citta), which is the Citta-cakra; the meaning is "starting from that self."
They become present in all the wheels of the scriptures. There is an elision of the word "beginning with" (ārabhya). || 2 ||

The messenger (dūtī), however, grants the accomplishment of the welfare of sentient beings through seeing, touching, kissing, and embracing; she is especially the eternal seat of yoga (yogapīṭha). || 3 ||

The word "dūtī" [in the verse] is the nominative plural, while [the word "tāḥ"] is the accusative singular. The particle "tu" is used for emphasis. "That messenger (dūtī) bestows the accomplishment of the welfare of sentient beings"—here, "that" refers to those messengers (*dūtī* / *dūtayaḥ*). How so? He says: "seeing and likewise touching. "Seeing" means apprehension, that is, direct perception. "Touching" means the mind of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā-citta*). If these two should occur, then...

The meaning is "bestowing all accomplishments. Regarding the passage beginning with *cumbana*: they are called *cumbanāḥ* because they are kissed; they are called *gūhanāḥ* because they are concealed.

The suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). The "yoga-seat" (*yogapīṭha*) refers to the seats of the Yoginīs and so forth. Regarding the word "especially" (*viśeṣataḥ*): it refers to specific techniques such as the various postures (*bandha*) prescribed in the treatises on erotics (*kāmaśāstra*). || 3 ||
As many as there are assemblies of yoga, they are remembered as bringing about all accomplishments;
one should give away one's entire being, and never otherwise.

"As many as" means those situated on all the seats (*pīṭha*) and so forth without exception. By what [means]? He says: "The assemblies of yoga" (*yogasaṅghātā*); the meaning is "the multitudes of *yoginīs*. What do they do? He says: "It is remembered as effecting all accomplishments" (*sarvasiddhikaraṃ smṛtam*). They are remembered as effectors of all accomplishments. The neuter gender and the singular ending are due to the nature of the sense. Alternatively, [it may be understood] as a nominative plural, with the vowel *ā* [as the case-ending].

And due to the etymological rule (*nairukta-vidhi*), there is both the shortening of one vowel and its elision (*lopa*). "That which is to be given" (*deyam*) means it must be bestowed as the true essence of all things (*sarvasadbhāva*). Since by this means the true essence (*sadbhāva*) comes to be in every way, so too should the food-offering (*caru-bhojana*) and other such items be given to those who have been thus characterized.
Because they thereby attain accomplishment (*siddhi*), he says: "But never otherwise. The particle *tu* (but) serves for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). || 4 ||
Whether she be a mother, a sister, a daughter, or indeed a wife, whoever stands as a messenger and constantly imparts the mantra—this indeed is recorded as the prescribed rule for him. || 5 ||

By this [means], he states that the yoginīs should be affectionate like a mother and so forth: "The mother, sister, daughter, or wife—these indeed abide as messengers. "Wife" refers to one who has but a single husband. "For him to whom she would constantly give the mantra, that is indeed remembered as the rule. This means that for whichever yogin the yoginī gives the mantra and herself, she, having received it, shall accomplish the siddhi.
One should offer [it]; for him, the rule of the Mantra system is prescribed, because that [system] has that as its purpose. Or, "mantra" may mean conversation. || 5 ||
I shall now describe a certain *samaya* that is difficult to find within the Yoga Tantras:
if a man or a woman moves on the left side, they attain accomplishment (*siddhi*) and reach their desired goals. (6)

"I shall speak of another *samaya*": here, *samayān* is a form resulting from the elision of the dual or plural case-ending; "another" (*anyatva*) refers to [a substance] other than the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth. Even in the reading "I shall speak of the *samayas* again" (*samayān atha vakṣye'ham*), it is the same. Alternatively, it may mean "another *samaya*" (*samayam anyam*). As for the elision of the case-ending, there is the elision of the vowel *a* in the word *atha*. Or, *samayāni* is a neuter designation. He states the *samaya*: "On the left... (*vāme...*)

"Neti," and so forth. "Nara" means a person. Having stationed either a man or a woman on the left, another man or woman who proceeds is known to be a yogin or a yoginī in the Śrī Cakrasaṃvara. And for this reason, one attains the desired accomplishments;
they become certain. || 6 ||
It is known that even if he is situated in a house or field far away, the preceptor who is devoted to Śrī Heruka and the Mothers of Yoga [are perceived]. (7)

Therefore, he says: "It is known even from afar. Even when the previously mentioned characteristics are not seen, the messenger (dūta) or female messenger (dūtī) is recognized by their movement to the left. Where the messenger is, he says: "In the house," and so forth. "The supreme yoga of Śrī Heruka" means that in which Śrī Heruka is supreme or most excellent; it should not be such that Śrī Heruka is not supreme in that yoga.

It is indeed so. The intended meaning is that the yoga which is centered on Śrī Heruka is the supreme yoga. By means of this yoga, it should be understood that the master (ācārya), the mothers of yoga, and the yoginīs are the most excellent. || 7 ||
In this tantra, practitioners and virtuous people alike must not be despised, nor should they be reviled; rather, they should be honored according to one's ability.

He asks, "Why? and says: "In this tantra, the practitioners are indeed virtuous. Regarding the word "in this" (*asmin*), there is the substitution of *na* for the locative case-ending. Within the section of the first plural number from the word *sādhu*, there is the substitution of *nā*. The meaning is that in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara* tantras, the most excellent practitioners are truly virtuous. Therefore, they are not to be disregarded on account of their smallness.
They are to be understood, nor should they be reviled; therefore, they are to be honored according to one's ability—that is, in accordance with one's means. || 8 ||
These eight, beginning with Kākāsyā, indeed increase devotion and faith;
they are the constant cause of spiritual accomplishments (siddhis) and the preservation of the rules of conduct (samayas).

He asks how devotion itself arises toward them, and says: "Kākāsyā," and so forth. The eight goddesses beginning with Kākāsyā increase devotion and faith; they are the cause of the *siddhis*. Those forms of Kākāsyā and the others are the causes of the *siddhis*. He asks which eight [they are], and says: "Of the *samayas*," and so forth. The word "and" (*ca*) is used for emphasis. It refers to the observance of the *samayas*.
First. || 9 ||
Free from association with other deities and unclouded by the delusion of desire,
he practiced the conduct and activities of non-duality without obstruction.

One who has desisted from it should not eat it due to association with other deities. To the question "In what state [should one be]?", he says: "deluded by desire. The meaning is that first one was engaged through delusion regarding the objects of desire (*kāma*), and subsequently one desisted.

That desisting is the second [state]. Where there exists no duality or conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), that is non-duality (*advaita*); this state of being free from conceptual construction is the third.

In that collection: "obstructed" (*pratihata*) refers to resistance; "unobstructed" (*apratihata*) refers to the increase of one's own accepted and certain tenets, which is firm resolute conviction—the fourth. Regarding the "samayas," which are the *yoginīs*, their "conduct" (*ācāra*) consists of the enjoyment of desire and so forth; activity (*ceṣṭita*) therein is their functional engagement—the fifth. || 10 ||

The worship of the Sovereign Lady (Nārīśvarī), the practice of celibacy, the maintenance [of vows], freedom from anger, and the movement of the ear—these are the eight rules of conduct (samayācāra). || 11 ||

"By the sovereignty of Nārī, [there is] *samanthāna*. Sovereignty (*īśvaryam*) means mastery (*aiśvaryam*). The suffix *vṛddhi* is not mandatory; thus it is not *anīśvaryam*. That which does not exist is "non-sovereignty" (*nārīśvarya*), here used without a case-ending. Where is that? He says: "In *samanthāna*," which refers to the *vajra*-expansion of the Yoginī. Therein, sovereignty itself is the sixth. To the question "Where is there non-attachment to celibacy (*brahmacarya*)?", he says: "In the *tathādhāna*," that is, in the *tathatās*.

The seventh [cause] is non-attachment to that very generation and undertaking of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*). "Non-anger" (*akrodha*) means the absence of anger; it is intended as turning away [from objects]. The sense organs are the "hearers" (*śrotra*); the "range" (*sañcāra*) is the collection of objects because they move within them. The particle *ca* is used for emphasis. Turning away from attachment to the collection of objects is the eighth cause. Thus, there are eight causes. Eight.

Devotion arises toward those things in which the causes of accomplishment reside; they alone are to be worshipped. Why is this so? He says: "Because they are the conduct of the *samaya*," that is, because of the practice of the Yoginīs. (11)
Those who are established in their practice must always be recognized by practitioners as perfected ones;
they are common to all tantras and must not be harmed by those without cause.

The practitioners should know that the eight commitments (*samaya*), beginning with the preservation of the pledge, are the causes of accomplishment (*siddhi*). For those established in the practice, they are "accomplished" (*siddha*), meaning certain. This is common to all tantras. To explain how these are the causes of accomplishment, he says: "They are not to be killed," meaning they are not to be slain. By whom? He says: "by killers who are without cause. By those who are without cause—[the text continues: *pratya-*... [fragmentary].
By means of the instruments of knowledge, such as perception and the rest. || 12 ||
It is grasped by faith alone, neither by hand nor by eye;
this secret is not to be revealed and must be guarded with great effort. (13)

Since they are grasped by faith alone, he says: "not with the hand, nor with the eye. And for that reason, he says it is to be kept secret: "it is not to be revealed," and so forth. This is the Octad of Samayas. 13.
The wise one should move the little finger; the messengers are stationed there.
Whether pure, impure, or mixed—such is the threefold state of the practitioner.
"A man who is a seeker, pure, an illuminator, and endowed with virtues.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Examining Disciples and the Vows," in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 26.

He describes the procedure for the arousal of passion through the messenger (*dūtī*)—beginning with the words "the little finger" (*kaniṣṭhām*), and so forth. One should move or stimulate the channel (*nāḍī*) at the tip of the bird’s mouth (*khagamukha*), which resembles a *bandhūka* flower, by means of the seed-syllable (*kiṃbīja*) resembling a flower, placed within the hollow formed by the tips of the ring and middle fingers. For what purpose? He says: "for the messengers" (*dūtaya*), and so forth. This refers to the established state of the messengers, their own abiding condition, and the state of flowing with intoxication (*mada*). [This concludes] the examination of the disciple.
"Pure," and so forth. "Pure" means one whose intention (*āśaya*) is purified. "Impure" is the opposite; "mixed" refers to one who is a combination of both.

There are three kinds of practitioners (*sādhakas*). The "worshipper" (*ārādhaka*) is one who possesses firm conviction regarding qualities and those possessing qualities through their connection with the fruits of action.
The "pure" one is one who follows what is taught in the scriptures, who is an illuminator for the wise, and who bears qualities such as non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion. Therefore...
In this very manner, one who knows the principles of policy [should act]. || 14-15 ||

"Disciples" (śiṣya) refers to those who are instructed and established in their own teaching. "Examination of them" (śiṣyaparīkṣā) means a thorough inspection, an observation by means of both virtues and faults. "Vow" (saṃvara) means the commitment (samaya). That by which it is prescribed is the "chapter" (paṭala); thus, it is [the chapter] on that. It is the twenty-sixth.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛtti*. 26.
The twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Worship and Offering of the Vow of Conduct.
Now, the hero’s vow of conduct (*vīracaryāvrata*), which accomplishes all *yoginīs*:
having understood the distinctions of its characteristics, one proceeds toward swift accomplishment.

The word *atha* (now) should be understood as follows: immediately after the power of the mantra and the characteristics of the Yoginīs—which are the causes for accomplishing the observance of the pledge (*samaya*) and so forth—the vow of conduct (*caryāvrata*) occurs. "Conduct" (*caryā*) refers to the practice of yoga; it is called a "vow" (*vrata*) because one engages in it with single-minded devotion. Having raised the question of what that conduct consists of and by whom it is to be practiced, he says: "The Hero," and so forth. The particle *tu* serves to emphasize; [it means] only after knowing the various characteristics of the Yoginīs—everything...
The hero becomes a practitioner of the yoginīs. Why? For what reason? It says: "Swift accomplishment proceeds. (1)
Traveling from village to village, his two messengers possess beautiful characteristics; those two messengers are like the edge of a sword, yet they are purifying and increase merit.

Regarding the phrase "wandering from village to village": in every multitude of people, the movement of that yogin is like a thunderbolt (*vajra*); from that, the messengers (*dūtayaḥ*) proceed—this is how it should be understood. The sense is that they become manifest. To the question "How are they to be known?", he says:

"Form is the defining characteristic" (*rūpalakṣaṇam*). Form itself is the characteristic, the cause of recognition; and that has been explained previously. [He further states: "The messengers are like the edge of a sword."

The two messengers (*dūtī*) and the sword-edge vow (*asidhārāvrata*): these two are pure. Therefore, they increase merit. In whose opinion that sword-edge vow is pure, it is said to be pure because of the acceptance of its underlying intention. Between these two, the sword-edge vow consists of lying upon a bed with a beautiful woman after placing a freshly sharpened sword between them. Alternatively, the two messengers and the sword-edges are equal.

Because it is difficult to practice [otherwise]. Furthermore, the sight of female messengers (dūtīs) is extremely purifying, increases merit, is as sharp as the edge of a sword, and accomplishes one's purpose;
the word "ca" is used for conjunction. || 2 ||
Through contact with such female messengers, the practitioner likewise attains accomplishment;
they achieve success very quickly, even without recitation, meditation, or ritual worship.

Therefore, he says: "One attains accomplishment through contact. Through contact such as the sight of the *dūtī* (messenger) and so forth, the practitioner attains accomplishment. To the question "Why?", he says: "The *dūtīs*, etc. Even the *dūtīs* become accomplished—that is, they manifest themselves—through the sight and other [means] of such a yogin; for, even without external recitation (*japa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and worship, in a very short time, [the goal is reached] after incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).

Because of the negation of [external] limits. Alternatively, this is a hyperbolic praise (*atiśayokti*) of such a yogin, meaning that even without mantra-recitation, maṇḍala-circles, meditations, the fivefold offerings, or the worship of deities, the female messengers (*dūtayaḥ*) are accomplished. Regarding the term "female messengers" (*dūtayaḥ*): through contact with the female messengers, one attains accomplishment; it means that practitioners achieve success even without recitation and so forth, simply through non-discrimination (*avicārāt*). [The compound *dūtisamparkāt* means] through contact with the female messengers...
Some say that the majesty has been described. || 3 ||
Worships proceed, as do mantras, mudrās, and practitioners;
there is no worship higher than this—such is the certainty of the scripture. (4)
Practitioners intent on accomplishment should always delight in the path of the messenger (dūtī).
Endowed with the knowledge of mantra and vidyā, the practitioner, being well-composed, should constantly partake of the sacrificial pap (caru).

He states that worship and other rites proceed from the mere sight of the messenger (*dūtī*) with the words "and worship," and so forth. "Mantras and mudrās" refers to *mantramudrā*. "This" refers to the sight of the messenger and so on. "Of the scripture" refers to the *Yoginī-tantra* known as the *Śrī-saṃvara*.
For this very reason, practitioners (*sādhakas*) become devoted to the path of the messenger and established in the instructions of the *yoginīs*. "Always" means at all times.

"Intent on accomplishment" (*siddhitatparāḥ*) means devoted to that. Regarding the variant reading "practitioners intent on accomplishment for those who delight in the path of the *dūtīs*": the word "since" (*yasmāt*) is used here. The genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇe*). Among those who delight in the path of the *dūtīs*, whoever is intent on accomplishment becomes a practitioner of that. He states the specific method of propitiation: "and the *caru*," etc. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate the acts of propitiation. The *caru* [is to be prepared] in one place—

One should always provide food with respect and without interruption for a long time to the yoginīs. "Endowed with mantra and vidyā" means accompanied by the recitation of mantras and so forth. "The practitioner who is well-concentrated" means one by whom yoga is established (*āhita*) in the perfectly equal Śrī Heruka. In the alternative reading *sarvayogapravṛttasya*, the genitive case is used in the sense of the nominative. [This applies] to the stable, the moving, and so forth.

Because of the engagement in the yoga of emptiness; and because one who is heedless lacks the qualification [for this practice], the term "well-composed" (*susamāhita*) has a further meaning [beyond mere concentration]. (4–5)
One should act for the sake of all castes and should not discriminate regarding what is to be eaten;
in reality, he is indivisible, and two messengers are employed in his practice.

"One should practice [eating] with all castes" means that one should eat together in one place with all castes. There is no distinction made as to whether this food is edible or inedible. Why should one perform everything in this way? He says: "Because, in reality, it is indivisible for him.

For that practitioner of conduct (*caryā-yogin*), everything is indivisible because, in truth, it is of a single nature. Even the female messengers (*dūtīs*) are indivisible due to the non-duality of all things.
Therefore he says: "The messengers" and "the two means. The two means are non-conceptuality and the messengers. (6)
One should accomplish two kinds [of goals], for indeed the messengers alone,
when impelled by proximity to the means of accomplishment, bring about the attainments.

And he says that there are two things to be accomplished (*sādhya*): "The means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is indeed twofold. [Namely,] worldly happiness which is accompanied by affliction (*saṃkleśa*), and supramundane [happiness] which is free from affliction (*niṣkleśa*). For the portion consisting of the means (*sādhana-bhāga*) is indeed one alone. The word "indeed" (*hi*) is used for the sake of absolute certainty. What is this? He says: "The female messengers (*dūtayaḥ*).
The meaning is that for the sake of accomplishing both, the female messengers alone are the means and nothing else. Because, through their grace, there is non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpatā*).

It will succeed. To the question "Whence comes their favor?", he says: "Impelled. Their favors have been brought forth by accomplishing their intentions as previously described, for the sake of their presence in the accomplishment of both types of success (*siddhi*). "Then his reality is indivisible"—that is, his *tattva* (reality), which is his essential nature, is indivisible; his female messengers (*dūtī*) are likewise so. "Two means" means two means. The equipment of merit (*puṇyasaṃbhāra*).

And the *yoginīs* [are also included] for one who is practicing and accomplishing the two types of *siddhi*. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "for the messengers (*dūtī*) are indeed one": the messengers constitute the single portion of the means (*sādhana*). This is because they are the proximate cause for *siddhi*; such is the explanation according to an alternative reading (*pāṭhāntara*). And here there is an expansion of the text: "The sites of the sacred fields (*kṣetra*) are perfected, and the *ḍākinīs* are gathered here. Abiding there..."
"One should perform *japa* and fetch the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) in one place; those situated there sport [there]. This text is to be introduced as follows:
regarding the phrase "made in the heart," he says "in the field," etc. One should "fetch," that is, take food. || 7 ||
He has been consecrated on the festival of the Guru, is well-equipped with the mechanical instruments,
has correctly instructed the messengers, and is habituated to the application of mudrās.

He says that one who has indeed received consecration is "dear to the Yoginīs," beginning with the words "guru" and so forth. "Guru-parva" refers to the specific rites such as the water-consecration and others, which have been transmitted in succession through the lineage of gurus. One who has obtained [consecration] by means of these is "one who has received consecration. "Abhiṣikta" means consecration. That in which the appropriate [attire], such as the master's [robes] and so forth, has been donned for the consecration is described thus. The term "śaiṣyaka" is used in the sense of "fit for a disciple. He is "well-restrained."

"Very well-restrained. In the reading *sumantrita*, it means "one who has recited the mantra. In the alternative reading *samanvita*, it means "one who has obtained the oral tradition (*sampradāya*). "'Well-spoken by the female messengers' (*dūtayaḥ samyaguktam*)" means it was beautifully spoken by the female messengers (*dūtīs*). "By the dharma of the disciple" (*śaiṣyakeṇa dharmeṇa*) means [the teacher is] a disciple because there is no distinction in their dharma; this is due to the non-difference between these two. And thus, such a yogi is "dear to the yoginīs"—this is the intended meaning. Why indeed?

He says: "And one whose nature is the union with the mudrā. This means that by means of the union with the mudrā, the knowledge of innate bliss (sahajānanda) is attained; this is what is to be experienced by him.
Therefore, the word "and" (ca) has the sense of "because" (yasmāt). || 8 ||
Here, the body of complete knowledge is whole; there, it is born as a physical body.
Having risen at dawn, the one whose self is consciousness should ritualistically construct the form.

One who has realized that becomes Śrī Heruka, whose body is the complete embodiment of gnosis (*jñāna*). "The complete one is there, born of the body"—this is a word without a case ending (*nirvibhaktika*) and is pronounced with a protracted vowel (*pluta*). He explains the sequence of meditation for the sake of becoming Śrī Heruka, beginning with the words "At dawn" (*prātaḥ*), and so forth. "At dawn" means at daybreak. "Having arisen" means having risen from bed. "He becomes the self of consciousness" (*cittātmā*): he is such because his very self (*ātman*) or essential nature (*svarūpa*) is nothing but consciousness (*citta-mātra*). What?

Having said "having done thus," he says: "having shattered the body. The meaning is that one should meditate on emptiness after having divided the body—consisting of the aggregates and so forth—into pieces by means of the weapon of wisdom. || 9 ||
One should practice the "anointing" scriptures located within the body;
having thus purified the body, one should then utter the pervasive mantra.
To explain what precedes this "thus," he says: "One should practice the anointing and the scriptures residing within the body.

They are called *śāstras* because beings (*sattvas*) are taught (*śiṣyante*) by them; thus, they are the Tathāgatas. One should place those [Tathāgatas] within the body, established in the eyes and other sense organs.
The anointings are, in the ultimate sense, devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Alternatively, *śāstra* refers to the training (*śikṣā*) and the ritual manual (*kalpa*).

Grammar, etymology, prosody, and astronomy are the six auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅga*) of the Vedas. The meaning is that these have been transcended as "anointings" (*abhyaṅga*), and thus they are no longer accessible [to him]. Regarding the passage beginning with "purifier" (*pavitrī*): immediately after the purification of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, he is indeed purified by emptiness. One should recite the mantra: *oṃ svabhāvaśuddhāḥ sarvadharmāḥ svabhāvaśuddho 'ham*.
One should utter it. "He" refers to the yogi; it is "extended" (tata), meaning "widely extended" because it is taught in various tantras. || 10 ||
One established in yoga should demonstrate the stages of yoga and must not transgress the scriptures;
the practitioner should not revile others and should not overstep those who are engaged in the practice.

The "places of yoga" (yogasthānāni) mean the places of meditative absorption (samādhisthānāni), that is to say, the locations of the two armor-mantras (kavacadvayasthānāni). "One should show" means that one should preside over them with their respective mantras or with the deities born from them. Thus, only a mere indication of the direction for visualization (bhāvanā) has been shown. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "one should not transgress the scriptures," some say it means one should not transgress the Yoginīs, or else, that one should know the emblems (cihnāni) of the deities.

The sense is that a practitioner of the *caryā* may, for the sake of play, even observe the meaning of the Vedas through mockery at times. "A person observing the *samaya* should not revile" means that the practitioner of the *caryā* who observes the *samaya* should not revile [others], nor should he give rise to such thoughts. "He should not transgress against those who are devoted" refers to those devoted to the venerable *Cakrasaṃvara*. (11)
One who desires liberation and seeks that goal should enjoy happiness with them and practice the conduct of the pledge (samayācāra), even if delusion should arise.

"By them" means by the *yoginīs*. "Bliss" refers to the bliss of sexual union and so forth. "Seeking liberation and seeking that" means one who desires liberation and one who desires pleasure. The connection is that, having performed the "gestures" (*ceṣṭita*) as taught in the treatises on erotics (*kāmaśāstra*), one should sleep together with them. "Vaibhrama" means arising from playful charm (*vilāsa*). "It is joined" (*yujyate*) means it is appropriate; the meaning is that if one should perform those gestures, [then it is appropriate]. If for the sake of the gesture...
They long for that [state] until it arrives. || 12 ||

And at night he should always remain naked, and he should always be smeared with black and red [pigments]. His clothing should be made from the limbs of living beings, as should his necklace and bracelets. (13)
Adorned with earrings, a sacred thread, and a garland of skulls,
he has a necklace upon his neck and a girdle that makes a jingling sound.

Adorned with a crown of matted locks and a headband, falsely decorated with hair and other ornaments, [he holds] a vajra and a lotus, and [is accompanied by] the sound of a khaṭvāṅga and a ḍamaruka drum, and the syllable HŪṂ. || 15 ||

"At night," and so forth. "Black and red" means the black fortnight and the red [fortnight]. "The necklace (*kaṇṭhikā*) and so on" refers to those fashioned from human hair; "the crest (*cūḍā*)" refers to a collection of bracelets (*valaya*). "The sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) and the girdle (*mekhalā*)" are also fashioned from hair. "Jingling sounds" refers to anklets (*nūpura*); the meaning is that one should wear the necklace and the other ornaments together with their tinkling sounds. "The matted-hair crown (*jaṭāmakuṭa*)" means a crown made of matted locks. "And the insignia-belt (*aṅkapaṭṭa*)" refers to the hero's sash (*vīrapaṭṭa*).

"Adorned with false hair and so forth" means fashioned from the hair, yak-tail whisks, and other materials of others. "Vajra-lotus-marked skull" refers to a skull marked with a vajra and a lotus; he is thus [described] because he exists together with the sounds of the vajra-khaṭvāṅga and ḍamaru drum, and the syllable *hūṃ*. (13–15)
Adorned with the three armors, clothed in garments made of animal skins, and surrounded by all the heroes and yoginīs, one who seeks happiness should move about happily.

The "all-heroic" (*sarvavīra*) refers to the three wheels (*cakratraya*) wherein all heroes reside; the *yoginīs* of that [system] are Pracaṇḍā and the others. The intended meaning is that these are to be meditated upon by that practitioner (*yogin*). For this very reason, he is adorned with the three armors (*kavacatraya*).

The three wheel-turning goddesses constitute the three armors because they repel the weapons of Māra. The underlying intention is that he is endowed with the meditation on the thirty-six deities. [This applies to] the limbs of living beings—
Regarding "clothing as a dwelling": it should be understood that one should make a dwelling with a garment of skin. *Vāsana* means clothing or covering;

the suffix *ghañ* is used here in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*). He provides the instruction for the phrase "one seeking pleasure should move [the woman] toward pleasure" [with the following verse]. || 16 ||
Having completely cast aside the sacred thread, the practitioner intent on accomplishment should maintain purity as established by Śrī Heruka and be bound by the five mudrās. (17)
Adorned with a necklace, bracelets, earrings, and a crest-jewel,
he possesses a sacred thread and ashes that remain constant at all times.
One should always practice openly at night, but keep it secret during the day;
one should maintain the secret knowledge of ritual action while remaining peaceful and free from weariness.

And purity should be known as threefold, established within one's own stream [of consciousness], free from the distinctions of caste or non-caste, and devoid of the binding of tufts of hair on the face or the topknot. || 20 ||

"And having completely cast off the sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta), [one attains] purity as established by Śrī Heruka. The word "and" (ca) serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned. The intention is that one abandons the purity produced by the sacrificial thread and other such items prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, and instead abides in the purity established by the yoga of Śrī Heruka. The practitioner, intent upon accomplishment, is bound by the five mudrās.
Adorned with a necklace, bracelets, earrings, and a crest-jewel.
"The sacred thread and the ashes are to be maintained at all times;
however, one should always wear them openly at night, but keep them concealed during the day.
Thus, [one should maintain] ritual action and knowledge in great secrecy, being tranquil and free from fatigue.

"And purity is to be known as threefold, established within its own stream"—this is an additional passage. Its meaning is as follows: the intention is that [the ritual] action should be performed in connection with the families (kula) of Vajra, Ratna, Padma, Karma, and Tathāgata. At night, it emerges manifest, connected to the five families (*pañcakula*). The particle *tu* has the sense of "exceedingly. During the day, it is well-concealed.

One should cause [this] to be done; or rather, it is for the purpose of restriction, so that there may be no fault regarding the rejection of sentient beings. Through action and service, knowledge—that is, the knowledge of innate bliss (sahajānanda)—is well-guarded. He is tranquil, compassionate, and free from weariness. His purity is threefold, and that consists in the non-restraint of passion and the other [afflictions]. Alternatively, it refers to what will be explained later, beginning with "the role of the messenger" (dūtya). Therefore—
"Established in one's own stream, which is one's own mind. *Varṇas* are the Brāhmaṇas and so forth; *avarṇas* are the lowest-born (*antya-jas*). "Mouth" means the primary [caste];

"exclusion" (*ākṣepa*) means that which is not primary. A "tuft" (*śikhā*) is a crest-lock; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the girdle of muñja grass, ashes, matted hair, and the like are included.
"Devoid of their binding" means devoid of their wearing or maintenance. (17–20)
First, the mission as a messenger; second, the Soma sacrifice is desired;
and third, the consumption [of the Soma] together is declared to be purity. (21)
From the diligent maintenance of this purity, the purification of purity arises;
and for a yogi who has attained it through gradual stages, what accomplishment would not come to pass? (22)

He states another purification—beginning with "But the *dūtya*," and so forth. *Dūtya* means the female messenger (*dūtī*). There is the elision of one *bindu*. "Soma" refers to the *bodhicitta*. That which is the consumption [of it] in one place is the meaning of *caru*. Regarding *caru*: there is the elision of one *bindu*. And that is the third purification. By maintaining this purification, once the purity of purification has been attained in due order, for whom would success not be achieved?

It is said: "It arises. By thoroughly maintaining these purifications, one attains purity through purification; for whom, then, would the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) not arise? || 21–22 ||
And as it is stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, so it is stated in the *Cakrasaṃvara*; likewise,
it is fully explained in the *Guhyatantra* and the *Paramādya*,
and in the *Mahāvajrabhairava*, which bestows the accomplishments of recitation, vows, and so forth.
The mantra-practitioner shall accomplish this very thing in an instant through meditation alone. || 24 ||

"Saṃvara" refers to the *Saṃvarottara*. "Guhyatantra" refers to the *Guhyakośa* and so forth. "Tathā" means without restraint. "Eva" is used as a restrictive particle. The word "ca" (and) serves to aggregate the rules of conduct (*ācāra*). The vow (*vrata*) and the recitation (*japa*) constitute the observance (*niyama*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the restraint of the senses and so forth are included; thus, she who grants success through these is the deity who bestows the accomplishment of recitation, vows, and the like. This is established in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* and other texts by means of recitation and so forth.

"Siddhi" is the collective meaning [of the term]. Here, however, in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara*, the intention is that this very meditation on Śrī Heruka alone is the means for accomplishing the siddhi of Mahāmudrā. Therefore, it is said: "The yogin shall accomplish [it] in an instant. (23–24)
But for those devoted to the path of yoga, this purification should be practiced;
the merit of such purifications cannot be described by even one person. (25)

Praising purity itself, he says: "By yoga," and so forth. Yoga is the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) in mind-only (*cittamātra*). That alone is the path to perfect enlightenment (*saṃbodhimārga*);
among those devoted to that, one should practice this aforementioned purity (*śauca*) of the Śrī Heruka yoga. He states the purpose of purity with the words: "Of purities," and so forth.
The female messengers (*dūtī*) and others are called "purities" because they are the causes of purity; the merit derived from them cannot be expressed by a single mouth.
It cannot be described. || 25 ||
The practitioner is the expansion of qualities; his face consists of many hundreds of thousands of faces.
He is the purification of the great wisdom of Śrī Heruka, the means for accomplishing all characteristics. || 26 ||
He asks "Why? and says: "The practitioner is one whose virtues are extensive. This means that because the practitioner is expanded by the quality of purity (*śauca*).
He asks "By what means is it possible? and says: "But the faces are many. When there are indeed many faces, then it is possible;
this is stated using the singular number for the sake of the genus (*jāti*). He says "thousand-faced" to indicate that even two or more constitutes "many."

"Thousand-faced" means having a count of a thousand faces, that is, possessing a thousand faces. To explain why such a practitioner is so described, he says "Śrī... and so forth. Śrī Heruka himself is the great gnosis (*mahājñāna*), which is pure and free from afflictions (*niṣkleśa*). That in which all the characteristics of qualities such as the ten powers (*daśabala*) are present is "possessing all characteristics" (*sarvalakṣaṇa*). The sense is that his union (*yoga*) with that [Heruka] is likewise of such a nature. (26)
And for the practitioner, the drinking of the water of bliss and non-duality itself;
by that, the self of the yoga of non-duality is pure and destroys sin.
Regarding "and for the practitioner": *ca* means "because. For the practitioner, the "water of bliss" is the *bodhicitta*; [it refers to] the drinking of that.
The phrase "the self of non-dual yoga, liberated from all sins" should be connected with "by drinking the water of bliss. Why? He says:
"It is pure and destroys sin. The meaning is that for this reason, the water of bliss is of such a nature. || 27 ||
Freed from all sins by even touching or speaking [to him], that best of men conducts himself with a pure body, free from disease. (28)
With a self purified of all evil, one shall obtain the glory of the Tathāgatas;
likewise, through successive births, one is born into the families of the Tathāgatas. (29)
"Even from touching or conversing" means with the practitioner. "All sins," such as the five crimes of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*).

"Pure body, free from affliction": it should be understood that it is called the "pure body" because it is free from affliction. "The person practices the water of bliss"—this is easily understood. "In birth after birth" means he is born into the family of the Tathāgatas in every successive life. (28–29)
Having thus always performed worship, the yogi should devotedly offer the bali-oblation;
he becomes a righteous king who acts according to his own will.

"Thus, [perform] worship" means that one should worship the Yoginīs and offer the *bali* oblation. As for when that should be given, he says: "It should be given. This refers to the procedure for the *bali*. "At will" means those rites desired by oneself, such as rites for pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth. || 30 ||
And the bali offering as well as the worship should be given according to the prescribed rule, on whichever tenth lunar day occurs during either the dark fortnight or the bright fortnight. (31)
These Vajra goddesses are to be worshipped with great effort, even with wines and meats.
When they are worshipped by a devoted person who has attained delight in Śrī Heruka, they become pleased in heart and grant boons, for the boons are held in their very hands. (32)
At night, the observer of the vow should offer the bali-oblation with his hair loose and naked;
through yoga, being the very self of Śrī Heruka, he propitiates the Mothers. (33)
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Worship and Offering of the Vow of Conduct," in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

The procedure here is that stated in another tantra. It specifies the particular time for worship with the words beginning "on the black [fortnight]," and so forth. The word *vā* (or) refers to the ninth and fourteenth days. The particle *tu* (but/and) has the sense of distinction or conjunction. In the alternative reading, "on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, but on the [tenth] of the bright fortnight," the word *tu* conjoins the tenth and ninth days. As for the phrase "the remainder which," it refers to whichever is the tenth or the ninth day.
It occurs as follows: worship should be performed on the fourteenth day, as well as on the tenth and ninth days. What else? He says:
"On these [days], the Vajra goddesses should be thoroughly worshipped with effort by means of liquor and even meat.
When they have been worshipped by a person of devotion who has attained delight in Śrī Heruka..."
"Because those whose minds are contented become givers of boons, for boons are held in their hands.
Thus, on these lunar days (tithis), one should exert effort in worship; "held in their hands" means that the desired boons (varāḥ) are within their grasp.
The rest is easily understood. (31–34)
That [chapter] in which the conduct, vows, worship, and offerings are prescribed is thus [described]; it is the twenty-seventh, the twenty-seventh.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛtti*. || 27 ||
The twenty-eighth chapter, on the rule for the unity of the color of the internal fire-oblation;
thereafter,
the practitioner whose self is perfectly purified should worship the supreme Self.
Nirvāṇa is the hero who has emerged, worshipped by all the Buddhas and others. || 1 ||

He speaks the chapter on Equanimity (*samatāpaṭala*), beginning with "Then, worship" (*tato pūjā*) and so forth. The word *tataḥ* should also be understood here in the sense of "therefore"; alternatively, the change to *u* (in *tato*) is due to its being an archaic Vedic form (*ārṣa*). Since perfect enlightenment (*saṃbodhi*) cannot occur without equanimity, the meaning is: "therefore, one should worship oneself.
One whose self—the mind—is purified by both external and secret worship is "one of perfectly purified self" (*suviśuddhātmā*). What kind of self?

Thus he says: "Nirvāṇa has gone forth as the Hero. Nirvāṇa is the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*), because external objects of the intellect are no longer perceived. Immediately after that, he has gone with certainty; he is established. One should worship him through the worship of practice—that is, the self, the mind, which abides in innate joy (*sahajānanda*). Alternatively, by virtue of being incomparable, he has gone to, or realized, innate joy; the self has understood it.

Those of unrefined intellect mock him who, failing to understand the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*) without [proper] instruction, points to it as being prior to innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*). For they, perceiving "cessation" as the emission of the *bodhicitta*, deceive themselves; by them, innate bliss is not attained here. Therefore, having established this for the protection of one's own mind, remain vigilant. What, then, would happen from that?

To this he says: "All [Buddhas]," and so forth. The meaning is that when [the deity] is worshipped, all the Buddhas and others become worshipped. This is because of the elision of the nominative plural ending in the word *sarvabuddhādi*. When the vowel *ā* in *pūjita* is shortened to *i*, it is established that "one becomes a Buddha" (*buddhavat*) within one's own self (*ātmani*), thus "Buddha, Buddha. In the reading *sarvabuddhādipūjitam*, from that [root], it means "born from all the Buddhas and others."
"It would be honored," [he said]. || 1 ||
The yoginīs of Sarvavīra—both the stationary and the moving, as well as the sisters who follow his conduct and abide in union with Soma—one should worship. (2)
