Furthermore, he says "all" and so forth to show that everything indeed is the Buddha. Regarding "of the All-Hero" (*sarvavīrasya*): this is the abstract state of the first plural [dual] form.
"Immovable" refers to trees and the like; "movable" refers to humans and the like. This is the worship of reality (*tattvapūjā*). Regarding "one should worship the brothers and the movements":

the particle *tu* is used for conjunction. "Brothers" are those together with the disciples (*śrāvaka*). They are called "movements" because they move within these [beings], remaining established in their own tradition (*svāgama*).

The *cārāḥ* (wanderers) are those who abide in equanimity within that union (*saṅgama*)—the yoga—with *soma*, which is the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*); thus they are "those established in union with *soma*.
The nominative case is used in the sense of the accusative; the meaning is that one should worship them as well. || 2 ||
Together with one's brother or son, regarding the arising of pleasure and pain,
one should not reveal there the knowledge, nor likewise the mantra and the mudrā.

"One should not reveal this knowledge there, even together with one's brothers, sons, or friends, for it is the source of both happiness and suffering. The connection is that one should not reveal this knowledge to those brothers. "Together with" means equally with the sons of the brothers and with certain friends by means of this knowledge. Furthermore, because happiness and suffering arise from these [relationships] as "this" (i.e., as objects of attachment), it is so described; nevertheless, it remains unstained by those two, for it is the very essence of happiness.

Because it is a constituent part of suffering for one who is subject to [the cycle of existence]. Although it is common [to all], it is uncommon because it is to be known only by the skillful. In the ultimate sense, it is "non-manifestation" because it is impossible to manifest. It is called "interpolation" (*prakṣepa*) because even those [skillful ones] insert it into their own compositions as if it were scripture.

It is called "corrupter of all" (*sarvadūṣaka*) because it defiles the fruits of all actions and so forth. The intended meaning is that one should not reveal this even to these two types of people. Among these—

Due to living together, due to being opposed by nature, and due to showing contempt, they go to hell; therefore, it should be understood that they do not even deserve the status of disciples. Another meaning is stated: the brother is Ānanda, because he is the convention of the Dharma; the son is Paramānanda; the one who is with the single [consort] is Viramānanda; he whose arising and abiding consist in the equanimity of pleasure and pain is thus [described]. This...

Innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). In that state, innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*) does not manifest as an agent, because there is an absence of manifestation. Nor does it manifest itself, because of the contradiction of an action directed toward itself. Discrimination such as "this is to be done" and "this is not to be done" is an imposition. The meaning is that the characteristic of innate bliss is that the entire mass of afflictions such as passion, which corrupts everything, and all things such as the body, do not exist therein.
This very point is stated again and again, because this alone is the means for accomplishing the supreme human goal.
One who has performed the conduct of the observance (samayācāra) should always consume the sacrificial oblation (caru);
one should not give the mantra to anyone, nor should one destroy the oral instruction (upadeśa). || 4 ||
One should give instruction according to the truth to those who abide by the samaya;
having abandoned the dūtī, one should not, deluded by desire, go to another woman.

"Caruṃ ca," and so forth. "Pavitrāṇi" refers to the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). To the question "What is the purpose of consuming them? he says: "One who has performed the *samaya*-practice. *Samaya* here is characterized by the consumption of beef and other such substances. He asks, "By what cause? and answers: "Always" (*sadā*). "Sada" means a dwelling; "sada" [here] implies a state of despondency due to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). The third case ending is used in the sense of a cause. For the power of jewels, mantras, and medicinal herbs is indeed inconceivable. "Mantra" refers to the mantra and so forth.

"Of someone" refers to a king or similar authority. "He should not destroy the instruction" means that once he has been requested, he should not grant water for irrigation and so forth out of mere greed; rather, he should grant the instruction according to what is truly required. Therefore, the word *tu* (but) indicates a distinction. "The messenger" (*dūtī*) is one who observes the pledges (*samayinī*).
The particle *ca* (and) denotes conjunction, while *tu* (but) denotes restriction. [The author asks: "Maddened by passion, would this man not go to any woman whatsoever? || 4-5 ||
The protection of the messenger always leads to liberation; even if she has transgressed, one should feed her.
One should certainly not show her disrespect, even if she remains one of low birth.

"The protection of the messenger (dūtī) is always liberation. The protection of the messenger—the external woman—is her safeguarding through the recitation of armor-mantras (*kavaca*). By means of that, there is the pacification of all seizing spirits (*graha*). Alternatively, the protection of the messenger consists in making her devoted exclusively to oneself through the practice of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*); from that comes liberation, due to the constant pursuit of reality (*tattva*). Some say this is because of the scriptural injunction: "One should not eat the leftovers of another. [This applies to] the Tathāgata...

Others say that for the *dūtīs* born of [specific] lineages, there is public service and protection; thus, one should enjoy them even by transgressing [conventional norms]. Since the *dūtīs* are gripped by pride, one should not show them respect during sexual union. Even by seizing them by the hair and so forth, one should cause them to experience the bliss of union. Therefore it is said: "One should certainly not offer them honor. One should enjoy them by force, not by [showing them] respect.
Because of the statement, "food with honor," one should feed [the deity] happily even if [the recipient] is of low birth. || 6 ||

Mothers, sisters, daughters, and wives stand as obstacles; through them, one's ascetic merit is inevitably diminished, or else one's progress becomes crooked and spiritual accomplishments are likewise lost.

He states when success (*siddhi*) occurs: "When [the women] are affectionate like mothers," and so forth. The meaning is that when they become as loving as mothers and the like, then there is success. However, he says that when they become perverse (*vakra*), then even the accomplishments become perverse: "The austerity (*tapas*) performed since beginningless time goes to ruin," and so forth. Why? He says: "Or because of the perverse," where *vā* means "because. This is because the heart of the messenger (*dūtī*)—
Likewise, even the accomplishments (siddhis) become crooked; that is to say, they turn away from one. || 7 ||

One should attract [the deity] together with the supreme [consort]; such is the certainty regarding the ritual substance. In this world, one who follows the left-hand path (vāmācāra) should always step forward with the left foot first.
Regarding what is to be done with such a messenger (*dūtī*), he says: "one should attract," and so forth. That which is the supreme *bodhicitta* is accompanied by *rajas*;

therefore, it is "more than half" (*sārdhamadhika*). Such is the determination regarding the substance (*dravya*). The substance is *bodhicitta*, and its faultless grasping is the "determination. As for the "left-handed practice" (*vāmācāra*) in the world, it is easily understood that one should step forward with the left foot first. (8)
Turning with the left hand, honoring with the left raised upward;
merely taking [the offering] with the left, one performs the left-hand libation and consumption. || 9 ||

“Turning with the left hand” means turning the body while remaining steady with the left hand. “Those who worship with the raised left” means that by the word “raised” (*ūrdhva*) is meant the *vajra*; thus, the yogins are those who worship according to the intention of the yoginīs. The passage beginning with “left” and so forth is easy to understand. (9)

One who does not violate his vows, who is complete in his observances, a practitioner intent upon his task, and who eats the sacrificial porridge (caru) together with others according to the rules and the Kula tradition; || 10 ||
"One who does not destroy the vow, one who is full of vows. The "non-vow" (*avrata*) refers to the vows of the Brāhmaṇas and others; it is the restriction of conduct such as the *samaya*.

"Subservient to what has been performed" (*kṛtanighna*) means intent upon that which has been done, such as the meditation on the deity and so forth. The *samayas* are the Yoginīs, and the *cāra* is the conduct of the *Kula*.
In one place, in a certain region, he is a consumer of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*). || 10 ||
The practice of the five castes is proclaimed as the four castes;
the one whose practice is of a single caste is the practitioner of yoga who worships with perfection.

He who practices and partakes among the five castes (*pañcavarṇa*) is one whose conduct is among the five castes (*pañcavarṇasamācāra*). Why? Because it is said, "and he is proclaimed as being beyond the four castes" (*acaturvarṇaśca kīrtitaḥ*). One for whom the four castes do not exist is such a yogi, because [the castes] are merely conceptual constructs in the world.
A yogi of this nature is proclaimed and described in the midst of the *yoginīs*. Alternatively, one who possesses the four castes is likewise [referred to].

He is of four castes (*caturvarṇa*) because he is the yogin Śrī Heruka; the substitution of *u* for *o* is due to his being a sage (*ārṣatvāt*). To the question "In what sense is there no [distinction of] four castes?", he says: he whose conduct and certainty regarding the castes is one is "one whose conduct regarding the castes is single" (*ekavarṇasamācāra*). The intended meaning is that even while being the yogin Śrī Heruka, by virtue of the purity of his single conduct regarding the castes, he possesses the four faces of the four castes. || 11 ||
If one prepares a triangular maṇḍala using cow flesh, horse flesh, dog flesh, and that of variegated animals, even the Buddha himself will certainly perish.
He describes the expansion of ritual action for the purpose of destroying those who harm the Three Jewels and others, beginning with the words "cow-flesh" and so forth.

One should perform the construction of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and other requirements according to the prescribed rules suitable for *homa*. Having kindled the fire with pungent oils and other materials used as implements for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), one should visualize Khandarohā entering within through the right nostril and exiting through the path of the anus; then, by means of her—

Having visualized the one to be accomplished (sādhya) as naked and overwhelmed, drawn in by means of the hand-marks of the vajra-hook and the knife, and having been cut into pieces by that very [weapon], one should kill him—released with the pride of the Great Wrath—while maintaining the conviction that the flesh of cows and so forth is his own flesh. One should offer oblations with the root mantra using variegated cocks and the like. 12.
The food of the heroes is likewise endowed with mantra and mudrā;
it is the manifestation of Śrī Heruka, a ritual service free from [ordinary] treatises. (13)
One should constantly practice retention and provide protection through every action; one should [attain] yoga, which is non-dual knowledge, and the mind should remain fixed on the single point.

An external woman consists of mudrā and mantra; it is said that eating together with her is praised for those heroes—beginning with the words "mantra," etc. "Endowed with mantra and mudrā" means endowed with mantra and endowed with equanimity (*samatā*). In that meal, one should perform the emanation of Śrī Heruka within oneself and the ritual service (*upacāra*) of the goddesses toward the yoginīs. And this [is taught] in all the Yoginī Tantras.

He says "that which is desired to be spoken" and so forth—namely, *śrīheruka* etc. Furthermore, he says "the maintenance" and so forth, meaning that at other times as well, the constant maintenance (*dhāraṇa*) of the *Śrīheruka-yoga* must be performed. Regarding "yoga": it refers to the yoga. "Yoga" is a qualifier for the maintenance, meaning that which possesses yoga.
Regarding "non-dual knowledge" (*advayajñāna*): one who knows the non-duality of *Śrīheruka* is thus [described]. And "the mind" (*cetas*)... from that, one...
The state of being a word. || 13-14 ||
So that he may achieve success without obstacles—no one else is as renowned for this—as his messenger, who is excellent, divine, diligent, and accompanied by her attendants. (15)

He says "nirvighna" and so forth, [meaning]: "Just as this [practice] is without obstacle for the sake of accomplishment, no other means is perceived. And her messenger (dūtī) is excellent, most superior; such a one is divine and fit for accomplishment.
She is accompanied by patience (*kṣānti*). || 15 ||

One who is unattached [to worldly things] through the union of passion, yet possesses the discernment of the substances of yoga and is devoted to the instructions of the Guru, is equal to the god Kubera in wealth for that purpose. 16.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, the procedure for the single color of the internal fire-oblation, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
"Unattached through union with passion": having attained external union with passion, the yogi should always remain unattached—that is, dispassionate.

Yoga is *samādhi*; "one for whom there is a distinction between those two, yoga and the substance (*dravya*)"—that is, yoga and the object of consumption (*bhakṣya*)—is so described. His state, namely "the distinction between yoga and the substance," must be cultivated. Alternatively, it refers to the distribution of the substance born of yoga, which is the *bodhicitta*.

The meaning of *vibhāgatā* (division) is that one possesses a share in enjoyment (*bhoga*) together with wisdom (*prajñā*). It is called *vibhāga* because its portion (*bhāga*) is in a specific state; the abstract state of being that is *vibhāgatā*.

He says "the guru," etc., [meaning] that yogins who are eager for the teacher’s instruction may come to be [thus]. The sense is: "May they be well-attached when the instruction on the yoga of Śrī Heruka is given by the gurus. Therefore, they are "for that purpose" (*tadarthāḥ*). Furthermore, "wealth" (*dhana*) refers to faith and so forth.

And thus it is said: "The wealth of faith, the wealth of wisdom, the wealth of learning, the wealth of vigor, the wealth of joy, the wealth of meditative concentration, and the wealth of mindfulness. Because he invariably bestows these upon those who possess desire by accomplishing their aims, Śrī Heruka and those equal to him are "givers of wealth" (dhanada). || 16 ||

Because of the internal fire-sacrifice (*adhyātmahoma*) and because it is excluded from worldly fire-sacrifices, these are prescribed as the unity of the castes (*varṇaikatva*); since this chapter [contains] that, it is the twenty-eighth chapter, the "Chapter on the Internal Fire-Sacrifice and the Prescription for the Unity of the Castes.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 28.
The twenty-ninth chapter: The Procedure for the Characteristics, Powers, and States of the Female Messengers (Dūtī).
Now, furthermore, the knowledge of the characteristics of the female messengers is fully set forth, by which one correctly understands the Ḍākinīs who abide by the pledge (samaya).
Since there is no practice without the activity of "heat" (*ūṣma*), he speaks this chapter in order to explain its meaning, beginning with "Now" (*atha*) and so forth.

"Now" means immediately after the explanation of the internal fire-oblation (*adhyātmika-homa*) and other such rites. "Another" (*aparam*) means another accomplishment. To the question "What is that?", he says "It has been indicated" (*samuddiṣṭam*).

The meaning is that another summary indication has been made. To the question "For what purpose?", he says "For the sake of knowing the characteristics of the female messenger" (*dūtī-lakṣaṇa-jñānataḥ*).
For the sake of knowing their characteristics: by means of which one correctly understands that the ḍākinīs abide by the samaya. The nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental.
In an instant, she sees her brother, her father, or even her master—
she who has a thick tongue, tawny eyes, a harsh voice, and reddish-brown hair.

He sees his heroic brother, his father, Śrī Heruka, as his own lord; indeed, the Lord himself [bestows] lordship upon him in an instant through the power of mantra. "Stout," and so forth: she whose eyes are tawny is thus described; "rough" in touch; she whose hair on the head is tawny is thus described. (2)
She is the common source of all accomplishments, always devoted to recitation and vows;
she is endowed with the power of remembrance and possesses the status of a messenger and other such roles.

He says that it is common to all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*) with the words: "common to all accomplishments. "Recollection" (*smaraṇa*) means contemplation; "endowed with that" means accompanied by such application. To the question "Of what is there contemplation?", he says: "By the messenger," and so forth. "Endowed with the word" (*padānvitam*): from the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the protection of the pledge (*samaya*) is understood. "Word" (*pada*) means knowledge; "endowed with that" means joined with recollection. By this, it is said that [this practice] is for one who is devoted to the pledge (*samaya*).
The meditation on the messenger (dūtī) should be performed. || 3 ||
The twenty-four supreme ḍākinīs bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
one who seeks to accomplish all desires and aims should daily recite the root mantra. (4)
And from this, the mantra is born, which bestows the fruit of the play of yoga, pacifies all Māras, and [pervades] the three worlds with all that is moving and unmoving. || 5 ||

He states how many there are of these messengers (*dūtīs*): "The twenty-four supreme *ḍākinīs* bestow the fruits of enjoyment and liberation. By way of illustration, this refers to the twenty-four *ḍākinīs* beginning with Pracaṇḍā; however, here it should be understood that the twelve are also included. To the question of why they should be meditated upon, he says: "Enjoyment" (*bhukti*) refers to heaven and so forth; "liberation" (*mukti*) is the removal of the bonds of the afflictions (*kleśas*) and the like. These are the two fruits.

They are so called because they bestow [attainments] pre-eminently. One should recite the root mantra through the meditation on them as residing within the maṇḍala of the Lord Śrī Heruka; thus he says "the root," etc., which is easy to understand. The three worlds are conquered, meaning they are brought under control. For this very reason, they grant the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (4–5)
The practitioner who is devoted to spiritual accomplishment must be endowed with both mantra and mudrā;
for embodied beings, a mantra devoid of mudrā does not bring about the presence [of the deity]. (6)

To the question "Why is it so?", he says: "Mantra," and so forth. *Mantra* is speech that impels the reality (*tattva*). *Mudrā* refers to the deity. Endowed with these two as the means to be accomplished, that practitioner becomes intent upon *siddhi*. To the question "Why is the mantra alone not recited?", he says: "Mudrā," and so forth. *Devabhāvanā* (the cultivation of the divine) is the proximity (*sānnidhya*), which is the direct realization; the agent is the mantra, and [realization] is the object. It is not [the case that... (Note: The final sentence fragment appears to be an incomplete negation or a transition to a further point.)
The meaning is that he does not attain [rebirth]. This is because the embodied one—the yogin—possesses a distinguished body. || 6 ||
It must be understood through diligent application, just as the practice of heat (*ūṣmakriyā*) occurs within oneself;
for those who hate the Great Yoga (*mahāyoga*), which accomplishes all desires and goals. (7)
Having passed through a hundred births as a dog, one is even born among the Caṇḍālas;
just as someone seeking ghee might, out of faith, churn water.
Yet ghee is not produced; there is only physical exhaustion.
Otherwise, the wearing of auspicious ornaments and even worship would be in vain.
Because it is the cause of the means of livelihood, it is resorted to by those engaged in other yogas;
or it is the land of Mahāyoga where the heroes dwell.
Even among beings who are Caṇḍālas or Mlecchas, one should designate that place as [one's own];
there I shall always abide for the sake of favoring those beings. (11)
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*, concerning the procedure for the characteristics of the female messengers (*dūtī*), their powers, and their states. 29.

And that proximity to the mantra is to be understood and attained through *abhiyoga*—that is, through practice that is respectful, uninterrupted, and long-lasting. To the question "What is that?", he says: "Just as the function of heat within oneself. *Sattva* refers to the vajra-nature;

*ūṣma* is the [magical] power such as pacifying (*śāntika*), enriching (*pauṣṭika*), or subjugating (*abhicāra*) rites; its *kriyā* is the accomplishment thereof. Just as that [power] exists within oneself, so too does the capacity [to accomplish it].

This means that very same efficacy. Regarding those who harm the Three Jewels, one should demonstrate efficacy by inflicting suffering and so forth upon them even in this very life. Furthermore, he says "those who... and so forth, to show that the power of mantra exists even in the next world. "Mahāyoga" refers to the yoga of Śrī Heruka. The remainder is easy to understand. He says "just as... and so forth to show that there is no other achiever of awakening than Mahāyoga. Faith—

The sense is that through such conviction, there is no fruit whatsoever from the practice of another yoga. Another yoga is maintained because it serves as a cause for auspiciousness; or rather, it is like worship. To show that the maintenance of another yoga is not for the sake of the next world, he says: "another yoga. Even the dwelling place of the Śrī Heruka yogins generates merit.

Thus he said: "Those who uphold the great yoga," and so forth. Even a region such as that of the Caṇḍālas, which is inhabited by heroes—that place one should likewise conceive of as a sacred land (*saddeśa*). For the sake of bestowing grace upon those sentient beings belonging to that land presided over by the yogin of Śrī Heruka, I abide there eternally. (7–11)

Power (*śakti*) is the power of mantra. State (*avasthā*) refers to the abiding for the sake of sentient beings in a place inhabited by those fit for Śrī Heruka; it is the state of power characterized by the *dūtī*. That which establishes these for the sake of knowledge is the chapter (*paṭala*); thus, it is "the [thirty-ninth]. It is the thirty-ninth (*ūnatriṃśattama*).
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. || 29 ||
The thirtieth chapter: The Ritual for Extracting the Mantras of the Wall-Binding.
Now I shall describe another arrangement that is very difficult to obtain;
by the mere knowledge of which the practitioner swiftly attains accomplishment.

The word *atha* means "thereafter"; I shall now describe another *prastāra* following the extraction (*uddhāra*) of the root mantra (*mūlamantra*). It is called a *prastāra* because letters (*varṇa*) and measures (*mātrā*) are spread out (*āstīryante*) within it. It consists of a continuous series of forty-nine grid-lines. To the question "Of what nature is this?", he says: "Extremely difficult to obtain" (*sudurlabha*). Since the four-faced mantra is extracted from this, it is thus [described].

He asks what the distinction is regarding the mantra itself that is to be extracted, and says "by which," etc. "By which" means by the mantra. "Swift accomplishment for the practitioner" means that by it there is the pacification of obstacles. || 1 ||
On a level and delightful patch of ground, having smeared it with sandalwood paste, which is fragrant with sweet scents and strewn with heaps of flowers. || 2 ||
In a place filled with rows of lamps and delightful with the fragrance of incense,
one should perform the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkaraṇa*) and then carry out the binding of the directions (*diśābandha*).
Then, having formed a *muraja-bandha* consisting of nine circular lines,
one who is well-composed should write down the phonemes and prosodic measures and then spread them out.

He states where one should spread [the seat]: "on the ground," and so forth. What is intended by "sandalwood and the five nectars" (*pañcāmṛta*) is that which brings delight to one who knows its true nature. "Fragrant scent" refers to sandalwood and the like. The meaning is that the area of the ground should be smeared with fragrant scents mixed with the five nectars. "Flower fragrance" refers to *campaka* and other such flowers. "Incense" refers to ball-incense (*piṇḍadhūpa*) and the like. In such a place, which is empty, one should contemplate emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Having meditated upon the preliminary rites such as the binding of the directions (*digbandha*), one should spread out, that is, lay down, the "mere letters" (*varṇamātra*). By "mere letters" is meant the vowels beginning with *a* and the consonants beginning with *ka*; these letters alone constitute the "mere letters. Having done what? He says: "having inscribed" (*samālikhya*). That is, having arranged them in an even manner according to the sequence of the vowels and consonants. Having done what prior to the inscribing? He says: "like a drum" (*muraja*) and so forth. This refers to the arrangement resembling that of a drum.

That which has such an arrangement is the *prastāra* (the grid). Because it faces away from the grasping of vowels and consonants through both direct and reverse orders, it possesses a similarity to a drum (*muraja*). || 2-4 ||
The practitioner should extract the Hero situated therein, who accomplishes all desires and goals;
he should [extract] the vowels and consonants in both direct and reverse order.

The *vīra* is the mantra. "The accomplisher of all desired aims" is an epithet of the mantra. To the question, "Whence should one extract the *vīra*? he says: "The practitioner [extracts] the vowels and consonants in direct and reverse order. The vowels are *a* and so forth;
the consonants are *ka* and so forth, because they have the nature of sound (*dhvani*). One should extract them from there. (5)
One should cause this number of virtuous acts to be performed for the Sage;
having gathered them within thirty-two compartments, they are then divided by the fifth.
"Contained within this number" means that one should extract it in such a way that it falls within the number of the grid cells (*koṣṭhaka*).
Anticipating the question of whose statement this is, he says "of the Sage. Regarding "having grasped [the letters] in thirty-two grid cells": the word *koṣṭha* is used here without a case ending.
Starting from the grid cell presided over by the letter *ka*, the thirty-second grid cell, which is presided over by the letter *sa*, is taken.

By counting starting from the letter *ka*, the letter *sa* itself is to be understood. In all such cases, by the mention of a "cell" (*koṣṭhaka*), the syllable residing in that cell is taken, because of its functional utility. Regarding the reading "the third of the cells," starting from the palatal *śa* (occupying a cell), the third [letter] occupying a dental *sa* is taken. As for the phrase "pierced by the fifth," it is distinguished by the vowel *u*.
[The verse] is completed. || 6 ||
Having taken half of half of one hundred (i.e., twenty-five), it is divided into twenty-four;
the thirty-sixth square is divided by three squares.

"Having taken half of half of a hundred" means that, starting from the square presided over by the letter *ka* and counting, one reaches the letter *ma*. Likewise, "divided twenty-four times" means starting from the square presided over by the letter *ka*, it is divided twenty-four times; that is, the twenty-fourth [letter], which is *bha*. By that, half of half of a hundred is divided at the bottom part, [occupying] the thirty-sixth square by way of three squares.
It is divided. Starting from the one presided over by the letter *a*, it reaches the thirty-sixth, which is presided over by the letter *na*. This is the third group of three cells.
Starting from the cell presided over by the letter *a*, the letter *i* is used to divide it. || 7 ||
Then, having taken thirty-two, it is divided by five;
then, having taken twenty-five, one should join them with twenty-four. (8)
"Then, having taken the thirty-second, it is pierced by the fifth cell. Here, "then" (*tataḥ*) means starting from that which is presided over by the letter *ka*.

The word "tu" (*then*) has the sense of "indeed" (*eva*) or a conjunction (*samuccaye*). Likewise, in the preceding case as well: "Then, having taken the twenty-fifth, one should join the twenty-fourth.
The "twenty-fifth" is the twenty-fifth [letter], which is presided over by the letter *ma*. "Then" (*tataḥ*) refers to that which is presided over by the letter *ka*. "Twenty-fourth" refers to...
The twenty-fourth [letter] is the syllable *bha*, and that is in the third case; the meaning is that one should join the letter *ma* at the bottom with the letter *bha*. || 8 ||
Taking thirty-three and honoring fifteen squares, joined with the fifth, this is considered a most excellent and beautiful [arrangement]. (9)
"Taking the thirty-third, honored as the fifteenth in the treasury. This refers to the sequence.

Starting from that which is presided over by the letter *ka*, the thirty-third is that which is presided over by the letter *ha*. Starting from that which is presided over by the letter *a*, the fifteenth is that which is presided over by the *anusvāra*.
"Joined with the fifth, it is considered beautiful and supreme. Starting from that which is presided over by the letter *a*, there is the state of being the fifth. Five—
The seed-syllable *m-e-n-a* is auspicious because of its efficacy in accomplishing all purposes. || 9 ||
"Endowed with twenty-two and indeed twenty-seven—having taken all this together, it is called the first step. (10)

"Endowed with the twenty-second, and likewise the twenty-seventh. "The twenty-second" refers to that which is presided over by the letter *pha*. "The twenty-seventh," from that which is presided over by the vowel *a*, refers to that which is presided over by the letter *ṭa*. Taking all of this together constitutes the first word; it is called the first word because it is stated to be the first mantra-sentence. (10)
The nineteenth letter from the grid, joined with the son of fire (Ra), and divided by three grids, shall become the syllable. || 11 ||
The eighth seed-syllable from the *ya*-group, joined with the thirty-sixth square, and likewise the word [formed] in this manner, is the accomplisher of all desires and goals. (12)
"The nineteenth cell from the one presided over by Fire’s son, conjoined with that which is divided by three cells starting from the one presided over by A.
This means: the nineteenth [cell] from the cell presided over by A is the one presided over by Ga. "Fire’s son" (vahniputra) refers to the letter Ra.
[The letter] divided by the triad of cells starting from the one presided over by A is the one presided over by I. And the eighth seed-syllable from the Ya-group is the thirty-sixth.

"Furthermore, it is joined with the word *eva*. [This means: the letter *ya* is the class (*varga*) of *ya*, thus it is the *ya*-class; from that, the eighth seed-syllable is *ha*. Regarding "the thirty-sixth cell," starting from the cell presided over by *a*, the thirty-sixth cell is presided over by *na*. Furthermore, such is the word. The letters *ca* and *eva* are used for the purposes of conjunction (*samuccaya*) and restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), respectively. (11–12)
Then, having taken the self-arisen [Svayambhū] from the treasury, conjoined with the fifth [vowel], and adorned above by the bindu. || 13 ||
The second step is said to be named "Accomplisher of All Aims" (Sarvārthasādhaka);
it consists of nineteen squares and is divided by the twenty-seventh [line].
But when joined with the third [digit], together with the thirty-third, and with the second cell, joined with the twentieth, it is auspicious and supremely beneficial. (15)

"Then, having taken the *svayambhū*": *svayambhū* is the letter *ha*. "From there" means from the word *gṛhṇa gṛhṇa*. "Joined with the fifth from the *koṣṭha*" means the fifth vowel (*u*) from the one presided over by *a* (i.e., *ā*), which is itself presided over by *a*. "Adorned above with a *bindu*" means that here, in every case, it is not the half-moon (*ardhacandra*) [that serves as the head-ornament], because it is adorned merely by the *bindu*. It is called "the achiever of all desires and aims."
The meaning is that it is well-known by this designation. The syllable *phaṭ* is to be understood from what precedes: "joined above with the *bindu*.

Therefore, having taken the twenty-second [letter] from there, and likewise the eleventh—according to a certain reading, the twenty-second is presided over by the letter *ka*, while the eleventh is presided over by *pha* and the [thirteenth] by *ṭa*. Thus, the syllable *phaṭ* is easily understood.
This is the second word: "The nineteenth square, however, divided by the twenty-seventh, joined with the third.

The nineteenth [letter] is presided over by *a* (the letter *ga*), while the twenty-seventh is presided over by *r*. Having taken the thirty-third, joined with the twentieth of the second square, it is beautiful and supreme.

Regarding the term *hitam*: from the thirty-third [letter], which is presided over by the letter *ka*, the second [letter] is that presided over by the letter *a*; from the one presided over by the letter *ka*, the twentieth is that presided over by the letter *na*. (13–15)
One should extract, with a well-concentrated mind, the twenty-one squares as well as the twenty-sixth, along with the position for the double repetition.

"Twenty-one squares, likewise joined with the twenty-sixth"—the meaning is that from the letter presided over by *ka* (the first), the letter *pa* (the twenty-first) is to be taken. The particle *tu* is used for conjunction. "Likewise" (*tathā*) means that from the letter presided over by *ka*, the twenty-sixth [letter] presided over by *ya* is to be taken. "And the word repeated twice"—the meaning is that there is a similar word nearby as a second instance, according to the rule. || 16 ||
Then, taking from the first square in reverse order,
it is joined with the end of the fourth [square] and likewise honored by the fifteenth.
Then, taking from the first square in reverse order, it is conjoined with the end of the fourth; likewise, it is "worshipped as the fifteenth.

The connection is as follows: then, from the reverse arrangement, having first taken the very letter *ha* situated at the beginning from the [square] presided over by the letter *ha*, the third word is stated. From that which is presided over by the letter *a*, the fourth is that which is presided over by the letter *ī*; [this is] its end.
It is presided over by the syllable *ukāra*. The rest is easily understood. || 17 ||
For those desiring dharma, artha, and mokṣa, the third pada is spoken;
it is the second seed from the square, from the thirty-sixth square.

The third word is "the word of Dharma and so forth"; another word must be supplied [after it]. Here too, the syllable *phaṭ* is to be carried over. Thus ends the third word. Regarding the phrase "the second seed from the square": it is [the seed] presided over by the letter *a*.
The second seed of the deities is that which is presided over by the letter *ā*. The particle *tu* is used for emphasis. "From the thirty-sixth square" means from the thirty-sixth cell.
The meaning is that, beginning from the syllable *ka* presided over by the letter *da*, one should take only the syllable *na* which is presided over by the letter *na*. || 18 ||
Likewise, the twenty-sixth is indeed called the fourth square;
taking the thirty-third, it is honored by the thirteen cells.

It should be understood that the fourth word is spoken by taking the letter *na* and the letter *m*. The remainder is easy to understand. "The thirty-third" refers to the letter *ha*. "The thirteenth in the chest" [refers to the letter *a*] as presided over by the vowel *a*. || 19 ||
The practitioner should take the tenth from the square [presided over by the letter *a*], moving in reverse order,
as well as the nineteenth from that same square.
From the cell presided over by the letter *ka*, from the twenty-third cell;
it is joined with the second cell and adorned above with a *bindu*. || 21 ||
Then, having likewise taken the eighth [syllable], which is the earthly one,
the wise one should cause it to be split by fire, joined with the ending syllables *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*.

"The practitioner [is found] by counting ten from the cell in reverse order. This means that the tenth from the letter *ha* (which occupies the cell) is the letter *bha*. "The nineteenth from the cell" refers to the nineteenth from the letter *a*, which is the letter *ga*. "From the twenty-third cell" refers to the twenty-third cell from the letter *ka*, which is the letter *ba*.

The meaning is that, therefore, the letter *va* alone is to be grasped as being presided over by *a*. From that which is presided over by *a*, the second [letter] is that which is presided over by *ā*.
"Adorned above with a *bindu*" means the *bindu* itself is merely a dot. The seed-syllable *va* belongs to the earth element. "From that" refers to the arrangement (*prastāra*).
The eighth [letter] is from that which is presided over by *ka*. The passage beginning with "by fire" and so forth is easy to understand. Here too, the syllable *phaṭ* follows.
It should be recited. Regarding the phrase "joined with *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* at the end": this means that *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* are joined at its end; thus it is "joined with *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* at the end.

The suffix ending in *-niṣṭhā* (the past passive participle) has been placed after the word it qualifies. This is a word without a case-ending (*nirvibhaktika*), and it is to be pronounced with a protracted vowel (*pluta*). || 20–22 ||
This mantra, named Trailokyavijaya, is adorned with four words;
all of them are illuminated by the syllable Oṃ and joined at the end with Huṃ Phaṭ. (23)

"Etat" refers to the mantra-phrase which is the *samaya*. It is called "Trailokyavijaya" because it conquers the three worlds—Hari, Hara, and Hariṇyagarbha—without exception. The rest is easily understood. Regarding "Oṃ" and so forth: there are four mantra-words illuminated by the *praṇava* (Oṃ); thus, the nature of the *praṇava* has been stated. As for *hūṃ* and *phaṭ*: those [mantra-words] to which *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* were previously joined at the beginning and at the end [are here specified].

The same applies to those mantras. Then this mantra follows: Oṃ sumbha niḥsumbha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ | Oṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ | Oṃ gṛhṇāpaya gṛhṇāpaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ | Oṃ ānaya ho bhagavān vajra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ. || 23 ||
This mantra of the Sovereign Wheel of Knowledge has never existed before, nor will it ever exist again, within the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, the *Paramādya*, the *Saṃvara*, or the *Vajrabhairava*. (24)
For the protection of that [mandala], especially against all evil beings, there is a mandala joined with the four wrathful deities and endowed with the eight forms.
By merely obtaining this, one indeed dies through lack of discernment;
yet, by reciting it through the yoga of the wheel, the fruit of all accomplishments arises.
Regarding the term *vidyārājacakravartī*: they are called *vidyārājas* because they shine (*rājante*) by means of the *vidyās*, that is, the deities.

Among all other *vidyārājas*, this mantra is for the protection of the maṇḍala found in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* and other such works, which is presided over by the *cakravartin*. This very point is stated as follows:
In the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, the *Paramādya*, the *Saṃvara*, and the *Vajrabhairava*,
he is joined with the four wrathful deities and endowed with the eight forms.

"The maṇḍala is for his protection, specifically against all malevolent beings. Thus, the eight forms are the eight world-protectors (*lokapāla*). Regarding "against all malevolent beings": it is for the sake of protecting the maṇḍala from all malevolent beings. "By this" refers to the mantra; "malevolent" refers to anyone who dies [by its power]. "From the application of the wheel" means from oneself into the Wisdom consort (*prajñā*), and from there...
Through recitation while entering into the self, there arises the fruit of all accomplishments. || 24–26 ||
Oṃ sumbha niḥsumbha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ | Oṃ gṛhṇa gṛhṇa hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ gṛhṇāpaya gṛhṇāpaya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ ānaya ho bhagavān vajra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ || 27 ||
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, the procedure for extracting the mantra of the *muraja-bandha*, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

He states the collection of mantras, saying that there are four mantra-words, beginning with *oṃ*. Here, the other two syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ* are concealed. That which prescribes the extraction of the mantra in the *muraja-bandha* arrangement is the "Chapter" (*paṭala*); thus, it is so called. It is the thirtieth, the *triṃśattama*.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. || 30 ||
The thirty-first chapter on the ritual procedures for consuming, offering oblations, performing bali-offerings, and hand-homa; following that,
the destruction of all [obstacles] by means of "great flesh" (mahāmāṃsa) is known as the Vajra-born.
This is likewise the destroyer of all cruel beings and is itself formidable.
In this same manner, the consumption of dog and pig meat, as well as that of cocks,
should be performed for the purposes of eating, fire-offerings, and ritual oblations without hesitation.
The twenty-seventh [chapter] has taught the worship and the ritual of offerings (*balikriyā*); in the twenty-eighth, the ritual of fire-offerings (*homakriyā*) is taught.

To explain that, he now states the chapter beginning with the word *tataḥ*. "From the fire-offering" (*homāt*). "For all" (*sarveṣām*) means for the benefactors, such as the Guru, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth.
"Born of the Vajra" (*vajrajam*) refers to the body, speech, and so on. It is also stated in the *Śrīsamāja*: "By means of 'great meat' (*mahāmāṃsa*), for all..."

"It is known as 'born of the vajra' because it causes destruction. Or, "born of the vajra" means born of indivisible gnosis (*abhedyajñāna*). Why is this so? He says: "This," and so forth. "This" means "this very one. And that meat-homa is "the destroyer of all cruel things" and likewise "terrible"; the meaning is that it is performed with that great flesh (*mahāmāṃsa*). It is superior to other types of *homa* for the following reason:

It has been said: "Gentleness is not appropriate toward those who are extremely cruel and fierce. This statement is for the purpose of prohibiting their descent into the lower realms (*apāya*). They are to be warded off from that state in this manner. "In this manner" means: [one should employ] a destroyer who is fierce. Even the oblation of the flesh of animals and the like is intended. By the word "having eaten" (*bhakṣya*), eating is meant for the sake of worship; the meaning is that the rites of worship and so forth should be performed with the very flesh of those [beings].
"What might be intended by this?"—such is conceptual deliberation (*vikalpa-vicāra*); its opposite is non-deliberation (*avicāra*). (1.2)
The entire kingdom, without exception or remainder, is accomplished and fully realized;
these three are the sources from which conch shells, mother-of-pearl, and pearls arise.
Who could defile the skull of those whose very bodies are the knowledge of the Dharma—the Hero adorned with a garland of skulls and decorated with the crescent moon? (4)

To the question "What then?", he says: "It is accomplished," and so forth. "Entirely" means all; "the remaining [attainments]" refers to the lower accomplishments such as the sword (*khaḍga*) and others, while "without remainder" refers to Buddhahood. "All kingdoms" refers to the status of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*). This refers to the seizing of these things even when they have not been killed by oneself. Furthermore, he states that for the practitioner of the *caryā*, the skull alone should serve as the vessel: "The conch," and so forth. "Released," etc.

The pearl-producing creature is a specific type of living being; even its particular bone is referred to by the word "pearl. Just as conch shells and other such items are considered pure by the Vaidikas, so too is the skull [pure], though it is a different part of a living being. To demonstrate this, he says: "The three arise from causes. The causes are karma, the afflictions (*kleśa*), and the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth. These three—conch shells and the others—[are the examples].
[They arise] from a specific cause; a human being is likewise [so]. Therefore, how could a proponent of the Vedas disparage the skull? [Objection:

If it is argued that its use in medicines and the like renders it pure compared to conch shells and other objects, [then why is no other purpose for other people seen? Even by the Blessed One, no practical utility was perceived in the skull. For a jewel is not a common property of all people by its very nature.

[Regarding] knowledge: in reference to whom is there censure? He says—“of those whose bodies are the knowledge of phenomena. This refers to yogins whose very body (*śarīra*), that is, their essential nature (*svarūpa*), is the realization (*bodha*) of phenomena (*dharmas*) such as the aggregates (*skandhas*) by means of their emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and so forth. The genitive case is used here in the sense of the locative. For this very reason, he asks: “By what could one censure even Śrī Heruka, who bears that [knowledge]?”—beginning with the words “skull” (*kapāla*) and so forth. [The phrase] “to join the skull” (*kapālaṃ melitum*)...

"He possesses this [garland]," thus he is *kapālamālī* (the wearer of the skull-garland). Alternatively, by virtue of belonging to the *śikhādi* group, the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is applied as *kapālamālāsyāsti*, meaning "he who has a skull-garland. He is so called because he wears a garland of five skulls on his head. He is a *vīra* (hero) because of his freedom from attachment (*niḥsaṅgatvāt*). He is *candrārdhakṛtabhūṣaṇaḥ* (one whose ornament is fashioned from the half-moon), meaning that the half-moon itself serves as his crafted decoration.
He wears the half-moon due to the purity of his stainless and perfect manifestation (*nirmāṇa*). || 3-4 ||
In this very way, that which is born of heroes is remembered as belonging to the heroes.
The practitioner should display the secret signs (*chommakas*) with the left hand. (5)

Among even the heroes, he from whom those who are heroes such as Hari, Hara, and others are born—by whom could that well-known one be disparaged? "One should show the five secret signs (chommakas)": the five goddesses, Vajravārāhī and the others, have been mentioned; one should show them, that is, meditate upon them, within the five skull-cups situated in the crown of matted hair. "The practitioner [should hold] the left hand," however.
The connection is "he should show. The word "tu" (but) indicates a distinction. The intended meaning is that he should give the pledges (samaya) and so forth held in his left hand. || 5 ||
For this is the abode of heroes and the source of the secret signs (chommaka);
the entire universe, the three worlds with all that is moving and unmoving, has originated from Vāma.

To the question "Why? he says: "Of the heroes," and so forth. "Of the heroes" refers to Vajrasattva and the others. "This abode" is the left hand. "Hi" means because. Why? Because from the left hand proceeds the activity of the heroes and heroines who are designated by secret signs (*saṃketa*). He says that this [world] is purified by that [left hand]: "The left," and so forth. "The left" is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). "From empty phenomena..."

Because of the statement, "Empty phenomena alone arise," *vāmā* is *prajñā*, and the entire world arising from that—consisting of the aggregates (*skandhas*) and so forth—is [the result]. For there is nothing in the three worlds that performs any purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) through means (*upāya*) alone; by such statements, he demonstrates that it is likewise so externally as well. || 6 ||
Vajrasattva resides in the body, and likewise Vairocana in the creeper;
in that very same way, Padmanartaka is for the Guru.
The Hero, the bestower of all accomplishments, resides in the Dhārā [finger];
in the Kaniṣṭhā [finger] is the imperishable one whose body is the womb of space.
And in the nails is Hayagrīva; likewise, Mālaya has been spoken of [there]. These are the causes for the arising of the left-hand path among all heroes. || 9 ||

He describes the worship of the hands: "Vajrasattva" and so forth. Vajrasattva is to be meditated upon in the body, that is, on the thumb; Vairocana on the creeper, that is, on the index finger; for the Guru, Padyanartaka (the Lord of the Lotus Dance) on the middle finger; on the stream, that is, on the ring finger, is the Hero Śrī Heruka; and on the little finger is Ākāśagarbha. [The word] "tanuḥ" is without a case ending; it means subtle and difficult to perceive.

Because its nature is consciousness (*bodha*). It does not pass away, thus it is *avyaya* (imperishable). Ākāśagarbha is Vajrasūrya. Hayagrīva is in all the fingers and nails; the word "and" (*ca*) is used for conjunction. He states that these also arise from the left side—namely, "the abode" (*ālaya*). That in which the nature of self-grasping and so forth dissolves and is no longer perceived through investigation, and from which deities such as Vajrasattva are born, is the "abode. Regarding the word "these": [The text continues: ...[the deities] are generated. The syllable *ma* is the seed-syllable of Mañjuśrī. The syllable *ya* is the seed-syllable of Kṣitigarbha. The syllable *ra* is the seed-syllable of Akṣobhya. The syllable *va* is the seed-syllable of Vajrapāṇi. The syllable *ta* is the seed-syllable of Ratnapāṇi. The syllable *tha* is the seed-syllable of Vighnāntaka. The syllable *da* is the seed-syllable of Yamāntaka. The syllable *dha* is the seed-syllable of Padmāntaka. The syllable *na* is the seed-syllable of Amṛtakuṇḍalin. The syllable *pa* is the seed-syllable of Acala. The syllable *pha* is the seed-syllable of Ṭakkirāja. The syllable *ba* is the seed-syllable of Nīladaṇḍa. The syllable *bha* is the seed-syllable of Mahābala. The syllable *ya* is the seed-syllable of Uṣṇīṣacakravartin. The syllable *la* is the seed-syllable of Sumbharāja. The syllable *va* is the seed-syllable of Vajravega. The syllable *śa* is the seed-syllable of Vajrajvālānalārka. The syllable *ṣa* is the seed-syllable of Vajradaṇḍa. The syllable *sa* is the seed-syllable of Vajrakhadga. The syllable *ha* is the seed-syllable of Vajramusala. The syllable *kṣa* is the seed-syllable of Vajrānkuśa. The syllable *ja* is the seed-syllable of Vajrapāśa. The syllable *jha* is the seed-syllable of Vajrasphoṭa. The syllable *ña* is the seed-syllable of Vajrāveśa. The syllable *cha* is the seed-syllable of Vajratunda. The syllable *ca* is the seed-syllable of Vajracaṇḍa. The syllable *ṭa* is the seed-syllable of Vajrakrodha. The syllable *ṭha* is the seed-syllable of Vajrabhairava. The syllable *ḍa* is the seed-syllable of Vajramahākāla. The syllable *ḍha* is the seed-syllable of Vajrayakṣa. The syllable *ṇa* is the seed-syllable of Vajrarākṣasa. The syllable *ta* is the seed-syllable of Vajrapiśāca. The syllable *tha* is the seed-syllable of Vajragandharva. The syllable *da* is the seed-syllable of Vajrakinnara. The syllable *dha* is the seed-syllable of Vajrapretarāja. The syllable *na* is the seed-syllable of Vajracandika. The syllable *pa* is the seed-syllable of Vajrapannaga. The syllable *pha* is the seed-syllable of Vajramātarā. The syllable *ba* is the seed-syllable of Vajrakumārikā. The syllable *bha* is the seed-syllable of Vajramantrī. The syllable *ya* is the seed-syllable of Vajradūtī. The syllable *ra* is the seed-syllable of Vajrakanyā. The syllable *la* is the seed-syllable of Vajradāsī. The syllable *va* is the seed-syllable of Vajradākinī. The syllable *śa* is the seed-syllable of Vajramukhī. The syllable *ṣa* is the seed-syllable of Vajranetrī. The syllable *sa* is the seed-syllable of Vajralocanā. The syllable *ha* is the seed-syllable of Vajrajihvā. The syllable *kṣa* is the seed-syllable of Vajrakarṇikā. The syllable *ja* is the seed-syllable of Vajraghrāṇā. The syllable *jha* is the seed-syllable of Vajrasparśā. The syllable *ña* is the seed-syllable of Vajrasaṃsparśā. The syllable *cha* is the seed-syllable of Vajrarasanā. The syllable *ca* is the seed-syllable of Vajragātrā. The syllable *ṭa* is the seed-syllable of Vajrasaṃsthānā. The syllable *ṭha* is the seed-syllable of Vajrasaṃskāra. The syllable *ḍa* is the seed-syllable of Vajrasaṃjñā. The syllable *ḍha* is the seed-syllable of Vajrarūpā. The syllable *ṇa* is the seed-syllable of Vajradharmā. The syllable *ta* is the seed-syllable of Vajravāk. The syllable *tha* is the seed-syllable of Vajracittā. The syllable *da* is the seed-syllable of Vajrakāyā. The syllable *dha* is the seed-syllable of Vajravajrā. The syllable *na* is the seed-syllable of Vajrasattvā. The syllable *pa* is the seed-syllable of Vajraratnā. The syllable *pha* is the seed-syllable of Vajradharmā. The syllable *ba* is the seed-syllable of Vajrakarmā. The syllable *bha* is the seed-syllable of Vajralokeśvarī. The syllable *ya* is the seed-syllable of Vajratārā. The syllable *ra* is the seed-syllable of Vajrapāṇḍaravāsinī. The syllable *la* is the seed-syllable of Vajramāmakī. The syllable *va* is the seed-syllable of Vajrasarasvatī. The syllable *śa* is the seed-syllable of Vajragaurī. The syllable *ṣa* is the seed-syllable of Vajracaurī. The syllable *sa* is the seed-syllable of Vajravettālī. The syllable *ha* is the seed-syllable of Vajraghasmarī. The syllable *kṣa* is the seed-syllable of Vajrapukkasī. The syllable *ja* is the seed-syllable of Vajraśabarī. The syllable *jha* is the seed-syllable of Vajraḍombinī. The syllable *ña* is the seed-syllable of Vajracāmuṇḍā. The syllable *cha* is the seed-syllable of Vajralāmā. The syllable *ca* is the seed-syllable of Vajrakhandarohā. The syllable *ṭa* is the seed-syllable of Vajrasurābhakṣī. The syllable *ṭha* is the seed-syllable of Vajramāṃsabhakṣī. The syllable *ḍa* is the seed-syllable of Vajrarudhirabhakṣī. The syllable *ḍha* is the seed-syllable of Vajraśukrabhakṣī. The syllable *ṇa* is the seed-syllable of Vaj
The nominative case is used in the sense of the genitive. The hand, which originates from Vāma, is the cause of all these heroes. (7–9)
On the palm of the hand, one should show Śrī Heruka eager for union with Vajravārāhī;
on the back, however, all the Ḍākinīs—[thus one should show the fivefold self]. (10)
This placement of the hands (kara-nyāsa) brings about the union with all that is dear;
thus, according to this prescribed method, one should worship the supreme Hero.
Earth is known as Locanā, the water element is remembered as Māmakī;
fire is known as Pāṇḍarā, and wind is proclaimed as Tārā.

"In the palm of the hand" means in the center of the hand. "Śrī Heruka-Vajravārāhī" means Vajravārāhī who has entered into union with Śrī Heruka; therefore, she is eager for the assembly (*samāgama*). "But on the back, all the ḍākinīs" means that all the ḍākinīs are on the sides and so forth, because the word "but" (*tu*) indicates that the back is being characterized [as the location]. This is what is stated: in the middle of the hand is an eight-petaled lotus.
In its pericarp is Vajravārāhī, who has entered into union with Śrī Heruka. On the eastern petal is Ḍākinī; on the northern, Lāmā; on the western, Khaṇḍarohā;

on the southern, Rupiṇī; in the northeast, Yāminī; in the southeast, Mohanī; in the southwest, Sañcāriṇī; and in the northwest, Trāsanī—thus one should visualize. This constitutes the *karanyāsa* (hand-placement), which brings about the meeting with all that is dear.

Regarding the term *kara*: that ritual procedure in which the placement of deities (*devatānyāsa*) is performed upon the hands is called *karanyāsa*. It is so named because by means of it, all things dear [to the practitioner] come together.
In this manner, according to this sequence, one should worship the Hero (*vīra*). He states another set of names for the *Ḍākinīs* and others, beginning with "Earth," etc. (vv. 10–12).
The kissing [seal] is in the void; likewise are the perfections.
In the center is the abode of all heroes, but the wise one should release it at the back. 13.

*Cumbikā* is another name for Vajravārāhī; she herself is in the void, that is, in emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The meaning is "for the sake of the purification of emptiness. Therefore, they are called *pāramitās*. Those who are the *pāramitās* of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, and meditative concentration—beginning with Ḍākinī and ending with Vajravārāhī—are to be understood in sequence. The word "likewise" (*tathā*) indicates that the *prajñāpāramitā* is conjoined with the five *pāramitās*.

Thus he provides the sutra-commentary: "In the center, however, the abode of all heroes. This should be understood to mean that one should see the abode—the place of play—of all the heroes, such as Vajrapada and the others, in the center. The intended meaning is "in the middle of the hand," by virtue of the purification of the site for the play of all the heroes.
"The wise one should discharge it upon its back" means that one should see all the deities on the back of the hand, like reflections in a mirror.
By the word "but" (tu), he indicates the specific meaning that one should contemplate [the Self] upon the hand and on the back; therefore, whoever is the seer is the wise one. || 13 ||

This secret is not to be disclosed; it must be concealed with great effort. In this way, one should initiate the hero alone and then undertake the *caru* offering—the *Sarvavīrasamāyoga-Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*. 14.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*, concerning the ritual procedures for the consumption of food, fire offerings, bali offerings, and hand gestures (*hastacchoma*). 31.

"One should show the five secret signs (*chommaka*). It should be understood that the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) are also designated by the term *chommaka*. Consequently, this refers to the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*). In that very context, there are the five nectars: having produced [the syllables] born from the seed-syllables *vuṃ*, *āṃ*, *jrīṃ*, *khaṃ*, and *hūṃ*, which consist of Vairocana and the other [Buddhas] and are empowered by the three syllables, [one recites] for Pracaṇḍā and the others: *oṃ pracaṇḍe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.

"Phaṭ! Thus, having first uttered the names of all [the deities], one should offer twenty-four libations (*tarpaṇa*) with the ring finger and thumb joined at the mouth, saying "Oṃ Khaṇḍakapālin Hūṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ Phaṭ," and then place one [libation] upon the tongue. This should be understood as another meaning for the "enjoyment of the five nectars" (*pañcāmṛtopabhoga*).
Thereafter, the worship (*pūjā*) should take place. It should also be understood that the secret signs (*chommaka*) are to be given preceded by the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*).

It should be understood that one should likewise taste the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) in a skull-cup or similar vessel, preceded by the ritual placement of the hands (*karanyāsa*), because the meaning of the Tantra is so vast. "One should kiss the hero" means one should worship him. "Therein, it shall be one" means that by this rite of the five nectars and so forth, one should eat the *caru*—which is not to be eaten [ordinarily]—contained within a single vessel. He states the fruit of enjoying the *caru*: "All heroes..."
"Samāyoga-Ḍākinījāla-saṃvara" means that one becomes Heruka. || 14 ||

The ritual procedures for consuming food, performing fire offerings (*homa*), and making sacrificial oblations (*bali*), as well as other secret signs (*chomma*), are prescribed herein; therefore, it is called a "chapter" (*paṭala*).
It is the thirty-first, the thirty-first [chapter].
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 31.
The thirty-second chapter: the ritual procedure for the generation stage of the accomplishment of animals, beasts, and vetālas.
Hereafter, the assembly of foods and drinks is fully explained, by which correct practice success quickly arises. (1)

Now he speaks the chapter on the ritual substances for the means of worship and so forth, beginning with "ataḥ param" (beyond this). Beyond the explanation of worship and so forth, that which is fixed is about to be fully explained. What is it? He says: "the assembly for eating and drinking.
That by which the eating—that is, the enjoyment—of things to be eaten, such as sacrificial animals and the like, comes together; such is the power of mantra. By which...

"By means of the union of food and drink" refers to that [practice] wherein there is a perfectly beautiful arrangement such as deity-yoga and so forth through the union of food and drink. "Accomplishment" (siddhi) is the accomplishment of the Mahāmudrā. "Swiftly" means in this very life. || 1 ||
The taming of animals is also accomplished according to the previously stated sequence;
and the five types of animals are the donkey, human, tortoise, camel, jackal, horse, and so forth. || 2 ||

He states the materials for worship and so forth with the words "of the *paśus*" (*paśūnām*), etc. "Extraction" (*karṣaṇam*) means drawing out [the best] from among the *siddhas* and *paśus* in general—that is, their selection and separation. The word "and" (*caiva*) implies that only the most excellent *paśus* are to be accepted.
He then describes what kind of practitioner accomplishes this: "one who accomplishes worship by means of *paśus* through the application of the deity according to the sequence previously mentioned."

He who is thus described is the practitioner of the previously mentioned sequence. As to who those animals (*paśu*) to be drawn forth are, he says: "animals," and so forth. The word *ca* has the sense of the particle *api*. "In that way" means that they are explained just as the animals [are]. A donkey is a *gardabha*. A human (*mānuṣa*) is well known. Some say it refers to a forest-dweller (*vanamānuṣa*). A tortoise is a *kacchapa*. A camel is a long-necked animal (*dīrghakandhara*). A jackal is a *śṛgāla*.
This is well known. When the nominative plural ending is elided in the compound *khara-mānuṣa-kūrma-uṣṭra-śṛgāla*, these five are indeed the most excellent.

In the phrase "with horses and so forth" (*hayādibhiḥ*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*). From the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the dog and the cow are also included. || 2 ||
These are the limbs for the accomplishment of the animal sacrifice and the means for attaining supernatural powers.
Among the castes, the Brāhmaṇa is the animal; among quadrupeds, the elephant is said to be the animal. (3)

"These are the limbs for the accomplishment of *paśu*. Those whose very nature (*svarūpa*) is excellence (*prakṛṣṭā*) as their limb (*aṅga*)—that is, their accomplishment—are so described. He states that even ordinary accomplishment is obtained from them: "and also the means of accomplishment. Accomplishments such as *ākarṣaṇa* (attraction) and *vetāḍa* (vampire/animated corpse) are also the result of the practice of the means. The word "only" (*eva*) serves to restrict the meaning; the particle "and" (*ca*) is used for the conjunction of accomplishments. Furthermore, he speaks of the attraction of *paśu*:

Regarding the passage beginning with "of the classes" (*varṇānām*): they cover (*vṛṇvanti*) success, thus the *varṇas* are human beings. Among humans, by way of class (*varṇataḥ*), the Brahmin is the "beast" (*paśu*). Among quadrupeds such as donkeys and the like, the elephant is [the beast]. Therefore he says: "Among quadrupeds, the elephant is said [to be the beast]. There is also a word *hasti* ending in the vowel *i*. || 3 ||
Among birds, the swan alone is victorious; among animals, the tortoise is supreme;
and among the gods, the movement of the mouth is said to be expressed in various forms. (4)

"And among birds, the swan alone. He also mentions the dragging of birds, which follows from the context of dragging: the meaning is that among crows and the like, the swan alone is the best; and by the word "alone" (ca), he implies it is specifically the royal swan (*rājahaṃsa*). "Among animals, the one conquered by the tortoise": among aquatic animals, the tortoise is the best, and he is "conquered by the tortoise," meaning he is surpassed by the tortoise, who is the most excellent. And he is *niraṅkuśa* (unrestrained), for whom—
This is the established tradition: "The movement of the mouths of the gods. The goat, the buffalo, and the cock—these are called "mouth-movers" (*mukhacālana*) because they move their mouths.
To whom does this movement of the mouth belong? He says: those who sport in various forms are "gods" (*deva*), such as the Dānavas and others. (4)
These are designated as "animals," the mandala for accomplishing supernatural powers:
the crow, the crane, the jackal, the twice-born (parrot), the great mantra-reciter (peacock), the curlew, the sarasa crane, and the kadamba crane.

"These are designated as 'animals' (paśu), and this is the mandala for accomplishing siddhi. These animals and this bird have been described by the Buddhas who are equal [to one another]. It is so called because it is both a means for accomplishing siddhi and a mandala. Regarding that, he speaks of the drawing of the birds for the purpose of worship, beginning with "crow" and so forth. The jackal is well known as *puṇḍarī*. The parrot is the great mantra-holder among the twice-born (*dvija*). The *krauñca* is the *rava*-...

This is the distinction. The intention is that the crow, the crane, the jackal, the twice-born (brahmin), the great mantra-master, the curlew, the sārasa crane, and the kādamba goose are the superior ones.

Among these too, the *haṃsa* is the most excellent, as was stated previously. In that context, if the word *haṃsa* is intended by some to refer to a kṣatriya or a particular type of yoga, then this [present] interpretation does not apply. || 5 ||
The accomplishment of eating, fire-offerings, and ritual offerings becomes available for one who desires it;
[this is achieved] with the milk of a black female dog, combined with black beans and rice.
One should offer oblations into the mouth of the corpse with the mantra, free from hesitation;
the best of practitioners should perform the homa for one hundred and eight times.

He asks, "What is the purpose of these? and replies: "The consumption of food, the fire-oblation (*homa*), and the ritual offering (*bali*). He asks, "What is achieved by this? and replies: "Success (*siddhi*) becomes available for one who desires it. This means that through crows and other such birds—beauty-enhancing like the *kādamba*—the performance of the consumption of food, the fire-oblation, and the ritual offering constitutes its accomplishment. [This refers to] the consumption of food, the fire-oblation, and the ritual offering involving crows, cranes, jackals, twice-born birds (*dvija*), great mantrikas, curlews (*krauñca*), cranes (*sārasa*), and *kādambaka* birds.

*Kriyāsiddhi* is a complete term. He explains the *sādhana* of the Great Preta, beginning with "black" (*kṛṣṇa*) and so forth. Performing the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) with the *sumbha-mantra* and the root mantra, one who has obtained the [auspicious] sign should take an unbroken, non-putrid corpse to a cremation ground at midnight. With black dog’s milk, he should smear [the corpse] and perform a fire offering (*homa*) into its mouth using black beans and rice grains with their husks, using that very same mantra.
One should perform this. He says exactly this: "The milk of a black bitch is to be offered by the best of practitioners," and so forth. (6–7)
Then the preta rose up and said, "I am your servant.
He also brought forth from Pātāla a sword and the power to seize and restrain the planets.

It demonstrates the state of having previously performed service by way of its excellence: "Pātāla" refers to the accomplishment of Pātāla; that is to say, the accomplishment of entering into a subterranean cavern (*bila*).

"Arise" refers to traveling through the atmosphere. "And the sword" refers to the accomplishment of the sword (*khaḍgasiddhi*). From the word "or" (*vā*), the accomplishment of the discus (*cakra*) and so forth is implied. "Seizing" refers to the suppression of obstacles. "Subduing" refers to the crushing of the wicked. (8)
Having bestowed a pill, collyrium, a treasure, an ointment for the feet, or an elixir—granting thus a single accomplishment—one then departs; it is not otherwise.
"Or [it is] a pill, collyrium, a treasure, an ointment for the feet, or an elixir"—the word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaye*). The rest is easily understood.
Having granted one or another of these accomplishments (*siddhi*), he departs; it is not otherwise, because of its fixed nature. || 9 ||
In this tantra, there are undoubtedly the lower and upper messengers (dūtīs) who have attained perfection;
likewise, there are the Goṣṭhopalikās and the remaining Śuṣkaśiras.

"The lower and upper messengers are perfected in this tantra; of this there is no doubt. This means that the lower yoginīs reside on the earth, while the upper yoginīs reside in the atmosphere; from them, perfection arises. "And likewise the cow-pen stones" refers to dried cow-dung from a cow-pen. "The rest are dried veins" means that the rest are cowrie shells, which are dried veins.
The *riṣṭhakas*. "Then" means for that purpose, the rosary (*akṣasūtra*). || 10 ||
One should make an unbreakable rosary from great conch-shell or from tortoise shell;
this very rosary bestows unsurpassed accomplishment. (11)

One should make a rosary from the bone of a tortoise; this is mandatory for the accomplishment of a *vetāḍa*. For the rites of pacification (*śānti*), nourishment (*puṣṭi*), subjugation (*vaśya*), and sorcery (*abhicāra*), as well as for the *putrañjīva* and all other ritual actions mentioned in the *Catuṣpīṭha*, beads (*gulikā*) are to be used. || 11 ||
Four-armed and four-faced, or likewise having as many arms as desired; with a white body, yet exceedingly fierce, and possessing a truly terrifying form. || 12 ||
Beholding Vajravārāhī, who bears her own color and weapons, and the Hero adorned with a garland of skulls and his body smeared with ashes. (13)

"Four-armed," and so forth. The connection is that, in the practice for the Vetāḍa, one should meditate on [the deity] as four-armed, holding a vajra, a trident, a skull-cup, and a sword (or khaṭvāṅga). The Blessed One has four faces—white, dark blue, red, and yellow—corresponding to the east, north, and so on. Regarding the phrase "up to a hundred thousand arms," the sense is that there is no fixed rule concerning the number of faces or arms; furthermore, oral instruction must be consulted. Alternatively, [one may visualize him] as follows:

The whiteness and four-facedness are indeed [as described]. The emblems are according to the instruction. Therefore, it should be understood that this is the case elsewhere as well, based on the instruction. "In that manner" means according to the instruction. "But gazing upon Vajravārāhī, who bears her color and weapons" means she bears the vajra, skull-cup, and so forth. From this, her four-facedness is established. The Blessed Lord is white, and the Blessed Lady is also white. (12–13)
His body is adorned with mudrās and other ornaments; he is marked by matted locks and a crown, and holds a trident;
his face is slightly terrifying with bared fangs, and he is seated upon a great corpse.
Then, having understood this according to the rule, the yogi should meditate upon all the deities;
the practitioner should do so at all times.
For those distinguished by such qualities, success becomes a desirable woman. (15)
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, the procedure for the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*) in the practice of the animal, the beast, and the *vetāla*, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

Having understood this sequence of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanākrama*), one should at all times cultivate the thirty-six deities in three groups; this is the meaning. Regarding the state of having a hundred thousand arms and faces and so forth: in all the right [hands] there is a vajra, and likewise in the left hands a trident, or else a *khaṭvāṅga* and a skull-cup.
All the faces are white. Everything else is to be understood according to the sequence of the *sādhana*. (14–15)

Animals are birds; beasts are donkeys and so forth; a *vetāla* is a *preta*. That which prescribes the sequence for the production of their accomplishment (*sādhana*) is this chapter (*paṭala*), and it is the thirty-second.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 32.
The thirty-third chapter: The Ritual for the Worship and Service of Secret Offerings.
Beyond this, there is nothing else; he is a practitioner in all yogas who performs [the rites] with whatever food, drink, fish, meat, and so forth are available according to his ability. (1)

Now, showing that worship and other rites should be performed preceded by hospitality (*satkāra*), he says "ataḥ" and so forth. The connection is as follows: "then, for the practitioner who performs worship and so on, [the results] occur in such a way—both supreme and non-supreme. This locative case (*nimitta-saptamī*) refers to "among the attainments (*prāpti*) which are the unions (*yoga*) with all the objects to be accomplished. Demonstrating hospitality, he says "bhakṣya" and so forth. "Edible food..."

“Gokudahanādi” (cow-slaughter and so forth). “Bhojya” refers to food such as curd, ghee, sugar-candy, and sweetmeats (*laḍḍuka*). Because there are many things to be eaten, "bhojya" specifically denotes curd and the like. “Matsyāḥ” are fish such as the *rohit* and others. “Māṃsāni” are meats such as goat and so forth. By the word “ādi” (and so forth), other specific edibles and the like are also included according to availability. It should be understood from the context that the practitioner (*sādhaka*) is to perform, or will perform, the worship (*pūjā*) with these. Thus [is] the worship.

The sense is that one who is about to act is an uncommon practitioner (*sādhaka*). Regarding the phrase "according to one's capacity" (*yathāśaktitaḥ*): the sense is that whatever capacity one possesses should be employed therein; thus, there is no transgression of one's capacity. || 1 ||
Even when [the usual offerings] are not available, one should diligently prepare the five kinds of edible foods and so forth;
indeed, one should always perform an elaborate feast of various foods and drinks at night.

However, when the capacity to produce the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) is absent, one must also perform and partake of the five nectars through meditation, consisting of the five types of food and so forth, by means of diligent effort and according to the rule. One should always do this at night; during the day, one should first prepare and consume the food and other items, but at night it must be done as a fixed rule. This is because the word "but" (*tu*) has that specific meaning [of restriction]. || 2 ||
And then the messenger (dūtī) should eat; indeed, the practitioner especially should place her head upon his own body, having worshipped her as the non-dual hero.
"And then the messenger (dūtī) should eat. "Eaten" (*adyata*) means food (*at*), such as edible items; "should eat" (*adyāt*) means she should consume.

"Having placed her head on her own limb" means taking the skull-cup (*kapāla*) in her own hand, she should then eat the food. The collective meaning is that one should perform the worship together with the messenger. Regarding "worshipped through the non-duality of the Hero" (*vīrādvayaprapūjitam*): even the worship of union (*samāpatti-pūjā*) is performed by the Hero together with her.

The meaning is "to be accomplished. Regarding the reading *svotsaṅge* found in some manuscripts, it should be explained there as follows: having placed the source of the lotus-dharma (*kamaladharmodaya*) upon one's own lap by means of the Hero (*vīra*), that which is worshipped as the non-duality of the Hero (*vīrādvaya*) is to be accomplished. || 3 ||
Whether it be one's mother, sister, daughter, female relative, or wife—
one should perform this rite of liberation from bondage according to the prescribed injunctions.

Whether they be mother, sister, daughter, female relative, or wife—these five yoginīs are as affectionate as mothers and the like; together with them, one should effect a liberation that is thoroughly released from bonds. || 4 ||
Then the mantras will be perfected until the dissolution of the world;
having assumed the form of the preceptor, the practitioner receives the worship.

"Then the mantras are accomplished," [says] the deity. To the question "In what length of time?", he says: "until the dissolution of the summoned. This means until there is a dissolution—that is, a transformation—of the summoned afflictions (*kleśas*). He states that such an honoring of the Yoginīs must be performed with the words beginning "the teacher" (*ācārya*), etc. Having assumed such a form of one's own within the teacher, I accept the worship; therefore...
Regarding the phrase "being one who accomplishes siddhi," the Blessed One said: "For when such a teacher is worshipped, Vajradhara is worshipped;
by worshipping him, all the Tathāgatas are worshipped"—this is the intended meaning. || 5 ||
There is no doubt that the practitioner, being well-composed, should perform the posture of the heroes (vīrāsana), the mudrā, and likewise singing, dancing, and so forth.
