As long as all embodied beings wander in saṃsāra, overwhelmed by suffering and grief, they do not become knowers of yoga. (7)
Then the practitioner should worship the mudrā with his whole being;
when worshipped, they desire what is worthy of worship, but if treated with disrespect, they consume [the practitioner] with fire.
I take up the seat, the station, the mudrā, and the insignia of the heroes; the song accompanied by vajra-words; and the dance with the *ālīḍha* posture and so forth.
And thus the practitioner, well-composed and whose self is the yoga of the deity—[the text] speaks of the majesty of the Śrī Heruka yoga, beginning with "as long as" (*yāvat*) and so on:
as long as they wander in saṃsāra, so long does the knowledge of the Śrī Heruka yoga not arise. [The word] "and" (*ca*)...
Because that much is the purpose. And those who are not delighted even with that—whom does he mean? He says: "as many as all embodied beings. This means:
as many as there are, indeed, all embodied beings. One should worship the *mudrā*, which is the deity. To the question "What is that?", he says: "being worshipped," and so forth.
That which worships is the "object of worship" (*pūjya*); the meaning is "the worshipper" (*pūjaka*). (6–8)
The Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) is primordially accomplished; in the Yoga Tantras, human beings are to be worshipped with great effort, after which, O Hero, one should practice heroism.

The deity Mahāmudrā is primordially established and naturally accomplished. To the question, "How is it that the world does not know her who is such? he says: "The human being" (*mānava*). One is called a "human being" because one "blows toward" (*vāti*) or attains the afflictions (*kleśa*) such as pride (*māna*). The meaning is that due to being a "human being," one is ignorant of that [Mahāmudrā]. Likewise, she is to be worshipped; the meaning is that she should be honored according to the previously mentioned ritual. Subsequently, one should practice the state of a hero and heroine.
Having first abandoned conceptual construction, one should then practice the state of non-conceptuality of the hero's mind. || 9 ||
Having thus performed worship, the practitioner who has emerged from the netherworld [attains] pacification,
nourishment, subjugation, attraction, killing, eradication, and so forth.
For paralyzing, immobilizing, creating enmity, and likewise for subduing, one should worship [the deity] for the accomplishment of the rite; it will be achieved without difficulty. 11.
In all rites whatsoever, there is no doubt for the practitioner. || 12 ||
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, the Ritual for Secret Worship and Hospitality, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

Thus, first of all, there is the worship. Thereafter, by means of that, one becomes an achiever of all siddhis, such as those of Pātāla and so forth. Regarding "peace" (śānti) and so on, it is easily understood. || 10–12 ||
Secret worship consists of honoring with food and so forth, while respect consists of reverence, prostration, and the like. That by which these two are performed is a "chapter" (*paṭala*);
thus it is so called. It is the thirty-third, the thirty-third [chapter].
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 33.
The thirty-fourth chapter: the ritual procedure for the non-dual messenger (advayadūtī) and the fire-oblation (homa) of summoning.
Now follows the detailed ritual expansion known as the "Wheel" (cakra) of the Ḍākinījāla, by means of which that [practice] swiftly succeeds for the practitioner; of this there is no doubt.

The word "atha" (now/then) indicates that this follows immediately after the description of worship and honor. It should be understood as: "I shall explain the detailed ritual procedure known as the *ḍākinījālacakra*. The state (*bhāva*) of the *ḍākinīs* is *ḍākinya*; that itself is a "net" (*jāla*) because it binds through the letters of the alphabet, such as *ka*, *ca*, and so forth, like a net. The "wheel" (*cakra*) is its mandala. That by which this is explained is the "detailed ritual procedure" (*vidhivistara*), in which the ritual action (*karman*) resides.
It is so. The "elaboration of the ritual" refers to the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *ḍākinīs* and so forth. To the question "What is that?", he says "In which," etc.
"She" refers to Khaṇḍarohā. It should be understood that she "is accomplished. || 1 ||
One should join all the heroes and ḍākinīs with the lotuses;
likewise, one should place the station of the avadhūtī between the eyebrows.
Then, one should not offer anything else into the fire except through the mouth of Vīrocchuṣma;
likewise, five oblations should quickly be offered with beef and blood.

In the twenty-four lotuses of the *Sarvavīra* maṇḍala, the ḍākinīs, accompanied by twenty-four heroes, are to be placed. Therefore, it says: "one should employ them. Regarding the reading "niyojayet," it means "one should employ them"; even with the reading "niyojitāḥ" (employed), the meaning is the same. Here, the word *puṣkara* denotes a petal; hence the plural number. One should deposit [them] in the middle of the eyebrows.

"Likewise, the station of the Avadhūtī"—by this, the third eye of all the deities, beginning with the Vīras, is indicated. Because it is located on the forehead, which corresponds to the nose between the eyebrows, and because it destroys evil, the Avadhūtī is "mere mind" (*cittamātra*).
Its station is its sign, the third eye. The forehead is also the abode of the Vīra. By this, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the deities is shown. Such is she.

The yoginīs should perform the oblation. One should not offer anything other than the "heroic dried flesh" (*vīrocchuṣma*) through the mouth; that is, one should offer while characterized by a face possessed of wrath—that is, a fierce countenance. The meaning is that no other substance is to be offered, but rather beef alone. The passage beginning with *gavi* is easy to understand. First, five oblations are to be given. (2–3)
Then, one should offer nine oblations while the sacrificial fire is blazing;
one should behold the single-faced [deity] who faces all directions, appearing like an ocean of garlands of flames.
One should likewise [worship] the four-faced Vīreśa and the abode of the heroes and heroines;
on the petals are the four female messengers (dūtīs), and the non-dual bliss of the Cakravīras.

"Then one should offer nine oblations into the blazing fire"—this is easily understood. Having offered into the mouth of the fire, one should then offer into the mouth of the deity; thus he says "blazing," and so forth. One should visualize a wheel in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). It faces all directions. Because it has four gates, it is the four-faced Śrī Heruka. The wheel is the abode of heroes, characterized by heroes. It is joined with yoginīs accompanied by heroes.

The intended meaning is that one should behold [them]. Regarding the phrase "and four female messengers (dūtīs) on the petals": "on the petals" refers to the sequence of the [four] classes. On the petals starting from the east, there are four ḍākinīs, according to the verse: "Ḍākinī, as well as Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rūpiṇī. The term "heroine of the wheel" (cakravīrā) means she who abides through the experience of the non-dual true bliss residing within the three wheels. By means of the yoginīs residing in the three wheels—
It should be applied thus: "it exists" [referring to] that non-dual bliss, by means of those who have attained the state of the non-dual hero. || 4-5 ||
One should present Khaṇḍarohā externally according to her prescribed form;
however, one should show her as established in her own essential nature within the center of the wheel.

"One should place Khaṇḍarohā on the outside" means that one should position Khaṇḍarohā upon the petal at the back. "But one should show her situated in her own forms within the center of the wheel"—here, the first word *tu* has the sense of a distinction (*viśeṣa*), while the second has the sense of emphasis (*eva*).

One should show and meditate upon her in her own forms—that is, in forms corresponding to the ritual action, such as white and so forth in rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and the like. [The phrase] "Khaṇḍarohā on the outside... [is thus explained].

That which was stated regarding "one should give" in the ritual of Nyāsa is intended to indicate her preeminence in all rites; it should be understood that one should employ her in [rites such as] summoning and so forth. || 6 ||
This wheel, which bestows all accomplishments, has been pointed out to you;
one should cause the wheel to shine forth in accordance with the specific ritual action.

"This is what has been indicated by the wheel, which bestows all accomplishments. This collection of deities indicated in the wheel bestows all accomplishments; this the practitioner seeks for you. "In accordance with the rite"—this should be understood as follows: it has been stated that one should offer the full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the mouth of the deity who has been meditated upon according to the color corresponding to the rite. And it is not only in the context of the fire-offering (*homa*) that [the rite] conforms to the action...
There is beauty of form, but it exists elsewhere as well; in the reading "the accomplisher of all siddhis," it is the practitioner who is distinguished. || 7 ||
O Hero, as it has been briefly explained in the Ocean of Knowledge, [practitioners] attain accomplishment through the non-dual yoga of the messenger; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, the Ritual for the Non-dual Messenger’s Fire Offering and Summoning, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
He explains how the assembly of deities is indicated by the [mandala] wheel with the words "the ocean of vidyās," and so forth.
"By the hero" means that one should offer oblations while in union with the heroine, the messenger (dūtī), who is Vajradhara. || 8 ||

The fire sacrifice (*homa*) characterized by the non-dual messenger (*advaya-dūtī*) is that by which attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*) is performed; therefore, it is the chapter [dealing with] that. It is the thirty-fourth.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 34.
The thirty-fifth chapter: The Ritual for Deceiving Death through Non-dual Action and Time.
Now follows the most excellent and supreme ritual, characterized by its proper sequence;
it consists of non-dual yoga as worship, well-applied to each respective rite.

The word "atha" (now) indicates that this follows immediately after the description of the placement of the deities (*devatānyāsa*). It should be understood that the "supreme rite" (*karmavara*) consists of the recitation of mantras (*mantrajāpa*), which is preeminent because it accomplishes one's desired aims in rites such as pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "characterized by the proper sequence": it means it is recognized as being characterized by the sequence of fierce rites (*krūrakarma*) and so on, according to their respective order. To the question of how the mantra should be recited, he says: "worship" (*pūjā*).

It should be performed; of what nature? It is that worship which is well-applied to each ritual action, whose essence (ātman) is non-duality (advaya)—that is, the yoga or meditative absorption consisting of the embrace of Vajravārāhī. || 1 ||
Those mantras which bring about renown are their divisions in due order;
one should cause that mantra, beginning with the letter and the messenger (varṇadūtī), to revolve with the speed of an arrow.

"Those mantras which bring about accomplishment are their divisions, according to the sequence. Those whose nature is to effect the accomplishment of practice are such [mantras], namely the root-mantras and so forth. When employed in practices such as pacification (*śāntika*), they are to be seen as divisions. He states the division without overstepping the sequence, beginning with "the letters" (*varṇa*) and so forth. Those heroes for whom the female messengers (*dūtī*) are primary are "those beginning with the female messengers" (*dūtyādayaḥ*).

The *varṇas* such as Khaṇḍakapālī and others, as well as the *dūtīs* and so forth, are as if being described; that in which these *varṇas* reside is the mantra of Śrī Heruka, consisting of eight words and so on. It should be understood that one should recite (*japet*) that mantra. To the question "How?", he says: "One should wander with the speed of an arrow.
The term "with the speed of an arrow" (*śaravegena*) implies the elision of the instrumental case ending; thus, the mantra should wander all around with the speed of an arrow. (2)
The mantras, joined together, are then separated by means of entry;
thereafter, the garland of seed-syllables is swallowed and established within the syllable *hūṃ*.
He says that very thing: "mutually," and so forth. The word *tu* (but) indicates a distinction. Regarding the rite of pacification (*śāntika*), the concise meaning is as follows:

those mantras whose syllables are joined in mutual positions—like a rope being twisted between the palms—and which have moved back and forth repeatedly, are called "mutually joined" (*anyonyaghaṭita*). As for "pierced by entry" (*praveśena bhedita*): having entered within from one's own mouth, [they are then projected] again through the path of the vajra.

The meaning of the distinction in entry is as follows: [the mantras] are not emitted, but enter the heart of the Goddess via the path of the verse (*padyamārga*), then proceed to her mouth, and from there enter one's own mouth. In the rite for the cruel [deeds], the sequence is: entering from one's own mouth into the mouth of the Goddess, then emerging via the path of the verse and entering the *vajra*, and finally reaching one's own mouth and then the mouth of the Goddess. Describing the fulfillment of this procedure, he says:

"Then, one should contemplate the seed-garland as being swallowed," means that one should visualize the mantra-garland with its syllables closely joined to one another. "Established within the *hūṃ* syllable" means that the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) is established between two *hūṃ* syllables; thus, at the end of the mantra to be recited, it is: *hūṃ devadattaṃ māraya hūṃ*. This is the interlacing (*vidarbhaṇa*) preceded by *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ* at the beginning of the position. || 3 ||
But through cessation, it becomes attainable; yet it does not go to a single state.
By means of the *sampuṭa* (encasement), through the process of encasement, and by the binding of the *vajra-śṛṅkhala* (vajra-chain). || 4 ||
One should pierce with the vajra and then whirl the picchaka;
likewise, one should attract it as if with a hook, and similarly employ the mallet for agitation.

Therefore, he says: "But through suppression (*nirodha*), that which is to be accomplished may arise; it does not go to a single state. The particle *tu* (but) is for emphasis. "Through suppression by means of the two *hūṃ*s" means by way of encapsulation (*saṃpuṭībhāva*). This refers to the rite of pacification (*śāntika*). "Oṃ devadattāya svāhā oṃ"—this is the interlacing (*vidarbhaṇa*) as before; this is the encapsulating interlacing, which is the state of encapsulation. It is the suppression by means of the two *oṃ*s at the beginning and the end.

"Vajra," and so forth. This is the explanation for the phrase "established within the syllable HŪṂ. In the rite of cruelty (*krūra-vidhi*), one should pierce with the "vajra" known as the syllable HŪṂ. Piercing consists of taking up the syllable HŪṂ at both the beginning and the end of the name of the target (*sādhya*). To the question "By what means?", he says: "by the binding of the vajra-chain" (*vajra-śṛṅkhala-bandhana*). That by which a vajra-chain is bound is thus described. Then, one should whirl the vajra like a peacock-feather fan (*picchaka*).
"One should whirl the mantra"—this is how it should be understood. By means of the mantra, the swiftness of entry and exit through the mouths and other [orifices] of Wisdom and Means is demonstrated.
In rites for the cruel, Khaṇḍarohā is black and holds a vajra in her hand; in rites for pacification, she is white and holds a khaṭvāṅga in her left hand.
"One should attract as if with a hook": when there is an attraction, then the interlacing [of syllables] is: *jaḥ*, "attract Devadatta, *jaḥ*."

As before. By the word "hook" (aṅkuśa), the syllable *jaḥ* is meant. Reciting the root mantra, by means of the mantra’s radiance, one pierces the heart of the target with the red Khaṇḍarohā who holds a hook in her hand and draws him forth. For agitation, it is likewise with the club (*muṣala*). For agitating an army and so forth, the interlacing (*vidarbhaṇa*) is:
*hūṃ* [name], such as Devadatta, *kṣobhaya hūṃ*. And Khaṇḍarohā is endowed with her own color.
The meaning of the word "tathā" (likewise) is "with pestle in hand. || 4-5 ||
For eating, it is said to be a thunderbolt; for piercing, an arrow is joined to it;
and for deceiving Time and Death, a khaṭvāṅga staff is joined to the body.
The skull-cup, serving as the vessel for the offering water, is assigned to the mouth by means of the weapon-mantra.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, the section on the ritual for deceiving death through the timing of non-dual action, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 35.
In the act of eating—that is, consuming—Khaṇḍarohā herself assumes her own form; the ritual expansion (*vidarbhaṇa*) is: *phaṭ devadattaṃ bhakṣaya phaṭ*.
In piercing—that is, perforating—Khaṇḍarohā holds an arrow in her hand; the ritual expansion is: *phaṭ devadattaṃ vedhaya phaṭ*.
Furthermore, regarding the evasion of untimely death, the skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) is joined to the body; in the evasion of untimely death, the skull-topped staff is [placed] on the left.

Dhāriṇī is Khaṇḍarohā. The syllable *HŪṂ* is white, emitting thousands of streams of flowing nectar. The *vidarbhaṇa* (interlacing) is: *HŪṂ devadattaṃ jīvaya HŪṂ*. It is said that in all rites, after the mantra has been made radiant, an *argha* offering should be given to the mouth of Khaṇḍarohā with a skull-cup (*kapāla*).

This refers to the phrase "the skull-cup as the *argha* vessel" (*kapālārghapātraṃ tu vaktra*); the meaning of the word *tu* is [to emphasize this]. Regarding the phrase "conjoined with the weapon-mantra" (*astraniyojitam*), [it refers to] the giving of the *argha*.
The sense is that one should meditate upon Khaṇḍarohā as applying weapons such as the goad and so forth to the limbs of the face of the person to be subdued (sādhya). || 6-7 ||

"Non-dual action" refers to the performance of rites such as pacification (*śāntika*) through meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), as well as the deception of death at its appointed time; because this is prescribed therein, it is called that [chapter]. It is the thirty-fifth, the thirty-fifth.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 35.
The thirty-sixth chapter: The Ritual for the Attraction of the Worship of Reality.
Now, the great worship of mudrās is proclaimed as the application of mantras;
these mudrās and worship indeed bring about swift accomplishment—of this there is no doubt.

The word *atha* means immediately after the non-dual ritual (*advayakarma*). "Mudrā" refers to the worship of the external mudrā. To the question "Of what kind?", he says: it is "proclaimed by the placement of the three-syllable mantra," meaning the mudrā is proclaimed through the placement of the mantra; that is its worship. And the mantra consists of three syllables.
For these [mantras] bring about swift accomplishment (*āśusiddhi*). The word *hi* means "because. || 1 ||
Having joined the mantra to the two lingas, the non-dual hero and ḍākinī; likewise, the practitioner of mantra should perform the union of the ḍākinīs with their heart-mantras. (2)
The wise one should churn the Yoginī, whose body is pure, according to his desire;
having realized the non-duality of the hero-worship, he should perform the ritual with diligence. (3)

He speaks of the conjunction with mantra, beginning with "mantra" and so forth. The connection is as follows: having joined the three-syllable mantra, one should churn the Yoginī. Regarding "the two signs": this refers to the sign (*liṅga*) of the two, namely wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*). He states this very point: "the non-duality of Ḍākinī and Vīra. The meaning is that the sign belongs to that non-duality in which both Ḍākinī—meaning *ḍākinya*—and Vīra are present.

Having produced the vajra with the syllable *hūṃ* and the lotus with the syllable *oṃ*, and having produced the vajra-jewel with the syllable *āḥ* and the filaments of the lotus with the syllable *maḥ*, one should place the three syllables upon the body and so forth, and then churn the yoginīs. "The pure body as desired" means that the worship of non-dual absorption has been explained in this way. The hero-worship consists of fish, meat, and so forth; thus, having understood non-duality, one performs it.
One should diligently and with concentrated mind perform the ritual actions, such as those for pacification and so forth. || 2-3 ||
Having analyzed according to his own will, the mantra-practitioner should indeed apply it in reverse;
for the purposes of restraint and favor, he should bring about the state of the ritual action.

Having distinguished them by dividing them individually, one should apply the rites such as *śāntika* (pacification) and so forth, which are otherwise contrary and mutually distinct. He states that very point by means of the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) with the words beginning "nigraha" (restraint). "Nigrahānugrahāḥ" refers to purposes or objectives; the locative case here is used in the sense of the cause (*nimitta-saptamī*). || 4 ||
Distinguished by the divisions of reality and applied to the pathways of the channels, one should accomplish the purpose of the practice, both external and internal. (5)
By this, one may swiftly accomplish [the subjugation] of gods, asuras, and humans alike.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, the Ritual for Attraction through the Worship of Reality, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

He provides the explanation for what was indicated by the words "mutually joined" (*anyonyaghaṭitā*) and so forth, starting with "divided" (*bheditā*) and so on. The mantras previously mentioned are joined in sequence within the channels (*nāḍī*) and the paths of the verses (*padya*). This is because they constitute their very nature. [This is done] by means of the differentiation of the principles (*tattva*) and the differentiation of the expansion of ritual actions (*karmaprasara*). One should accomplish them for the purpose of practical application; that is, for the sake of illustration, one should accomplish rites such as pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth. By this means, success (*siddhi*) is attained, and not otherwise.
One whose undertaking has been perfected shall accomplish everything. || 5-6 ||

For the sake of accomplishing the expansion of the activities of the principles (*tattva*), worship is the means of attracting them; that by which this is established is the chapter (*paṭala*). This is the thirty-sixth chapter. Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 36.
The thirty-seventh chapter: The Procedure for the Authority of Internal Mastery.
Now I shall proclaim another [practice], the accomplishment of one who has overcome the physical form;
the mantras and the ḍākinīs, mutually entwined, are joined together in one place.

Now, with the words beginning with "atha," he begins to explain the method of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). The word "atha" indicates the immediate succession to the ritual actions accomplished through recitation (*japa*).

"Anyatama" refers to the means (*upāya*). "I shall explain correctly" means I shall analyze and fully declare the correct practice. "Vigrahākrāntasādhaka" means the means that accomplishes those beings who have entered into a physical body (*vigraha*); that is the meaning. This—

Regarding "burning" (*dāha*): it means that the mantras and *ḍākinīs*, which are mutually entwined, are joined together in one place. Having combined these three—the root mantra, the king of vidyās, and the *ḍākinī* mantra—one should accomplish the medicinal elixir (*bhaiṣajya*). This is the meaning. || 1 ||
One should cause the food already consumed and vomited to be ejected by means of recitation at the end [of the mantra];
then, after a full seven nights have passed, one should employ it in eating and other such activities. || 2 ||
By this, they come under one's control for as long as life lasts; there is no doubt.
Having drunk the ghee of a tawny cow, one should vomit it at the conclusion of the recitation.
Then, he should smear his own face with that [substance];
if [the person] is constantly angry, he shall be brought under control by the mere sight [of him]. || 4 ||
Having anointed [the body] with sesame oil mixed with rice flour,
the practitioner of mantra should fashion a *śaṅkulikā* and employ it by means of consumption.

He says this very thing: "Eaten," and so forth. "One should cause vomiting by means of the end of the recitation" means that one should rinse what has been eaten and vomited, then eat it again and vomit it. Having mixed it with unrefined camphor, one should recite the three mantras for seven nights at the three junctions of the day. Then, when giving it in food and other such things, it will happen as stated. Having drunk the ghee of a tawny cow—tawny cow's ghee—over which the mantra has been recited seven times...
One should vomit. With that [substance], one should anoint oneself and the face. "Then" means immediately after the anointing. Regarding "having been anointed," and so forth:
after the body has been anointed, sesame oil should be taken. The particle *tu* is used for the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*) in the ritual application. "Combined with rice-flour" means:
having made a small cake (*śaṃkulikā*) from rice-flour and cooked it in that oil, one should give it by means of eating. The particle *tu* here has the sense of "indeed" (*evārthe*).
In all cases, the recitation of the mantra is to be understood as such. || 2-5 ||
If one does not abandon the ritual action, [the deity] remains forever under control for as long as one lives;
having eaten black sesame seeds mixed with *rājikā* mustard that have been vomited out.
One should grind kuṣṭha, apāmārga, karaja, udara, and kīṭaka with one's own blood and then saturate them with semen.
One should employ food, drink, collyrium, garments, and ointments;
by this means, there is no doubt that subjugation lasts for as long as one lives.

"If it does not release the karma, then it is not liberated. Having eaten black sesame seeds together with *rājikā* mustard, along with *kuṣṭha*, *apāmārga*, and the *karaja-udara-kīṭaka* [insect], [one should induce vomiting]. Here, "and" (*ca*) is used for conjunction (*samuccaya*), while "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction (*viśeṣa*). Having eaten black sesame seeds together with *rājikā* mustard, they are to be vomited up. *Kuṣṭha* is to be drunk seven times.

*Nirgata* means "gone out" or "emerged. *Karaja* means "a fingernail. *Udarakīṭaka* means "a small worm emerged from the belly. *Khāna* means "food" or "that which is eaten. *Lopa* refers to [the loss] of a limb. (6–8)
An oblation of beef, with the deities smeared with its blood, brings [the target] under control at that very moment; if he does not come, he dies.
Having visualized meat before him, the wise practitioner should perform the fire offering (*homa*).
At the conclusion of the *homa*, having offered the sacrificial cake (*bali*), he shall attract the three worlds in an instant.
Success will be achieved within seven nights. 10.
"Anointed with blood for the sake of the oblation by means of the offering of beef"—this means the offerings of beef are anointed with its blood.

Through the oblation of beef smeared with cow's blood, the knowledge of the deity to be accomplished becomes subject to one's control. Alternatively, "deity" refers to a worldly deity, and the meat is that of the cow itself; therefore he says, "of that," meaning in front of the Śrī Heruka painting.
Alternatively, there should be a ritual pit for all rites (sārvakarmika-kuṇḍa) either before or behind the image of that deity or its face. Success shall be attained within seven nights;
that is, success comes from performing oblations at the three junctions of the day during those seven nights. || 9-10 ||
The characteristic of the conduct of the samaya is difficult to find within the three worlds;
it must always be concealed with effort by oneself through secret mantras. (11)
One of meager fortune does not obtain the hidden meaning, nor does he achieve success;
it is obtained by practitioners of little merit only when I am pleased. (12)
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, the procedure for the rite of internal subjugation, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

"Difficult to obtain" refers to the rite for subjugation (*vaśya*). It is called "the characteristic of the conduct of the pledge" (*samayācāralakṣaṇa*) because it is observed by yogins through the practices of the pledge. "One of meager fortune" means one who has little merit from previous lives. Regarding the phrase "by those of little merit":
this [attainment] is not obtained by these practitioners who possess little present merit; however, it is obtained by me when I am pleased. (11–12)

The rite of subjugation (*vaśya-karma*) performed for the purpose of bringing [others] under control is the subject matter here; that by which the section on subjugation—the method of oblations (*homa*) using medicinal herbs and so forth—is prescribed, that is this chapter, namely the thirty-seventh.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter in the *Śrī-Hakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 37.
The thirty-eighth chapter: The Ritual Procedure for the Secret Abodes of the Yoginīs and the Dwellings of the Heroes.

Then follow the secret signs (*chommaka*) of the ḍākinīs, the characteristics of the body, and likewise the classification of the limbs of the heroes; whatever is to be accomplished, that is already accomplished.

Since this has been stated in the Tantra as something entirely secret, he says "therefore," and so forth. *Chommakas* are the secret signs mentioned in the text, such as "Ḍā is a man," and so on. *Tur* indicates a distinction. *Ḍākinīs* refers to Pracaṇḍā and the others. *Body* refers to the hands and other limbs.

For the purpose of giving the *chommaka*, its characteristic consists of the class of marks, scents, and so forth belonging to the *ḍākinī* lineage. The classification of the hero's body includes [the distinctions of] color and face.
"Arms and so forth; likewise," thus it is to be concealed. || 1 ||
Vīreśvara neither writes it nor recites it before anyone;
he should conceal it in every way, for the practice of the Left (vāmācāra) is well-guarded. 2.

It should also be understood that the yogin Vīreśvara neither writes nor speaks of the secret signs (*chommaka*) and so forth, nor of the piercing of the heroic limbs (*vīrāṅgabheda*). "In the presence of someone" means in front of those belonging to other tantras and the like. "One should not recite" refers to the tantra. "Well-concealed by those of left-handed conduct" means that the secret signs and so forth are well-guarded by the practitioners of the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara* who follow the left-handed path (*vāmācāra*). (2)
If a practitioner of mantra recites the secret-characterized ḍākinīs through negligence,
I do not see thousands of ḍākinīs in their various forms appearing before him.
That evil-minded one is not to be eaten. || 3 ||

"Out of negligence, the practitioner recites the *Guhyalakṣaṇa-ḍākinī*. This means that if one recites, writes, or speaks the *ḍākinī* [text] contained in a book out of negligence—that is, through a lack of attention to one's own duties—I do not look upon him; the meaning is that I do not grant him success (*siddhi*) and so forth. Furthermore, he says: "Thousands of *ḍākinīs* will devour him in many ways. "Devourable" (*bhakṣyaka*) refers to one who is to be eaten.
The meaning is that this occurs for him. The word "na" (not) indicates a shaking of the head [in negation]. Why? He says: "He is evil-natured," and so forth.
In the phrase "he is evil-natured" (*durātmaka*), the suffix *aṇ* is used in its own sense; thus, it means "one who is very evil-natured. "Self" (*ātman*) refers to the distinguished mind. || 3 ||
He is a destroyer of the sacred pledge, one of evil conduct, and a slayer of Brahmins—of this there is no doubt.
This wicked-souled fool is a sinner, a rogue, and one who has been utterly deceived.
The *samayas* are the principles of mantra and mudrā; the *brahmans* are the Buddhas. One who practices only evil is "of evil conduct" (*pāpācāra*).

Therefore, one whose conduct is wicked and whose established rule is unrighteous is "of corrupt conduct" (*durācāra*). "Foolish" means extremely deluded. "Deceived" means through separation from what is desired. "This one" refers to the author of the recitation and so forth. (4)
I am not his protector when he is being devoured by the yoginīs;
in the midst of the guhyakas, that practitioner is nothing but a sacrificial animal.

And I am not the protector of that evil-minded one of wicked form as he is being devoured by the yoginīs. Why is this so? It is said: *guhyakāḥ* are the yoginīs who conceal, cover, and protect. The word *tu* has the sense of "even. Among even those who are protectresses, he is merely a sacrificial animal, a goat, because he is to be slain due to his great offense; such is the practitioner (*sādhaka*).
Therefore, the word "tu" (but) indicates a distinction. || 5 ||
He who betrays his guru and betrays the samaya is fallen from the world of the Buddhas;
however, he who protects the tantra of Śrī Heruka, whose appearance is formidable, [is not]. (6)
"Fallen," and so forth. The "Buddha-world" (*buddhaloka*) refers to the manifestation of the Buddha in the world; the sense is that one would even fall from that.

And this consists of both betrayal of the guru and betrayal of the *samaya*. However, he who protects—that is, guards—the *tantra*, the "terrifying vision of Śrī Heruka," because it generates fear in those who have not realized the reality (*tattva*). (6)
I, together with the ḍākinīs, shall show favor to that one of auspicious countenance;
the gurus will grant their approval, and the practitioners will keep it secret.

I am his benefactor; "benefaction" (*anugraha*) means a particular kind of affection. [The term] *ḍākinī* is used with the elision of the third case ending. He is a benefactor in such a way that his face is auspicious and beautiful. They give their approval; even the gurus grant him their consent. They conceal him; other practitioners, upon seeing him, embrace him, thinking, "This is the casting of his wings."
Alternatively, this meaning is that among the virtuous in the worlds, there is both the revealing and the concealing [of faults]. || 7 ||
He is eternally beloved by the yoginīs, and for him there is no doubt regarding the attainment of siddhi;
the practitioner attains heroism and becomes the sovereign of the sky-goers in the three worlds.
The practitioner who desires the state of a hero becomes honored everywhere;
yoga proceeds for him, and he attains the oral tradition.

"Desiring heroism" means one who desires the state of a hero (*vīratva*). For such a person, yoga proceeds; that is, the yoga of continuous application (*prabandhanayoga*), which is meditative absorption (*samādhi*), proceeds.
He finds—that is, he obtains from the presence of the guru—the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*) and the assent regarding the forms of the objects of knowledge perfected by the disciple. (8–9)
But having seen the heroic Ācārya who maintains the vow of Śrī Heruka, the practitioner, rejoicing at every sight of him, [should act] with this mantra: || 10 ||

"Heroic" (*vīra*) means being fearless in the course of worldly life. "One who observes the vow of Śrī Heruka" means one who maintains what is prescribed in his own scripture. The connection is that another practitioner should rejoice upon seeing such heroism. "Having seen, having seen indeed, with this mantra"—this means that the practitioner, characterized by the yoga of Śrī Heruka, having seen and indeed seen others who are like him...
The sense is that one should rejoice. || 10 ||
One should recite the hero who is supreme among root-mantras seven times, interspersed with the *praṇava* and the syllable *hūṃ*. || 11 ||
Having bowed with effort to those [deities] who are worshipped by all the Buddhas and others, one will undoubtedly always sport with the Great Hero. 12.
The connection is as follows: while reciting the root mantra as previously described, one should bow down to those who uphold the vow of Śrī Heruka and rejoice with effort.
To the question "What then? he says: "Worshipped by all Buddhas and others. This implies there would be worship by Vajradhara and the rest.
Regarding that prostration, he asks "How so? and replies: because that yogin is engaged in the play (*krīḍā*) of the Great Hero, Śrī Heruka, [he worships] them.
This may be for yogins who observe it. || 11-12 ||
Vārāhī resides in their hearts, established in non-duality with the Vīrayoginīs;
therefore, by the sight of that merit of that noble-born being, [the goal is attained]. 13.

Regarding the question "What [happens] for those who remember?", he says: "Of them," and so forth. "Those whose heroes reside in their hearts" (*hṛdisthavīrāḥ*) refers to those who maintain the vow of Śrī Heruka; here, the singular genitive case is used in the sense of the plural nominative. Regarding the phrase "abiding non-dually with the Yoginīs": according to the rules of etymology (*nirukti*), the plural form takes the substitute *am*. Thus, the meaning is as follows: why are they such? Because for those yogins...
"The goddesses abide in a non-dual form. Therefore, because of the "virtuous birth" (*sujanman*) [of the practitioner], there is the "vision of merit" (*puṇyadarśana*) for living beings.
How does this belong to him? Because, through the vision of the merit of that one who maintains the vow of Śrī Heruka, living beings come to have a "beautiful arising" (*śobhanotpāda*). || 13 ||
On riverbanks and at the ocean, on mountains and at crossroads, at ponds, wells, lotus-pools, deserted dwellings, and along gateways. || 14 ||
Thus, with eyes bloodshot with passion, the ḍākinīs stand everywhere—in the Mahābhairava cremation ground, in the netherworld (pātāla), and likewise as sky-farers (khecarī). || 15 ||
Together with those many terrifying and mighty Vetālas,
the great hero sports at his pleasure.
In hollows, caves, and secret places, that hidden human Yoginī sports with the practitioner in those various locations and regions. (17)
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Secret Abode of the Heroes, the Region of the Yoginīs’ Place of Accomplishment," in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.
He states the place for play with the words "river," and so forth. "With eyes reddened" means due to the passion of seeing one who observes the vow of Śrī Heruka.

The word "ca" (and) expresses joy. "Kuhara" means a cave; "gahvara" means the interior of a mountain; "guhya" means a dense forest. "Gūḍhamānuṣyayoginīsthāna" refers to a place where human yoginīs are hidden. This is an adjective qualifying all [the locations] beginning with the river. (14–17)
The locations of the Yoginīs themselves are prescribed as the abodes of the secret heroes; because of this, this chapter is so designated. It is the thirty-eighth, the *aṣṭatriṃśattama*.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 38.
The thirty-ninth chapter: The Ritual Section on the Great Laughter of Vision.
Now, the great accomplished yogin, displaying the eightfold laughter-mantra to him, bestows it upon him; of this there is no doubt.

"Then" (*atha*) means immediately after the locations of the *yoginīs*, sequentially through laughter. "Eightfold" (*aṣṭavidha*) refers to how it occurs; thus, the great adept-yogi (*mahāsiddhiyogī*) is the yogi of Śrī Heruka in the great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*), that is, in the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā. And here the mantra is: *kili kili cili cili sili sili dhili dhili*. This is the remainder of the mantra of the King of Vidyās; by this, it is eightfold.
Laughter: "Hā hā he he ho ho hūṃ hūṃ"—thus, laughter is of eight kinds by means of the mantra of the Goddess. The passage beginning with "Then" (*tataḥ*) and so forth is easy to understand. || 1 ||
With a terrible and loud sound, the fearsome ḍākinīs,
upon hearing it, tremble before that hero and flee in all directions.
If the hero does not become afraid, he is seized by those ḍākinīs with their left hands and led together with them to their own city. || 3 ||
He says that one must not fear even when surrounded by Yoginīs who are terrifying: "They flee from that hero who is afraid. The word "ca" (and) means "because.

"From that" means from the surrounding. "The hero does not fear. If the hero does not fear, then he is seized by them by the left hand and led to their own city; thus, both results are achieved. He states this: "Then, having seized him by the left hand..."
"They lead him to their own city" means "together with the ḍākinīs," [expressed] by the elision of the instrumental case-ending (*tṛtīyālope*). || 2-3 ||
One who desires the power of Śrī Heruka is led to the state of Khecarī;
delighting there eternally, he shall go to Sukhāvatī. || 4 ||
Neither old age nor death exists anywhere for the practitioner whose very body is the mantra. || 5 ||
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, the Chapter on the Ritual of the Terrifying Laughter of Vision, in the glorious *Herukābhidhāna*. 39.

"By one desiring union with Śrī Heruka" means by one who yearns for union with Śrī Heruka. "The state of Khecarī" refers to Sukhāvatī; this very place is explained as "one's own city. "Nowhere is there old age or death" because those two arise from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). The sense is that when that [construction] is abandoned, they are abandoned. To the question "Why is there the abandonment of conceptual construction?", he says: "The practitioner has the mantra as his body. Mantra...
The direct realization of the true nature of all phenomena; the sense is that [the yogin] is of the same essence as them. || 4-5 ||
"Vision" (*darśana*) is the perception of the *ḍākinīs*, and "loud laughter" (*aṭṭahāsa*); that by which these two are prescribed is the chapter (*paṭala*), and thus it is so called.
It is the thirty-ninth (the forty-ninth).
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 39.
The fortieth chapter: The procedure for practicing the great mudrā that subjugates by means of the five colors.
Thereafter, I shall fully explain that by which one may bring a mortal under control;
by this, the hero established in the ritual of mantra-yoga attains success within a month.

Now he teaches the chapter on the fire-offering (*homa*) for subjugation alone, beginning with "Then," and so forth. Since beings, once subjugated, can be directed toward one's own teaching, therefore I shall explain it. To the question "What is that?", he says: "by which one may bring a mortal under control. This means: by which fire-offering one may bring an unsubjugated being under control. And how long does that take to be accomplished?
Thus he said: "Success is achieved in a month. What kind of hero? One who abides by the ritual procedure of mantra-yoga; that is to say, one who begins with the mantras and so forth. || 1 ||
Flesh combined with fish-meat and liquor, even in every circumstance, [brings about] the Lord of Heroes for the practitioner within seven days. (2)
If one devoted to the night-homa performs it three times a day for one hundred and eight repetitions, he bestows the great siddhi.

Within seven days, one shall bring under control the king together with his army by means of half [the portion], the heroic minister by half of that, and the [ordinary] minister by half of that again.

To the question, "By the application of what is success achieved? he says: "Meat" and "fishes" as previously mentioned. It should be understood that the external *homa* is performed with meat, while the internal [homa] is performed with fish. Even in every state, the Lord of Heroes, Śrī Heruka, possesses four arms and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "within seven days": having performed the offering of one hundred and eight oblations three times a day for three months, then by means of the *homa* performed on the seventh day, the objective is accomplished.

It bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*) upon the practitioner. Regarding the phrase "devoted to the fire-oblation (*homa*) at night": "night" (*niśā*) is a technical term for wisdom (*prajñā*); the intended meaning is that one should perform the oblation while joined with wisdom. He states this very point in the passage beginning with "one hundred," etc., where "in all tantras" (*sarvatantraḥ*) indicates a collective application. Regarding the phrase "but by half": it means by fifty-four oblations. Regarding the phrase "but by half of that": it means by twenty-seven. [He bestows] the minister [the power over] peace and war...
The connection is that one should bring [the enemy] under control, such as by means of [the aforementioned] and so forth. || 2-4 ||
For the thirty-two neighboring kings, one should perform oblations according to the sequence of thirty-two fire-offerings;
for a Brāhmaṇa, however, one should perform twenty oblations over the course of seven days.
In this manner, one should offer oblations seven times for a Kṣatriya and five for a Vaiśya;
for a Śūdra there should be three, but for one of the lowest caste (antyaja), one should offer only one.
Seated upon a single seat, the heroic practitioner, following the lineage tradition, shall attract all sentient beings by means of the power of the mantra. (7)

In the case of neighboring kings and others, thirty-two oblations should be offered in the evening for the sake of those who practice yoga and so forth. "One should perform the fire-offering according to the sequence of oblations" means that he demonstrates that the oblations are to be given according to the sequence of castes. He states this very point in the verse beginning with "twenty," etc.:
one should give twenty oblations for a Brāhmaṇa; for a Śūdra, only three—that is, three oblations. One should offer one [oblation]... [etc.]

"An outcaste" (antyaja) means that one should offer [the oblation] once—that is, one should give a single oblation—for the sake of the *caṇḍāla*s and others. "Resorting to a single seat" means having resorted to Śrī Heruka. (5–7)
Acting thus, the mortal hero who fulfills his desire according to the prescribed rule and practices the yoga of the deity shall attain a fortunate aeon (bhadrakalpa). || 8 ||
The practitioner will be pleasing to the ḍākinīs; there is no doubt about this. || 9 ||
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Practicing the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) for Subjugation through the Five Colors," in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

Showing that a person may be devoid of observances (*niyama*), vows (*vrata*), and so forth, he says: "But at will," and so on. One may enjoy forms, sounds, and the rest at will—that is, according to ritual injunctions, specifically the ritual injunctions for deity yoga (*devatā-yoga*). The intention is that one who practices the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*).
To the question "What then? he replies: "One would obtain. The ellipsis is "the accomplishment of subjugation" (*vaśīkaraṇa-siddhi*). (8–9)
The subjugation of the five colors is performed, and preceded by that, the practice of Mahāmudrā is prescribed; because this chapter [deals with] that, it is so called.
It is the fortieth [chapter].
Thus ends the fortieth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 40.
The forty-first chapter: The ritual procedure for the arrangement of the twenty-four-syllable maṇḍala.
Now follows the most excellent and supreme rite, by which practitioners come to know [the methods of] subjugation, attraction, inciting enmity, killing, and expulsion, and so forth.
Yawning, paralysis, delusion, and indeed pinning; the seizing away of speech, as well as muteness, deafness, and blindness. (2)
Causing impotence, causing emasculation, and the transformation of form—these twelve great rites the practitioner should always accomplish. (3)
Success comes for the practitioner by mere remembrance; of this there is no doubt.
Among all the most excellent places, the Ḍākinīs are all-pervasive in the sacred seats (pīṭhas) and so forth.

Regarding the question as to what kind of accomplishment of action (*karmasiddhi*) belongs to a yogin who has attained power, the word "atha" [is used]. Thereupon the Blessed One said: "The supreme action, the most excellent. It should be understood that this is because it carries the desired object with excellence.
To the question "In what way?", he says: "By which practitioners know. Just as the knowledge of the practitioner is supreme, so too—what is that?

He says: "Subjugation," and so forth. Now, he will speak of the supreme ritual action (*karmavara*). In some recensions, the reading is easily understood. Subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*) are one, as are killing (*māraṇa*) and expulsion (*uccāṭana*); thus, these twelve are the expansions of ritual action (*karmaprasara*). From the mere recollection or thought of these great rituals (*mahākarma*), their accomplishment arises for the practitioner. [This concerns] the abode of the twenty-four Yoginīs.

Another says: "In all the supreme [places]. This means in all the most excellent *pīṭhas* and so forth; the term "*pīṭhādi*" (beginning with *pīṭhas*) involves the elision of the locative case ending.

The phrase "all-pervading" (*sarvavyāpinī*) results from the elision of the nominative plural ending. The word "but" (*tu*) specifies that there are exactly twenty-four *ḍākinīs* in the *pīṭhas* and so forth. (1–4)
Those who are born in various regions, endowed with knowledge within their own wombs, are called ḍākinīs; they are the mistresses of the vajra-maṇḍala. (5)
In Kulatā, in a secluded place, and likewise in the city of Sindhū,
in Suvarṇadvīpa, and also in Saurāṣṭra, she is Gṛhadevatā.
In Pretapuri, in the region of Himavat, in Kāñcī, in the country of Lampāka, as well as in Kaliṅga, Kośala, Triśakuni, and Roḍraka; || 7 ||
In Kāmarūpa, Mālava, Devīkoṭṭa, and Rāmeśvara;
in Godāvarī and Urva, as well as in Oḍḍiyāna and Jālandhara. || 8 ||
The daughters of Pullīra, Malaya, and the others pervade the non-dual state of the Hero;
they are all capable of assuming any form at will for the sake of quelling the speed of the mind.
"In one's own wombs" means among those of one's own caste. "The mistresses of the Vajra-maṇḍala" refers to the consorts of the Śrī Heruka maṇḍala.

By the words "in Kulatā," etc., he states the locations; when designating them by the term "pīṭha" and so forth, and then specifying them as "in Kulatā" and so on, it should be understood that these very places, beginning with the cremation grounds and ending with the *pīṭhas*, are intended. This is for the sake of instruction. [This includes] Pullīramalaya and so forth.

By these words, the *pīṭhas* and so forth are to be understood. [The term] "gṛhadevatā" (house-deity) results from the elision of the locative case. [The term] "triśakuni" uses the nominative in the sense of the locative; such is the meaning of the word "tathā" (likewise). To the question of where the Vajramaṇḍalanāyikās are located, it is said: "in Kulatā," and so on. He says that in these regions, such as Arbuda and others—namely Oḍiyāna, Jālandhara, Pullīra...
Those for whom Malaya is the first are Pullīramalaya, Jālandhara, Arbuda, Kulatā, and so forth.

This [specific] order of enumeration is intended as an instruction that, having begun with Pullīramalaya, [the yoginīs] reside in Jālandhara, Oḍiyāna, Arbuda, and the others. By this, the placement (nyāsa) of the Yoginīs within the mandala and the body at Pullīramalaya and the other sites is explained.

"Possessing daughters, the maiden is pervaded by non-duality with the heroes. This means that because maidens (*kanyā*) always remain in that very state, their nature (*śīla*) is pervaded by non-duality (*advayatva*) with the heroes such as Khaṇḍakapālī and others; thus it is [called] *vīrādvayavyāpinī*. There is also an elision of the case-ending (*vibhakti-lopa*). *Puṃ jāṃ oṃ aṃ goṃ rāṃ deṃ māṃ kāṃ oṃ triṃ koṃ kaṃ laṃ kāṃ hiṃ preṃ gṛṃ sāṃ suṃ naṃ siṃ maṃ kuṃ.* Thus.

The twenty-four syllables are the secreted mantra-nature. From these—along with the half-moon (*ardhacandra*), the bindu, and the *nāda*—the goddesses such as Pracaṇḍā and the others, born from the mantras "Oṃ kara kara pracaṇḍe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ" and so forth, are to be meditated upon as residing in their bodies within the [sites] such as Pullīramalaya and the rest, arising in due order. "Possessing the power of desire-forms" (*kāmarūpiṇyaḥ*) means that their forms are dependent solely upon their own will.

He asks, "For what purpose? and says: "To bring about the cessation of the mind's impulse. When the mind is engaged in a particular purpose, once that purpose is accomplished, the impulse of the mind ceases from it. (5-9)
The six Yoginīs are in Kulatā; the six Mothers are in the land of Maru;
Lāmā is in the land of Sindh, and the Kulanāyikās are in the city.
In Lampāka and Saurāṣṭra, the family deities reside;
in Pretapurī, the Great Maiden, the Ḍākinī Saharūpiṇī, dwells. (11)
It is said that she dwells with her daughter on the Himālaya and in Kāñcī;
in the region of Pañcāla she is the household deity, and in Kaliṅga she is the observer of vows. (12)
In Kośala, they are the Piśitāśanas; in Pretapurī, they are the Vajraḍākinīs; and in Sthūleśvara and Triśakuni, they are born from the Kula of Khaṇḍarohā. (13)
In Pullīramalaya and on the Golden Mountain (Kanakādri), there were twenty-one thousand women born of the Caṇḍāla caste. || 14 ||
He says "the six yoginīs," etc., to explain that those of that same class who wander in the outer regions are being set forth.
Among those residing within the body or within the mandalas at Pullīramalaya and so forth, Pracaṇḍā and the others are to be known in their respective order;
however, in the outer regions, those of that same class may be arranged in whatever way is appropriate. These are Vajravārāhī, Yāminī, and the other five, known as the six Mothers.

In the Maru region, they have the forms of the Seven Mothers; they are of the *lāmā* lineage and are the leaders of the family (*kulanāyikā*). Born from the family of Śrī Heruka, they are the family deities (*kuladevatā*) in Lampāka and Saurāṣṭra; the meaning is that they are to be worshipped in the form of the family deities. In Pretapurī, they are the Great Maidens (*mahākanyā*), the Ḍākinīs who possess various forms; this means the Ḍākinīs are in the form of maidens and belong to the *rupiṇī* lineage. In the Himālaya...

And in Kāñcī, they are known as Sabālikā; that is, those belonging to the class of Sabālikās. In the region of Pañcāla, they are the Gṛhadevatās (Household Deities) in the abode of the Gṛhadevatā; and in Kaliṅga, they are the Vratadhāriṇīs (Vow-holders). In Kośala, they are the Piśitāśanās (Flesh-eaters), who consume great meat. In Pretapurī, they are the Vajraḍākinīs; that is, the Yoginīs born in Pretapurī who possess non-dual knowledge. In Sthūleśvara and other such places, they are the Khaṇḍa-... [fragmentary].
"Born in Rohākula; at Pullīramalaya and on the Golden Mountain. Here, the mention of "twenty-one thousand women of the lowest castes" is intended to indicate their great abundance. (10–14)
For as many as there are other yoginīs of Śrī Heruka among the remaining [deities], they are the mistresses of his maṇḍala in the Great Yoga of Śrī Heruka. (15)
"Indeed, as many as there are among the others" means that in other regions as well, there are likewise [such]. "As many as" (*yāvantyaḥ*) is the plural form of *yāvat*.

Regarding "the Yoginīs of Śrī Heruka," the nominative plural ending has been elided; thus, there are thirty-six Yoginīs who are the members of the mandala (*maṇḍaleya*) of Śrī Heruka. "Great Churning" (*mahāmanthānam*) refers to the nature of Wisdom and Means (*prajñopāya*); or, Śrī Heruka is endowed with that Means.
The meaning is that among those [goddesses] who possess the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*), the central lady of the mandala, Vajravārāhī, has entered into union with him.

The "Great Churning" (*mahāmanthāna*) is the emanation (*nirmāṇa*) which is indivisible. Since their emanation is to be accomplished by Śrī Heruka, some say she is the central lady of the mandala of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) of Śrī Heruka. (15)
The three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, are pervaded by the twenty-four ḍākinīs;
for this is the commitment (samaya) of the ḍākinīs, which has been fashioned and meditated upon. 16.
"Twenty-four": the moving and non-moving world, which is the nature of body, speech, and mind, is pervaded by these twenty-four.

Why is this so? He says: "For this is the *samaya* (pledge/teaching) of the *ḍākinīs*. *Samaya* means instruction. How extensive is this? He says: "It is 'unmeasured' (*nirmita*). It is so called because from it the measured (*mita*)—that is, the limit or quantity—is gone. Is this their direct fruit?
Thus he says: "And that [mind] is cultivated. This means that its supernatural powers (vibhūti) have arisen. || 16 ||

Whatever [practice] such as meditation may exist on the surface of the earth during the Full Moon, one should always follow the left-hand path (vāmācāra), remain naked, and be concentrated at night. || 17 ||

"Whatever meditation and so forth may exist on the surface of the earth during the Full Moon"—whatever meditations and such are connected with mantras, mudrās, and so on, those belong to the ḍākinīs alone. "On the earth" means when the surface of the entire full earth is one's own form (*svarūpa*). "Naked" means without covering. "At night" means in the state of equality (*samatā*). || 17 ||
The heroic yoginīs and all the heroes born of heroes are pleased;
worship of the Self-Arisen One should be performed with the offering of the dance of mudrās. All tasks, without exception, are accomplished through the worship of the left. 18.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, the procedure for the placement of the twenty-four-syllable maṇḍala, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

To the question "What is the purpose of that?", he says "all," and so forth. Those who arise from the Hero, Śrī Heruka, are the "Hero-born" (vīrasambhavāḥ), namely the heroes such as Khaṇḍakapāla and others; and the yoginīs, such as Pracaṇḍā and others, are satisfied. By means of the *mudrā*, which is the union with the deity, there is the offering of dance, and not through ordinary [worldly] nature. Therefore, worship should be performed constantly by one who is self-arisen and endowed with the *rajas*.
"By means of the bodhicitta. Thus, the purity of worship has been stated, because the worship of the left is supreme. || 18 ||

The twenty-four secret syllables beginning with *pu* constitute the maṇḍala; it is that which prescribes the placement (*nyāsa*) of the assembly of that many yoginīs, and thus this chapter is so designated. It is the forty-first.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. || 41 ||
The forty-second chapter: The Ritual Procedure for the Illusion of the Form of the Laughter-Mantra Yoginī.
Then the hero, having drunk the flower-water, should recollect this mantra.
Likewise, the practitioner should perform a dance there together with the mudrā.
One should perform the consumption of meat at night, governed by the mantra;
having drunk and likewise given this curd-whey (mastu) with it, it brings happiness. (2)

Having been touched, the woman of noble family laughs; by means of truth, she becomes a celibate practitioner. At the conclusion of the rite, through the mudrās of laughter, she then becomes one who possesses pride in her gaze.
Explaining the laughter indicated in the thirty-ninth chapter, he speaks this chapter on its mantra and so forth, beginning with the words "Then" (*tataḥ*) and so on.

Since this laughter does not arise without the mantra and other factors, the hero is one endowed with the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*). One should recollect or recite this mantra of eight syllables or seven syllables. Having done what? Having drunk the flower-water, which is the *bodhicitta* mixed with menstrual blood (*rajas*).

Then one should perform the dance with the *vajrapada* together with the consort (*mudrā*). The connection is that one should partake of a meal of flesh at night. Of what nature is it? It is "triply constrained" (*triyantrita*), meaning constrained by the three [bodies] and so forth. To the question "by what means?", he says: "by this. This refers to the invocation. He states the mantra: "May there be the bringing of bliss"—*oṃ astu sukha*.

"Vahaṃ hūṃ"—this is the mantra. In some places it is "Oṃ sukhāvaha hūṃ. Having consecrated the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth with this very [mantra], one should employ them. Regarding the statement "having drunk and likewise having given," he says that for others as well, one should give after touching [the substance] and becoming blissful, and likewise give preceded by the mantra, and then laugh.

Therefore, he says: "she laughs. If the reading is *pṛṣṭvā* (having asked), it should be construed as: having asked, "Are you happy?", she should laugh. A person of noble lineage (*mahākulī*) and one who observes the great vow (*mahāvratin*) means one engaged in the practice (*caryāyogin*). Regarding "by truth, [she is] a celibate student" (*brahmacāriṇī*): it should be understood that "truth is Brahman" and "asceticism (*tapas*) is Brahman"; and here, asceticism is what is being described. Such an external consort (*bāhyamudrā*) should laugh. Having done what? He says: "the one to be accomplished" (*sādhya-*).

"Attains," etc. That which is to be attained is the *sādhya*, and that which attains it is the *sādhaka*. At the conclusion of tasting those five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), having seen her characterized by the mudrā of laughter, one should perform laughter. Of what nature is she? "Proud of her gaze" (*dṛṣṭigarvā*). She is so called because she possesses pride (*garva*) through her gaze (*dṛṣṭi*), that is, through being seen. Such is the consciousness (*saṃvit*) that arises. "By this" refers to [the sounds] such as *kili kili* and so forth, and *hā hā* and so forth. This is laughter.

Laughter is the accomplishment of the *ṇyat* suffix. The connection is that the former practitioner should laugh by means of tasting the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*). And since that [laughter] is his "external mudrā," it should be applied in exactly that way; thus, it is established that there is laughter for both wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*). Regarding the words "by truth" and so forth, some maintain that a certain other yoginī, having seen the practitioner in such a state, would laugh. (1–3)
Whether by night or by day, one should indeed perform laughter with this;
likewise, O Hero, listen to the nature of the Śuṇḍa as it truly exists. || 4 ||
Then there was dancing, the shedding of tears out of devotion, as well as self-exertion,
the leaping over the thunderbolt, and likewise worship while naked.
This is the sequence of the groups of mudrās for all the Vāmeśvarīs:
exhaling, impelling, laughing, and the wonderful dance of erotic passion.
Whatever one should perform in front of Viśva, one should recollect the mudrās and mantras;
the eightfold laughter—hā hā, he he—is most dear to Viśveśvarī.

"At night" refers to the *viramānanda* (bliss of cessation), which is the nature of the subsiding of the flavor of conceptualization regarding external objects. "During the day" refers to the *sahaja* (innate) state, which is the nature of pure self-awareness alone; the word "or" (*vā*) serves to indicate the conjunction of these two, namely *ānanda* and *paramānanda*. Thus, it points toward the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness), which is the thorough knowledge of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-parijñāna*). The sense is that whatever is performed within the realization of the innate (*sahaja-avabodha*) attains the state of reality (*tattva-daśā*). [The text continues: "Externally..."
The meaning is quite clear. Having seen that yogin, the yoginīs residing in the sacred seats (pīṭhas) and elsewhere display unprecedented forms and actions; thus he says "rūpa" and so forth.

The action (*karma*) of form—that is, of one's own nature (*svarūpa*)—is secret (*guhya*); such being its nature, it is revealed because it is to be manifested, just as it exists for the heroes (*vīras*), who are the Tathāgatas.

He says that very thing: "Dancing," and so forth. First there is dancing, and then it occurs through the falling of tears from the eyes; thus, the dramatic gesture (*abhinaya*) is expressed without case-endings out of devotion. "Personal exertion" means rising up by oneself. By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), offerings (*argha*) and so forth are included. In the reading "likewise the bristling of the hair through devotion," it refers to horripilation (*romāñca*) through affection. He describes the practitioner’s activity contained within that: "Of the vajra," and so forth. Leaping—

The meaning is "excess" (*atiśaya*), which refers to the "arising of the vajra. In the reading *alaṅghanam*, the sense of "excess" remains the same, as it means "to be surpassed completely" or "to be surpassed by me first. In the reading *ālambanam*, it means "attainment," specifically the act of attaining that [vajra] by the Yoginī;
thus he says: "likewise, nakedness and worship. "Likewise" means by way of being unrestrained (*niravagraha*). This applies to all the Vāmeśvarīs, that is, the Yoginīs.

It is for this very reason that it belongs to the yogins. The word "tu" (but/rather) indicates a distinction. This sequence of the group of mudrās, as well as the vajra-leaping and so forth, should be performed specifically with the *recaka* and other [breath-control techniques]. One should personally perform the manifestation in front—that is, before the yoginīs who have previously performed the ritual actions. The "mudrā-mantra" refers to the laughter-mudrā mantra. He states that very thing: "hā hā he he," and so forth. "Hā hā he he" constitutes the eightfold laughter.
The connection is that one should recollect the *hāsa-mudrā*. By the word "others" (*apareṣām*), the inclusion of "ho ho hūṃ hūṃ" is intended, because of the statement:

"Words ending in the plural, such as these, serve as indicators of a group. The second half of this mantra, beginning with "kili kilī," is also included. Regarding the phrase "the supreme beloved of Viśveśvarī": these syllables belong pre-eminently to the Yoginī.
"Priyāḥ" means dear ones. In the reading "viśeṣacaryāḥ paraṃ priyāḥ," it refers to the performance of specific activities such as dancing and so forth. (4–7)
For in their presence, there arises a cry of "Alas! and the shedding of weeping tears;
by that very means, she becomes dear to them when properly joined with meditation and mantra.
The yoginīs of the heroes experience pleasure along with horripilation and other sensations;
those who are conceived as "left" (vāmā) perform the leaping over the vajra.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, the procedure for the laughter-mantra and the form of the Yoginīs, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

Then they utter cries ending in "Hā! Hā! Therefore it is said: "For here, in their presence, there is the cry 'Hā! Hā! It is further stated that they constantly shed tears of weeping: "They bring forth tears of weeping. Along with that very shedding of tears, even the cry of "Hā!
Hā! becomes dear to them. Why is this so? It is said: "Because they are well-joined with meditation and mantra. That is, by means of meditation and mantra.

The sense is that those *yoginīs*, being well-joined and restrained, would become joyful upon seeing someone of their own kind. Through the mutual affection of both the *yoginīs* and the *yogins*, there arises mutual horripilation and so forth. To whom, then, is the "vajra-leaping" performed? He says:
"of the vajra," and so on. It is before those *yoginīs* who have been designated as "left" (*vāmā*) and identified through the observation of signs (*saṃketa*) and the like.
Such [passages] as these are to be understood. || 8–9 ||

The laughter-mantra and the illusory form of the Yoginī are prescribed therein; because it is that by which this is established, it is called a "chapter" (*paṭala*). It is the forty-second, the forty-fourth [sic].
Thus ends the forty-second chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 42.
The forty-third chapter: The Ritual Manual for the Accomplishment of the Upahṛdaya Rite.
Now I shall describe the visualization of the heroic non-dual man;
for one who knows the rules regarding the distinctions of locations, meditative cultivation is always most dear.

Now follow the gazes, the naked worship, and the ritual procedures for the seven-syllable mantra; he speaks the chapter on the ritual procedure for the seven syllables, beginning with "atha" and so forth.
"Atha" (now) means immediately after the explanation of the laughter and other [expressions]; the connection is that he will explain the gazes and so forth. "Nara" refers to the supreme among men.
"Having known" means having understood the disposition (*āśaya*) of those to be trained (*vineya*), because the state of the supported depends upon the support. || 1 ||
Whether at a crossroads, in a house, at a site for heroes, or on a mountain,
the ḍākinīs behold the place of the covenant even from afar.

With the words beginning "at a crossroads," he describes the different locations; the sense is that the meditation (*bhāvanā*) should be performed right here. Or "in the house" means, first of all, in the house itself. He states the purpose of the gathering with the words beginning "looking on"; they are present for the sake of the *samaya* and so forth.
The ritual application of the Nagnapūjanamudrā is now described further:
having cast off another garment, one should desire the mudrā and touch her with it. (3)

"The ritual application of the *mudrā* of naked worship is explained hereafter"—thus concludes the instruction on naked worship (*nagnapūjā*). Regarding the ritual action, he says "having cast off," and so forth. Having cast off other garments or skins and the like, and having become naked, one should desire the *mudrā*; that is, one should touch her with that [act].
The meaning is that by means of that ritual action, one shall become happy. || 3 ||
In this very manner, acting as the principal authority, one should cause all the rites to be performed;
likewise, perform the binding of the directions with the root mantras and with four others.

"Thus" means that nakedness and wearing garments of skin are enjoined. "All activities" refers to eating and so forth. The "root mantra" consists of eight syllables. [For the slaying of those who perform cruel deeds after overpowering them, there is another: the "Sumbha mantra" consists of four syllables. The instruction is that these two should be recited upon seeing the Yoginī. By implication, the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) and other rites should be performed at the time of meditation and so forth. Therefore, he says:

"Perform likewise with the four for the binding of the directions (*digbandha*). An alternative reading is *digbandhāvartayan tathā*, meaning "performing the rotations of the binding of the directions.

It should be explained as: "Perform likewise by means of the mantra itself for the rotations of the binding of the directions. Regarding the word "perform" (*kuru*): it refers to all rites such as worship and so forth.

In the alternative reading, *mūlamantraistathā cānyairdigbandhāścaturbhistathā kuru*, it means: "Perform all rites with the root-mantras (*mūlamantra*) and likewise with others; perform likewise with the four for the binding of the directions."

One should apply [the instruction] as follows: "Perform the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) with four other four-line verses. The term *digbandha* here involves the elision of the accusative case ending.
Furthermore, there are two instances of the word *tathā*; it should be explained to mean "in such and such a manner," that is, by means of various distinct methods. || 4 ||
Even by the hosts of gods in heaven, she could not be seen during her worship;
having cast up a handful of flowers, she became a celestial being (khecarī) in the sky above, perfectly complete.
No flower fallen there from the [offered] garland is seen upon the ground;
one may bring under control a thousand *khecarīs* residing therein.
The *Gopī* said: "In worship, he would not be seen even by the hosts of gods in heaven. She speaks of the power of the seven-syllable mantra:

"Having raised a full handful of flowers upward, one becomes a *khecarī*. The meaning is: having raised—that is, tossed upward—a full handful of flowers over which the seven-syllable mantra has been recited (*japta*), one becomes a *khecarī*. And that *khecarī* would be a *khecara*, one who dwells in the sky (*antarīkṣastha*). [This refers to] the *añjali*.

The feminine gender is due to the usage of the *ṛṣi* (Vedic/authoritative source). Therefore, he says: "Not there," and so forth. Because the flower seen right there does not fall to the ground, [it is said to be] "a thousand," and so on; this is easily understood. || 5–6 ||
Having also drawn forth Vāgīśa and Mātṛkā, he knows them in their proper order,
as well as the divine, divine discourse, and likewise the movement of the luminaries.
In subterranean villages, forests, and cities, at crossroads, under a solitary tree, in the abodes of heroes, on mountain peaks, or likewise in the sky; || 8 ||

He knows Vāgīśa Bṛhaspati, his mother Vāṇī, and divine matters—that is, events occurring in heaven. Divine stories are the accounts of divine yoginīs. He knows the movement of the luminaries, that is, the planets. Regarding "the netherworld" (pātāla): he knows whatever has occurred within the seven netherworlds. Regarding "village," and so forth: [he knows what occurs] in Nandigrāma and other such places; in the forest, that is, in the great wilderness.

In cities such as Vardhamāna and others; in a hero’s house, which is a dwelling-place presided over by Kṣetrapāla and other deities; in the sky, that is, in the atmosphere; on a peak, that is, on a mountain summit. (7–8)
They remember the *hṛdaya* and *upahṛdaya* mantras and are not seen by gods or humans;
therefore, practitioners always remain in these places.
Those who remember and recite the seven-syllable *hṛdaya* and *upahṛdaya* in these locations are not seen by gods or humans.

The meaning is that in these places, the accomplishment of invisibility (*adṛśyasiddhi*) results from that recitation. Therefore, the conclusion is that practitioners always reside in these regions; the sense is that this mantra is to be recited in these very locations. || 9 ||
Having meditated upon the seven-syllabled mantra of red color at the top of a tree,
one may quickly cause even broken mountains to bend, or otherwise [achieve other results].
Having projected [the self] into his own body, he should lie upon the ground on a seat of darbha grass;
he should mutter the seven-syllabled mantra one hundred and eight times.
In a dream, he shall reveal everything that is desired by the mind,
whether it be an untimely death, something lost, or whatever other matter may have occurred.

By means of the recitation of the mantra upon a sword, his thumb, water, a lamp, or a mirror, the practitioner, through constant union with the Self, should cause Prasena to descend [into the reflection]. 13.

"Consisting of seven syllables" means that he whose syllables consist of the number seven is so described. Having meditated upon him at the tip of a tree, one should bend the tree. "Unbroken" and "undivided"—thus is shown the state of being bound by will. "Mountains" refers to stone mountains. "For his own body" means for the sake of his own purpose. There is a reading, "ātma-kāma," which is easily understood. Ātma-...

Regarding the phrase "on the body": having assigned the six syllables to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and the syllable *phaṭ* to the mind (*manas*), one should lie down on a seat of *darbha* grass. The rest is easily understood. The mantra declares that one's lifespan shall last for this many years; or else, it refers to Śrī Heruka. "Struck by death" (*mṛtyuhata*) means one who has gone from the presence of death. "Destroyed" (*naṣṭa*) means having become invisible. From the region—

The phrase "all" is a summary that includes other effects situated within the interval. She refers to the deity. Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times over a sword or similar object, one should cause the light of the Prasena to descend. || 10–13 ||
Having meditated thus and recited [the mantra] seven times, he should reveal what is auspicious and inauspicious;
then the hero, having applied the seven-syllable mantra according to its divisions. (14)
Having reflected upon the diseased person, one should recite the mantra a thousand times while focusing on the center of the sun;
in an instant, one should visualize a thumb-sized consciousness, resembling the form of a crystal, and show it to the one afflicted by disease. 15.
By the mere sight [of it], the destruction of disease occurs without a doubt;
the sick person shall become free from illness, like the autumnal moon.

One should show a sword or similar object to a girl or a young woman; those two will declare whether it is auspicious or inauspicious. Now, with the words beginning with "atha," he explains the pacification of disease: having clearly inscribed or written the seven-syllable mantra within a sun-disc using *gorocanā* or other substances, or having visualized it, one should contemplate the sick person in its center and recite [the mantra] one thousand times. According to the specific division:

[The word] *vidarbhaṇataḥ* [means] from the process of interweaving. Because of its purity, it resembles the form of crystal. One should show that [mantra] as afflicted by disease; that is to say, one should see and meditate upon it. In the alternative reading *sphaṭikākṣarasadṛśam*, the mantra is such that its beautiful syllables are white like crystal. One should contemplate such a mantra upon the hand for the sake of [curing] disease.
One should show it to the afflicted person. The accusative case is to be explained as having the sense of the dative. "In an instant, [one should visualize] the size of a thumb":

one should meditate on consciousness (*vijñāna*) in his heart, equal in measure to a thumb and like pure crystal. Of what nature is it? It is that from which all various diseases arise; thus, one should contemplate the body and the consciousness as being liberated from all diseases and recite the mantra.
