The collective meaning [of verses 14–16].
Having thus placed the wheel within the moon in the left hand—
resembling crystal and letters— one who has been afflicted by all diseases is thereby liberated.
He states another yoga, beginning with "the moon" (*śaśi*) and so forth. A *cakraka* is that which has its left hand;

having visualized the lunar disc in the left hand, one should place a nine-square wheel there, with *oṃ* in its center. In the east is *hrīḥ*; in the south, *ha*; in the west, *hṛ*; in the north, *hlāṃ*.
Again, in the center is *hūṃ*, and in the four corners is *phaṭ*. This is the seven-syllable mantra.

Excluding the letter *ṭa*, there are seven syllables; some say it is the syllable *oṃ*. Therefore, he says: "shining like crystal-syllables. Because the seven syllables are white like crystal, that wheel (*cakra*) is so called because it shines—that is, is manifest—through their distribution. Furthermore, how is it? It is that in which all diseases are laid down (*vinyasta*). [It is] the wheel of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*) situated in the center.
One should meditate upon the left hand according to this instruction. || 17 ||
Fever, possession by spirits and the like, epilepsy, colic, leprosy, and likewise all diseases born of poison—of these there is no doubt. (18)

Regarding the verse beginning with *jvara* and so forth: the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārtha*). Since it is from [this mantra] that the disease and affliction of those bitten by venomous creatures and the like are destroyed, it is "the destroyer of the disease of those bitten by venomous creatures within the circle. By the word "and the like" (*ādi*), poisons such as those of stationary origin (*sthāvara*) are included. The particle *tu* is used for emphasis. It is "the one from whom all mental anxieties (*ādhayaḥ*) have departed," thus it is "the remover of all diseases" (*sarvavyādhi*). || 18 ||
Having meditated upon the syllable of the lunar disc, they flee in the ten directions;
at night, one should indeed grind beef with the three sweets in a secret place.
Having mastered the seven-syllable mantra, one should perform eight thousand oblations;
on the following day, the practitioner of the mantra shall obtain a thousand palas of gold.
By performing ten thousand oblations, one shall also obtain Surāṣṭra;
or else, one may contemplate the King of Mantras anywhere at all.
He is born right there at that very moment; of this there is no doubt.
Through the white [syllable] peace is produced, while through the black [syllable] one may cause death in an instant.
By means of [the mantra] colored red, one becomes subjugated and there is immediate attraction;
by means of yellow, there is the overcoming of all—this is the certainty of the scripture. (23)
By means of yellow alone, one gains prowess in ships, machines, elephants, and armies;
by the mere thought of white, one is certainly liberated from death. 24.
Even if seized by hundreds of great serpents, he quickly awakens from their fangs; likewise, even if rendered unconscious by poison, he regains consciousness upon seeing [the deity]. (25)
One seized by fever, planetary spirits, or epilepsy will become terrified upon seeing [the practitioner's] hand;
moreover, a person should always form a fist in battle and mentally recite [the mantra]. (26)
For as long as the fist is not released, everything indeed succeeds;
for even an enemy with raised weapon is [held at bay] as long as the fist remains bound.
Even if one so desires, it is simply not possible to cast away one's weapons;
for indeed, in all undertakings, it is exactly thus that success is achieved.

"Regarding the phrase *śaśibimbākṣaram* (the syllables on the moon-disc): having seen and meditated upon the left hand with the seven syllables placed upon the moon-disc as before, one should show it to one afflicted by disease, or one should wipe away [the affliction] with it. Regarding the phrase *vidravanti diśo daśam* (they flow forth into the ten directions): these are the rays of those syllables. Having the nature of flowing nectar, they "flow forth"—that is, they pervade—the ten directions, beginning with the east. Such..."
The meaning is that one should show the left hand with the *rūpākṣara* [mudrā] and wipe away [the obstacles] with it.

He describes the fire-oblation (*homa*) with the words beginning "cow-flesh" (*gomāṃsa*). "Triple-sweet" (*trimadhura*) refers to molasses, honey, and sugar. Alternatively, regarding the "King of Mantras":
he states that wherever one contemplates it for the sake of pacification and so forth, there pacification and the like arise; "then, at that time, it arises—of this there is no doubt."

Regarding the term "doubt" (*saṃśaya*), he states the recitation (*jāpa*) [of the mantra] beginning with "with white," etc., up to "one should immediately attract. Or else, having seen [the deity] as red-colored, one should perform the seven-syllable [mantra] with the left hand. With the words "or else," etc., he demonstrates the signs of accomplishment (*siddhi-liṅga*), showing that for the reciter of the mantra, everything is accomplished in this very manner. (19–28)
With leaves, flowers, fruits, betel, and likewise with food—this is the first application of the body; the second is that which pertains to one's capacity. (29)
The third [is found] indeed from speech, and the fourth is not perceived,
even upon the earth girdled by the ocean and covered with trees.

By means of this king of mantras, accomplishment is attained here without a doubt; within the three realms of existence, including all that is moving and unmoving, both the beneficial and the harmful can indeed be accomplished.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, the procedure for the accomplishment of the rites of the *upahṛdaya*, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 43.

"With betel leaves" means with useful items; "with various betels" refers to the maintenance of the body (*śarīrayoga*). "The second [is attained] by power" means he becomes powerful; the sense is that even non-human beings become his servants. "The third is indeed through speech"—the sense is the perfection of speech (*vāk-siddhi*). "The king of mantras has been meditated upon" is the meaning. It is said: "Mantra, mantra—thus it is proclaimed."
"Speech that impels toward reality. Through speech, body, and mind, the yogi is the performer of curses and favors. (29–31)
The "Heart and Upahr̥daya Ritual Action" refers to that by which the task to be accomplished—such as the rite of scattering flowers—is performed;
thus it is called a *paṭala*. This is the forty-third [chapter], the thirty-fourth [in some reckonings].
Thus ends the forty-third chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 43.
The forty-fourth chapter: The Ritual Procedure for the Seven-Syllable Mantra of the Six Yoginīs.
Now, having fully accomplished the messenger (dūtī) by means of the seven-syllable [mantra], whatever rite one undertakes therein is swiftly perfected at that very moment.
Having performed the placement of the six Yoginīs according to the rite of the seven syllables, one should fashion the wheel situated in the hand according to that same procedure.
Having meditated upon him who bears a form, the King of Mantras, accompanied by the exhortation from the left, reveals his hand to whomsoever [he intends], having uttered it through his own mouth.

"Now," [it is said]. The expansion of the ritual activities of the mantras of the six Yoginīs is introduced. That expansion of ritual activity is that in which the messenger (dūtī) is accomplished and becomes manifest. Having done what is it introduced? He says: "having commenced the ritual. It should be understood that the expansion of ritual activity is introduced after performing rituals such as summoning (ākarṣaṇa) and so forth. By what means? He says: "having fully mastered those joined with the seven syllables. Saṃvi...
The mantra of the six Yoginīs is to be accomplished and mastered by means of devotion. Its "conjunctions" refer to the meditations on their union.
He states the ritual action, beginning with "in the hand," and so forth: *Oṃ hāṃ hrīṃ hreṃ huṃ hūṃ phaṭ*—this is the seven-syllable mantra. The six Yoginīs are those [deities];

having placed those seven-syllable six Yoginīs in the middle of the hands, one should attract the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*)—this is the connection. [This refers to] the placement (*vinyāsa*).

To explain this, he says "six," and so forth. The wheel situated in the configuration of six spokes—that which is used for attraction—is the "wheel situated in six"; this is an adverbial modifier. Therefore, it is specific. "Left" (*vāma*) is a modifier of the hand; one should attract that [object] in such a way that the wheel is situated in six, while showing the hand to whomsoever [one intends]. Hence, he says: "he shows."

Regarding the phrase "the hand of whom": having done what, and to whom does he show his hand? He says: having meditated upon the *cakra* (wheel) which bears the form of that which is to be drawn forth. Again, having done what? He says: "having uttered with the mouth the King of Mantras," where the accusative case ending has been dropped. It is specified as "with the mouth" because it is to be visualized (*bhāvanīya*) as the seven-syllable mantra belonging to the six Yoginīs. Of what nature is this mantra?
He said: "Accompanied by the *codanā*. Having visualized a six-spoked wheel in the left hand, one should place *oṃ* in its center.

On the five spokes, one should arrange the six syllables: *hāṃ hrīṃ hraiṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. Visualizing the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) being led there by a net of rays from that [wheel] in the form of a hook, one should offer the hand equipped with the wheel to him: *oṃ hāṃ hrīṃ hraiṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
The collective meaning is that by reciting the mantra accompanied by the injunction "Draw Devadatta hither," while displaying the hand-gesture (mudrā), one draws him forth. || 1-3 ||
One should certainly draw [the target] using red sandalwood, black mustard, the dust from the foot of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), and likewise salt. (4)
Having unified them and examined them, one should then churn them with both hands;
at night, one should offer oblations to the Yoginī in the fire of a Caṇḍāla according to the prescribed rule.

Or one should offer the powder into the funeral fire; the person to be influenced will become submissive. Having begun this ritual application, one should likewise recite [the mantra] up to one hundred times.
By that [mantra], the one who is to be accomplished is certainly drawn forth;
for when this application is perfected, one may bring wealth and men under one's control.
I do not speak otherwise; having taken the dust from his feet, one should mix it with iron filings and wrap it in a cloth from a cremation ground.
Having recited [the mantra] seven times at a crossroads, one should dig eight finger-breadths into the earth;
there, one should conceal that powder together with the name of the enemy.
If one should recite [the mantra] over cow's milk, he will be defeated;
however, by using that same powder with effort, there shall be a restoration once again.
Moreover, by taking that powder, success is indeed attained without a doubt;
having added the five types of intoxicants, it should be wrapped in a cloth from a cremation ground.
One should write the name of the enemy there and perform the recitation one hundred times;
by concealing that in a cremation ground, the target will become insane.
Having carefully uprooted it and bathed it with cow's milk, one who is liberated returns to the state of attainment; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*, the ritual procedure for the seven-syllable [mantra] of the six yoginīs. 44.

Having ground red sandalwood and so forth with both hands while reciting the mantra, the yogin should offer them as an oblation into the funeral pyre fire or the fire of a *caṇḍāla*, accompanied by the same injunction. Regarding "according to the rule": the rule (*vidhi*) consists of the preparation and arrangement of the red sandalwood and other materials. This oblation is a practice performed by an eminent yogin based upon the refuge of Śrī Heruka. Those very substances—red sandalwood and the rest—are to be reduced to powder for the sake of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
And [the mantra] connected with the feet. "Endowed with the name of the enemy" means accompanied by the injunction. "With pure cow's milk" means with the milk of a cow;
this is the sense of "restoration. The remainder is easily understood. || 4-13 ||

The six Yoginīs consist of the nature of seven syllables; that chapter in which their activities, such as summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*) and so forth, are prescribed is thus [described]. This is the forty-fourth [chapter]. Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 44.
The forty-fifth chapter: The Ritual Procedure for the Attraction of the Accomplishment of Speech and Action of the Six Yoginīs.
Now follows the supreme and most excellent rite that effects the accomplishment of speech.
Having gathered one hundred and eight red *karavīra* flowers,
one should cause them to be consecrated by reciting [the mantra] one hundred times over cow's milk.

Now, with the mantra of the armor (*kavaca*) of the six yoginīs, he explains the chapter on the expansion of the ritual applications of the remaining six syllables of the mantra, beginning with "atha" and so forth.
"Atha" (now) means immediately after the explanation of the expansion of the ritual applications of the mantra consisting of the seven syllables of the armor of the six yoginīs;
it should be understood that the "supreme rite" pertains to the six-syllable mantra. [The mantra is: OṂ VAṂ YOṂ MOṂ HRĪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ PHAṬ.

The mantra is its ritual action, which accomplishes its specific attainment (*siddhi*). The attainment through speech is direct realization. He says this very thing in the passage beginning with "karavīra" and so forth. One should take one hundred and eight red *karavīra* flowers and, having carefully prepared them with cow’s milk, sprinkle them while reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times. || 1 ||
One should strike the top of the *liṅga* with a flower over which the mantra has been recited once;
one should perform this day after day for seven days with a well-concentrated mind. || 2 ||
Then, on the eleventh day, let flowers be taken;
having gone to a great river, one should cause each one to flow away.

Then, with each flower consecrated by reciting [the mantra] once, one should strike the top of the *liṅga*. One should do this for seven days, remaining well-composed as a yogi of the deity. Then, on the eleventh day—meaning after the seven days have passed; the word "tu" has the sense of "indeed"—until the eleventh day arrives, those four intervening days are not to be included [in the count]. However, [one should continue until then].

During those days, the mantra should also be recited there at the three junctions of the day. The word *tu* (but/then) is used for emphasis. On the eleventh day, it should be grasped—meaning it should be properly grasped after having been thoroughly examined so as not to be mistaken. Regarding the act of tying (*granthanam*), which is a general action, the instruction is that the string for tying should be made from the bark of the *karavīra*. He states the specific detail: "But the flowers... The word *tu* here has the sense of *eva* (indeed/emphatic).

The meaning is that they are indeed those very flowers. "Mahānadī" means a river free from drying up. The particle *tu* is used for conjunction (*samuccaye*), for the sense of "but" (*vai*), for the sense of "at that time" (*tadātve*), or for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).
It is certainly never otherwise. (2-3)
One should employ all of those by reciting [the mantra] once in successive order;
as for the western flower, it should be cast against the current in a river.
Having taken that [liquid] mixed with water, one should drink it without touching it with the teeth;
thus the practitioner attains mastery of speech, as revealed in the Guhyatantra.

He explains how the *pravāhaṇa* (the winding) is performed: "all of them in successive order. At the time of striking, one should perform the placement of the first flower and so forth in a row; likewise, the stringing is done according to that same sequence—that is the *pravāhaṇa*. Some say it refers to the sequence of the time of stringing. Others say that the "western flower" refers to the western flower at the time of striking and the western flower at the time of stringing.
"Pratistrotaṃ prapāti(vāhitaṃ)": it flows against the current; having overcome the force of the current, it moves upstream by the power of mantra.
The remainder is easily understood. "One whose speech is perfected" refers to such a practitioner (*sādhaka*). The sense is that this section has emerged from the *Guhyatantra*. (4–5)

Having bound the *yoginīyogamudrā*, the mantra-practitioner, facing the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, visualizing [the mantra] situated within the very belly of that person to be accomplished.
The wise man, with his mind fixed upon that [deity], should move the little finger at the three junctions of the day;
even a slayer of a Brahmin shall bring Indra and others under his control within seven days.
Having fashioned an image of the person to be subdued with the powder of red sandalwood, its limbs smeared with the three pungent spices (trikaṭuka) and anointed with beeswax; || 8 ||
Having pierced her at the secret place with a copper needle,
the wise practitioner should heat her for seven days with smokeless coals of khadira wood.
Then, by reciting [the mantra] one hundred times, the king, the vassal lords, and the family priest,
along with the harem and its retinue, will be swiftly drawn forth.
One should have the king, together with his retinue, written upon birch bark;
one should write the name, interwoven [with mantras], using the lac of a *preta* and yellow pigment (*rocanā*). 11.
Facing whom one should recite [the mantra], one should heat [that person] with a fire of *khadira* wood;
for the sake of success, one should heat them in a cemetery until the wax has melted.
It draws toward itself the king who is being tormented—that universal monarch—[using] the dust from his feet and red sandalwood of the person to be accomplished. (13)

Having assumed the yoginī-yoga-mudrā cross-legged posture and performed the vajra-bandha, one should join the tips of the two middle fingers with the tips of the two thumbs, and having raised the two index fingers, join their tips together; this is what some call the yoginī-yoga-mudrā.
Even when the reading is "yonimudrā" in certain places, it is this very same mudrā. It should also be understood that the recitation follows immediately after. How?

He says that one should recite [the mantra], beginning with "of the person to be acted upon" (*sādhyasya*) and so forth. Having placed the little finger—the six-syllable garland of the six Yoginīs—along with the *vidarbha* [interlacing] within the yantra, and having inserted it into the belly of an effigy of the person to be acted upon made from the dust of that person's feet and other materials; one should move it, that is, recite. How should one recite? He says: facing the effigy of the person to be acted upon, remaining with the mind fixed on that [effigy] during the three junctions of the day.

One should bring Śakra and the others under control by means of recitation for seven weeks, totaling one hundred and eight [recitations] per week. These extend up to seven hundred and fifty-six [recitations]. One should effect the summoning by means of these totals ending in hundreds. "Then" refers to the complete assembly of conditions. The remainder is easily understood. (6–13)
The practitioner, having gathered together the ashes discarded in a cremation ground,
should diligently heat them with smokeless charcoal from the Khadira tree.
Having rubbed that dust with both hands, one should perform the fire-oblation (homayet).
Having performed the oblation until success is attained, one should indeed take up that very dust.
Having restrained the breath, one should certainly bury that [victim] there when she has been cast down;
she will then become unconscious, deprived of consciousness, afflicted, and utterly bewildered. || 16 ||

One should bury the dust of an effigy being burned, or of ashes discarded from a cremation ground that have been dried; "of it" means of the dust from the burnt offering (*homadhūli*). The rest is easily understood. (14–16)
Arriving with the speed of the wind, she descends upon the practitioner.
The wise one should cause her to act as either a sacrificial victim (paśu) or a messenger (dūtī), or he should divide her [between them]. 17.
Then indeed one should perform the rite and the seizing of the messenger;
taking a fresh Karavīra creeper of the length of an arm. (18)
Having inscribed the mantra upon it for whichever rite the practitioner intends, he should cast that creeper even into a blazing fire. || 19 ||
Having quickly seized it from there while it has not yet been burnt,
one should whirl it around seven times while recollecting Yama and having empowered it with the mantra recited seven times.
With the words beginning with "paśum" (the animal), he states another ritual application: one should cause a man or a woman to perform the rite as desired by oneself.
For that very reason follows the taking of the messenger (dūtī) and the subduing of the messenger. Regarding the phrase "moist, the measure of an arm":
it means moist and the length of an arm. Having taken a *karavīra* creeper, upon which the mantra has been inscribed—meaning, by interlacing the name of the person [with the mantra].

The meaning is: "having written that very mantra. Regarding the phrase "but for the performer": whether it be a man or a woman, in the case of the opposite [gender], [the rite is performed] with the six-syllable *yoginī-kavaca-aparākṣara* mantra. "He" refers to the man; "she" refers to the woman. (17–20)
At that very moment, she comes in the form of an excellent woman with the speed of the wind.
The practitioner, during the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism, should take a red karavīra flower over which the mantra has been recited one hundred times. || 21 ||
A flower smeared with gorocana and placed in water, having been taken down into a great river and held in water reaching up to the navel. || 22 ||
Placed within the hollow of the palms and consecrated one thousand times with the mantra,
he should drink it while holding both hands filled with water.
Therefore, he says: "or in an excellent woman, in her own form. Regarding "in an excellent woman," it means *varastrīm*.

He states another application for the accomplishment of speech (*vāk-siddhi*): "the red flower of the *karavīra*," and so forth. Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times under the constellation Puṣya, it should be taken. Then, that flower, smeared with *gorocanā*, is combined with water and *madana*.

There, one should perform one hundred and eight recitations. Then, having entered knee-deep water in a great river, one should recite [the mantra] one thousand times with both hands. After the thousand recitations, the flower—complete with its filaments and so forth and not broken—which was placed in the joined palms (*añjali*) of the practitioner by the assistant-practitioner (*uttarasādhaka*), [is taken]. "With water" means: where that flower, which was held in the hollow of the assistant-practitioner's two hands, [is then taken] with one's own two hands.
By means of one's own [effort]. || 21-13 ||
Then success shall be his; indeed, the practitioner attains mastery over speech.
He will certainly attract a king or a queen by means of his mind alone. (24)
He quickly brings gods, asuras, and humans under his control;
when enraged, he can slay them with his voice and even effect their eradication.
The practitioner restrains [them] with his speech, saying "So be it";
likewise, he can paralyze a river, a cart, a machine, or even the ocean by mere words alone.
By means of speech, one creates elephants, horses, clouds, men, or even birds; indeed, one brings to pass everything that is desired by the mind.

He states the purpose of the accomplishment of speech (*vāksiddhi*) with the words beginning "the king," etc.: "One who is enraged may kill by means of speech, and likewise effect the expulsion (*uccāṭana*) of that [person]. "The expulsion of one who is not equal" is *asyoccāṭanam*. "Elephant, horse, and likewise cloud"—that is, *gajavājitathāmeghāḥ*; [one effects the expulsion] of those. "Wherever the mind desires" means: wherever there is a desire of the mind, there [one performs] the summoning (*karṣaṇa*) and so forth.
He performs [it]. || 24–27 ||
Now, as for the practice of attraction which causes the enchantment of all women:
having gathered red flowers, one should collect those of the *karavīra*. (28)
Having empowered it with the mantra recited seven times by means of the Vidyā, one should place that flower within the vulva; having encased it, one should apply it to the secret place. || 29 ||
The practitioner, possessing the yoga of non-dual knowledge, should recite the mantra one hundred times;
then, the adept should take a single flower from among those situated within the womb.
Whomever one strikes with a flower, that person shall instantly become submissive—
distraught, deprived of consciousness, and rendered subject to another's will in all the joints of the limbs.
And he quickly brings [the object] under his control if the conviction is firm;
this is the accomplishment of conviction, which unfailingly effects subjugation. (32)
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*, the chapter on the ritual procedure for the attraction of the accomplishments of body and speech of the six yoginīs. || 45 ||

With the words "attraction" (*ākarṣaṇa*) and so forth, he states another application; that is easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "if the consciousness (*pratyaya*) ceases": consciousness resides in that which possesses sentience, but not in wood, stone, or the like. (28–32)

The mantra consisting of the six-syllable *apara-mantra* which is the armor-mantra (*kavaca-mantra*) of the Six Yoginīs is the subject; its ritual action is the "action of the Six Yoginīs" (*ṣaḍyoginī-karma*).
That [action] is the summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*) through the perfection of speech (*vāk-siddhi*), namely the accomplishment of speech; that by which this chapter is established is thus described.
It is the forty-fifth [chapter], the one following the forty-fourth.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*.
The forty-sixth chapter: The Ritual Procedure for the Five *Ha*-Syllables.
Now follows the [procedure] for the five *ha*-syllables, which accomplishes all rites;
by the mere knowledge of which, swift accomplishment proceeds.
Now he states the ritual function (*karman*) of the five *hakāra*s, beginning with "atha" and so forth. "Now, the ritual procedure of the five *hakāra*s is set forth.

Regarding the phrase "of the five *hakāra*s": it refers to the ritual function—the task—of the five *hakāra*s; or alternatively, it refers to the yogi who accomplishes that [function], [the practitioner] of the expansion of the *hakāra*. (1)

One should crush the two hands with the five *ha*-syllables: *hā*, *hī*, *hai*, *hau*, and *haḥ*. If one does so even with the mouth of one who is under incantation (*codanā*), it causes blood to flow at that very moment and kills the enemy.
One should rub one's own blood contained in a skull-cup with the blood from the ring finger until it dries up;
then the target will perish. || 3 ||
If, being enraged with blazing eyes and bloodshot pupils, one recites [the mantra] with fiery intensity,
one swiftly kills the king along with his army, forces, and vehicles.

He states the five *hakāras*: *hā*, *hī*, *hai*, *hau*, *haḥ*—this is the pentad of *hakāras*. Without the sixth vowel, the *hakāra* is distinguished by the remaining five vowels from the extraction of the six-vīra armor mantra (*ṣaḍvīrakavaca-mantra*). The connection is that one should rub together the two hands joined with the five arrows by means of the five *hakāras*. Therefore, he says: "the two hands which [consist of] the five *hakāras*."

"Five *ha*s in the hands": having visualized a five-spoked wheel in the two hands, or having actually drawn it there, one should visualize or write the five syllables within it and then crush those two hands; this is the collective meaning. Since the word "five" refers to individual instances (*vyakti*), even when including the vowel *u*, there are six *ha*s: *hā, hī, hū, hai, hau, haḥ*. Thus, the mantra consists of five *ha*s.

Some say it is the six-syllable mantra. Regarding "blood even from the mouth": having pierced the five vessels with a needle-like mouth, one should visualize the blood being drawn out and residing within the skull; then, at that very moment, he kills the enemy.
He states another application: "the blood of a dog," and so forth. "Anāmikā" means childless; her blood...

The *rajas* undergoes drying; that is to say, it becomes heated. This effect is achieved simply by the recitation (*japa*) of the five *ha*-syllables. By the words "if [the practitioner] is angry," and so forth, he describes the accomplishment of the recitation: having smeared both palms with poison, *rājikā*, and other substances, and having written the five *ha*-syllables upon them as before using yellow orpiment, crystal, or other materials with a pen made from a crow’s wing feather, one should also perform it through meditation.

Having seen it thus, one should crush the dust from the feet of the target with both hands over a fire of *khadira* charcoal embers and offer it as an oblation while preceded by the section on the name. By that very mantra, the enemy then vomits blood from the mouth and dies; so say some. (2–4)
One should offer oblations to the cat, the mongoose, the dog, the crow, the crane, the jackal, and the ḍākinī;
for these bring swift accomplishment in this tantra, of this there is no doubt. (5)
He states the application of the *homa* sacrifice: "With the flesh of a cat," and so forth. *Ibhya* means a lord (*īśvara*). *Jambuka* is used here due to the archaic nature of the text (*ārṣatvāt*).

With the flesh of these [animals], one performs a *homa* preceded by an offering (*bali*) to the *ḍākinīs*. One should practice that *ḍākinī-bali-homa*. One should offer the *ḍākinī-bali* as a *homa*. The sense is that one should offer that flesh into the fire while interspersing it with this mantra. It brings about swift accomplishment (*āśusiddhi*).
These, namely cats and so forth, bring about the attainment of sovereignty and other such powers. || 5 ||

Having made a rope from the hair of hares and other such animals, and having consecrated it one thousand times with mantras, whoever one ties it around their neck becomes exactly like that [animal]. || 6 ||
Having consecrated one's hand a thousand times with mantras and joined each syllable with *karavīra* flowers, one should touch a pregnant woman;
it causes the fetus to transfer. When released, there is liberation. Whomever one threatens, that person dies; [whomsoever one touches,] one brings back to life again. || 7 ||
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, the Chapter on the Ritual Procedure for the Five *Ha*-Syllables, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 46.
"Of rabbits and so forth"—by the word "and so forth," jackals and others are included. "With the hand" is a form without a case ending (*nirvibhaktika*).

Having consecrated the hand one thousand times with mantras, one should touch a pregnant woman with it along with *karavīra* flowers. To the question "What is the result of that?", he says: "The fetus," and so forth. "Joining each syllable one by one"—this refers to the application of the ritual (*karmayoga*) following five hundred thousand recitations (*pañcalakṣajāpa*).
This is the intended meaning. Regarding "liberation upon being released": when her body is released by the hand, there is liberation in the form of the discharge of the fetus. || 6-7 ||

Regarding the applications of the mantras for the armor of the six yoginīs, there is the yoga of Vajravārāhī; elsewhere, there is the yoga of Śrī Heruka. That chapter in which the accomplishment of the pressing of the hands through the five *hakāra* actions is prescribed is thus [designated]. It is the forty-sixth [chapter].
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*.
The forty-seventh chapter: The Ritual Procedure for All Activities of the Mantra of All Buddha-Ḍākinīs.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain that which is in the heart of all ḍākinīs;
by its mere utterance, there arises the fruit of all accomplishments.

Now he explains the expansion of the ritual activities of the *upahṛdaya* mantra of Vajravārāhī, beginning with "atha ata" and so forth. "Atha" (now) means immediately after the explanation of the expansion of the fivefold ritual activities of the letter *ha*. The connection is: "I shall fully proclaim the *sarvaḍākinī* [mantra] in its heart.
*Sarva-ḍākinī* refers to the heart-mantra of Vajravārāhī; "in its heart" (*tasya hṛdi*) means the heart [mantra]. The meaning is: the *upahṛdaya* mantra of Vajravārāhī.

*Oṃ vajravairocanīye svāhā*. From this, I shall fully explain that from which the arising of the fruit of all accomplishments (*siddhi*) occurs. Therefore, he says "by this" and so forth: by means of this [mantra] when recited, I shall fully explain the arising of the fruit of all accomplishments, because its *upahṛdaya* (near-heart mantra) is about to be taught. If it is asked, "How is it the heart-mantra of all *ḍākinīs*?", it is because of the expansion of its ritual activity (*karmaprasara*).
Because it has been cultivated with certainty. || 1 ||

Then, by reciting the great vidyā of the ḍākinī, one brings all castes under one's control. By constant recitation, one generates great prosperity. Having prepared a ritual stake (*kīlaka*) made of human bone and consecrated it eight hundred times with the mantra six finger-breadths in length, if one buries it at someone’s door, that person’s lineage will be destroyed. If one buries it in a field, a cow-pen, or a place where buffaloes, elephants, or horses are kept, it will affect that [place].
Destruction occurs. || 2 ||
"Tataḥ" means for the sake of the fruit. "Ḍākinīmahāvidyā" refers to that which is being recited; thus, by that [mantra].
"Ṣaḍaṅgulā" is without a case-ending. "Gotrocchāda" means that even his lineages (jātayaḥ) become utterly destroyed—this is the sense. || 2 ||

Now, one who desires to bring a king or a royal minister under control should, being wise, fashion an image out of clay at the gate of the palace and place it eight finger-breadths in height. On the first day, one should offer one hundred thousand oblations of three *mātuluṅga* fruits mixed with flowers; [the target] becomes submissive. By this very mantra, [one achieves] attraction, paralyzing, drying up, and deluding.
It causes the loss of speech through paralysis, induces blindness and muteness, and effects expulsion. || 3 ||

"A clay image" means that its name, written on birch bark or similar material and pierced with the relevant mantra, should be placed in its heart and concealed at the royal gate. "Eight finger-breadths" means that one should dig eight finger-breadths deep and conceal it there. Then, elsewhere, three wood-apple flowers (*mātuluṅga*) should be offered as oblations; thereafter, another sixteen thousand of those very same flowers should be offered. || 3 ||

Now, for one who wishes to turn a man into a woman: one should collect the flowers of a dead man, the fruits of the *kākāṇḍī* plant, and the skin, nails, and so forth from the feet of a hungry man; these should be made into equal portions and ground with the blood of a rabbit. One should then form eleven pills and dry them in the shade. Thus, having bound [one pill] on the hand on an auspicious day, on the twelfth day, for whomever...
If he places powder on the head, she becomes a woman. || 4 ||

Now, if one wishes to turn a man into a dog, one should place *puṣpaloha* on the head of a mongoose and recite the mantra eight thousand times over seven nights. On the eighth day, having mixed it with saffron and empowered it one hundred and eight times, one should offer the powder as a burnt oblation (*juhuyāt*). Whosoever has that ash placed upon his head becomes a dog. To restore him to his original state, [one should perform this] at night or during the twilight (*sandhyā*).
Having performed a great worship of the Ḍākinī, one should then offer a bali-oblation; thereby, one becomes [her] very nature. || 5 ||

One who wishes to turn a non-substance into a substance should offer one hundred and eight oblations of golden fruits; it becomes a substance. One should offer oblations of *harītakī*; it returns to its natural state. Now, one who wishes to cause madness should offer oblations of the dwelling of a great bird (*mahāśakuni*);
on the seventh day, madness occurs. To bring it back, however, one should offer oblations of husks; it is pacified.

During a lunar eclipse, having collected the hair of a female cat, if one offers it as an oblation while reciting a mantra containing the name of a person, that person, upon being made to take the ashes and place them on his own head, becomes a cat; he returns to his natural state once more when [the rite] is overcome. || 6 ||

Having consecrated a rope made of crow-tendons with mantras, if one ties it around someone's neck, that person becomes a crow. In this same way, one assumes the form of a crow, a pigeon, a peacock, a parrot, an owl, a hawk, or a vulture. Having made a rope from cow-hair and consecrated it eight hundred times, if one ties it around someone's neck, that person becomes a cow. Whichever sentient being [it may be]...

Having taken a cord of sinew and consecrated it with mantras, one binds it around the neck; he becomes like that [creature]. Having made a cord from any four-legged animal and consecrated it, one binds it around the neck; he assumes the form of that [animal]. Upon release, there is liberation. Having consecrated grain and cast it into the house of a great lord of wealth, and having sprinkled oneself with the remainder for seven nights, one attracts all riches.
The end of the section. || 7 ||
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, the Chapter on the Ritual Procedures for All Actions of the Mantra of All Buddhas and Ḍākinīs, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

*Kākāṇḍī* fruits are *mahākāla* fruits. A hungry crow. *Puṣpaloha* is an iron insect. *Kanaka* is the *dhuttūraka* plant. *Mahāśakuni* is a bat. *Kākasnāyu* is a crow’s tendon. Regarding the word "with the remainder" (*śeṣeṇa*), it means subsequently. This is what is intended: after throwing the grain, one should [sprinkle] oneself with water consecrated by that mantra.
By means of the consecration (sekha), one who has recited [the mantra] for seven nights attracts riches. || 4-7 ||

That by which the mantra-activities of all the Buddhas and Ḍākinīs are performed is called a "chapter" (paṭala); this is the forty-seventh (saptacālīśatimaḥ). Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 47.
The eightieth chapter, the ritual procedure for the secret maṇḍala which is the abode of all heroes and ḍākinīs.
Now I shall further proclaim another auspicious [teaching] concerning all ḍākinīs:
the heart-mantra of all yoginīs, which accomplishes all desired aims.

The word *atha* (now) refers to the point immediately following the explanation of the expansion of the ritual application of the *upahṛdaya* mantra. "I shall fully proclaim another mantra, and that is the *hṛdaya*.

Therefore, he says: *sarvaḍākinī*. That is the *hṛdaya* wherein all *ḍākinīs* reside. Regarding the phrase *yacchubham*: it has the sense of "because"; because it is auspicious (*śubha*), and because from it the *ḍākinīs* are born, and through its recitation (*jāpa*) they become manifest. [It is for] all of them...
Because he accomplishes all desired aims for sentient beings, the yogi becomes one who accomplishes all desired aims. || 1 ||
By the mere remembrance of whom even the three worlds tremble, and by the mere constant recollection of whom perfect accomplishment is attained in due course. (2)

By the mere recollection of which even the three worlds tremble, and by the mere recollection of which even the three worlds tremble, and from which perfect accomplishment and complete enlightenment arise in due order—that heart-mantra I shall now fully proclaim; thus it should be connected. || 2 ||
Hā svā ṭpha hūṃ hūṃ yenīrṇavajrava yenīkiḍāddhaburvasa oṃ. || 3 ||
He states that heart-mantra: "hā sva" and so forth. The mantra is concealed. It should be recited as: *oṃ sarvabuddhaḍākinīye vajravarṇanīye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. (3)
This mantra is perfected through recitation; it is auspicious and performs all rites.
It belongs to the ḍākinīs and yoginīs, as well as to Khaṇḍarohā and Lāmā.

This mantra is "accomplished through recitation alone," meaning it is devoid of [the need for] writing and so forth. Consequently, those yogins whose nature it is to perform all the previously mentioned rites are "performers of all rites" (*sarvakarmakarāḥ*). They are "auspicious" (*śubhāḥ*), which means pure. In the reading *sarvakarmākaraḥ śubhaḥ*, this is an epithet of the mantra. To the question "Whose mantra is this?", he says: "Of the ḍākinīs," that is, of the ḍākinī. [The word] *yogi-*...
"Nīnām" refers to Rupiṇī. "Tu" is used for conjunction. "Khaṇḍarohā, Lāmaya, and likewise"—the meaning is that this applies to Khaṇḍarohā and Lāmaya as well. || 4 ||
Thus has the mantra of all the yoginīs been proclaimed;
whether in the netherworld, in heaven, or likewise again in the mortal realm.
Whatever action is performed, this mantra— which brings about all accomplishments and is auspicious— accomplishes it all, being the achiever of every siddhi.
There is nothing superior to this in the three worlds, because it is unsurpassed and reveals the divine means. (7)

"Likewise for all" means for all [deities] such as Vajravārāhī and the others. "Such a mantra" refers to this kind of mantra. He explains its designation as "the performer of all activities" with the words beginning with "pātāla" (the underworld). "It exists" means it is known throughout the three worlds. "The accomplisher of all siddhis" means that there is no other means of accomplishment superior to this. Why is this mantra the accomplisher of all?
Thus he says: "The unsurpassed," and so forth. "This" refers to the Heart. It is called "the indicator of divine means" because it points out the divine methods. || 5-7 ||
I shall describe the abode of all ḍākinīs concisely, and not in detail:
having depicted a divine mountain where various flowers and fruits arise. (8)
Above that, one should constantly meditate upon the Ḍākinīs and the Lāmās,
as well as the Yoginīs, Khaṇḍarohā, and the hero among heroes of the Vīras.

Pointing out the *yoginīnyāsa* that has been indicated, he says "all," and so forth. Although one should have said "having meditated upon" (*bhāvayitvā*), the fact that "having written" (*likhitvā*) is stated is because even by writing it in this way, there is accomplishment. "The mountain" refers to Sumeru. "One should constantly meditate upon it above" means a palace (*kūṭāgāra*) that is constant in its continuity. Likewise, above the palace, the *ḍākinīs* and others are to be meditated upon by the practitioner.
Not in sequence. Therefore, he says "the ḍākinīs," and so forth. Regarding "of the heroes":

it should be understood that the twenty-four yoginīs, beginning with Pracaṇḍā, are to be meditated upon together with the heroes, beginning with Khaṇḍakapālī. Since there is a plural number in "the ḍākinīs" and so forth, Kākāsyā and the others are also included. And one should meditate on the hero, who is indeed Śrī Heruka himself; thus the connection is to be made. (8–9)
"Hā hā he he" is the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara* of the twenty-four heroes;
likewise [it belongs to] Vajrasattva, Vairocana, and Padmanarteśvara. (10)
Śrī Vajraheruka, Ākāśagarbha, and Hayagrīva;
Ratnavajra, Mahābala, Virūpākṣa, and likewise Bhairava. (11)
Vajrabhadra, Subhadra, and indeed Vajrahūṃkāra;
Mahāvīra, Vajrajaṭila, Aṅkuri, and Vajradehaka. || 12 ||
Vajraprabha, Amitābha, Surāvairin, and Vikaṭadaṃṣṭrin,
as well as Kaṅkāla, Mahākaṅkāla, and Khaṇḍakapālin at the beginning.
The entire world is pervaded without exception by the twenty-four heroes;
likewise, there are the ḍākinīs of the heroes, as well as the yoginīs such as Pracaṇḍā and the rest. (14)

The practitioner should perceive [the deities] as residing in the wheels during all ritual activities; desiring success and being well-composed, he should constantly contemplate himself as the essence of the wheel. || 15 ||

He explains what kind and how many those heroes (*vīra*) are with the words "Hā hā he he," and so forth; the meaning is that one should contemplate the twenty-four heroes characterized by laughter. The phrase "one should contemplate the *ḍākinījālasaṃvara*" is a reference back to the previous summary.

He provides a detailed enumeration of the heroes in their sequential order with the words "Vajrasattva," and so forth; the term "should contemplate" (*bhāvayet*) is to be connected everywhere [in the following list].

The second [line] begins with "by Khaṇḍakapālin, etc. The word "etc. refers to the beginning; the meaning is that one should meditate on Mahākaṅkāla and the others together with Khaṇḍakapālin who stands at the beginning. He provides a conclusion by way of number: "of the twenty-four heroes. The entire maṇḍala and the body consist of twenty-four heroes; therefore he says:

"Jagat" [is used] because it denotes the body. Khaṇḍakapālī, Mahākaṅkāla, Kaṅkāla, Vikaṭadaṃṣṭrī, Surāvairī, Amitābha, Vajraprabha, Vajradeha, Aṅkurika, Vajrajaṭila, Mahāvīra, Vajrahūṃkāra, Subhadra, Vajrabhadra, Bhairava, Virūpākṣa, Mahābala, Ratnavajra, Hayagrīva.

Ākāśagarbha, Śrī Heruka, Padmanarteśvara, Vairocana, and Vajrasattva—by means of these eight, beginning with Khaṇḍakapāla and ending with Vajradeha, the Mind Wheel (cittacakra) is black, being black [in color]. By means of those beginning with Aṅkura and ending with Virūpākṣa, who are red, the Speech Wheel (vākcakra) is red. By means of those beginning with Mahābala and ending with Vajrasattva, who are white, the Body Wheel (kāyacakram) is white. These [deities] possess two arms.

Alternatively, according to the opinion of the Ācārya, he may have four arms. One should visualize Khaṇḍakapāla and the others, joined with Pracaṇḍā and the rest, on the following locations: the head, the crest-lock, the right ear, the back of the head, the left ear, the space between the eyebrows, the two eyes, the two roots of the arms, the two armpits, the pair of breasts, the navel, the nose, the mouth, the throat, the heart, the penis, the lingam, the anus, the thighs, the shanks, the toes, the backs of the feet, the big toes, and the two knees. Thus, by these...

The pervasion of the body. He states the summary meaning: "Of the heroes, the heroes" refers to the *ḍākinīs*; they alone are the *yoginīs*, and they are [the goddesses] beginning with Pracaṇḍā. They are to be seen as residing in the wheels (*cakras*). By this, the pervasion of the wheels is indicated. In all activities...

To the question "By what [means] are pacification and the other rites performed?", he says: "by the practitioner" (*sādhaka*). If one is a practitioner, then it is by means of this [mantra] that they are accomplished.

Concluding this, he says: "One should constantly meditate on the nature of the *cakra*. The meaning is that one should meditate on the assembly of heroes and heroines as being of the nature of the *cakra*. (10–15)
One should recite the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara* according to the previously mentioned procedure;
it is the great wheel, the locus of all accomplishments, and likewise the abode of all accomplishments. (16)
He speaks of the conclusion of the worship with the words "by that which was previously mentioned," and so forth; the meaning is: by means of the outer, secret, mental, and essential-nature worships.
He speaks of the object of worship with the words "the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*"; "the Great Wheel" (*mahācakra*) and "the attainment of great siddhis" (*mahāsiddhyālāṃ*) are synonymous terms. || 16 ||
The well-spoken words of ten million Buddhas and likewise ten million Heroes, each surrounded by a retinue numbering ten million Yoginīs. (17)

He states the view of the Tathāgatas of the past and so forth as follows: "The well-spoken," and so on. This tantra is the well-spoken word of ten million Buddhas; the genitive case here denotes the agent. And likewise, "the very ten million of heroes. By means of the term "ten million" (*koṭi*), he expresses the great number of yoginīs: "Each one, however, is surrounded by a retinue numbering ten million yoginīs. Thus, each individual yoginī [is accompanied by such a multitude].
They were surrounded by yoginīs numbering in the tens of millions. || 17 ||
The Yoginīs, the Ḍākinīs, Khaṇḍarohā, and Rupiṇī, as well as Lāmā and the others, are auspicious and bringers of all accomplishments. || 18 ||
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, the ritual procedure for the secret maṇḍala that is the abode of all heroes and ḍākinīs, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*.

These are the twelve *ḍākinīs* and so forth, the twenty-four such as *Pracaṇḍā*, and Vajravārāhī. He speaks of these very ones with the words "the yoginīs" and so on. By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), all of them are included. To the question "Why are these to be worshipped?", he says:
"They bring about all accomplishments and are auspicious. (18)

The heart-mantra of Vajravārāhī, the abode of all ḍākinīs, and that maṇḍala which is to be kept secret—since these two are prescribed herein, it is called a "chapter" (paṭala). It is the forty-eighth [chapter]. Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. 48.
The forty-ninth chapter: The Ritual Procedure for Transforming Form to be Accomplished through Seven Births.
Now I shall describe another [practice], the ritual for animals according to the rule, by the mere knowledge of which swift accomplishment proceeds. (1)

The mantra-practitioner, having fashioned sacrificial animals out of rice flour in the proper sequence—namely, a donkey, a human, a tortoise, a camel, a jackal, a horse, and so forth—[should proceed]. (2)
Among them, Viśvavarāha and these others are indeed remembered as sacrificial animals (paśus).
From among these, I shall declare the ritual procedure and how their characteristics should be.

Now, explaining the process of becoming Śrī Heruka, he says "atha" and so forth. "Atha" means after the statement of the heart-mantra of Vajravārāhī and the rest. "Paśukarma" (the act with animals): the act performed by means of animals is *paśukarma*, characterized by the attainment [of results] over seven lifetimes. "Made of rice-flour": *śāli* is a specific type of grain produced in the winter; it refers to the flour made from its grains.
A "vikāra" is that which undergoes transformation; such is the *paśu*.
He describes the *paśu* with the words beginning with "donkey" (*khara*) and so forth. "Therein" refers to seven births. A "viśvavarāha" is a specific type of deer of various colors.
He is to be consecrated along with the donkey and the others; the meaning is that he is one among these. And by means of these, the ritual action has already been performed previously.
This has been clarified. [The phrase] "starting from the donkey" refers to births as a human, a camel, a goat, and so forth, up to seven births; and that [is observed] through these very [births].
Regarding the words "from these," etc.: one should connect this by thinking, "I shall explain how that karma and its characteristics come to be from these seven human births. (1–3)
Those who [commit these acts] for one birth, two births, or three, four, and five;
and even those for six or seven births—they are undoubtedly beasts. (4)
He whose speech is melodious and who gazes with unblinking eyes shall be truthful in word, pleasant in appearance, and always devoted to the true Dharma. (5)
For one whose body is always fragrant attains birth as a human being;
indeed, one endowed with these characteristics has arisen from seven previous births.
By merely tasting it, one shall assume a divine form;
likewise for whoever applies it as a tilaka, whether by smelling it or merely touching it.
He becomes an accomplished one instantly; he may assume whatever form he desires.
Having taken the *rocanā* from his heart, it should be held by the wise man on the left.

Clarifying this very point, he says: "Those who have one birth, two births, or three, four, or five; and even those with six or seven births—they are beasts, of this there is no doubt. They are called "beasts" because of their similarity to beasts due to the authority of the *ārṣa* [scripture]. He states the defining characteristic: "fragrant," and so forth. He states the ritual action: "by that," and so forth. The meaning is that upon merely smelling or touching it, one becomes a possessor of a divine form.

Whoever applies the *tilaka* becomes an accomplished one (*siddha*) instantly. He assumes whatever form he desires; for there is an alternative reading: "he indeed assumes whatever form he desires. To the question of by what means the *tilaka* should be made, he says: "with *rocanā*, etc. [The word] "having taken" refers to the two [substances], by changing the case ending. (4–8)
Having recited the heart-mantra, one should apply a tilaka to him;
and whatever being’s form one desires to assume, [one should do so].
By means of a sectarian mark (tilaka) made with that respective substance, one becomes that very form; of this there is no doubt.
Having taken the juice of the *vṛkṣaparṇī* plant together with yellow pigment (*rocanā*) and *budha*, [one should apply it].
Having made a tilaka on the forehead, one becomes that very form; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, one should tie the hair of the sacrificial animal upon the hand and the head.
If one mixes the five parts of a tree and likewise combines them with its hair,
and binds it upon the hand and head, one will undoubtedly take on that very form.
Furthermore, a man who practices yoga and performs recitation is certainly not incapable;
he may indeed block the path to accomplishments such as the attainment of power through austerity, suffering, or propitiation. (13)

Regarding the phrase "with the heart-mantra": he explains what constitutes the "assumption of one's own desired form" for Śrī Heruka and Vajravārāhī by saying "of whom," and so forth. "On the hand-top" means at the base of the arm; by the word *kara* (hand), the hand together with the arm is meant. "Its five limbs" refers to the five limbs—Vairocana and the others—as well as the leaves, flowers, and so forth, of whichever sacrificial animal (*paśu*) or tree one desires to assume the form of through yogic practice.

"Sitajāpī" means one who meditates while reciting; it does not mean one who is incapable, but rather one who is indeed capable. Regarding "mokṣe mokṣaḥ" (liberation in liberation), he asks why one does not remain here even in this state in the form of an animal or similar being, and answers with "kaṣṭa... and so forth. This means the state of being an animal (tiryaggati). || 9–13 ||
Or by an elephant, horse, donkey, tortoise, camel, boar, or jackal; or by a crow, owl, and so forth, a vulture, a curlew, a hawk, or a crane. (14)
He shall indeed become handsome, deformed, or divine in form; he becomes a great heroic yogi capable of assuming any form at will—of this there is no doubt. || 15 ||
There is no accomplishment higher than this to be found in the three worlds. || 16 ||
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*, the chapter on the procedure for transforming the form to be accomplished through seven births. 49.

He states whose forms he assumes with the words "elephant, horse," and so forth. The instrumental case is used in the sense of the genitive; the meaning is "he assumes the form of these," and the meaning is also "he assumes beauty and so on. [Their specification follows: in this ritual action, offerings (*bali*) and enjoyments (*bhoga*) must be performed by means of elephants and the others. From that, one obtains beauty and the like. Here too, there is the operation of both hearts. There is nothing beyond this.
The power established through seven births is the power established by nature. || 14-16 ||

The transformation of form (*rūpaparivartana*)—that is, assuming the form of an animal and so forth—which is to be accomplished through seven births, is prescribed by this; therefore, it is called that *paṭala*. It is the forty-ninth (*ūnapañcāśattama*). Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. 49.
The fiftieth chapter: The procedure for indicating the ground for the sacrificial hearth (*pīṭha*) and so forth for the *vaśya* rite.
Now I shall explain the procedure for the fire sacrifice (*homavidhi*), by which, through its correct performance, the certain accomplishment of subjugation (*vaśya*) swiftly proceeds. (1)

"Now" (*atha*) means: immediately after the description of the transformation of form accomplished through seven births. I shall explain the ritual procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*) of the eightfold laughter-mantra beginning with *hā hā* and *he he*. The meaning is: that by which, through the oblation of beef, the swift accomplishment of the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*) proceeds. || 1 ||
Having soaked beef with liquor, one should offer it as a homa-oblation with the left hand;
even a Buddha comes under one's control, let alone insignificant mortals.
By offering spittle, a tooth-stick, and likewise the dust from one's own body, along with liquor bearing one's own name, into the fire, one shall bring the three worlds under control.
By performing a fire sacrifice (homa) with dust, blood, vomit, excrement, and human hair, instantaneous attraction (ākarṣaṇa) will occur. || 4 ||
Alternatively, the wise practitioner may perform the fire-oblation with hair vomited from his own body;
by employing the nimba tree, he shall immediately achieve enmity.
Being composed, one should offer as an oblation into a fire of *dhatura* the bitter oil named after [the target], using crow feathers; this brings about immediate expulsion and death.

He describes the fire-offering (*homa*) with the words beginning with "ga" and so forth. *Niṣṭhīvana* is phlegm issuing from the throat. *Śvakeśāḥ* means the hair of a dog. Regarding "sadyam ākarṣaṇam": that which moves, goes, and comes is *sat*, which is the seed-syllable *yaṃ*. That by which one draws that very [syllable] toward oneself is *ākarṣaṇam*. Visualizing the person to be subdued (*sādhya*) as coming while situated upon a wind-mandala generated from the syllable *yaṃ*, [one visualizes them] with the blood of a menstruating woman and so forth...
One should perform the *homa* with [the syllable] *bhūḥ*; this is the summary. "The body of a dog" is *śvakāya*. "He who perishes immediately" is *sadyojīvan*;
its eradication and killing [is the result]. (2–6)
Whether awake, asleep, rising, eating, or even engaged in sexual union, the mantra-practitioner should always recite the mantra at all times; for him, no obstacle shall arise.
One should offer one hundred oblations with the meat of a Jambūka;
within three months, his family's poverty shall be destroyed.
If someone, the practitioner, should perform a fire-oblation with great human flesh mixed with wine one hundred and eight times for three watches of the night.
For one who has practiced all the stages without exception, the Ḍākinī, being satisfied and brought under control within six months, will grant him a kingdom; of this there is no doubt.
One should meditate upon all the deities and perform fire offerings for two watches;
by that very means, one shall attain the state of a sky-walker (khecarī) with one's own body. || 11 ||
One should offer as oblation the flesh raised by a jackal, both internally and externally;
thus, the power that sets all accomplishments in motion will quickly come into one's hand.

He states the fruit for one who recites [the mantra] constantly: *jāgrataḥ* means while awake; *suptaḥ* means while asleep, having gone to bed; *kṛtaḥ* means while performing an action; *uttiṣṭha* means having risen from sleep or from sitting; *mithunaḥ* means one who possesses sexual union; *māram* refers to the mind (*citta*), because it possesses Māras such as the aggregates (*skandhas*) and so forth, according to the statement: "The mind itself is the Great Māra."

"The mantra practitioner should recite [the mantra] for Mahākāla; there is no fixed time," is an alternative reading (*pāṭhāntara*). The meaning therein is that one need not observe a specific time for the recitation. And the laughter-mantra (*hāsamantra*) is: *oṃ hā hā he he ho ho haṃ haṃ phaṭ svāhā*. *Oṃ kili kili sili sili cili cili dhili dhili phaṭ svāhā*.

And: "A hundred oblations. One should constantly offer one hundred oblations three times [per day] using *arka* bark and other substances. And one should meditate upon all the deities; one should perform the fire-sacrifice (*homa*) for two *praharas*. Then, the meditation on the deities is joined with all cow-flesh and liquor. "With jackal-flesh and liquor" means the decayed flesh of a jackal. The deity is to be offered [this]. Internally and externally.
Thus, because of its utility: one who desires to perform oblations in the fire of the sacrificial pit [should know] that which sets all accomplishments in motion. (7–12)
One should perform the recitation of the mantra at night and cause the enemy kingdoms to fall;
by doing this every day, one will become a king oneself. || 13 ||
There is nothing superior to this found anywhere in the three worlds;
thus, the yogi, assuming various forms, may die at his own will.
By performing one hundred thousand oblations of *bilva*, *palāśa*, and likewise *udumbara* wood, one quickly becomes a lord of great wealth. || 15 ||
One desiring royal power should offer beef mixed with liquor;
having attained Yogeśvarī, who indeed could remain in poverty? (16)

The recitation of mantra; here, "recitation" refers to meditation performed with mantra, which is the service of mantra. Regarding the phrase "alone at night," he says: "one should cause the kingdoms to fall. He states the reasoning: "Having attained the Yogīśvarī, who indeed would remain in poverty?
Where the Yogīśvarīs—the goddesses—are the lords (īśā), such is that mantra of laughter (*hāsa*). One who is poor is indeed "poverty" (*daridratā*). (13–16)
They are accomplished with ease by means of the jackal-homa;
one who performs the jackal-homa quickly becomes equal to the Giver of Wealth (Kubera). || 17 ||
Even one who lacks vows, conduct, and purity shall attain success once possessed [by the deity].
[One should avoid] excessive quantities of kushmāṇḍa, mung beans, black gram, and chickpeas. (18)
By binding the mouth with honey, *madhucchardis*, black mustard, and house-grown *tāla* leaves, the yogi becomes a master of his own will, remaining established wherever he may be. (19)

"According to one's pleasure" (*yathāsukhena*) implies there is no fixed rule; this very state of being "according to one's pleasure" is indicated by the passage beginning with "one who does not observe vows" (*avratacārī*). "Possessed" (*āviṣṭām*) means authorized by the deity. "By means of a dream" refers to the perception of signs. "Dūrvā grass, honey, vomit, and the residue of honey" (*madhūtsiṣṭam*); "the leaf of the *mālatī* tree taken from the house" and "suspended smoke"—all of these [should be kept] in one part of his house. One should conceal the mantra that has been recited.
For him, it becomes as has been described. || 17-19 ||
Now I shall further explain the yoginīs of the lands, seats, and so forth, who are the limbs and sub-limbs of Śrī Heruka, consisting of both the stable and the mobile. (20)
The *pīṭha* is on the stage of *pramuditā*, and likewise the *upapīṭha* is *vimalā*;
*kṣetra* is to be known as *prabhākarī*, and *upakṣetra* as *arciṣmatī*.
Chandoha is Abhimukhī, and Upacchandoha is Sudurjayā;
Dūraṅgamā is in Melā, and Acalā is the Upamelaka.
Sādhumati is the cremation ground, and Dharmamegha is the supreme cremation ground;
having consecrated Śrī Heruka, these are the internal stages (bhūmis). || 23 ||

"Then" (*atha*) means immediately after the description of all the ritual applications (*prayoga*). "I shall proclaim another"—to what does he refer? He says: "The Yoginīs of the *bhūmis*, *pīṭhas*, and so forth. Those of which the *pīṭhas* are the first are the *pīṭhas* and so forth, namely the sacred sites (*sthāna*) such as the *upapīṭhas*. The *bhūmis* themselves are the *pīṭhas* and so forth, due to the elision of the accusative case-ending. "Yoginī" refers to the [names] of the Yoginīs. "Limbs and sub-limbs" (*aṅgāṅgam*): the limbs are the hands and so forth.

Its limbs are the joints (*parvan*) and so forth; its head is the *rupaskandha*; its powers are sensation (*vedanā*) and the rest. The limbs and sub-limbs of Śrī Heruka consist of the earth, the pedestal (*pīṭha*), and the aggregates (*skandha*) and so on. The connection is: "I shall explain all the limbs as being of the nature of means (*upāya*). *Upapīṭha* is [derived] from *papīṭha* by the elision of the letter *u*. Having ascertained and determined Śrī Heruka, he says that these earths are to be deposited upon his limbs: [The text continues: ...the earths are to be placed upon those limbs. He says: [further details follow].
"These are the internal stages" means that these are the internal stages. || 20–23 ||
On the stage of the ten perfections, let the Yoginī speak in the tongues of barbarians;
whether in heaven, among mortals, or in the netherworld, she is the stable and immovable essence within the body of the Hero.
In Pullīra and the other [pīṭhas], as previously described, resides the Great Yoga of Śrī Heruka, the Lord who is the master of all desires, existing both externally and internally. (25)
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces on all sides,
it exists pervading everything, heard of everywhere in the world.
Then, one should accomplish success with a mind joined in meditation;
this secret reality has been proclaimed for the benefit of practitioners. (27)
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, the procedure for the instruction on the ground for the subjugation fire-offering, the seats, and so forth, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. 50.

"Regarding the ten perfections on the stages": the ten stages, beginning with the Joyous (*pramuditā*), are the ten perfections—generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, aspiration, power, skillful means, and gnosis. "Let the barbarians speak" refers to the barbarian language of the *yoginīs*.
By the words "In heaven," etc., the three wheels are indicated. Having mastered the great yoga of Śrī Heruka, one should accomplish the siddhi.

It should be applied. Some maintain that the qualifiers beginning with "from all sides" refer to this very [mudrā] as the *siṃhavikrīḍitāmudrā*. In that case, the hand is the vajra, and the foot is the anus. (24–27)
The "Instruction on the Grounds for the Vaśya-homa and the Pīṭhas" is that text by which the grounds for the vaśya-homa, the pīṭhas, and so forth are pointed out.
It is a "vidhi" (injunction) because it prescribes the reality of the matter through various methods; the chapter (*paṭala*) consists of that. It is the fiftieth, meaning the *pañcāśattama*.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara-vivṛti*. || 50 ||
[The Summary of the Cultivation, etc. The Fifty-First Chapter.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the tradition that is very difficult to obtain;
it was spoken by me in the Tantra using the secret code-language of the heroes (*vīrasaṅketa*), and it must be kept hidden.
Now he speaks the chapter on the summary of the meaning of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth, beginning with "atha" and so on. "Atha" (now) marks the conclusion of the teaching.

"Ataḥ" (therefore): because nothing is accomplished without the manifestation of the deity, the connection is that "therefore I shall proclaim the tradition (*āmnāya*). Tradition is the lineage of authoritative instruction. "Sudurlabham" (extremely difficult to obtain) means that those who fully understand it are rare.
Wherein that tradition is thus [recorded]: it is to be concealed for the sake of removing the faults of those who would cause harm. "By me alone" means by myself. Why? He says: "In the *tantra*.
That by which things are strung together (*tantryante*) and refined (*saṃskriyante*) is thus called a *tantra*, namely the one known as the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara*.
"Spoken in code" (*saṅketabhāṣita*) means spoken by means of symbolic conventions. It was spoken in code by the heroes, the Tathāgatas. The convention used here is indeed unprecedented.
This is the state of affairs. Consequently, one should not suspect the existence of correct words (*śabda*) and corrupt words (*apaśabda*), for a word alone does not convey meaning;

rather, it does so with the aid of convention (*saṅketa*). And since that convention has been established even by heroes, it is well said that [the language] is "spoken according to the convention of the heroes" (*vīrasaṅketabhāṣita*). || 1 ||

Having first [contemplated] the emptiness of the causes and so forth, one should recite "Āli Kāli" while wearing the lower garment, the five mudrās, and so on, as well as the consort's limbs and the lattice of stakes. (2)
Then, what is the intended meaning even by means of the conventional term? It is the garment, namely the tiger skin and the elephant hide.

Regarding "possessing the five mudrās and so forth": the five mudrās consist of the necklace (*kaṇṭhikā*), crest-jewel (*cūḍaka*), armlet (*keyūra*), earring (*kuṇḍala*), and sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*). That which has these as its primary ornaments includes the neck-ornament, the garland of heads, the girdle, and so on. [The limb of Wisdom] is the embrace with the vajra and the vajra-bell.
One should perform the ritual of staking; this is the staking. The cage is made of vajra; because this is an illustrative term, it includes the vajra-fortress and so forth. || 2 ||
From the initial *pravṛtti-nāda* up to the yoga of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*),
[one attains] the bliss of nourishment by nectar and the consecration by hand.
One should protect [the deity] with the Great Armor (Mahākavaca) and perform worship with the Universal Mantra (Sarvamantra).
Thus, this fourteenth reality has been explained in brief.

Regarding the phrase "the activity, the sound, and so forth": "activity" (*pravṛtti*) refers to the purification of the aggregate of form and the other aggregates. "Sound" (*nāda*) is the drop (*bindu*), which has the shape of a preceding line; here, the letter *ma* situated above the syllable *hūṃ* is to be understood. And that [letter *ma*] should be known as being of the very nature of the drop (*bindu*). Both the sound and the letter *ma* are "sound-and-*ma*" (*nādamau*). Those things beginning with the half-moon and so forth, of which these two are the first, are "those beginning with sound" (*nādamādīni*). And the activity...

And the *nāda* and so forth refer to the *nāda* and so forth of the process of manifestation (*pravṛtti*). "Up to the yoga of withdrawal" means that withdrawal is preceded by emanation, because this [process] culminates in that. "The bliss of nourishment with nectar" refers to the accomplishment of the nourishment with the five nectars. "Dwelling" refers to the pentad of seals (*mudrā*) and so forth, the pinning down (*kīla*), the cage (*pañjara*), and the emptiness consisting of the causes such as the utterance of *Ālikāli*. [This is followed by] *nāda*, the *bindu*, and withdrawal.

Yoga, the nourishment of nectar (*amṛtāpyāyana*), bliss (*nirvṛti*), hand-worship (*hastapūjā*), consecration (*abhiṣecana*), and the worship of the mantra preceded by the protection of the great armor (*mahākavacarakṣā*)—these fourteen principles (*tattva*) have been stated as primary. Therefore, he says: "This is the fourteenth principle. That which has fourteen parts is called "fourteen" (*caturdaśa*). The subject matter of the Tantra is thus summarized. Hence, he says: "In brief. (3–4)
The best of men who practices this, his soul purified of all sins,
attains the stage of a Tathāgata in birth after birth.
Born into the family of the Tathāgatas, he becomes a righteous king;
yet, due to his former sins, he is deficient in all the [major] marks.

By this [verse], he who practices or conducts himself in this very manner—that is to say, trains in this way—becomes one whose self is purified of all sins; for there is an obligatory connection between the relative pronoun (*yaḥ*) and the demonstrative pronoun (*sa*). One whose "all sins"—namely, the five immediate transgressions (*pañcānantarya*) and so forth—are "purified" is thus described; and since the word *ātman* is used here as a synonym for *citta*, such a person is a yogi.

"Karmas do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons; having reached the necessary conditions and the [proper] time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings. Thus, there is no destruction of karma without its fruit; even through a means, there is only purification. There is no one who [can effect] its destruction.

There is no other means [for its destruction]. This is because of the scriptural statement: "They do not perish without having borne fruit. Since the word *khalu* carries the sense of certainty, the fruit itself is indeed the means for that destruction. Furthermore, even if action (*karman*) were itself another means, once the fruit characterized as the destruction of the previous action has been produced, there would be an utter cessation [of karma], because it lacks the capacity to produce any further fruit.

If it is argued that such a specific means, while producing its destruction, simultaneously produces the nature of supreme, uncontaminated great bliss—just as a lamp, while removing darkness, produces light—the answer is: it does not actually remove the darkness; rather, it simply produces light. When that light is produced, the darkness departs of its own accord. [The same applies to] the means—

Why should its greatness not be accepted, such that it would become fruitless? It is not contradictory [to say] that "actions do not [apply] to one who does not know the means," and so forth. And he attains the stage of the Tathāgata; he attains the stage of the knowledge of the Tathāgata, which consists in the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*). If this were not the case—due to the absence of reaching the ultimate limit of the excellence of cultivation—then what [would happen]?

To this he says: "Born in every birth into the family of the Tathāgatas. One whose family is the Tathāgata is born from such a progenitor; thus, the fifth case is used here. "In every birth" means in births as a god or in births as a human.
"He becomes a righteous king," like Sumati, Kośala, and others. Even for one who is extremely wicked, somehow...

He asks what would happen if one were to practice the fourteen principles (*tattva*), and says "yathā" and so forth. One who has committed and accumulated sinful karma through the activities of body, speech, and mind, and who is bound by it in the beginning, middle, and end, is "one whose sins are as before" (*yathāpūrvādipāpa*).

The genitive case in *yathāpūrvādipāpasya* is used in the sense of the nominative (i.e., "he who is such"). Furthermore, he is one who is devoid of all the characteristics of a true person (*puruṣa*). (5–6)
He who constantly meditates upon this [goddess] becomes the lord of all desires on earth,
like a vessel filled with ghee placed in the midst of a fire.
Just as clarified butter melts when heated and disappears from two vessels over time, so too does evil perish through the name of Śrī Heruka. (8)

Now, he who meditates upon this Śrī Heruka, who consists of the fourteen principles (*tattva*), becomes the lord of all desires on earth. When the mass of his sins has been rendered powerless, the fruit of action born of meditation alone ripens. Alternatively, when the destruction of prior sins and so forth has been accomplished on earth through meditation, one becomes the lord of all desires. How? By means of [the deity] possessing the form of arms, faces, and so forth.
It is said that by meditating upon Śrī Heruka, one's prior sinful karma is destroyed—this is expressed in the passage beginning with "ghṛta" (clarified butter), etc.

Just as a vessel filled with clarified butter is placed in the midst of fire, what would happen then? It says: "dravantaṃ dravate sarpiḥ" (the melting clarified butter melts). If, while the clarified butter is melting in the vessel, it causes a substance characterized by water to melt—that is, it reaches a state of melting and becomes mixed with water—[then...]
This is the meaning. To the question "What then? he says: "Time perishes. Having reached a long period of time (*kālaṃ*), the water perishes.

He indicates that as long as the water does not perish, the ghee does not perish; this is the inherent power of things (*vastuśakti*). Since the vessel is also the support for the vessel's contents, the fire is also called a "vessel" (*bhāṇḍa*). Likewise, he says this very thing—that karma is exhausted: "In the same way, evil..."
"It perishes" means that it causes beings who are attached [to existence] to fall into the ocean of *saṃsāra*; thus, "evil" (*pāpa*) refers to common karma.

When the fire of the knowledge of emptiness and the vessel in the form of Śrī Heruka are cultivated, because of the destruction of the karma characterized by attachment to the grasped and so forth—which has been deposited within the aggregates (*skandha*) and so on—the aggregates and so forth become free from fault. Furthermore, emptiness—
Because it is established as such, that very thing is faulty due to its lack of effective action (*arthakriyā*) as it truly is. And so it has been said:
"O Vajragarbha, O Greatly Compassionate One, beings are liberated by existence itself;
they are bound by existence and liberated through the thorough knowledge of it."
One who is free from afflictions but whose course is impaired does not attain enlightenment; yet one whose afflictions are rampant cannot even accomplish his own welfare.
Therefore, you must strive with steadfastly applied vigor to attain enlightenment.

"The afflictions have not been incinerated; rather, they have been reduced to the lightness of a blade of grass. And: "Regarding *Śrīheruka*: *Śrī* is non-dual gnosis; *Ha* is the emptiness of causes and so forth; *Ru* is the departure from the array (*vyūha*); *Ka* means it does not abide anywhere."
