Thus, [he] consists of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*). "From his name" (*nāmataḥ*) means from the name itself. For this very reason, the word *iti* has the sense of the genitive case. "Bowing" (*namana*) means subordination, that is, becoming dependent upon sovereignty (*prabhutva*). (7–8)
Whether merely contemplated during meditation, recited, studied, or written down,
one obtains the enjoyment of heaven or else becomes a universal monarch (cakravartin).
At the time of death, however, the yogi sees Śrī Heruka and the other heroes and yoginīs, their hands busily occupied with various flowers and bearing various banners and streamers. (10)
Amidst the sounds of various musical instruments and the offering of diverse songs, that which is called death leads the faint-hearted to the state of the sky-farer. 11.

To the question "Under what conditions? he says: "In meditation" (*dhyāne*). Meditation (*dhyāna*) means reflection (*cintā*). Recitation (*pāṭha*) is general; self-study (*svādhyāya*) is one-pointed reflection; and writing (*likhana*) is [the practice]. Even if one has personally attained the status of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), or if the yoga of Śrī Heruka and the Yoginīs is unaccomplished, or if the performance of recitation and so forth is incomplete, should death occur, then what happens? To this he says: "Consciousness," etc. [The] yogi...
The "Nā" refers to the hero-yogi (vīra-yogī-puruṣa). Regarding "Śrīherukādivīrayoginī," the third-case plural ending has been elided. Regarding "nānā":
because of the empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna) through musical instruments and so forth, the activity of Śrīheruka and the others is perceived even in a slight degree. (9–11)
Thus, having known this great tantra of the Śrī Cakrasaṃvara, which is difficult to find on earth even for gods and great heroes, [if one does so] without devotion— || 12 ||
The torment of suffering shall be his constant and perpetual lot.
[He shall wear] a necklace, a crest-ornament, armlets, earrings, and the sacred thread. 13.
With the sounds of the girdles and small bells on their necks, head-garlands, and waist-bands,
they resembled a swarm of bees upon the filaments of the mountain-peak lotus.
He says this very thing in the passage beginning with "evam" (thus) and so forth. "The God" is Śrī Heruka. "The great heroes" are Khaṇḍakapālī and the others.

"The yoginīs" are Vajravārāhī and the others. They are difficult to see with the fleshly eye. If a person, even after knowing and understanding the great tantra, the glorious *Cakrasaṃvara*, lacks devotion—that is, becomes devoid of devotion—then poverty arises for him and he is tormented by sufferings.

Since it is so, he shows the conclusion of the teaching beginning with "the necklace" (*kaṇṭhikā*) and so forth. The singular number in "necklace, crest-jewel, and armlet" (*kaṇṭhikā-cūḍa-keyūram*) is due to a collective compound (*samāhāra*). "The neck," and so forth, is as before; this is the conclusion regarding the ornaments. "Upon the filaments at the summit of the mountain" is the conclusion regarding the location. "And the *āli-kāli*" is the conclusion regarding the five aspects; the meaning is "the vowels and consonants" (*āli-kālī*).
The letter *ca* [at the beginning of a compound] signifies the remainder of the form in the sense of accumulation (*uccaya*). || 12-14 ||
Having approached the Lord of Gaurī, who is embraced by the limbs of Vajra-ghaṇṭā, and who is joined by a host of twenty-four heroes and yoginīs; || 15 ||

"Gaurī" is in the instrumental case in the sense of accompaniment (*sahārthe*). This is the withdrawal of the seat (*āsana*). "Embraced by the vajra and the bell" is the withdrawal of the embrace of the hand-symbols (*cihna*). These two symbols serve as an illustration for the other symbols. "Half of twenty-four" refers to Kākāsyā and the others, twelve being half of twenty-four. The heroines (*vīrayoginī*) joined with the heroes (*vīra*) are twenty-four; their groups (*vṛnda*) [are to be understood].
The groups of heroic yoginīs; the short vowel [in "vīra"] is due to Vedic usage. The word "conjoined" (saṃyukta) signifies the summary of the thirty-six yoginīs. || 15 ||
One should meditate upon the supreme state of the Great King Śrī Heruka, who, possessing the yoga of the central consort, is accompanied by all the heroes, the yoginīs, and the assembly. 16.
All were satisfied and became non-dual, acting as the agents of creation and destruction;
beings possessed of various inclinations were awakened through various modes of conduct. || 17 ||

"Wherein the Great King Śrī Heruka [resides]" is the summary of the principal deity (*nāyaka*). "The place" (*pada*) is the substantive (*viśeṣya*). This is the summary of the entire maṇḍala in the form of the support and the supported. Having spoken in brief, he speaks again in extreme brevity with the words beginning with "all," etc. "All heroes"—here the singular genitive case is used in the sense of "all. [Likewise] the yoginīs. Thus, together with his retinue.

"Accompanied by an assembly" means *saparṣat* (with an assembly). "Possessing the yoga of the churned" refers to Vajravārāhī; she is the one with whom he is joined in yoga. The short vowel [in *mathya*] is due to its being an archaic (Vedic) form. In the reading *madhyayogavān*, it refers to the intermediate, untainted bliss (*anāsrava-sukha*). Having heard the Dharma beginning with "Now, therefore, the secret... and ending with "...possessing the yoga of the churned," all the previously mentioned heroes (*vīra*) and heroines (*vīreśvarī*) were satisfied.

Because they have attained the essence of the Dharma, they have become twofold through joy and have thus doubled [in number]. Emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) is radiance; withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) is the contraction of those things that were radiated. The heroes (*vīra*) and yoginīs listen to the Dharma for the sake of the welfare of others. For the benefit of those to be trained by Śrī Heruka, the Blessed One, having been requested by Vajravārāhī, likewise manifested such an assembly engaged in listening to the Dharma, and [taught] the Dharma.
He gave this instruction. To the question "Why is there such devotion to Śrī Heruka?", he says: "Various," and so forth.

"Those who ascertain various meanings" refers to those whose modes of conduct (*caryā*)—that is, their behaviors—are of various forms, characterized by being householders and so on. "Awakened by various conducts" means they have been led to realization and established in the thought, "Do this! || 16–17 ||
Taught through various means for disciples of diverse dispositions, it is so that through this instruction on the profound Dharma, there may arise resolute conviction. (18)
One should not utter reproach; one should remember the inconceivable nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
For this is not my domain, nor do I know the true nature of phenomena.

To the question "Why is it so?", he says: "It was taught through various means for disciples of diverse methods, so that there might be conviction through the instruction of the profound Dharma. If there were some degree of conviction among those to be trained by the methods of the Śrāvakas and others, then conviction was taught through various means—that is, by way of diverse paths. With what intention was such a statement made? He says:

"By the teaching of the profound Dharma": the "teaching" (*nirdeśa*) or exposition of the profound Dharma—which consists of the non-duality of wisdom and skillful means—is the cause by which liberation has been taught through various methods (*nānānaya*). The meaning is that whatever inclination toward the Dharma (*dharmādhimukti*) [beings possess], that was taught to them. One should not raise the objection as to why there is such diversity of inclinations; for the inconceivable nature of phenomena (*acintyadharmatā*) must be kept in mind, or alternatively—
They have been taught through various means and in the forms of various deities; the underlying intention is that sentient beings themselves are presented in the form of deities.

In the Mantra Mahāyāna, which consists of wisdom and skillful means, since one may practice according to one's own inclination, such a conviction (adhimokṣa) is appropriate. Nevertheless, he asks: "What would happen if it were not so? and replies with the words beginning "profound," etc. The limb of wisdom has profound emptiness as its intrinsic nature; this is the Dharma.

The limbs of method consist of the forms of the arms, faces, and so forth. That which is both profound and the Dharma is the "Profound Dharma. The tantra called the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara*, by means of which that Profound Dharma is taught, is the "Instruction on the Profound Dharma. If those to be trained (vineyas) lack faith in this [teaching], they should not be rejected; rather, what should be done for them? He says: "They should be remembered."

"Regarding 'the nature of the inconceivable' (*cintyadharmatā*): the nature of inconceivable phenomena—that is, of meditative cultivations (*bhāvanā*)—must be recollected and taught. The meaning is that the very form of these cultivations is always inconceivable. Within these phenomena, such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, there is no object of mine in the form of something to be grasped or the like.
For what reason? He says: 'By which,' etc. I do not know the form of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), suchness (*tathatā*), or emptiness (*śūnyatā*)."
Because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself; as it has been said: "The mind does not know the mind.
Cognition that is devoid of the grasped object and so forth is *cittamātra* (mind-only), which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Thus it is said:
"There exists no emptiness whatsoever other than consciousness."
"Since it is held that discrimination consists in being distinct from what has been seen. (18–19)
Those great-souled ones, the perfectly awakened Buddhas and their sons as well, know this:
it remains established whether Buddhas arise or do not arise. (20)
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is always inconceivable and free from decrease or increase; having reflected thus, one should not criticize any worldly beings. 21.

He states who it is that knows: "They know," and so forth. They are the perfectly awakened ones (*samyagbuddha*), meaning those possessing perfect awakening. They are the great-souled ones (*mahātman*), meaning those of vast intellect. Those for whom they are sons are their sons—the Bodhisattvas—since, having become Bodhisattvas, they become Buddhas. Alternatively, "their sons" refers to the sons of those Buddhas, because they are born from them; the self (*ātman*) of the Buddhas [is the source].

Dharma. Because they awaken to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the Buddhas will fully awaken to it; likewise, Bodhisattvas are also designated as "awakening" because, through the absence of conceptual proliferation (*niyuta-abhāvita*), they know the *dharmatā*. As to when this *dharmatā* comes into being, he says:
"By the arising," and so forth. It is established by depending upon the arising of the Buddhas, remaining and persisting even in the absence of arising.
The meaning is: "even in the state of primordial nature (prakṛti). Regarding the word "always": because they remain eternally established in the form of a continuous flow of primordial nature.

"Inconceivable" means that such a thing is impossible to conceive—namely, that [the soul] increases for such a long time. Being devoid of decrease and increase, having thus weighed them and equalized them in the intellect whether conscious or unconscious, none of them are to be censured.
The worldly [ones]. || 20–21 ||

For their course is inconceivable, and the Buddha’s dramatic performance is inconceivable; through the various distinctions of the secret yoga of those who have mastered the performance of the sūtras, they manifest a conduct for introducing sentient beings, as if delighting in this or that [state]. || 22 ||

Thus, in the *Śrīherukābhidhāna*, the great king of tantras comprising one hundred thousand [verses], this is the fifty-first [chapter], the subsequent tantra known as the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara*, the great king of Yoginī tantras, which is the pinnacle of all treatises, the supreme success recited by the great hero Śrī Heruka, and the primordial accomplishment that is unconquered by any [other] knowledge.
The chapter is completed. || 51 ||
Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has explained their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.
This is the religious gift of one who follows the most excellent Mahāyāna.
Even for those mundane beings, the establishment of their course of existence is inconceivable; why is this so? He says: "The Buddha-play is inconceivable.
The Buddhas themselves are established in various forms, hence it is called a "play" (*nāṭaka*). He explains this very point with the words beginning with "sūtra":

*sūtra* refers to the *Sūtrānta*; *kriyā* refers to the *Kriyā-tantra*; *abhī* refers to the *Abhidharma*. The genitive case is used in the sense of the first [case]. *Caryā* refers to the *Caryā-*...

The *tantra* is the *yogatantra*, the secret *tantra*. The particle "tu" (but/and) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). "Sattvāvatāra" [is used] with the elision of the fourth case ending.

"Liberation" (*mukti*) is the removal of the bonds of the afflictions (*kleśa*). The phrase "for the purpose of" (*iti-arthe*) means for the sake of the inconceivable descent of sentient beings (*sattva*), which is differentiated by various distinctions. And that inconceivable descent of sentient beings is what the perfectly awakened ones (*sambuddha*) bring forth; this is the connection with the preceding [text]. And in each respective instance, they are as if delighted in worldly matters and so forth.

The *Ratna* [Tantras] are the perfectly awakened ones (*saṃbuddha*). The meaning is that the equality of passion (*rāga*) is inconceivable. Now, the *Sūtra* [Tantras] are the *sūtrāntas*. The *Vibhāṣā* is the ritual action (*kriyā*).

The *Abhidharma* is the Middle Way (*madhyamā*). The *Yogaguhyatantra* is the Yogācāra. By the passage beginning with "Now, therefore, I shall explain the secret (*rahasya*)," the secret is promised. By the textual passage beginning with "By the Middle and Supreme Breath," the Blessed One taught—

The word *vān* [refers to the author]. As for the agent indicated by *sarvā*, it has been shown by the Blessed One himself that she established the satisfaction of those to be trained (*vineya*) and so forth through the passage beginning with "All were satisfied" and ending with "delighting in this and that. Thus, the connection is as follows: the fifty-first chapter—characterized by such attributes as "the great king of tantras"—is concluded. || 22 ||

In that regard, as for what kind of *Śrīherukābhidhāna* it is, he states "Mahā... and so forth, showing the specific nominative singular qualifying words distinguished by the implied word "therein" (*tatra*).
It is "Great" (*mahat*) because it expands and nourishes the qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadharma*) by means of this; and it is a "Tantra" (*tantra*) because it is that which extends (*tanoti*).
Thus, it is the "King of Great Tantras" (*mahātantrarāja*) wherein that supreme, untainted great bliss (*paramānāsrava-mahāsukha*) shines. Such are its specific qualifiers.

It would be distinguished. That which consists of a *lakṣa* (one hundred thousand) and is equal to space (*khasama*) falls from its center; that which possesses this [falling] is "falling within a *lakṣa*" (*lakṣāntaḥ-pāti*). The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include the meaning of other systems (*tantrāntara*). This has been explained in successive order. He is like a king—a "king"—because he stands above all scriptures (*śāstra*) and all systems (*tantra*), and because he is their illuminator. For this very reason, the Blessed One bears the moon. Furthermore, the moon is stated to be the subject (*abhidheya*) [of the single light]. Śrī Heruka together with Vārāhī—[they are called] "Great" because they are the Great Yoginīs (*mahāyoginī*).
The thirty-six [deities] beginning with the Ḍākinīs; the twenty-four heroes (vīras) beginning with Khaṇḍakapāla; the mantras whose efficacy is realized through mere recitation;

the omniscience consisting of the knowledge of the characteristics and so forth of the Yoginīs as well as direct perception and other forms of knowledge; and the invincible Śaṅkara accompanied by Durgā—the "A" and other siddhis that are the primordial attainments. [This is] the sword of the invincible omniscience realized through the recitation of the great hero Śrī Heruka.

It is called *tathokta-tantra* because it expresses that [reality]. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is understood as expressing the purification of the elements (*bhūmi*) and so forth. It is called *uttara* because by means of this one crosses over (*uttaranti*) from existence (*bhava*);

[this is derived] from the root *paca-* with the suffix *ādyac*. *Tantra* refers to the accumulation of merit and wisdom (*puṇya-jñāna-saṃbhāra*). *Cakra* refers to the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).
Because it restrains (*saṃvṛṇoti*) the minds of sentient beings from evil paths by means of that glorious wheel (*śrī-cakra*), it is the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara*.

Śrī Heruka is so called because the tantra expresses him; thus the tantra is also referred to by that name. The term "Mahāyoginītantrarāja" (King of the Great Yoginī Tantras) is a compound word without case endings (*nirvibhaktika*), meaning "the great king of the Yoginī tantras. This is due to the abundance of instructions from the Yoginīs. Within this King of Great Tantras named Śrī Heruka—which contains one hundred thousand verses and is the sovereign of all subsequent scriptures—[this work stands].

"Thus ends the fifty-first [chapter], correctly obtained, in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvara*, the Great King of Yoginī Tantras, known as the *Śrīherukamahāvīrapaṭhitasiddhasarvajñāparāta* (the Supreme All-Knowing One Accomplished by the Recitation of the Great Hero Śrīheruka), which is the supreme tantra.

The phrase beginning with "Great King of Tantras" and ending with "Great King of Yoginī Tantras" is a collection of words ending in nominal and verbal suffixes (*suptiṅantapadasamuccaya*). It is finished (*samāpta*).
Thus, the phrase "in the fifty-one chapters" should be joined at the end of the title *Śrīherukābhidhāna*. Just as the words of the Guru’s commentary were recorded by me from memory,
so too does this statement of mine come forth from grasping its meaning.
Even when this distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted has been ascertained through valid means of knowledge,
doubt does not cease without the instruction of a guru.
Like a garland, I bear upon my head the command of my guru— which is captivating to both speech and mind— and which, being connected to him, dispels all delusion.
Through the perception that the world is a vibration of one's own mind,
let it be contemplated that one's own mind alone is determined [as reality].
Herein, there exists nothing other than one's own mind as the maṇḍala.
Without the planets, quickly [draw] the mandala.
Meditate upon the state of Śrī, the station of the deities,
for from that you shall go to the stainless, established state;
without the cessation of worldly existence (bhava) there is no peace (śama), and without peace there is none.
Existence is the non-differentiation within purity.
She became as if beloved toward these present principles, which are born from the lotus of the Śrī Cakrasaṃvara and are mines of the nectar-essence of secret instructions.
Those whose minds and intellects are pure through merit carry forth faith.
Indeed, having observed other eminent poets who were great composers, my intellect also took delight in accomplishing that same purpose;
for where one is fit, there he dances and sings on the occasion of a festival.
Due to such eagerness, would even an unworthy person not go there?
Having elucidated the world of Śrīcakrasaṃvara with clear terminology, like the sun illuminating the universe,
may people carry forth those virtues through whatever merit I have thereby acquired.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter in the *Śrīcakrasaṃvaravivṛti*. || 51 ||
The *Śrīcakrasaṃvarapañjikā* composed by the learned master Bhavabhaṭṭa is hereby completed.
Just as a lamp situated inside a jar does not shine outside,
but once that jar is broken, the flame of the lamp shines forth thereafter.
For one's own body is indeed the jar, and the lamp is indeed the reality;
when these are joined by the mouth of the Guru, the wisdom of the Buddha becomes manifest.
He perceives the sky as arisen from the sky, the space of space;
in this very manner, this "Prayogga" has been demonstrated by the mouth of the Guru.
